# A Letter from New York

The second line of the examination instructions had given him trouble since Sunday evening.

He had written it out in his room the night before — three attempts in the margin of his notebook page, each crossed — and then again this morning on the classroom board before the first class came up the east stair. He stood at the board with the chalk and read back what he had written: *When you do not know a word, consult the sense of the sentence.* The problem was *consult*, which required the student to have an intuition about what consulting a sentence meant, and it was exactly this intuition that he could not assume. He wiped the line.

He tried: *If you do not know a word, work from what the sentence needs it to mean.*

He stood back.

The German classroom occupied the second floor's east end, and in December it received the morning light in a way that was briefly pleasant before the cold coming off the north sill reasserted itself — the cold was better now, since Henry had planed the casement, but there was still a way the December light looked through those windows that was more like winter light pressing against glass than like light in a room. The examination sheets waited on the corner of his desk: three copies, typed himself on the school typewriter, which did not have the characters for *ü* or *ä*, requiring small substitutions he had worked out to preserve the sense if not the precision.

He read the second instruction line back. That would do. He had been a philologist for twenty years and had spent two days writing a sentence for the back of an examination sheet, which said something about either the importance of language or the particular liability of a mind that could not stop attending to it. He turned to lay the sheets on the desks and the bell from the floor below rang for the first class.

---

Parsons appeared during the interval between classes.

She came with the mail binder under her arm, the Tuesday delivery from the general store, which was also the post office, the mail sorted before school and walked up the hill in the binder. Marcus had Latin in twenty minutes. He knew, in the abstract, that nothing requiring an immediate response was likely to be in the binder, and he opened it anyway, as he always did, with the specific attention that he applied to anything arriving from outside Coldwater: the possibility that it was news.

The envelope from Dr. Feld was fourth from the top.

*Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars.* The letterhead on the envelope was the letterhead he had been receiving, in one form or another, since autumn 1940 — placement confirmation, credential documentation, quarterly notices about the wider network of displaced scholars the Committee maintained. Feld's own letters had been less frequent: two in 1941, one each in 1942 and the early part of 1943. Marcus had sent two postcards in the spring of this year, brief, reporting that his position continued and his address remained the same.

The envelope was thicker than a practical letter.

He opened it and read it standing. He had to sit down and read it again.

Feld was writing about a problem the Committee had encountered in tracking scholars who had been in transit during 1942 and into 1943. Some had arrived at their placements and failed to notify the office; this was not uncommon, and the Committee had means for re-establishing contact in most of those cases. Others were in Europe, unreachable for reasons that Feld described with a care that Marcus read as the careful prose of someone who did not yet know how to describe what was happening in Europe and was not going to guess. The third category was the one Feld lingered on: scholars who appeared to have been in transit and then ceased to be in transit, with no subsequent documentation and no record at any receiving institution.

Marcus knew that phrase. *Keine nachfolgende Dokumentation.* No subsequent documentation. The Emergency Committee used it the way a port authority used *vessel not arrived* — accurately, without affect. The period between his release from the camp and his arrival in Boston in August 1941 had been several weeks in which Marcus Klein existed in no file. The Committee had an address for him — the camp — that was no longer his address, and no forwarding address until he made contact from Boston. For those weeks, he had been a man of whom it could be written: *last documented at.* And then the next address.

The specific case was in the third page of the letter. Feld was careful with surnames, citing Committee privacy practice; he used initials where he could. A Dr. Felix K., he wrote — a linguist of German-Jewish origin, formerly of the University of Leipzig, who had been corresponding with the Committee from somewhere in Canada since early in 1943. His last letter to the office had been postmarked Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, September 22, 1943. In it he had told the Committee of his intention to travel south by sea, to reach Boston by late October; he had a contact in Boston. He had not written since. The Boston contact had heard nothing. The Committee had no other channel.

Feld was writing to Marcus partly because Marcus was placed in Maine — geographically relevant to a route running south from the Nova Scotia coast — and partly because he knew Marcus had been long enough on the Committee's rolls to have some reach into the network. Did Marcus know anything of a Dr. Felix K., Leipzig, a linguist?

Marcus read the letter through twice more.

He had a partial recollection — not a name, but something adjacent to a name, the way a word hovered at the edge of retrieval before either arriving or failing to arrive. A man at a philology conference in Vienna in 1936. Something at the intersection of Germanic philology and historical linguistics; he recalled a corridor in the Anatomiegebäude, the cold institutional light the building always had, two men talking in the specific Leipzig-accented German he had always found recognizable at a distance. He had been introduced. He had not spoken with the man at any length.

The name would not come. He might be constructing the memory from Feld's description rather than from the conference itself. A philologist could not always be trusted to distinguish reconstruction from recollection; it was one of the discipline's hazards he had never found a way around.

He set the letter on his desk.

Latin was beginning.

---

The German examination was the following Tuesday.

He read through Hannah Pfeiffer's paper first, which was not his usual order — he customarily worked alphabetically, which put Doris Hatch first and Hannah last — but which he found himself doing anyway. She had translated the passage from Goethe's correspondence correctly, which was not surprising; what stopped him was the word order. The passage was a letter Goethe had written to Schiller in October 1798 about the difficulty of rendering a natural scene in language without losing what had made the scene worth rendering. In the key sentence, the verb fell at the end, as German required. Most students, encountering this, pulled the verb forward; English demanded it, and the instinct was not wrong. Hannah Pfeiffer had left the verb where Goethe had placed it. The English she had produced was technically awkward and philologically correct, a sentence translated in the grammatical sense rather than the idiomatic one — you could see the German inside the English the way you could sometimes see the structure of a building inside the material it was built from.

He marked it correct and moved on to Doris Hatch.

He had not said anything. It was not the examination's occasion, and it was not entirely the German's occasion either; what she had given him told him something about where and how she had learned to read, which was not a conversation he was equipped to have in December with three weeks until Christmas break. He wrote *Good work* on her sheet and the same on Doris's and *This is improving* on Louise Pelletier's and meant all three, which was not always the case.

Latin was going well. Caesar's *De Bello Gallico*, the organization of the camp and the construction of the fortifications, twelve students working through the ablative absolutes with the patient incomprehension of people who found something merely difficult. After three students who found German faintly shameful, merely difficult was a relief he had not expected to feel as strongly as he did.

He encountered Henry Crow on Thursday afternoon in the second-floor hallway, Henry moving past with the supply cart.

"The window," Marcus said, which was not a complete sentence but arrived that way.

Henry looked at him.

"The north sill," Marcus said. "The cold isn't coming through the way it was."

"Block plane," Henry said. "And new caulk on the outside. It'll hold as long as the temperature stays above ten degrees. Below ten, the frame tightens." He added: "Might stick closed."

Marcus said he appreciated it.

Henry said it was his job and pushed the cart toward the supply closet at the hallway's end.

---

The school thinned in the last two weeks before Christmas break, the way it thinned every year — boys finding reasons to be on the water or in the timber, girls finding reasons to be needed at home, the teachers accepting these reasons with less scrutiny than they would have applied before the war. The building was quiet in the afternoons. Marcus finished the examination corrections and began preparing the January syllabus, working in the classroom for an hour after four o'clock because his room was colder than the classroom and the classroom had the east light for another forty minutes.

He had read Feld's letter three more times over the week. He had not replied.

---

He read it again that evening in his room, the lamp on, the letter flat on his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark that had been in place since half past four. There was no moon he could see and the cold pressed against the glass. The radiator on the south wall was running well, which it did not always do this early in December, and the room was warm enough that he could work at his desk without his coat.

He set the letter down. He took the German notebook from the shelf above his desk — more than half-full now, the compressed German hand running through its pages from April — and turned to the first blank leaf.

He wrote, in German, what he had:

*Felix K. Linguist. Leipzig. Zuletzt belegt in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, 22. September 1943. Beabsichtigte, Boston auf dem Seeweg zu erreichen, Ende Oktober.*

He looked at what he had written for a moment and then wrote below it:

*Ich glaube, ihn nicht zu kennen.*

He set down the pen. The 1936 Vienna corridor was still where it had been all week — present, the quality of the light available, the Leipzig-accented German available — and the name was still not there. He had searched the memory in the way you searched difficult German when you couldn't bring up a word: working around it, approaching from the surrounding context, trying the company the word had been in. It did not produce the name. He might be wrong about the conference. He might have assembled the memory from the description and mistaken the assembly for recollection.

He picked up the pen. Below the previous lines he wrote:

*Yarmouth nach Boston. Die Küste von Maine liegt dazwischen.*

He read the three lines back.

Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. He had not been there. He knew it as a port town on the southwestern coast, a transit point on the sea routes between the Atlantic provinces and New England — knew it in the way he knew most Maritime geography: from a map he had studied when he was trying to understand his own route south, the autumn of 1941. He could bring the coastline's shape from the map. He could not bring the harbor, the town's character, what it looked like from the water in late September. He had a place that was a location on a line rather than a place.

September 22, 1943. That was six weeks before the first heavy weather of the fall. A small vessel could make the run in favorable conditions in two to three days, or longer if the weather turned, or much longer, or not at all if the weather turned badly enough. It was a route that could be done. He did not know whether it had been.

He sat with the notebook open and the lamp on and thought about the phrase *zuletzt belegt in*.

Last documented in. The Emergency Committee's vocabulary for the point on the record where the thread ended. It was precise language; Feld was a precise man. He used the passive construction deliberately — *last documented in* rather than *last seen in* or *last known to be in* — because the documentation was what the Committee could stand behind, and he would not claim more certainty than the record gave him. The documentation ended at Yarmouth on September 22, 1943. What the documentation had been attached to continued, or did not continue, beyond that point, and the file had no way to say which.

He had been *last documented in* a place himself, in the summer of 1941. The documentation had said the camp; the camp had released him; for some weeks after that he had moved south without an address any file could reach him at. He had arrived in Boston, eventually, and written to the Emergency Committee from a boarding house on Commonwealth Avenue, and his file had been updated: Marcus Klein, Coldwater Reach, Maine, March 1942. Everything after that date was documented. Everything before August 1941, going back through Sherbrooke and London and Paris to Vienna, was documented also, in one archive or another. The gap between them was the condition Feld's phrase described, and Marcus had lived inside that condition and knew its particular quality: the sense of being in motion without leaving any trace of the motion, which was sometimes practical and sometimes something else.

Dr. Felix K. had been last documented in Yarmouth.

He did not write any of this in the notebook.

He put the pen down and opened the shortwave.

The BBC was not finding him tonight — 9.41 megacycles produced static and the fringe of something that might have been German, or might have been Dutch, sliding in and out at the edge of resolution. He moved the dial through the Brazilian Portuguese that appeared reliably above eleven megacycles, found a French signal that wavered between clarity and interference, found nothing else worth resting on. He moved down and found an American broadcast, clear and even, a news signal from somewhere in the domestic network. The Pacific: the Marshall Islands, conditions described with the precise optimism of someone who had been given permission to transmit and was being careful with it. He listened to the names of islands he had not known before the war and would not have had occasion to know. Maloelap. Wotje. He did not know where these were on a chart with any precision; he was assembling the Pacific the way he had assembled the Maine coast, location by location, from a distance, the geography of a war he was not in.

At nine-thirty he turned off the shortwave.

He took the Emergency Committee folder from the shelf between the English journal and the Stifter he had been reading since September. The folder held twelve letters now, going back to 1940, a paper record of his placement and its history. He put Feld's letter in the folder and put the folder back on the shelf.

He closed the German notebook and set it on the shelf above his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark, undiminished. He thought about Yarmouth, which he had not been to and did not know. He thought about the phrase *last documented in* and what came after it in the Committee's language: nothing, and then a date, and then the passive construction that meant someone had stopped being accountable to any record. He had been that. He knew the inside of it. The file noted the absence accurately and without editorial comment, which was the correct approach, and the absence itself remained — somewhere, in the space between the last documentation and whatever had come after — as a gap in the record that the record could acknowledge but not fill.

He turned off the lamp.

The room was dark and cold and smelled of woodsmoke from the furnace two floors below and of the particular density of cold books in a New England December, which he had come to know over the past two years without having been able to decide what he thought of it. He did not write anything more. The notebook was on the shelf, the folder was on the shelf, the shortwave sat silent on his desk. He did not move for a while. Outside the window the dark had the quality December dark always had at this latitude: complete, and cold, and indifferent to what was or wasn't documented in it.

# January Harbor

The inner cove had been icing since the second week of January — a thin skin at first, gray at the margins where the fresh water off the Reach mixed with the salt, then thickening toward the center until by the twenty-second it was opaque white ice that would not hold a man and would not let a boat through. It was not hard winter; the outer approach stayed open. The two draggers — the Callie B. and the Margaret Rose, Pelletier's — were tied at the outer dock and had been for nine days. The lobster boats were on their trailers at Farber's yard and at the Pelletier place up the road. The mail boat came Tuesdays and Fridays, worked the outer approach, tied at the deep-water slip, and was gone within the hour.

January harbor. Fewer reasons to be on the dock.

She did her rounds in the mornings. In summer the rounds took forty minutes: log, bilge checks, dock inspection, radio at 0800. In January they took twenty-five, with the fleet reduced and the radio check running once daily and the bilge pumps demanding less attention than they did in active season. She had learned, in her second winter at the post, not to stretch the rounds to fill the time. Owen had said something close to this before the fact, though she had arrived at it herself before she remembered that he had said it, and she was no longer certain whether she had arrived at it or remembered it, and she did not pursue the question.

She walked the outer dock each morning and noted the ice line in the log. January 22: inner cove ice approximately four inches, opaque. Outer approach clear. Callie B. and Margaret Rose, outer dock, checked and secure. Wind NNW at eleven knots. Barometer 30.14, steady. She checked the Callie B.'s bilge pump — running clean, had been since the boat was tied up — and noted it and went on.

The Callie B.'s bilge pump was what she had gone to check on the night of October 11. It had been running clean then too. She had made her note and left the dock at 2330. She had told Ennis this, and it was accurate.

She did not think about this on the dock. It presented itself and she noted it and moved on.

Back in the shack she ran the 0800 check on the BC-1206 — weather, traffic conditions, the harbor operations she monitored on the coast — and logged the result. Then she turned to the ledger.

She had been opening it to October since November. Not every morning; some mornings she skipped it. But she had opened it enough that it was a part of the mornings, and she had stopped asking herself why, the same way she had stopped asking herself why she rechecked the Callie B.'s bilge pump when she knew perfectly well it was running clean.

The gap was on the right-hand page, midway through the ledger. Pages 114 through 119: Ennis had taken them at 1008 on October 12, folded them into his document envelope with the efficiency of a man for whom this was ordinary procedure. What remained was a faint unevenness in the binding — not something you would notice if you weren't looking, but a different weight when you held the spread open. The stitching showed at the spine, pale thread where the section had gone.

The entry before the gap was October 8. Weather, tide, traffic, nothing unusual. Her handwriting, quick and competent. The entry after the gap was October 13: the body, the Coast Guard, the departure of the district lieutenant at 1008. Her handwriting again, abbreviated.

She held the spread open and looked at both sides of what wasn't there.

Then she closed the ledger and left it on the desk.

---

On Wednesdays she went to Merrill's for coffee. Owen had gone every morning; she had made it once a week, not from economy alone — once a week gave it something mornings would have worn smooth. In January, Merrill's had a particular quality: warm in a way the shack was never warm, and occupied in the particular way that the working middle generation occupied things in January, which was with a settled patience, people who had made their arrangements with winter and found a diner a reasonable place to sit with them.

She was on her second cup when Reg Farber came in.

She knew him as she knew most of the fishermen: by his boats first. Eight years of the Callie B. — the bilge pump, a mooring chain in '41, a registration discrepancy the fall before last — had given them a specific and sufficient acquaintance. Since October they had another kind: the kind produced by proximity to the same event. When they ran into each other at the dock or on the road, the body was there without being mentioned. This was common enough in a town of Coldwater's size. Most things that had happened were there without being mentioned.

Farber sat two stools down from her. The counterman brought him coffee without being asked. He looked into his cup.

He said: "I've been thinking about that fellow since October."

Eira said: "I expect most people have."

"My boy." He stopped. "He doesn't say much about it. Hard to tell what kids carry."

"No," she said.

He drank his coffee. She held her cup. Outside the front window the road was frozen and empty, the empty that Wednesday afternoon in January produced with particular thoroughness.

He said: "I was up late on the eleventh. Night before."

She set down her cup.

"Couldn't sleep." He said it without particular weight; insomnia in January was ordinary. "I was on the porch around eleven, eleven-thirty. I saw a boat come in." He paused. "Small wooden thing. No lights."

She waited.

"It tied up at the far end of the dock — past the dock extension, where you can't see from the road. I watched it for a few minutes. I've gone without navigation lights myself, close in, when I've been out later than I planned and I know the water. Didn't think much of it." He shook his head slowly. "Went back inside around midnight. It was gone by morning."

"When did it connect?" she said.

"Few weeks after. I was thinking about who the man could have been and I remembered seeing the boat and thought — I don't know." He looked at her. "I don't know that it's connected. I just had it sitting with me and didn't know where to put it."

"Did you report it to the Coast Guard?"

He turned his coffee cup on the counter. "No. Didn't think to. Should I?"

She said: "I'll mention it if it's relevant."

He said: "Probably isn't." He looked up at the counterman. "You have apple pie today?"

---

She walked home in the cold.

The road was frozen, the ruts from the last mud period locked into the surface now until spring. She kept to the margin where the ground was flat. January light at two-thirty had maybe ninety minutes in it before the sky gave up. She could feel it going.

What Farber didn't know: she had been on the dock. In the shadow of the Callie B.'s wheelhouse, twenty feet from the dock extension, close enough to hear the engine cut. She had seen the boat come in and she had watched it tie up. She had seen the man step off and stand at the foot of the dock for a moment, getting his bearings — the dark overcoat, the shoes that were wrong for the dock in the way they turned out to be wrong for everything. Thirty seconds, maybe less. Then he had turned and walked toward the breakwater. She had watched him go.

She had gone home and gone to bed. She had told Ennis she had checked the bilge pump, found it running clean, and left the dock at 2330. All of that was true. The truth as she had told it contained all of it except the boat and the man and those thirty seconds, which were not in the account she gave and not in the pages Ennis took and not anywhere except in her.

She had run the other version in October. Thoroughly, carefully, arriving at her conclusions the same way she arrived at conclusions about weather: by looking at the available information from each angle until the picture was clear. The conclusions held. She had not changed them.

What was different now was Farber.

He had been on his porch. He had seen the boat come in from the same direction she had seen it. He had watched it for a few minutes — his words — which meant he had stood in the cold in the dark doing his own version of what she had done from the shadow of the Callie B., and then he had gone inside and not thought much of it until he had, and he had carried it for three months because he didn't know where to put it, and he had put it down at Merrill's on a Wednesday in January because the occasion was there and the Wednesday was long.

He didn't connect the boat to the body with certainty. He had said so.

The road turned uphill past the Congregational church. The church windows held the last of the afternoon light for a moment and then let it go. The sky above the tree line was pale gray, moving toward the blue that came before dark.

She had been the only person who knew about the boat for three months. She had not thought about it in those terms — had not told herself each morning, *I am the only person who knows the boat was there.* But she had known it the way she knew the tide tables: as a condition, a baseline, reliable because it had been reliable yesterday and the day before and the month before that. She had counted on it without knowing she was counting on it.

Farber had put a second point of knowledge into the world. He had done it the way people did things without knowing what they were doing — honestly, without urgency, because he had been meaning to go through that drawer and the occasion presented itself.

She was not the only witness now. She was the witness who knew the most. Farber had seen the boat. She had the boat and the man: the thirty seconds on the dock, the overcoat, the shoes, the direction he walked. Farber was missing those thirty seconds and he would not know to look for them.

The short road to her house. The maple in the front yard was bare, the branches black against a sky that was almost dark now.

She went inside.

She took off Owen's peacoat and hung it on the peg. The kitchen was cold; she had banked the stove before leaving and it needed tending. She put wood on and adjusted the draft and waited until the flame took before she closed the stove door.

She did not go to the log. She had thought, walking home, that there might be a form for Farber's account — some way of putting it into the record where it could exist separate from what she chose to do with it. She stood at the kitchen table. She did not go to the log.

She made supper. She ate. She cleaned up.

The barometer at four-thirty was 30.18 and rising. Clear weather coming, and cold with it.

Reg Farber's information was somewhere in her now, without a ledger to put it in. She did not know what she would do with it. She had not done anything yet.

She went to bed.

# Found

The cows moved before she got the barn door open — a shifting, the soft thud of hooves on packed earth, a low sound one of them made to another in the dark. She had been hearing this for six years, since the first winter she was old enough to do the milking alone, and she still stopped for a moment when it happened: the sound of the herd gathering itself in the dark, the way they knew someone was at the door before the door opened.

February cold had drawn itself into the boards overnight. Her breath showed when she stepped through, and then the cows' breath showed too, a white fog rising from the near stalls in the lantern light, and she stood a moment in the smell of it — wet hay and grain, the close animal heat, the February cold that lived at shin level and in the beam joints and did not warm off entirely even when the herd had been standing in it for hours. The lantern made a small yellow circle on the earthen floor. Above it, darkness.

Four-thirty. She went to work.

Her section was the six Guernseys on the near side. She had been milking them, or cows like them, since she was eleven and her hands knew the work without asking her permission. The one who kicked left. The two who leaned into the pail. The last one, who needed settling before she would let you near her, who had been that way for two years and would probably always be that way. Hannah moved through them in the order she always moved through them, unhurried, the pail finding its place, her fingers working.

Her father was in the far stalls with his Holsteins, and she could hear the rhythm of his milking through the divider — pull and ring, pull and ring — as steady as it had been for as long as she had known what milking was. They had not spoken during morning milking in as long as she could remember. The barn had its own kind of quiet and they both kept it. This had been true before his English went away, which made it a barn thing and not a silence thing, though she did not separate them in her thinking.

February dark outside the barn door was total. She had been standing on the back step before she came down, her coat half-buttoned, and the hill above the property had been just a darker shape against a dark sky and the fields were nothing at all. July dark wanted something from you; it had insects in it, motion, the rustling of things that had business to do. February dark had no business. It settled in and waited.

She finished her third Guernsey, moved to the fourth.

Somewhere around five, the wind came over the roof peak and she heard a nail pull free — a ping against one of the far boards — and she looked over at the dark end of the barn where the sound had been, and couldn't see anything that had changed. She would check it in daylight. There was always something in February that needed checking in daylight.

---

At six, Lonzo Reed came with the four men.

She heard the keys first, always. Then the footsteps crossing the barnyard, the particular sound of four people being walked somewhere at six in the morning in cold they had not chosen. Then the drag of the door against the ice that had been building at the sill for ten days. Lonzo came through first with the Springfield, and then Werner, and Gerd, and the quiet one whose name she could never remember even though she heard it every morning — some difficulty between the German and the Maine of it — and then Karl last.

Lonzo had fallen in the first week of the month. He'd gone down hard on the icy patch near the barn door, the Springfield striking the ground before he did, and after that he walked from the icehouse to the barn with the deliberateness of an old man testing ice, each step settled before the next. He was not old, exactly, but he walked old on ice now.

The prisoners had not fallen. Karl had learned to read the ice sometime in January; she had noticed it without deciding to notice it: the widening of his step on the gray patches, the way his weight shifted back. He was nineteen and his body took what the ground taught it quickly. The other three were older and slower to adjust.

She did not look up when they came in.

The February arrangement was the same as January: the prisoners took the far stalls for mucking and for the cleanup work while she and her father managed the milking, and then when the Guernseys were done Karl and Werner carried the cans to the cooling tank. Her father worked the Holstein end. Lonzo Reed stood near the center beam with his rifle and his cold, stamping his feet occasionally on the earthen floor.

She finished her fifth Guernsey and moved to the last.

Karl came across the barn with a can in each hand, moving at the pace she had watched him find over the winter — not rushing, not dawdling, the workman's pace that got things done. He was aimed for the door. The icy patch near the sill was the same patch Lonzo had gone down on: the temperature dropped overnight and the melt off their boots refroze by morning and the ash she spread kept being absorbed into the gray surface and needing spreading again. She saw Karl hit the edge of it. His right foot went sideways, the can in his left hand knocked outward, and he caught himself in a single half-step — no drama in it, the body's fast knowledge — and set his feet right and kept going through the door.

The right can sloshed. He had not dropped it.

She was back at the last Guernsey, moving the pail, when she saw the paper on the floor.

---

It lay near the icy patch, close to where his foot had turned. A folded page, doubled twice. She could see from where she stood the wear at the folds — the paper darkened there, soft with handling, the kind of wear that came from something carried and taken out and folded back again, many times.

She looked at the door. It was closed.

She went to the page and picked it up.

There was a wooden ledge beside the door post, where people set things down when their hands were full — a glove, a harness strap. She could put the page there, where Karl would see it when he came back for the second pass on the cans. She held the page.

She looked at the far stalls. Werner and the others working, the sound of it regular. Her father's voice, once, in German, to one of his Holsteins. Lonzo Reed had gone out with Karl.

She unfolded the page.

A woman's handwriting — that was what she understood first, before the language sorted itself. Careful, narrow, slightly formal, the kind of handwriting that was tidy from intention and not from ease. The kind of handwriting that had been drilled into a girl and had stayed. The page had been folded and unfolded enough times that the creases held their shape even flat.

German. She understood this a moment after the handwriting, the way you caught the voice before you caught the words. And then, inside the German: Bavarian. Her ear for it was her father's ear — she had not learned it, had not been taught it, had absorbed it the way she had absorbed the sound of cows at four-thirty, from before she was old enough to know what learning was. This was not Dr. Klein's classroom German and not the German she had found in books. It was the German of home, some home she had never seen, the same dialect she had been hearing through the floor and through the icehouse window since April.

She read.

A neighbor's fence, replaced that autumn. Some difficulty with the materials, a delay, but it was finished and holding now, better than the old one. Potatoes more expensive than last year, as everything was. A cousin — her name appeared to be Els — had married in October: a small gathering, quietly done, the family had been there, the weather better than you would expect for October. The writer hadn't been able to come but had sent something with Els's sister. The cellar was holding better this winter than the winter before. The dog — a name she couldn't parse from the cursive — had been sick in December, something in the stomach, but had come back to himself; he was back to his old habits.

She read slowly. Her German was her father's German and this woman wrote in her father's register, the long comfortable sentences that carried everything without stopping to set pieces down separately.

Then, at the end of the paragraph about the cousin's wedding, this:

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.

She read it again.

Those who tried to go are gone. We pray for them.

The sentence was between a line about the October weather and a line about the cellar and it did not explain itself. The writer moved on after it to something about firewood. The war was not named in the letter, not once in the whole page, and yet versucht haben zu gehen was not a sentence about the cellar. Sind weg was not the dog being sick in December.

She didn't know who the people were. She had enough German to know that the sentence was specific — a real attempt, past tense, over; particular people this woman knew; a prayer for them by name, or rather for them in the place of their names, which were not given. She did not know where they had tried to go or what had become of them when they went. She had enough German for all of that and not enough for anything further.

The door scraped.

She folded the page on its creases and put it in her coat pocket and went back to the last Guernsey.

---

Karl came in again with Werner for the second pass on the cans. Lonzo Reed came through behind them, saying something about the ash and whether she had more of it. She told him where the bucket was.

She finished the last cow and carried her pail to the cooling tank. Her father came out of the far stalls and they moved the last of the milk across the barnyard to the cellar, two trips, without speaking. The cold that early in February cut straight down through the collar. The sky above the hill was just starting to separate itself from the darkness, gray coming up from the east.

She heard Lonzo lock the barn behind them.

---

That afternoon she sat at the kitchen table with her school notebook open.

She took the letter out of her coat pocket and unfolded it.

The handwriting first, again. Careful and narrow. In the kitchen light — the wood stove going, the gray February afternoon outside the window above the sink — the handwriting looked like someone who had sat down to write this with an intention to do it well, to send her son something careful. The page had been read smooth. He had been carrying it in his jacket pocket since whenever it arrived, October maybe or November, through the ice and the cold and the early mornings and the icy patch near the barn door, through whatever November and December and January were like in an icehouse in Maine.

She read it from the beginning.

The fence. The potatoes. Cousin Els. The cellar. The dog.

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.

She sat with it.

She could ask Dr. Klein. She had thought of him by name in the barn, the way you thought of someone when you had a question in the right subject. He was the only person in Coldwater who would know both the German and enough of the world beyond Coldwater to know what a sentence like that was the end of. But asking Dr. Klein meant taking the letter out of her pocket in front of someone, meant explaining where it had come from, meant saying what she had done with it when she found it.

She had not decided to do that yet.

She put the letter between the pages of her English literature notes — a Whitman passage she had been annotating, the words barely visible through the folded page — and closed the notebook and set it in her school bag.

The fire in the stove was going. She could hear her mother in the back room moving about, the particular footstep that said she was sweeping, and outside the February light doing what it always did at three-thirty, which was give up. She had taken something that did not belong to her and she knew that she had taken it and neither of these facts resolved the other.

She pulled her arithmetic toward her and began.

input.content:
# What the Letter Said

Doris and Louise went past the desk in the current of coat-buttoning and the momentum of girls who have decided the afternoon is elsewhere. He heard Louise's laugh in the hallway — specific, uncontainable, the kind of laugh that was a fact about a person rather than a response to anything — and then the stair door, and the building's afternoon quiet.

Three forms of werden remained on the board. The future auxiliary, arranged in a column: wird, werden, werdet. He had written them with more care than the lesson warranted, the chalk letters spaced as though for a class of thirty rather than three, and he went to the board now and took the eraser.

Hannah Pfeiffer had not moved. She was at the middle desk, coat already on, her school bag on the desk before her but not yet buckled. She had stayed after before — once to ask about an irregular verb, and once for a question about the subjunctive in indirect questions that had lengthened into the most useful grammatical conversation he had managed in Coldwater — and she had always had a reason when she stayed, which was not universally true of students who lingered.

He tapped the eraser against the chalk rail and set it down. He went to his desk and opened his lesson folder.

She said: "There's something I don't entirely understand."

He said: "In what?"

She opened not her German grammar but her English literature notebook — the one he had seen her annotating through several weeks of Latin period, which was not his — and she took from between the pages a folded sheet of paper and set it on the front edge of her desk. "German," she said. "A phrase I follow partly."

He came around the desk to look.

---

He picked up the page. The wear at its folds registered before anything else — the paper softened there, the surface slightly fibrous from being taken out and refolded many times, the specific quality of something attended to rather than carelessly handled. A single page, no header, no salutation: whatever address and identification the letter had carried were not on this page. The page began with the text itself, without preamble, and ended at the page's physical edge.

He had not asked where it came from. He would not ask.

A woman's hand. He understood this from the first line, and then from the particular use of wegen in the subordinate clause — Bavarian, or near enough; a formation that standard written German handled differently, a regional habit — and then from the letterforms themselves: the closing loops, the formation of the capitals, a schoolroom standard drilled in and retained without effort for forty or fifty years. He had been identifying regional written hands for twenty years. This one was not difficult.

He read from the beginning. She had asked about a phrase; he could not read a phrase. The letters on either side of it mattered for what it meant, and the letter's occasion mattered, and the whole domestic organization surrounding whatever had to be said mattered as much as what was said.

A neighbor's fence, replaced in autumn. Some difficulty with the materials, but holding now, better than the old one. Potato prices up. A cousin — Els — who had married in October: a small gathering, family present, weather better than October usually offered. The writer hadn't been able to attend but had sent something with Els's sister. The cellar better than last winter. A dog — the name blurred in the cursive — sick in December, something in the stomach, but recovered and back to his old habits.

He had been reading letters like this all his life — the domestic inventory that organized a world by its surfaces because the surfaces were what held. You said the fence, you said the cousin, you said the dog, and in saying them you maintained the world at its edges, kept the frame. He had received letters like this from Vienna, from Paris, from friends in places he would never return to. The inventory was a kind of loyalty: I am telling you the fence and the cousin and the dog because these things are still here. And sometimes, embedded in the inventory, between a wedding and firewood —

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.

He read the sentence. He read it again. He continued to the end of the page, which closed in the middle of a paragraph about the cellar and ended there, no signature.

He looked up.

She had underlined die versucht haben zu gehen. He had read through the underlining without registering it; the sentence had taken him before the notation did.

He folded the page on its existing creases and set it on the edge of the desk between them.

She said: "Versucht — tried. And zu gehen — to go. But I don't have the whole phrase."

He said: "Those who tried to go are gone."

She was very quiet.

"Wir beten für sie," he said. "We pray for them."

"People who left Germany?" she said.

"People who tried to leave. Germany, or Austria, or Czechoslovakia. In the years before the war made it impossible — 1939, 1940, 1941 — there were people who attempted to emigrate and did not succeed. Who started and were stopped. Or who started and were not heard from again." The coal furnace behind the wall made its sound — something in the metal, a faint contraction against the February cold. "Some of the people who tried to go arrived in places like this. Some of them didn't arrive anywhere."

She said: "She knows particular people."

"Yes. The double relative — die die — gives you a specific group. A real group she knows. The names aren't in the sentence. Just the category: those who tried." He looked at the line. "The placement tells you the rest. Between a cousin's October wedding and the firewood. Past tense — the past perfective. This is something she knows and is passing on. It is already over. The prayer confirms it."

Hannah looked at her hands for a moment. Then: "And the people who tried to go — they were from the same community?"

"From her community. Yes." He paused. "She writes tried, not went. Not left. They attempted and did not complete. That is what the sentence contains."

She sat with it. She had an adolescent's capacity for absorbing a sentence without immediately producing a response to it, which he had noticed before in this room. She let things arrive before she addressed them.

He did not say: I can date this letter to autumn 1943. A letter that mentions an October cousin's wedding and the onset of winter was written in late 1943, which meant that the people from their community who had tried to go in '39 or '40 or '41 had been gone for two years or more before she wrote this sentence, and the writing of it was not news but acknowledgment — telling her son in his POW camp in America what had become of the world he had come from. He did not say: the header is missing from this page, and I know what it means when a header is missing, and it tells me something about the path this page traveled to reach this room. He did not say: Yarmouth. He did not say the name from Feld's letter — the German-Jewish philologist, Leipzig, last documented Yarmouth Nova Scotia, September 1943 — and he did not say the coast of Maine between Yarmouth and Boston, and he did not say October.

He was close to saying these things to himself. He had been close since he picked up the page.

He handed the letter back to her.

---

She took it. She held it without immediately folding it, looking at the underlined phrase.

Then she looked up at him with the face that was not her classroom face. The classroom face was attentive and careful and gave nothing away. The other one, which appeared less often, was a girl thinking something and deciding whether to say it.

She said: "Were you one of them? The ones who tried to go?"

He was quiet for a moment.

"I am one of the ones who arrived," he said.

She received that.

"Vienna," he said. "Then Paris. London. Then Canada. Then here."

"Canada," she said.

"Briefly."

She did not ask about briefly. He had said the word with the register of a door that is shut, and she heard the register — he could see that she heard it — and left the door where it was. She had developed this particular skill somewhere. He knew where: the same place a girl would develop the skill of hearing her father through a floor, of reading the difference between a word that led somewhere and a word that was simply present in the room.

He said: "The leaving is not the hard part."

He had not intended to say this. It was true. He had known it was true for five or six years and had kept it in the notebook rather than giving it to rooms.

She looked at him.

"What is?" she said.

"The arriving," he said.

Which was a simplified version of the truth, close enough to the truth for a classroom in February, and as close as he had managed in language so far — the fuller version remained in the notebook, where he had been working on it since approximately Paris, and he had not yet found the sentence.

She was quiet for a moment. Then she said: "Yes."

Not I understand or I see. Just yes. Which was the right word, because it didn't claim more than she had.

She put the letter back between the annotation pages in the English literature notebook, closed it, buckled her school bag, and stood.

He said: "Good afternoon, Miss Pfeiffer."

She said: "Good afternoon." Then, at the door: "Thank you, Dr. Klein."

The door. The hallway. The stair door below. The building settling around its quiet.

---

He sat down at his desk.

The classroom arranged itself without him: the erased board, the three desks at their slight angles from the day's use, the chalk dust in the late February light. The coal furnace pressing its inadequate heat against the cold of the room, which absorbed it and remained cold. The east windows held February — condensation on the oldest frames, where the glass was thinnest and the fit loosest, the pines on the upper hill with their snow, the road below going toward four o'clock's early gray.

He reached for the letter from the edge of his desk and then stopped, because the letter was not there. She had taken it in her bag.

He put his hand flat on the surface.

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. He held the construction. In German — in the Bavarian formation, specifically — the double relative enacted the group before naming what happened to the group. Who they were first, before the fact of their going. The past perfective: had tried. Had been in the act of trying, had continued trying, had completed the trying, and it had not been enough. Sind weg: are gone. Not fled, not departed. Gone. Three words. Bavarian restraint doing the work of whatever the full account would require.

He thought about the woman who had written it. At a kitchen table somewhere, in a village whose letterforms he could place to within thirty or forty kilometers on the evidence of her handwriting — a village that lay within fifty kilometers of where a girl in his German class had grown up hearing her father's language, the dialect this woman wrote in, the register Hannah Pfeiffer's ear had been trained to by means she had never chosen. The world had a size. He had been learning this size since 1938, the same lesson in different rooms, in different languages, arriving each time as if for the first time. A mother at a table in Bavaria writing to her son in a POW icehouse in Maine, and the sentence she put between the cousin's wedding and the firewood, and the page separated from its header traveling from that table to this desk, and the girl who brought it to him, who carried in her speech the same dialect the letter was written in without knowing it — or without having said it.

He had told her the truth. What the phrase contained, what the construction meant, what kind of people the prayer was for. He had told her as much as was his to give from the letter she had given him, which was not the same as everything he had heard.

What he had heard was the letter's date — autumn 1943, recoverable from the cousin's October wedding and the cellar and the onset of winter — and what it meant to write that sentence in autumn 1943, which was that the people from their community had been gone long enough for the fact to be known and the prayer to be offered. He had heard the missing header, and what a missing header knew about itself. He had heard Yarmouth. He had heard the coast of Maine between Yarmouth and Boston, and what the coast of Maine held in October. He had heard a German-Jewish philologist, formerly of Leipzig, who had tried.

He held these things alongside each other and did not yet move them into sequence. They were adjacencies: real, probably connected, not yet proven. He had a habit of not closing adjacencies too quickly, a habit he had developed in the years when closing them too quickly had led to bad decisions in train stations and border offices. You looked at what you had; you wrote it down; you saw what it was.

Tonight he would write something in the notebook. He would look at what it looked like written down and decide from there.

He picked up his lesson folder and put it in his bag. His hat from the chair beside the desk. One of the student desks had drifted slightly from its usual position — the middle one, where she sat — and he moved it back, more carefully than necessary, the exactness a habit by now.

The world was a particular size. He had been learning this for six years, and the knowledge had not finished arriving.

He went out and closed the door.

input.content:
# A Report from Portland

By the last week of March the ice was going from the inner cove — pulling back from the edges first, a dark rim of open water widening an inch a day, the granite shelf of the shore returning in the mornings like something remembered. The center still held: opaque where it had been clear, four inches where it had been five, the surface pale and slightly sunken where the melt had come through and refrozen in February. She had been watching this progress for three weeks.

The Callie B. and the Margaret Rose had moved back to their slips on the twentieth. Farber first, because Farber was like that about weather and tide, and the Pelletiers a day behind. The lobster boats were still on trailers at Pelletier's yard — Kincaid's four, the two from the Dunbar brothers — waiting on the ice and on permits that came out of Portland at their own pace. She had six boats on the waiting list for the first week of April. The radio had been busy for two weeks: weather checks, supply questions, the kind of talk that accumulated when men had been on shore since January and the season was getting close.

She did her rounds at half past seven. Dock cleats, the drain at the float ramp, the fuel line, the BC-1206's daily check. The tide clock had gained a minute since she last reset it. She wound it, adjusted it, made a note. The spring smelled different from the other seasons — not better, she had stopped that mistake years ago — but specific: salt and diesel and the cold mud coming up where the dock skirting had held ice all winter, and underneath both, something opened that had been shut.

In the afternoon she wrote the permits. Six boats, six sets of documentation, the spring registration forms that had to be filed with Portland by April 15. She had been harbormaster for eight and a half years and the forms had not changed. She worked through them from top to bottom, the same order every year.

---

The letter came in Friday's mail.

It arrived with the February billings from the fuel cooperative — they were always late — a parts catalog from Portland Chandlery, and a Coastal Patrol circular about spring procedure. She took the stack back to the desk and dealt with them in order: bills, catalog, circular. The envelope from Boston was last.

Standard government stock, cream-colored, slightly heavy. Return address: First Coast Guard District, Headquarters, Boston, Massachusetts. Redirected through the Portland auxiliary, which had added a date stamp in blue ink, March 28 — nine days in transit.

She opened it and read it through.

---

The letter was a page and a half. Dated March 19. An administrative lieutenant she didn't know. At the bottom, a notation in smaller type indicating the original inquiry had been received from the Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, port authority and was being distributed to relevant coastal stations for information and response.

The substance: a party in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, had received no word from a man to whom they had either lent or rented a small wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet. The man had departed Yarmouth approximately September 28, 1943, reportedly heading south by sea, with the stated intention of making landfall in Massachusetts. He had not returned the boat. The owner had assumed, initially, that the occupant and the boat had reached their destination and that the boat had been sold or left somewhere. The missing-persons report had not been filed until February 1944, the letter noted, because the owner had been uncertain whether the report was his to make.

The description of the occupant: male, middle-aged, of continental European appearance, with limited English. No further identifying details available from the Yarmouth party.

The inquiry was being routed to coastal stations, the letter explained, because a body fitting some elements of the description — middle-aged male, civilian, no identification — had been recovered on the Maine coast in October 1943. The District was asking affected ports to provide any relevant information.

She set the letter on the desk. She read it again. Then she sat for a while with the radio on the south wall and the tide charts above it and the April light coming through the shack's east window.

---

What the letter had: a wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet. A single male occupant. Continental European appearance. Limited English. Departed Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, approximately September 28, 1943. Destination: Massachusetts, loosely.

What she had: a wooden boat, no lights, tied at the dock extension on the night of October 11, 1943. Gone before morning. A man stepping off the boat and standing at the foot of the dock extension before walking toward the breakwater. Dark overcoat, city cut. Leather shoes that had never been made for a dock. She had been in the shadow of the Callie B.'s wheelhouse, twenty feet away. She had watched him for twenty, thirty seconds. She had not seen his face.

She turned slightly and looked at the chart above the radio.

Yarmouth to Coldwater Reach. She had never made the crossing herself, but she knew the coast by chart and radio contact and the general arithmetic of small-boat passage. Yarmouth was in the southwest of Nova Scotia — a harbor town, working, the kind of place where you could rent a boat from someone who had one to rent. Once you cleared Cape Sable and came south along the outer coast you were in open water: the Atlantic running hard in autumn, the Bay of Fundy's tides working the approaches, no shelter until you reached the outer islands and could begin to work your way inshore. The crossing from Yarmouth to the midcoast of Maine was not impossible in a well-found boat with a good engine. In an eighteen-foot wooden motorboat, alone, in the last days of September — it was something you would undertake carefully, or not at all.

The end of September 1943 had closed badly on this coast. She had the record. Four days of northeast blow beginning the 27th, moderate on the 30th, another two days of wind and rain before it cleared around October 4. If he had departed on the 28th and run into the blow — and he would have run into it, there was no way not to, it had run from the Maritimes to Cape Ann — he would have had to find shelter somewhere and wait it out. An eighteen-foot wooden boat could have done this: put in behind an island, anchor in a cove, wait for the weather to settle. Then come out again and make what time he could.

September 28 to October 11 was thirteen days. Portland to Yarmouth by sea was roughly 200 miles along the coast. At that distance, with four days of bad weather in the middle, a small boat making eight or ten miles a day in the open and thirty or forty in a good stretch — thirteen days was not an impossible time. It was a long time. It was the arithmetic of someone who was being very careful, or very slow, or who had run into trouble more than once and recovered from it and continued south anyway.

She looked at the letter. Middle-aged. Continental European appearance. Limited English.

The man she had seen at the dock extension: a dark overcoat, city cut. Leather shoes. He had stood at the foot of the dock for thirty seconds before he moved. He had walked with the deliberate care of a man who was very tired or not well — she had noticed this and stored it in November and had not returned to it since. He had not spoken. He had not known she was there.

No papers. The Coast Guard had searched the body on October 12 and found nothing: pockets empty, no identification, nothing to give him a name or an address or a record of where he had come from. She had been present when Ennis conducted the search. She had watched him go through the coat and the trouser pockets — exterior, breast, inside — and come up with nothing.

A man traveling from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, in a borrowed boat, at the end of September, heading south toward Massachusetts, without papers. With limited English. With continental European appearance, which was the letter's language and not hers, but which was the right kind of language for what she had seen at the dock.

The letter did not contain a name.

---

The desk drawer stuck in the way it always did — the wood had swollen in February's wet and had not recovered fully — and she pressed it open and laid the letter at the back, behind the January freight manifests, which were thick and which she would not need again until the end-of-year accounting.

She should respond. The letter asked specifically for any relevant information; she had the authority to write a response and direct it through the Portland auxiliary to the District's administrative office. She would do this.

She closed the drawer. She opened the log and wrote the afternoon's conditions: wind NNW at ten knots, barometer 30.24 and rising, inner cove northwest corner open approximately one-third, outer dock in good order, registration forms filed for six vessels pending April permits. Tide times for the evening. She closed the log.

At three-thirty she did her afternoon rounds. Dock, drain, radio check. The cove had opened another half inch since morning.

---

She made supper and ate it at the table. She had done this every evening for eight and a half years, since there was no one else to do it and no one in the house who would eat it with her. The kitchen was Owen's kitchen: his shelf heights, his arrangement of the cups on the left side of the cabinet, the window latch he had repaired in September of 1935 and which she had not replaced because it worked. She sat with her plate and then with her tea and with what the letter had put in the room.

The man had come from Yarmouth. He had left on approximately September 28, heading south, in a small wooden boat. He had no papers and limited English and the kind of appearance that was described by phrases like continental European, which was what you wrote when you meant something more specific but did not have the specifics. He had arrived at Coldwater Reach on the night of October 11 after thirteen days of bad-weather passage and she had watched him walk to the breakwater.

He had been heading somewhere. This was what the letter had put into the room and would not take back. He had borrowed a boat in Yarmouth and gone south, and Yarmouth was not where you ended up — it was where you passed through on your way to somewhere else, somewhere with a wharf and a street address and a person who was expecting you. Massachusetts, loosely. Boston, probably. He had had a destination and a reason for the destination and people at the destination who had expected his arrival.

They had received instead the kind of silence that comes when someone does not arrive and cannot be found. The owner in Yarmouth had waited five months to file his report, uncertain whether it was his to file. There might be other people who had waited longer, who were more certain that it was not theirs to file, who had no way to report anything because reporting would require them to explain why they had been waiting for him.

She sat with this for some time. The March dark had come down on the cove and the harbor and the breakwater's red light was running at the end of its two hundred yards of granite. Five miles visible offshore. The same as always.

She did not write anything in the log.

She went to bed.

input.text:
First Coast Guard District, Headquarters, Boston, Massachusetts. [Date: March 19, 1944.]

Re: Inquiry received from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, port authority.

A party in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia has reported a small wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet, which was lent or rented to a male individual and has not been returned. The occupant departed Yarmouth approximately September 28, 1943, reportedly heading south by sea with the stated intention of making landfall in Massachusetts. The boat and occupant have not been accounted for. A missing-persons report was filed by the owner in February 1944.

Description of occupant: male, middle-aged, of continental European appearance, with limited English. No further identifying details available.

This inquiry is being routed to relevant coastal stations for information and response, as a body fitting some elements of the above description — middle-aged male, civilian, no identification — was recovered on the Maine coast in October 1943.

Affected ports are requested to provide any relevant information through the Portland auxiliary to this District's administrative office.
