# Sprechen

April came in wet. Not the clean wet of rain — the slow wet of thaw, the ground releasing what winter had put into it, the low fields going to mud first and the mud staying because more came from above every second day and the higher ground was only drier by comparison, not dry. The farm roads had been impassable for two weeks in March. Even now the ruts in the south drive were four inches deep in the mornings, filling again before her father had the manure spreader across them.

The work changed with it. In winter you moved inside: repair, preparation, the woodwork and the harness work and the ledger kept beside the stove. In spring you moved back out into ground that didn't want you yet, into the mud and the half-frozen furrows and the particular cold of April that was colder than March because you had stopped expecting it. Her father had been trying to get at the low corner of the north field for three weeks. The drainage ditch below the elbow had been frozen since November, was open now but choked — sediment, dead stems, the runoff from the upper pasture backing up in the bend — and the low corner itself was standing in two inches of water that would not move until the ditch moved. He had put the prisoners on it Monday morning: two of them with drainage spades working the choke from the outlet upstream, the other two on the sod itself, turning forks, breaking the strips where the ground was solid enough to turn.

Lonzo Reed walked the south fence line. He had his Springfield on his shoulder and his hands in the pockets of his coat and he walked one direction and then the other at the end of the field, doing the job that was achievable: watching when he could watch, being visible the rest of the time. The field was long and the four men were spread across most of its length. There was no position from which one man could hold all four in view. Hannah had understood this about the farm's arrangement since at least October. She thought Lonzo had understood it since before she did, and had found his accommodation — the walking, the visibility, the attention at the moments when attention was possible — and left the gap between that and the theoretical complete at the back of his mind, which was where it belonged.

She was at the north fence. Three posts needed resetting: frost had lifted them through February and March, tilting two of them noticeably and leaving the wire slack between the second and the third. She had the post driver, the tamping bar, a bucket of gravel from the drive apron. The work was not complicated. Pull the post, clean the base, repack the depth, tamp the gravel, check the plumb, move on. She had done it three years running now. Next spring she would do it again.

The north fence work put her at the far end of the field from Lonzo, and roughly thirty yards from where Karl Reinmar was turning sod.

She had not arranged this. The north fence needed the work it needed. The prisoners had been assigned to the north field. The farm's geometry put her where it put her, and she was not going to spend the morning deciding what it meant or didn't mean.

The letter was in her school notebook, in her coat pocket. She had been carrying it since February, between the Whitman annotation pages where nobody would open. She had read it perhaps fifteen times — not to learn anything new from it, her German was enough for most of it and she had Dr. Klein's English for the phrase that mattered — but because she had it and Karl Reinmar did not know she had it. She had not returned it. She had considered the ledge beside the barn door, where things were left for other people's hands; she had considered slipping it into the pocket of his canvas jacket during the milk-can work. She had looked at each option and put it down. The letter stayed in the notebook.

She thought about what Dr. Klein had said. *Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg.* He had given her the English: *Those who tried to go are gone.* He had said it quietly, without ceremony, looking at the page more than at her. And then: *The leaving is not the hard part.* She had not followed everything after that — the part about arriving, the brief word he used for Canada, the way he stopped himself partway through a sentence — but she had taken that line home and it had been there since, in the kitchen and in the barn and in the evenings when she heard the two voices through the glass of the icehouse window.

She thought about December. The fence post on the east side of the paddock, lifted by the frost, loose in its hole. Karl had found it before she did, had both hands on it to test it, and they had stood on either side of the fence with the cold between them for ninety seconds. He had said thirty-two words in uncertain English — *Fence. Post. Is loose — frost, I think. I can — with the tool — if you want.* She had answered. She had gone home afterward and decided to keep noticing what she noticed without deciding what it meant, and she had done this for four months, and now it was April and the ground was waterlogged and she was thirty yards from him with a post driver and a tamping bar.

She pulled the second fence post and cleaned the base.

She was going to speak to him in German.

She had known this for some time, not as a plan she had made and timed but as a thing that had already become true and was only waiting for the occasion. She could not have told anyone when she had decided it. Maybe when she read the letter at the kitchen table and put it in her notebook. Maybe when Dr. Klein said *the leaving is not the hard part.* Maybe earlier. She did not know how to locate when she had started moving toward something. She knew where she was.

She tamped the gravel and set the plumb. The post was straight. She moved to the third one.

Karl was twenty yards from her now, working a strip of turned sod. He had not looked up.

---

The occasion came on a Wednesday.

By four o'clock the light was going gray in the west and the temperature dropping, and Lonzo gathered the men in his customary way: a short two-note whistle, an arm wave, the walk from the field across the farmyard to the milking barn. The full cans needed moving before the evening escort back to the icehouse. Same procedure every afternoon.

Hannah was already in the barn. She had finished her portion of the afternoon milking — the late shift, her father's Guernseys, twelve animals in the south stanchion row — and was at the stanchions with the rinse pail when she heard the outer door.

Lonzo came through first, the way he always did, moving through the near end of the barn before the prisoners entered. He passed her without a word — that was usual too — and made his check of the space. Then the four men came through the door.

The three older ones went immediately to the far end. Fischer, Brandt, Walther: the motion of men who had done this a hundred times, moving to their positions at the carrying frames with the ease of a practiced routine. Karl came in last and took up his position near the door, where the two empty cans were waiting to be moved to the cold room.

The barn in April had its specific smell: winter still in the wood — straw, old manure, the cold settled into the rafters — and over it the new warmth the cows had been building since the temperature turned, something almost sweet, the particular heat of twelve animals at the end of a full day. She had known this smell her whole life. In winter it was comfort and in summer it was almost too much and in April it was both at once.

Lonzo said, to nobody in particular, in the mild and slightly apologetic tone he used when he was really talking to himself: I believe I could use a minute of cold air.

His boots on the door planks. The cold outside coming in briefly, then the door.

She had perhaps three minutes.

She moved the rinse pail to the corner. She turned.

Karl had the first empty can in his hands. He looked at her directly — no fence between them, no width of field — and he was nineteen years old and very still, the kind of stillness that is attention, not surprise.

She said, in Bavarian German, her father's Bavarian German, the kitchen German, the words she had grown up on before she had any other words:

Bist du von nah an Rosenheim?

He stopped moving.

He said — not the halting English he had been absorbing from Lonzo, not the vocabulary of weather and farm tasks and Lonzo Reed's fisherman's Maine, but his own German, the German of someone who thinks in German, the German of someone for whom German is the place the words come from:

Ja. Nah an Rosenheim. Du sprichst Bayrisch.

She said: Mein Vater ist Bayer.

He said: Ich weiß. Er hat mir gesagt. Wir reden manchmal.

She said: Ich weiß.

A pause. He looked at her steadily. He said: Verstehst du uns?

She said: Einiges.

He settled the can against his hip, looking at the middle distance for a moment — at the carrying frame, at whatever he was about to say — and said:

Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören.

She said: Ich weiß.

Then Lonzo's boots on the door planks, the cold coming back in with him, and Karl moved toward the far end with the can. Fischer said something in German. Karl answered in two words. The carrying frames went up. The sound of boots and iron-wheeled carts on the stone floor.

The three minutes were over.

---

She finished the barn and walked up to the farmhouse. She went at her usual pace. She was carrying something and she did not want to drop it by moving too fast.

Her mother was at the stove. Her father's coat was on the hook — he was still in the south field, the manure spreader still to get through the ruts. The kitchen was warm after the barn's April cool, and it smelled of supper beginning: something on the back burner, the five-o'clock smell of the kitchen in every season she could remember.

She sat down at the table and held what she had.

She had spoken Bavarian German to Karl Reinmar in her father's milking barn. He had answered in it. They had been in the same language for approximately two minutes, for approximately forty words.

She went through them.

Her opening: Bist du von nah an Rosenheim. Then his: Ja. Nah an Rosenheim. Du sprichst Bayrisch. She had grown up on Bavarian and he had heard her and said so. He had named it — the particular vowels, the particular verb placement, her father's dialect in her mouth — and said: you speak Bavarian. That was the acknowledgment. The first thing.

Then hers: Mein Vater ist Bayer. Then his: Ich weiß. Er hat mir gesagt. Wir reden manchmal. She had already known this. She had been listening to the two voices through the icehouse window since at least October — her father's German, Karl's German, the back-and-forth of the exchange she could not fully follow but could read by its rhythm. She had known they spoke. Karl did not know she had known. Now he did.

Then hers: Ich weiß. Confirmation, not news. Then his: Verstehst du uns? Then hers: Einiges. She had not lied. Her German was enough for most of it and not for all of it and he had asked honestly and she had answered honestly.

Then the last thing.

Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören.

She turned the sentence over in the way she did when a German word was doing more than she could immediately account for. Seltsam was a word she had from her father. He used it for things that were wrong in a way that was also right: the first warm day in March when you weren't prepared for it, the quality of the light after a storm, a calf in its first hour looking at the barn walls with its whole body. Seltsam. Strange and also true. Strange in a way that was not a complaint.

He had said es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören while he was looking at the middle distance — at the carrying frame, at the thing he was saying, not quite at her — and she had heard the strangeness and she had heard the other thing in it too. Something she was not imagining.

She was not imagining the implication.

Her mother moved the pot to the front burner. Hannah looked at her own hands, still cold from the barn, a faint smell of the rinse water still on them. Two minutes in the milking barn in April. It was the first time in her life she had spoken German to someone who was not her father, not Dr. Klein, not her own reflection testing phrases in the window glass before school. She had gone to Karl in his language and he had come back in it.

She thought about the letter. She had thought, for the few seconds before Lonzo's boots on the door planks, that this might be the moment — that she could reach into her coat and pull the notebook out and set the page in his hands. She had not done it. She was not sure why. The letter was still between the Whitman pages. She sat with it in her pocket and with what she had said and what he had said and let the kitchen be what the kitchen was.

---

After supper her father went to the icehouse window.

She could hear them from the kitchen, where she was doing the clearing. The sound came through the old single-pane glass above the sink, not words but the quality of words — the rhythm of the exchange, the structure of turns. She had been listening to this for months. She could read it now the way she read the farm by its sounds: what the cows told you before anything else did, what the specific direction of wind in the north ridge meant in November against what it meant in April.

Her father's German was the German he had been speaking his whole life, which in 1944 was fifty-five years of it. It was not just the language — it was everything the language held for him: the names for things she could not name in English, the Bavarian vocabulary for weather and calendar and the particular work of dairy farming, words he had given her before she had any other words at all. When he spoke it she heard everything he was inside it. Not the man who passed the bread at supper without speaking, not the man who had stopped giving his instructions in English two years ago. The man who had read to her in German when she was small. The man who had sung her the Bavarian songs until she could sing them back, not knowing she was learning them. His German had width. It had the weight of fifty years.

Karl's German with her father was the German of a younger man in the presence of an older one who knew things he wanted to know. She could hear the structure of it through the glass: her father's sentences longer, Karl's shorter, the occasional close back-and-forth when they found a subject they both knew from the same side — some matter of agricultural calendar, some question of soil that was the same soil in Bavaria and in Coldwater, Maine, if you were asking about the right thing. Karl asked questions. Her father answered. Sometimes her father made the short sound that meant a thing had been said correctly, that the understanding had landed. Karl's German with her father was young German still forming beside old German that had stopped forming forty years ago. It was the German of a twenty-year-old from fifty kilometers away learning the particular version of fifty kilometers away that had come to Maine.

In the barn it had been different.

She stood at the sink with the clearing water and tried to hold what was different about it. In the barn Karl had been more level. Not equal — she did not have his twenty years of German and he knew this; Einiges was the honest answer — but not the younger-man-receiving-instruction either. Something between. The German of speaking across to someone unexpected. He had heard her Bavarian and named it, and then he had answered, and the register he had used for the next forty words was not the register she heard through the window. More careful. Slightly more formal, the way you spoke to a stranger. But also something else — the formality of someone who was surprised into attention. He had not expected her to come to him in that language. The surprise was in his stillness. The surprise was in the word seltsam.

She was not from the home he meant. She had never been to Bavaria. She had never been south of Portland. The Bavarian she had was her father's Bavarian, brought across the Atlantic in 1922 and passed down through the kitchen and the barn floor and the songs she learned without knowing she was learning them, and it was as much a part of her as the farm. She was from Coldwater. She would always be from Coldwater.

But Karl had heard her father in her German. He had heard the fifty kilometers between where Albrecht Pfeiffer was born and where Karl Reinmar was born, carried across the ocean and through twenty-two winters and back out through Hannah's mouth on a Wednesday afternoon in April. He had said du sprichst Bayrisch and she had said mein Vater ist Bayer and he had said ich weiß, er hat mir gesagt — your father already told him. Her father had given Karl this, and Karl had received it, and it had been waiting between them in the barn.

Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören.

Strange, to hear it here. She sat with the word seltsam the way she sat with things she wasn't finished with. Strange and also true. Strange and also, underneath the strangeness — she thought she had heard this in the word, in the way he looked at the carrying frame when he said it — not wrong at all. Not wrong in the way that strange things you haven't decided about yet are not wrong. The kind of strange that means: I did not know this was here. I did not know it could be here.

She thought he might also have meant: I am glad it is.

She did not know this. She had not imagined it. There was a difference between the two.

---

She went to bed at half past nine.

She had done the thing she had been moving toward since she did not know when. The Wednesday had come and Lonzo had gone out for his three minutes of cold air and she had turned and said her father's words into the barn's April smell and Karl had answered in his own German, full and careful and from the same ground.

She did not know what it meant for the farm, for her parents, for the arrangement. She did not know whether Karl would carry it forward or whether the icehouse window would have a different quality now. She did not know whether the letter still in her notebook meant the same thing it had meant in February, or whether she should return it, or whether returning it was something entirely separate from what had happened in the barn.

She did not know how to locate when it had started: the fence post in December, the letter in February, Dr. Klein's classroom, the north fence in April and Karl thirty yards from her at the turning fork. Some combination of these and something underneath the combination she didn't have a name for. You could not always find where you began moving toward something. You found where you were when you got there.

She knew the thing had been real. Two minutes in the milking barn in April. Forty words in the language her father had brought from Bavaria to Coldwater, Maine. Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören. She had said Ich weiß, and she had meant it.

She went to sleep.

input.content:
# The Notebook

The three girls had gone at four o'clock. He stayed.

He had been carrying the German notebook since morning, in the inside pocket of his coat, and had not opened it. He set the exercise books on the teaching desk and took out his pen and sat for a moment in the empty classroom, looking at nothing in particular — the east window, the flat gray light coming through it, the chalk ledge where he had written today's conjugation exercise, which he now went up and erased. He cleaned the eraser against the ledge and the chalk dust fell. He sat back down.

The three girls: Priscilla Mack, Doris Farber, Hannah Pfeiffer. German enrollment for the current year and, he suspected, for the foreseeable future. There was no exam at the end of the year — he had asked the administration in September and they had looked at him as if he had inquired about something beside the point, which was perhaps accurate. He had been teaching from primary texts instead: nineteenth-century letters, simple prose, a few pages of Goethe in the original that he had typed out himself because there was no text available and he was not prepared to assign Faust. In the autumn the lesson that most occupied the three of them was the grammatical relationship between direct and indirect object; by February it had become the subjunctive; now, in late April, with the school year approaching its last five weeks, they were reading a short story about a journey by train, and the discussion of vocabulary had drifted twice into territory that had nothing to do with the train.

He read the exercise books in his usual order. Hannah Pfeiffer's was on top.

She had written about the farm in early May — the seed orders, the garden beds being turned, the smell of the earth before planting. He had assigned a composition requiring specific description rather than general: something familiar, but named precisely. She had done this, and what she had named precisely was Bavarian in its vocabulary and in a dozen small matters of grammar. The verb placement in two of her sentences was the placement her father used at home, not the placement the textbook taught, which were not the same position. He had been correcting exactly this for seven months — the small marks in the margin, the notation of standard form beside the regional form she had grown up on. He did not make the corrections this time. He wrote at the bottom of her composition: *Gut. Weiter so.* Good. Keep on like this. He set it aside.

He sat for a moment with his pen in his hand.

Her German had not become more standard over the year. It had become more specific — more precise in the register her father had given her, more accurate to the dialect her father had brought from Bavaria to Coldwater in 1922. When she wrote about the farm she wrote it in the vocabulary of the farm she had grown up on, which was the vocabulary of a farm fifty kilometers east of Munich, transplanted and maintained through two decades of Maine winters. He had been trying to correct this in the direction of the textbook. He was not sure, this evening, why.

He set the other two exercise books to the side and took out the notebook.

---

He had started the current volume in the previous spring. More than half the pages were filled — closer to two-thirds now, he estimated, riffling through without reading — and the writing was denser in the most recent quarter of the book than in the earlier sections, as if the record had been crowding itself. He had not noticed this before. He noticed it now.

He wrote the date at the top of a fresh page.

Then, in the private shorthand he had kept since his years as a junior lecturer in Vienna — subordination stripped away, bare sequences of fact, the record pared to what could not be argued with — he wrote what he had been assembling since December and had not yet assembled in one place.

*October 12, 1943. Unknown man, found at the Coldwater breakwater. No papers. No identification. Not from Coldwater. Clothing civilian: city coat, leather shoes. Approximate age: fifty, or a hard forty.*

He had known this since October. He had not written it here, in this form, until now. He was aware of the delay and did not intend to explain it, even in the private shorthand.

*December 1943. Letter from Dr. Feld, Emergency Committee. Felix K., linguist, formerly Leipzig. Last documented Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, September 22, 1943. Intended to reach Massachusetts by sea. No further word.*

He looked at that entry for a moment, then wrote the third.

*February 1944. Letter, Pfeiffer barn. Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Bavarian. Refers to people from the mother's community who attempted to emigrate before the war closed. Letter written late 1943.*

He put the pen down and worked the arithmetic.

Yarmouth, Nova Scotia to the Maine coast by small motorboat, autumn 1943. He had checked the coastal weather record in the Courier archives in January: a northeast blow between the twenty-seventh of September and the fourth of October, sustained, the kind of system that would have kept a boat of eighteen feet close to shore or laid up in shelter for some portion of the crossing. Last documented Yarmouth, September 22. Departure: certainly after that date — by some days, perhaps a week, to arrange the boat, watch the weather, do what a man preparing to cross an open coast does. Call it late September. Add ten to fourteen days of careful navigation southward, hugging the coast in the way a man would who did not know this coast and was alone on it. Arrival possibilities along the Maine coast: mid-October.

He wrote it: *Departure Yarmouth: late September, estimated. Crossing: ten to fourteen days, careful. Arrival along the Maine coast: mid-October.*

He looked at the page.

Below the arithmetic, without the qualifying architecture that attended everything he wrote for any other reader — without the subordinate clauses, without the hedging — he wrote two lines:

*This is probability, not evidence. One does not publish on probability.*

And then, below that:

*One also does not ignore a probability this high.*

He sat with it. The classroom was quiet; the building had gone still around him the way buildings went still on Friday afternoons, as if it had been waiting for the week to end. Outside the east window the spruce line at the back of the schoolyard held against the overcast sky.

He tried to remember the 1936 philology conference in Vienna. He had been there; he had attended the third session, eighteenth-century correspondence, which was close to his own work. He reconstructed the corridor on the second day, the height of the ceiling, the sound of a specific door with a heavy hinge. He had spoken with a man whose affiliation was Leipzig, or possibly Halle — a linguist, or someone adjacent to language history, which was adjacent enough to have been at the same session. The man's face would not come. He had met perhaps a hundred people over three days, and retained perhaps twenty of them fully, and the man from Leipzig or Halle was somewhere in the remainder: present as a sense rather than a face, a handshake that had or had not made an impression, possibly a name on a program card he had long since lost. He tried to imagine what a linguist from Leipzig in the 1930s would have looked like. He produced several faces, none of which he trusted. It was possible he was misremembering the affiliation entirely. It was possible he had never spoken to Felix K. at all.

He wrote: *1936 Vienna conference: possible meeting. Not certain.*

He closed the notebook.

---

He sat in the empty classroom with the notebook closed on the desk before him and let the problem sit, which was his practice. He had a problem; he had assembled it; he did not have its resolution. The habit of staying with the assembled thing rather than pushing it before it was ready was one he had learned over twenty years of scholarship and refined over the subsequent years in which there had been no shortage of problems that pushing made worse.

He knew Eira Bowman held something he did not have. He had known this since November — since seven minutes at the harbormaster's shack when she had attended to something she had decided not to raise, with the careful neutrality of a person working inside a chosen boundary. He recognized that quality; he had been practicing it himself, in several languages, for some years.

He had been considering, for several weeks, whether to bring what he had written to her.

The argument for it was not difficult. She had the official record, or what remained of it after the Coast Guard's October visit. She had whatever she had personally observed that had not gone into her statement, which — on the evidence of those seven minutes — was not nothing. If what he had assembled in the notebook was in any sense accurate, her information and his were adjacent to the same object, and the sum of the two might be more useful than either alone.

The argument against it took longer, because it was better.

He had a theory. He did not have evidence. That was not a technicality. It was the difference between the verifiable and the merely plausible, and in his experience — in the twenty years of his scholarship that had preceded the word scholarship ceasing to apply to him — the damage done by confusing the two was not recoverable. If he was wrong, if the man on the breakwater was someone with entirely different origins, then he had introduced a false story into the account of a woman already carrying something whose weight he could only estimate. A wrong theory was not a neutral addition to what she held. It was a second weight, and the wrong kind.

If he was right — if the man was Felix K., linguist of Leipzig, last documented Yarmouth on September 22 — then being right changed nothing that was still recoverable. The man was dead. His name was not in any official record and would not be restored to one by Marcus's theory. Going to Eira Bowman with a probable name was not the same thing as providing her with one.

He took the notebook out and opened it to the last page. Below the two lines about probability, he wrote a question in the private shorthand, without qualifying architecture:

*What do I intend to do with this?*

He left the question on the page. He put the notebook in his coat pocket, gathered his papers, and went out.

---

The walk back took nine minutes, as it always did. Down the school's back steps, through the alley past the hardware yard, up the hill to the elm at the corner of Henry's lot. The elm had leaves now — small, still partly furled, the pale green of the first weeks. The afternoon light was later than it had been a month ago. He did not linger under it.

Henry was at the kitchen table with the Rockland paper spread before him, open to a section that might have been the same section he had been reading since Thursday, or one that looked like it. The cup was at the far edge. Lillian was at the stove. There was a cup at Marcus's usual place; he sat down and wrapped both hands around it.

The kitchen had its sounds. The stove, the settling of the house, something outside — a screen door, two houses down — that opened and closed twice and then stopped. He sat and did not say anything particular, and nothing particular was said to him.

After a while Henry looked up from the paper and said: "You look like you've been working on something."

"Trying to," Marcus said.

Henry nodded. He looked at Marcus for a moment with the even and un-pressing regard he gave to most things, and returned to the paper. Nothing else was said on the subject.

Marcus sat for twenty minutes. Lillian mentioned that the sugar ration was short again and she was going to ask about the April allocation. He said he could stop in Monday. She said she would ask herself. The coffee was good. He drank it.

He said good night at half past five and went upstairs.

---

His room. The desk under the east window; the shortwave on the shelf above; the notebook's usual place between the English journal and the grammar workbook, where it was not because it was still in his coat pocket. He took it out and set it on the desk.

He sat in the chair by the window.

He did not turn on the shortwave. On Friday evenings he usually listened — the BBC at nine, CBS, whatever the coastal atmosphere permitted — but tonight he did not want more arriving from outside. He had enough.

The last light was going. The spruce line at the back of the schoolyard was visible, then less visible, then a shape against a marginally lighter dark. The season's lengthening: the evenings extending by a minute or two every night, accumulating. He had been noticing this change in the light at Coldwater for two springs now and had not yet decided whether he noticed it because he had finally started paying attention to this place, or because the place had become available to him in some way it had not been before, or whether there was a distinction between those two things.

He thought about Yarmouth. A harbor in Nova Scotia in late September, built from what he knew of harbors in general and of this coast's autumn weather: the gray-green chop, the cold in the water before the cold reached the air. A man borrowing a small motorboat. The open coast running south, the shoreline kept in sight. Boston at the far end of it — Massachusetts, a name and an address, whatever document or institution or Emergency Committee contact was there to receive him. Ten days on the coast. Fourteen. A lantern carried for the compass work and shuttered before the last approach, because there were places on this coast that were blacked out and he would not know which until he was close.

He thought about what a man does when he has found the dock in the dark and tied the boat and walked to the end of a breakwater at the end of a very long transit. He thought about sitting down. The specific quality of having stopped. What the back of a light standard's pedestal would feel like against a man's back if he sat down with his legs extended before him and let himself be still.

He thought about *die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg.* He had been holding the phrase since February, since the afternoon Hannah Pfeiffer had set the folded page on his desk and he had read what the mother had placed between the cousin's October wedding and the firewood paragraph. The Bavarian past perfect, which was also a way of saying: irreversibly, without return. Gone into the category of the gone. The mother at a kitchen table in Bavaria writing this to a son in an American prisoner-of-war camp, not saying what she was saying, saying it anyway.

He thought, briefly — not about the camp at Sherbrooke, he did not go there directly, had learned in the subsequent years not to go there directly — but about a morning in August 1941 when he had come out of a place with a document in his coat pocket classifying him as a resident alien enemy, which was accurate and was not the full picture of what he was, and had stood on a street in the same summer air as the previous day and the day before that, only now he was outside in it. He had spent the following months learning the difference between outside and somewhere. By the time he arrived in Coldwater he had begun to understand that the difference was other people, and a desk under a window, and a kitchen where someone put a cup at your place before you sat down. He had not expected these things to be the answer, and then they were.

He thought about Felix K. He thought about whether Felix K., at the end of the breakwater, had believed he was nearly arrived, or had understood that he was not going to arrive at all. He thought about whether it mattered which of those two things Felix K. had believed, in October, in the dark, at the end of a granite breakwater on a coast he had not known long enough to name.

He did not know whether it mattered.

He did not know whether the man on the breakwater was Felix K.

The notebook was on the desk. The question he had left in it — *What do I intend to do with this?* — did not answer itself in the dark. It would be there in the morning. It would be there next week. It would be there until he found something more to write below it.

He went to bed.

input.content:
# Ice Out

The ice had been pulling back from the northwest corner since the last week of March. Each morning she had checked it from the dock end before opening the shack — the strip of ice shelf along the cove's north wall narrowing by degrees, turning gray and porous, the color of something ceding ground. She logged the observations without commentary, the way she logged the barometer and the bilge on the Callie B. and the angle of the breakwater light at first dark: not expecting any particular morning's measurement to matter on its own, but keeping the increment because the day the increment did not come was a day that needed marking.

May 3, 1944. She opened the shack door at five-thirty-five and the inner cove was open water.

She stood in the doorway for a moment with her hand on the frame. The salt came in off the water the way it did in working season — not the thin cold salt of winter, which arrived only on high wind off the open bay, but the full harbor salt: diesel underneath it, the particular smell of the tide flat at low water and the channel bottom's specific mud and something above all of it that was specifically this harbor, this reach. It had been five months. She had not been keeping track of that, or had not let herself keep track, and standing in the door she noticed she had been keeping track.

She wrote in the log: *Ice out, inner cove, full extent. May 3, 1944. 0535 hours.*

She checked the tide clock. She had reset it Monday, as she always did on Monday mornings, and it was running true. She made the notation in the maintenance column.

She ran the radio: primary check, backup frequency, Coast Guard channel at Group Southwest Harbor, the weather broadcast from the Rockland station. Northeast, light and variable, high overcast, no precipitation through Sunday. She wrote it in the weather column.

Before the lobster boats went out she walked down to the second slip to check the Callie B.'s bilge pump. The pump had been running on slow-leak monitor since November — the port quarter taking water at its old rate, never more than expected, twice-weekly checks through the winter, one spike in January when the hard freeze put tension on the hull and the pump managed six inches over three days before things equalized. She had notified Farber in January; she had continued the checks. Now she ran the pump through its test cycle: float switch responding, intake clear, discharge running clean. She wrote it in the maintenance log. The pump was running clean.

The lobster boats went out before six. She counted them from the dock end: nine, which was the full complement for the harbor. The permits had been backed up in Portland — a classification question on the renewed forms that had to be resolved in writing — and had not cleared until the last day of April, but all nine boats had their papers and the nine boats went. Burgess first, as he had been first every season she could recall, leading out with the particular certainty of a man who was not waiting on anyone. Then the two brothers from the far end of the village, then the others in loose sequence, each one pushing through the channel mouth and picking up speed in the open water beyond the bar.

She watched them clear the breakwater.

At seven-sixteen the Callie B. went out, the Margaret Rose ten minutes behind it. She logged their departures. Reg Farber at the Callie B.'s wheel, standing slightly off-center in his usual way, raised a hand as he cleared the dock without looking toward it.

The radio was busy after eight. The weekly freight traffic from Rockland, a fishing advisory from Group Southwest Harbor, two exchanges on the lobster frequency that she monitored in case one of them was going to become a buoy-line dispute — one of them was, and she noted it. She ran the correction forms for the six seasonal mooring permits that had been in error since April: each one reviewed against the tonnage classification table, corrected, re-signed. Six minutes per form. She sealed the Portland envelope.

It happened every year — the harbor going from winter's compression back to its working configuration in the space of a single week. She was aware it should not still catch her slightly, after nine seasons, and every year it caught her slightly. How quickly it became itself again.

---

Reg Farber came to the shack on the Friday after ice-out.

He was a large man and the shack was not a large room and he had developed, over years, the practice of stopping at the threshold rather than coming in. This kept things workable. She had never named it aloud and did not name it now. He stopped in the threshold with his cap in both hands and said he had a question about the June M.

The June M. was his lobster boat, a thirty-two-foot wooden trap hauler he had been running for eleven years. She waited.

He laid it out the way he laid things out: in order, without additions. The June M.'s seasonal dock fee came due at the end of the month. He was behind on it. The mooring line had snapped in the hard January freeze — the temperature dropping faster than the almanac had called for, the line under more tension than it was designed to carry before he got to the dock to ease it. When it let go it took dock cleat number seven with it, midpoint starboard of the outer float. The cleat had been in questionable condition before the failure. He had not wanted a dispute about whose responsibility the replacement was, so he had paid for it himself: forty-two dollars for the hardware and the installation labor. He had also had a winter where the trawl catch was down and the fuel cost was up, but he mentioned these in the way of context rather than argument and moved past them.

He was asking if she could defer the June M.'s seasonal fee to July.

The light in the shack was the flat morning light that came through the south-facing window over the radio. She could hear the radio cycling through its scan in the background, the low static between intervals.

The fee schedule was fixed by the District office. She did not have formal discretion to defer a seasonal boat fee. The hardship fund was administered through Portland with an application process and a result that came in August when it came at all, and August was not July and July was not May. Farber was not a man in financial distress — he had been running two boats from this harbor for fifteen years — but forty-two dollars onto a low season was forty-two dollars, and she was not going to name the hardship fund as an answer to his question.

She pulled the spring maintenance folder from the back of the desk.

She had kept the maintenance log in calendar quarters since she took the desk over in 1936. One page per quarter, each dock fitting and installation numbered and noted by location. She found the October 1943 page. She ran her finger down the entries until she found what she had noted on the evening of October 11: *Outer dock, east float hardware survey. Cleat #7, midpoint starboard: bracket wear evident, seating slightly loose. Recommend assessment spring 1944.*

She had written that entry in the fall and filed it and it had been on her spring list. She had not gotten to it. The spring list had four items ahead of it.

She looked at the entry.

She said: "I'll need to look at the cleat."

"It's been replaced," Farber said. "New hardware, good installation."

"The condition of the original fitting is a maintenance question. It was flagged in my fall survey for spring assessment." She set the folder on the desk. "A fee review pending that inspection is within the standard process."

He said nothing for a moment. He was working the cap slightly with both hands, not nervousness, the physical version of waiting.

She wrote in the log: *June M. seasonal fee under review pending dock maintenance inspection — cleat #7, outer float, east of midpoint starboard. Per fall 1943 survey notation. Review to be completed prior to end of month.*

She dated it. She said: "Can you be at the dock Thursday morning?"

"Seven o'clock," he said. "I'll be there."

She said: "I'll write it up as I find it."

He held his cap for a moment. He said: "I appreciate that, Eira."

She didn't answer to that. He left.

She looked at the entry. The maintenance note from October was in the quarterly record, dated, in her handwriting. The spring inspection was overdue by her own log. Her authority to hold a seasonal fee pending a maintenance question was in the harbormaster's charter. The July timeline would follow from the inspection timeline without requiring the log to carry anything the log would not carry. The entry was accurate. It was complete.

She picked up the mooring permit form she had set aside when he knocked. The radio gave her the eleven o'clock weather update. She wrote it in the weather column and went back to the form.

---

Thursday morning at seven o'clock she was at the outer float.

Farber was already there. He was a man who arrived on time in the way that people who respected their own word arrived — without ostentation, just there. She acknowledged him with a nod. She knelt at cleat number seven.

The replacement hardware was in good condition: galvanized steel, properly bedded in the float decking, the seating solid. She checked the surrounding plank for movement; none. She checked the adjacent cleats on either side for comparison; both showed similar surface weathering, both solid. She stood up and made the notation in the inspection log she had brought: *Cleat #7, replacement hardware, installation sound. Base deck condition within acceptable range. Pre-existing bracket wear at original fitting location consistent with fall 1943 survey notation. Failure mode: line-tension overload, not fitting failure.* She initialed it and dated it.

She said: "The cleat's in order. The original fitting was fair wear."

Farber said: "I know that."

"The inspection supports the fee schedule adjustment. The review is closed."

He nodded. That was all. He went back to the June M., which was in the slip behind them, lines checked, ready for the day's run. She watched him go aboard and wrote the final notation in the inspection log.

The morning was overcast, the temperature forty-two degrees, the harbor in its first full working week. She walked back to the shack.

---

The Heron came in on Tuesdays and Fridays from Rockland — mail, packaged freight, occasionally a passenger traveling one direction or the other. She used the outermost slip, the longest approach in the harbor. Eira had assigned it in 1942.

The second Friday in May. She was working through the monthly mooring-line inspection — outer dock, section by section, each line lifted and checked for chafe at the attachment fitting and surface rust on the hardware — when she heard the Heron's horn off the breakwater. She was at section eleven. She kept working. The Heron needed twelve minutes from the breakwater to the dock and she had seven sections remaining.

She was coming down the outer dock when she saw Marcus Klein standing at the end of it.

He was there for the mail, or for the same kind of parcel the Emergency Committee sent up through the Rockland freight — she had seen him twice before on mail-boat Fridays, waiting for a box addressed in a Manhattan hand. He stood at the end of the dock the way he stood everywhere he stood: upright, coat buttoned regardless of the temperature, looking at the harbor with an attention that was not a harbor person's attention. She could not have said, exactly, what the difference was. He was watching the water. He was not reading it.

She kept moving.

He said: "Warmer."

She said: "Finally."

He moved in the direction of the Heron's slip, which was the direction she was moving. She kept her eye on the approach line.

He said: "The boats are back."

She said: "They are."

The Heron was throttling back at the right distance, coming in at the slight angle Ayers always corrected in the last fifty feet. She watched the approach.

He said: "Any word —"

She said: "Nothing from Portland."

He nodded. She was at the slip. The bow line came across and she held it while the Heron came alongside, then cleated it and checked the fender placement. Ayers said, "Morning, Eira." She said, "Morning." She went to check the stern line while the freight hatch opened.

She did not look back at Klein. She heard the hatch open and the shift of boxes. By the time she finished the stern line he had moved to the hatch, collecting whatever was addressed to him. She went back to section twelve.

The line at section twelve showed surface weathering on the starboard fitting — not structural, worth monitoring. She wrote it in the inspection log. She finished the remaining sections. The afternoon sea fog was beginning to come in off the bar, the familiar mid-May pattern, the visibility softening at the channel mouth without obscuring the breakwater light.

She walked back to the shack.

---

She wrote the day's entries at six in the evening.

Weather: overcast, high cirrus by early afternoon. Wind northeast seven to twelve knots, backing southwest by eighteen hundred hours. Sea fog, harbor approach, fifteen-thirty to seventeen hundred. No precipitation. Visibility unlimited otherwise.

Traffic: nine lobsters out, nine in. Callie B. out 0716, in 1638. Margaret Rose out 0724, in 1503. Heron arrived 1050, departed 1116. Two freight deliveries, afternoon, invoices attached.

*June M. seasonal fee review — closed. Cleat #7 dock inspection completed May 11. Replacement hardware satisfactory, installation sound. Pre-existing wear condition per fall 1943 survey confirmed; line failure attributed to tension overload, not fitting defect. Review complete. June M. seasonal fee rescheduled: due July 31, 1944.*

She blotted the entry and dated it.

She wrote the barometer reading — 30.09 inches, falling slowly — and the morning and evening tide observations. She wrote the mooring-line inspection summary: thirty-one sections inspected over two days, one notation for monitoring, no replacements required.

The shack had gone quiet around her. The radio was on the evening scan, low, cycling through the empty frequencies. Owen's log ledger was on the bottom shelf of the cabinet to her left, where she had moved it in February 1936 when she'd taken the desk over — his handwriting running from June 1891 through the last entry in November 1935, where it stopped. She had not moved it since. The current ledger, her third volume, was on the desk.

She had a quarter of the page left below the day's entries.

She wrote: *May. Ice out. Harbor open. All boats accounted for.*

She put the pen down. She blotted it. She looked at it for a moment.

Then she closed the log.

She schedules the inspection for Thursday morning at seven. He collects his package; she finishes the inspection. Evening: she writes the log's day entries, formally closes the Farber review, and writes the final line: 'May. Ice out. Harbor open. # June Radio

Four-thirty in June was different from any other four-thirty. The dark was shorter and thinner — already a gray line at the east edge of the fields when she opened the barn door, the horizon somewhere between night and something. The cows were already up. June made them impatient, all that summer weight on them, and they came to the stanchions without needing to be pressed. The hay was warm and dry and the barn's smell this month was not the closed winter smell but something looser, the boards having breathed themselves out all through May.

She moved through the milking the way she always did, can to can, one end of the row to the other. The light over the door came on automatically when she switched the barn circuit; she had not needed the kerosene lamp since April. By the time she finished the second row the gray outside had become something almost blue. By the time she was done and washing down the stanchions a quarter past six, the fields were fully lit.

She came out of the barn. The south field was high and green, the hay cutting maybe a week out. The silo, the icehouse, the farmhouse: the yard in the morning quiet, everything where it was.

Lonzo arrived at eight with the prisoners. He came through the front gate in his patient way with the Springfield on his shoulder and the four of them behind him: Fischer first, then Brandt, then Walther, then Karl last, looking at the fence posts or the middle distance the way he usually did. Lonzo said good morning toward the barn where she was standing. She nodded. They went to the south field for the morning's work and the day looked like a Tuesday in June.

---

The kitchen radio was on at breakfast, as it was every morning now. The habit had formed somewhere in the spring; she couldn't have named the day. Her father held the Rockland paper without reading it. Her mother stood at the stove with her back to the room. The radio cycled through its programs in the ordinary way.

She was pouring coffee into her cup.

The radio said: *Allied forces have landed on the coast of Normandy. The operation is underway.*

She set the coffee pot down. The cup was beside it, she had not poured, she did not remember stopping.

The radio kept talking.

Her father pushed back from the table. He crossed to the radio and turned it louder, both hands on the knob, and came back and sat down. He had his coat on from the morning barn check and he did not take it off. He sat at the table with his coat on.

The radio said: *A massive amphibious operation. Airborne divisions in the early morning hours. The Allies on French soil.*

She sat down. She had her coffee cup in front of her now, somehow; she didn't remember pouring. She picked it up and held it.

Her mother came in from the garden at quarter past nine and sat down at the table between them and stayed. The three of them in the kitchen with the radio going, eating and not eating. Hannah ate a piece of bread, then set the second piece down. Her father's food sat where her mother had put it. Her mother had her hands folded in front of her and her attention pointed somewhere ahead of herself, all the way into the radio, the way her silence collected itself when it had somewhere to go.

The CBS correspondent said: *Casualties are reported to be significant. The fighting continues at several points along the beachhead.*

The BBC faded in through static at ten-fifteen when the kitchen set picked up the signal — it did this some mornings, caught the BBC clear and others got nothing — and the BBC voice was more formal than CBS but said similar things: *Operation Overlord. The largest amphibious operation in history. Allied forces establishing positions.* She tried to hold the two accounts in sequence and could not. Two voices from two studios in London both saying Normandy, saying beaches, saying dawn.

Her father's hands were flat on the table.

Through the window over the sink she could see the south field.

Four figures out there, far enough that she could not read their faces, not even which one had stopped moving. At the northeast corner, one of them stood briefly apart from the others — she could tell it was Karl by his build, the particular width of his shoulders, the size of him she had been looking at across fences and through glass for more than a year. Then he bent down and went back to the row and he was not distinguishable from the others at that distance.

Camp operations would have told them. She did not know in what form or at what hour — roll call, a guard with a statement, something. But it would be strange if they hadn't known by now.

She took her plate to the counter and washed it and put it in the rack. Her father was still at the table. The radio was still talking.

---

She heated soup at noon and set it beside him. He ate it, which she noticed without looking at him directly, the bowl emptying while she ate her own soup standing at the counter. The radio had not been turned off. It said: *The Prime Minister addressed the House of Commons this morning. The King has spoken to the nation.* It said: *Fighting continues at the beachhead.* It said the names of the beaches and she could not retain them in order.

She went out at one o'clock. The north barn needed the afternoon hay brought down from the loft, and the east-pasture gate needed checking after the spring flooding had shifted the post on the hinge side. The farm did not stop for this. She pulled her jacket from the hook by the door and went out.

Outside the day was warm and cloudless and knew nothing about any of it. The fields were the fields. The sky was a June sky. She went to the north barn and spent the better part of an hour on the hay and the gate, and when she came out and crossed the south end of the yard she was taking the shorter way back to the kitchen, which meant passing along the fence line of the south field.

Karl was at the northeast corner, thirty yards from the fence. He was bent at the waist, working along the row, his head down. She could see his face clearly from this distance. It was his working face, the same one every day, and she could not read anything in it from here.

She did not stop.

There was nothing to say today and no place to say it — not with Lonzo twenty-five yards away eating his lunch off the tailgate, not with all of them visible from the farmhouse window, not with the morning still in her head and the radio going in the kitchen and no German that was the right German for the gap between the fence and the row and what this day was. She went back to the kitchen.

Her father was still at the table. He had turned the newspaper face-down at some point, which she had not seen him do.

---

By four o'clock he had moved to the parlor.

The parlor radio was the better set, the signal cleaner and the BBC coming in without the kitchen static. He was in the chair he used only in winter — the corner chair by the window, the one with the gray slipcover her mother put on every November and took off every April. The coat was off now, folded over the arm. He had not called her in.

She passed the doorway twice on errands and saw him there each time in the same position: hands in his lap, the radio on the side table. The quality of his stillness was the same one she had seen in December 1941, that Sunday, when she had been fourteen and had stood in the kitchen doorway not knowing whether to go in. Something very large was being absorbed very slowly and there was nothing left over for the surface of his face.

She went in and sat in the straight chair by the door. He did not look at her. The BBC correspondent was saying that additional forces were moving to reinforce the initial landings, that the situation continued to develop, that the casualties could not yet be fully accounted for. She sat for a while and then stood and went back to the kitchen.

Her mother came through a few minutes later with a cup of coffee and went into the parlor and set it on the side table next to the radio, next to his hand. She said nothing. He reached for the cup without looking up and drank from it and set it back down. Her mother came back to the kitchen.

Hannah watched her come back and turned to the stove and put the kettle on.

---

The prisoners came in from the field at five. She heard them through the open kitchen window — Lonzo's voice carrying across the yard without the words, and then the four of them moving through the yard to the icehouse, and then the icehouse door. Then quiet from that direction.

She made supper. By six her father had come in from the parlor and sat at the table and eaten, which surprised her — she had expected him to carry the day's stillness through to tonight unchanged. But he ate all of his supper, carefully, the way he did everything carefully. When he finished he set his fork down and sat for a moment and went back to the parlor.

Hannah washed the dishes. Her mother dried them and put them away. They had been doing this without talking all spring, longer than that, and tonight was the same except that the quiet in the kitchen had the weight of the day behind it. Her mother folded the dish towel and hung it on the hook. She looked at Hannah for a moment — not speaking, never speaking, but something in the look — and then went to bed.

Hannah dried her hands and went to the table.

She had *The Selected Poems of Robert Frost* open in front of her. She'd been working through it since the term ended, not because Marcus had assigned it but because she kept returning to it, kept finding the same pages. She was not reading now. She had the book open and the lamp on and the radio coming low from the parlor, where her father had turned it down after supper — she could hear it the way she heard rain, as a sound that was always there but was not a voice.

He came into the kitchen at half past eight.

She heard him before she saw him, his footsteps crossing the parlor floor. He came through the doorway and crossed the kitchen and stood at the window over the sink. He did not acknowledge her. He stood at the window the way you stand at a window when you are not trying to see something but cannot leave the glass.

Through the window: the yard, half-lit by the kitchen lamp. The icehouse at the far edge of the lamplight, its window dark.

He stood there for a long moment.

He said, to the window, to himself, to no one in the room: "Nun ist es fertig."

He did not explain it. He turned from the window and went upstairs. She heard his footsteps on the stairs, even and slow, the familiar weight of him on the second step that always creaked. The door at the top of the stairs opened and then closed.

The house was quiet.

The radio was still on in the parlor, very low, a program that had nothing to do with France — some orchestra in a studio somewhere, the sound barely carrying. She could hear it the way she heard the pump.

She did not move.

The kitchen lamp was on. Through the window the icehouse held no light. Karl was in the icehouse with Fischer and Brandt and Walther, in the dark across the yard, and whatever this day had been for them was behind the dark window and she had no way into it and it was not the night to try.

Her father had said: Nun ist es fertig.

She sat at the table. The fields were moving outside the open window, the long summer grass at the field edge, the nighthawks somewhere over the south field making the sound they made in June. She had heard it every June of her life. She heard it now.

The radio on low from the parlor. Karl in the dark across the yard.

What came next, she did not know.

input.summary: June 6, 1944. Hannah's chapter. Four movements through the day. (1) Before: four-thirty milking in the warm June barn, Lonzo arriving at eight with the prisoners, the south field, the day looking like a Tuesday. At breakfast the kitchen radio delivers the news of Normandy; Hannah sets down the coffee pot without noticing she has. (2) The table and the morning: Albrecht turns the radio louder and sits in his coat at the kitchen table for two hours; Magda comes in from the garden and stays; the three of them with the radio filling the kitchen, eating and not eating. Hannah can see the south field from the window — four figures, Karl at the northeast corner, too far to read anything. Camp operations would have told the prisoners; she does not know what Karl is feeling. At one o'clock she goes out because the farm doesn't stop; she passes near the south field on the shorter way back, thirty yards from Karl working with his head down; she does not stop. There is no sentence for today. (3) Late afternoon: Albrecht moves to the parlor and the better radio, sits in the winter chair (the one with the gray slipcover, used only in winter), hands in his lap, absorbing. Magda brings him coffee without being asked; he drinks it without comment. Hannah sits in the parlor's straight chair for a few minutes, then goes back to the kitchen. (4) Evening: after supper the prisoners are in the icehouse, Lonzo gone home, radio turned low in the parlor. Hannah is at the kitchen table with the Frost poems she's not reading. Albrecht comes in from the parlor, stands at the kitchen window looking out at the dark icehouse, and says — to the window, to no one — "Nun ist es fertig." He goes upstairs. The house is quiet. Hannah sits at the table, the radio on low from the parlor, the icehouse dark across the yard. Close (elliptical): what comes next she does not know.

# The Zenith

The Crow house was quiet when Marcus turned onto the back street at twenty minutes past four, the same time he always turned onto it on a Tuesday in June. He had stayed after the last Latin class to look at a student's Cicero translation, which had been adequate, and he was still thinking about how to grade an adequate translation in a way that was true — how to measure an approximation against an original without measuring the person against the work — when he heard it.

The parlor window was open two inches and through it the Zenith's voice reached him across the front yard. Not music. A man speaking carefully, without pause, in the particular cadence that radio voices took on when the news was large: a slight slowing, an economy of breath between phrases, as if the voice understood what it was carrying and was being careful with it.

He came up the porch steps. He could hear the words now.

*Allied forces have landed on the coast of France. Units of the American, British, and Canadian armies, under the supreme command of General Dwight Eisenhower, have this morning begun the liberation of Western Europe.*

He opened the door and stood in the hall.

Through the parlor doorway: Henry was in his chair, still in his work clothes, his cap on the side table beside him. Lillian was in the doorway between the kitchen and the parlor, a dish towel held in both hands in front of her in the manner of something forgotten — she had picked it up for a reason and the reason had become irrelevant.

Neither of them looked at him.

Marcus set his briefcase on the floor beside the umbrella stand. He crossed the hall. He sat on the parlor sofa without taking off his coat.

---

Lillian brought supper at half past six. She had made a pot roast, carrots, biscuits, and she set everything on the low table in front of the sofa without asking. She had moved the parlor table from its usual position against the wall and placed two chairs alongside the sofa — they ate at the parlor table, because no one was going to be in the kitchen this evening with the Zenith in the next room and the broadcast filling the house.

Marcus ate without being particularly aware of it. The food was warm. He was grateful in the way you are grateful for simple things when you cannot manage anything more complex.

He found the BBC at ten minutes past seven — he crossed the room and turned the dial past three stations of static and the faint outline of something that might have been a farm broadcast from Portland, and then the BBC came through, clear and precise, the presenter's voice carrying its characteristic quality of British reserve in the service of unprecedented information. He went back to the sofa.

The three of them listened through the seven o'clock BBC and the eight o'clock CBS and back to the BBC at quarter past eight. At some point Lillian refilled his coffee cup, real coffee, the kind she made, and he did not say anything when she did and she did not say anything when she did, and the Zenith continued.

---

He found it by accident at nine o'clock, turning the dial during a CBS break while looking for the BBC. He passed the frequency too quickly and had to rotate the dial back, slowly, until he found the place where two broadcasts occupied nearly the same position and one of them was losing.

German.

Not alongside the English but underneath it — the BBC European service, or something like it, the transmission aimed east, toward the occupied territories, toward listeners with clandestine receivers hidden in farmhouse cellars and back-room wardrobes, who were listening in a way that had consequences if they were caught. The German was formal and deliberate, the register of a language designed to be received once and understood immediately.

Henry said, "What's that?"

"A German broadcast," Marcus said. "The BBC. For occupied Europe."

Lillian had come back from the kitchen and was standing in the doorway again.

Marcus listened. The German ran alongside the English signal for another few seconds, then the English strengthened and the German became something felt more than heard, and then it was only English again. In the time it was audible —

Henry said, "What are they saying?"

Marcus translated without looking up from the dial. "They are saying the Allied landing was conducted at multiple points along the coast in the early morning hours. They are saying the German commanders did not expect the landing at this point on the coast. They are saying the element of surprise —"

The broadcast shifted. The English signal returned in full and the German was gone. The CBS presenter said something about airborne divisions, about paratroopers in the Norman fields before dawn.

Marcus let it go. He sat back on the sofa. He had taken off his coat at some point; it was across the arm of the sofa now.

Lillian sat in the armchair beside the lamp, which she had turned low. Henry was in his chair, still. The three of them in the low-lit parlor, the Zenith doing its work at the wall.

---

He was not trying to think about Paris.

His job in this room tonight was to track the dial, to find the BBC when it drifted, to translate if there was anything that needed translating. But Paris was present the way certain things were present: not summoned, not avoidable, there in the room the way the room was there.

He had been in Paris for fourteen months — from the spring of 1938 until May 1940, when he had left before the Germans came. He had not been there in June 1940, had not seen the flags going up in the Place de la Concorde or the soldiers coming down the Champs-Élysées. He had made the calculation earlier and it had been the right calculation, which he had not known until several weeks after making it, when the information began arriving about the people who had not made it. So Paris for him was not June 1940. It was the fourteen months before that, which he was allowed to carry as something other than catastrophe.

The reading room at the Bibliothèque nationale, where a man could sit from nine in the morning to five in the afternoon and the staff required only a reader's card. The Sainte-Chapelle in November rain. A café near the Odéon where he had spent three evenings working on a chapter about Klopstock, and the coffee was good, and the other patrons left him alone.

The Louvre. He had been to the Louvre more times in fourteen months than he had been to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in ten years in Vienna — something he had not expected of himself, which was one of the small revelations of living temporarily in a city, that you attended to it more carefully than to the city you were from.

German soldiers had been in the Louvre for four years.

He was hearing, on the Zenith, that this might be ending. That the soldiers could leave the streets of Paris, if the battle moved in the direction the announcer's careful optimism implied. He heard the announcer's optimism as calculated — the man knew what he was allowed to say tonight and what he was not, and so the optimism itself was a document of what was known versus what was hoped.

He could not quite hold all of it at once.

Paris across the Atlantic, in the dark, with the soldiers perhaps already receding from certain streets as the news receded from the Zenith's speakers and became repetition. A colleague from the École pratique des hautes études who had gone to London in early 1940, whose current address Marcus did not have and had not had for three years. A street his landlord's wife's cousin had known — the name of it he had written down once and lost the paper.

The apartment in Vienna had been taken over by whoever had taken over such apartments. The monograph on Klopstock was in a drawer there, or had been turned to other uses.

He turned the dial. Found the BBC. Left it there.

---

At ten o'clock the news became a different kind of news.

In the first hours, information had been emerging out of the static as it was established — each fact landing with the weight of something genuinely new. At ten o'clock the shape of the day had solidified, and what remained was the assembly and narrative: the same facts being fitted into order, the event having happened, the urgency lowering slightly and in its place a kind of steadiness, as if the Zenith had shifted registers from emergency to record.

Lillian took the dishes to the kitchen. She came back and stood in the doorway for a moment.

"I'm going up," she said.

"All right," Henry said.

She looked at Marcus with an expression he had learned to read as Lillian's particular form of care, which was direct without being sentimental. She said, "Get some sleep, Marcus."

"I will," he said. "Thank you, Lillian."

She went upstairs. The sounds of the second floor: the hallway, the bedroom door, the familiar sequences of an occupied house settling itself for the night.

Henry reached over and turned the Zenith down to just above silence. The announcer continued, barely audible. The lamp was still on but low. The room had settled into itself, the supper things gone, the chairs returned to something near their usual positions.

They sat for a while.

---

Henry said, "I'm going to sit on the porch for a bit."

Marcus got his coat from the sofa arm and followed.

The night was warm in the way that June nights in Maine were rarely warm, which was that it did not require defending against. The air was still. The back street ran dark between the houses, the elms making a canopy against the sky, which at this hour and in this season was not quite black — a deep blue still holding some reserve of the day's light, the horizon to the north not fully given up.

Mrs. Pelletier's light was on across the way, a yellow square. Otherwise the street was quiet.

Henry sat in the left chair. Marcus sat in the right. It was the arrangement they had, established without discussion — the specific chairs you chose becoming your chairs without anyone deciding. He had been in this town for two years and three months and this was one of the arrangements that had become his: this chair, this porch, this street.

The elm leaves were still. Somewhere further down the block a screen door opened and then closed.

They were quiet for a time.

Henry said: "You have people there?"

Marcus considered how to answer this. He said: "I did. I don't know."

Henry nodded. He did not follow it with another question.

The screen door was quiet. In the upper branches of the elm, something — a shift of air too subtle for the porch — moved the leaves slightly.

Marcus said, after a while: "It's a long way to go."

Henry said: "It is."

He was talking about the invasion — the logistics of it, the distance the soldiers had crossed to reach that beach before dawn. Marcus was talking about the same thing. He was also talking about the particular relationship he had to the distance between here and France — the months he had spent in Paris, the city now four years occupied, the colleagues he had not-known about for four years — and the weight of hearing, tonight, that the distance might be in the process of changing.

Henry's relationship to distance was not the same. His version of the distance between Coldwater Reach and somewhere else — between here and Norfolk, Virginia, between here and whatever else of the country existed between those two points and what that country was — was not the same as Marcus's. Both of them understood this, that their versions of this were not the same, without requiring it to be said. The porch contained both versions without either one being named.

Another quarter-hour. The elm leaves. The quiet of the town.

---

He went back inside at midnight.

The Zenith was still on in the parlor, turned to its lowest point, the voice barely carrying through the room. He turned it off on his way through. It seemed wrong to leave it speaking to an empty room.

The house was dark. Henry had come in a few minutes before him; the downstairs was quiet and settled.

He went upstairs.

His room was the way he had left it in the morning: the chair by the east window, the books on the desk, the shortwave on the corner table. The shortwave was dark. He had not turned it on all evening — what would it give him that the Zenith had not already given?

He sat in the chair by the window without turning on the lamp.

Through the glass: the back street below, the elm canopy, and above it the sky, which in June at midnight was a deep blue rather than black, the latitude and the season conspiring to hold some residual light at the northern horizon. He had not expected this of Maine when he arrived — that the sky held its color so long.

The window faced east.

He was aware of this in a way he was not, usually, aware of it. That east across the town was the harbor, and east across the harbor was the Atlantic, and east across the Atlantic was France, and France was where men had crossed in boats this morning before dawn, under fire, onto a beach he could not picture because he had not been to Normandy and had no image to place there. Only the radio's language: the coast of France, the Allied positions, the fighting at the beachhead. Coordinates without a landscape.

But Paris he had a landscape for.

He did not know what was in Paris tonight. He did not know if the café near the Odéon was still a café, or if the building was standing, or what a city looked like after four years of occupation — he could theorize but he had not been there, had not seen it, and the imagination of it felt presumptuous against the fact of whatever it actually was. He did not know what had happened to the colleagues who had remained after May 1940 with different calculations or slower ones or no calculations at all. He had been not-knowing about them for four years. The particular quality of the not-knowing had changed over those four years, had taken on a different weight, the way water acquires the shape of the vessel it is held in.

He did not open the notebook.

What was in the notebook was already there — the four entries in their shorthand, the arithmetic, the question at the bottom of the page still unanswered since April. Tonight was separate from the notebook. Tonight was its own thing.

He sat in the chair.

Somewhere across the Atlantic, on the beach at Normandy, men he had not met were doing something that might begin to change the shape of what had expelled him — the Anschluss, the fall of France, the specific accumulation of years that had ended with him sitting in a chair in a rented room in Maine, east-facing, at midnight in June, not knowing who was alive and who was not. He was trying to hold this thought — what it meant that the thing might be beginning to end — and he found he could not hold it all at once. Too large. The pieces wouldn't stay in order.

Paris, perhaps, in a year.

And then what? Return to what city, with what colleagues still there, to what apartment, for what purpose, to be which version of himself?

He did not know. He noticed he could not picture it cleanly, which might mean only that it was too far away and too uncertain to picture, or might mean something else about the picture itself.

He sat until the cold came in through the glass — June cold, not significant, but enough to make itself known at two in the morning through the old window frame. He stood. He went to the bed without opening the shortwave, without the lamp, and lay down in the room's dark.

The window faced east. The dark outside it was the direction of everything he had come from: the libraries, the reading rooms, the colleagues, the monograph in a drawer, the café that may or may not still be there, the man on the Coldwater breakwater who had tried to cross from the other side of the same distance and had not made it.

The lamp was off.

Outside, the elm leaves moved against the sky's last blue.

He closed his eyes.
