input.content:
# Zuhause

The cows were restless through most of December. It was the dark, or the cold, or the particular quality of deep winter that animals seemed to register before people did and which manifested in the barn as a low-grade generalized unease — not sickness, nothing clinical, just the small signs of discomfort she had learned to read in the years she'd been doing the four-fifteen milking. Hannah talked to them through the work the same as always: the low reassuring murmur that barn work required, not words exactly, just sound, the human voice as its own argument for calm. She had been doing this since she was old enough to carry a pail. She would probably do it when she was fifty.

The radio was on before she got back to the kitchen. It had been on since December sixteenth, which was the morning she'd heard the word Ardennes over breakfast and watched her father set down his coffee and not pick it up again. The Ardennes was a place she knew from Harton's atlas — a forest on the German border with Belgium, which had nothing to do with Maine, which was therefore precisely the place her father would listen to for twelve hours straight. The German army had pushed through it, or was still pushing, the news confused in the first days, the correspondents using a kind of controlled uncertainty that told you the situation on the ground was more uncertain than the broadcasts could sustain.

Her father was at the kitchen set in the mornings and the parlor set in the evenings, and on the twenty-second he had both going at once, a thing she had not seen since the summer of 1942 when the tankers were burning off Cape Cod. The Ardennes was different from that. The tankers were the war coming here — a thing to be frightened of in the specific way of physical nearness, the fire visible on the horizon, the smell of it. The Ardennes was the war going there: to the country he had left in 1922, to the fields that were not Maine fields, to whatever was or wasn't in the Bavarian farmland he had not heard from in two years, perhaps longer. She had lost count of when the letters had stopped and could not remember if he had ever told her exactly.

She made breakfast and brought him coffee. He said danke and went back to listening.

Lonzo Reed was on minimal winter detail and dressed accordingly. He had acquired a second pair of wool socks sometime in November and changed between them in the icehouse vestibule each morning before escort, hanging the first pair on the stove pipe and putting on the second. He did not explain this system. It simply existed when you happened to look. He had developed a method for standing inside the icehouse door during the worst mornings that left him sheltered from the wind without technically being inside, and Hannah had observed this over several weeks without comment. He was not a fool. He was a man in his late fifties standing guard in January for a dollar a day, and he had organized his situation accordingly.

The prisoners were on reduced winter work: wood for the icehouse, hay from the north mow, the milking escort when the weather allowed. Bauer had a cough that the cold made worse. Lonzo had decided, without saying so, to leave Bauer in on the mornings below ten degrees. This was not in his orders. It was not contrary to them in any literal sense that Hannah could identify. Bauer stayed in.

Karl came to the barn willingly, the same as always. He moved through the milking stalls with the economy of someone who had worked animals since before he could read. Hannah moved through them the same way, on the opposite side, and the work got done in the barn's usual quiet. They had not spoken much since October. No particular thing had been said to stop it — the winter had done it, the way cold does, slowing things to stillness and leaving them to start again when the air changed. She was not troubled by the stopping. She knew where it had been and she knew it was still there.

She went to school on the days she went, which in December was most of them and in January was four out of five — the road iced over on Tuesdays and Wednesdays of the second week, and she stayed to do the morning work and then the evening, and the school day was somewhere else, occurring without her. Marcus Klein would have set her the reading. He did not make a particular occasion of her absences, which she appreciated.

---

The Bulge resolved in the Allies' favor by the end of January. The papers said it and the radio said it and Harton's geography students moved the pins back across the map in the school hallway, east and east again until the line was approximately where it had been before December sixteenth. Hannah watched this happen over three mornings on her way to German class. The resolution was accurate. The satisfaction it produced in her was not equal to the relief she had expected and she did not know what to do with that, so she left it.

Her father was not better.

She had let herself believe, without examining the belief, that the Bulge resolving would move something in him the way the tides moved things. In and then out, the particular pressure going and the next thing arriving. But the Bulge going had left him quieter, not more open, and the quality of his stillness had changed in a way she had to look at carefully to name. He was in the barn before six now, which was earlier than she had ever found him there, and he stayed through the second milking and into the dark of the evening, past when the work required it. He was not sad, or not only sad. He was the face of a man who had handed something away and was now in the absence of the thing. She did not have a German word for it. She did not have an English one either.

He sat at the radio less. Her mother moved through the kitchen with the efficiency she had maintained across two years of silence: bringing him coffee in the parlor without being asked, the way she communicated everything now, by action without word. Magda communicated very precisely. Hannah had learned to read the quality of her mother's movements the same way she had learned to read her father's face — it had simply taken different practice.

What Hannah wanted to say to her father was not a question.

She had questions. She had accumulated them for three years of living inside a house that had reorganized itself around two different silences. Whether there was family still in Bavaria that she'd been told about too young to remember. What he heard when he listened to the radio and what it cost him to hear it. What the German word was for whatever had happened to him when the war started and then went on and then the letters stopped. These were questions and she had given up expecting answers to them — not in despair, just as a practical matter, the same way you gave up expecting a certain kind of weather in February and instead worked with what February brought.

What she wanted to say was not a question.

She wanted to say: she knew about him and Karl. The icehouse window, the evenings, the particular register she had heard in her father's voice — the third register, neither barn German nor supper German but something slower, with more room in it, the pace of two people finding shared ground. She had known since spring and had said nothing because she had not known how to say it without seeming to offer something she was not offering. She did not want to make it strange, the way saying the name of something ordinary can suddenly make it strange.

She wanted to say: she spoke German now. Not Morgen, not the supper-table yes-father words. She had spoken German to Karl in the barn in April, forty words, and he had answered, and she had understood, and she had not been afraid of the language. She had been afraid of other things — whether Lonzo would come in, what her father's face would do if he saw — but not of the language itself. She had been speaking it at the fence through the fall, the ordinary German of farm questions and weather, the language settling into her the same way the barn language had settled in when she was three and the cow language when she was four. It was hers now. It had always been hers.

She had not said this to anyone in the farmhouse. She had walked through this house for eight months with the language in her and had not brought it into the same room as her father's language, as if they were two things that should be kept separate, as if the fence that kept Karl in the paddock also ran through the kitchen. By mid-January she recognized this as a kind of cowardice she had dressed in the wrong name. She had been calling it caution. It was not caution.

---

On a Thursday evening in late January she came in from the barn and stopped in the mudroom. She still had her coat on. The lantern was in her left hand. Outside the mudroom window the cold was absolute, the temperature well below what it had been when she went out, the sky clear and indifferent. She had not planned Thursday. Thursday had simply arrived at the end of enough other Thursdays.

The kitchen was lit by the overhead and the stove's firebox glow. Her father was at the table. Not beside the radio — the radio was on the counter, its dial barely amber, turned so low it was barely registering, just the habit of having it on that he had not fully let go since December. He was sitting with both hands around his coffee cup. He was looking at the table's grain. She had seen this posture many times in the last year: turned inward toward whatever country existed behind his eyes. Not empty. He was never empty. Somewhere.

Her mother was at the far end of the table with her darning. The sock on the needle was Lonzo Reed's — she had been mending the farm socks since November when Lonzo held out a heel with a hole in it and Magda had taken it from him and nodded. The darning gave her hands something. Hannah thought of it as that, and perhaps her mother did too.

Hannah set the lantern on its peg. She came into the kitchen. She sat down across from her father.

She said, in German — his German, the Bavarian she had grown up hearing through the floor and at the supper table and in the barn when she was close enough to catch it: Papa. Ich muss dir was sagen.

Her father looked up.

He had not heard her speak German to him — deliberately, directly, aimed at him across a table — since before the war. Since she was fourteen at the oldest and it was still the house's ordinary language, before the ordinary had ended. He looked up and his face was the face she had been learning to read. She thought she was closer to it now than she had ever been, which was different from having it fully.

He said: Dann sag es.

She said: she knew about him and Karl. The window. The evenings. That Karl was from fifty kilometers from where he was born, that she knew that and had known it, and that she knew it was not nothing. She said: I speak German now. Not the words I grew up with. I speak it. I have been speaking it for eight months and I was afraid to say so to you, and I'm not afraid anymore.

He was quiet.

She let him be quiet. The stove worked. At the far end of the table her mother went on with the sock, the needle moving in the same small arc, steady. The clock on the shelf above the icebox ticked through the room — the clock with the white face and the brass pendulum that her father wound every Sunday morning the same time as the barn, the first task of the week. She could hear it clearly now.

He said, in German, more slowly than his German usually moved, as if he were finding each word before he let it into the sentence: Du hast das von mir.

She said: Ja.

He said: Ich weiß das.

A pause. She had learned, in three years of this house, that some pauses were meant to be filled and some were themselves the conversation — the space the other person needed to breathe in. She held this one.

Then, quietly — in English, the language he had not spoken to her, not once, not even in passing, in more than two years — he said: "Hannah."

Just her name.

Her mother did not look up from the darning. But her hands were still.

---

Hannah went to bed.

She lay in the dark and the farm settled around her the way it settled in deep winter: the boards in the cold, the cows in the barn making the low sustained sound they made at night, the clock sending its voice through two walls and a ceiling. She had been falling asleep in this room her whole life and had never heard the clock so clearly, and she could not say why tonight was different except that it was.

She did not know what her father's name in English meant. She knew too many things it might mean, and too many things it couldn't mean, and she could not sort the combinations in a single night. She did not try very hard. She was eighteen and tired from the barn and from what she had done at the kitchen table, and the tiredness was not unpleasant.

She knew this: he had said it. He had found the language he had set down two years ago and picked it back up long enough to say her name. He had not offered a reason or a gesture toward reason. He had not announced what he was doing or explained the doing of it. He had just said her name, in English, at the kitchen table in January, and the English was real — not a slip, not something that slipped out — real and deliberate and directed at her specifically, which was the person it had always been for.

She thought about the word zuhause.

She had been trying for years to know what it meant in this house. Her father's German and her mother's silence and Karl through the icehouse window speaking to her father in the register of a young man learning from an older one, and the school German that was Hochdeutsch when she expected Bavarian, and the barn German that was in between, and the language at the fence with Karl that had gradually stopped being between anything and started being its own thing. She had been looking for the word that covered all of it and finding that no single word did, that what fit Bavaria didn't fit Maine and what fit Maine didn't fit the kitchen in the evenings when everything was German and she was standing at the edge of it.

Tonight it meant the kitchen in January. The stove's glow. The clock that her father wound every Sunday and which kept time the way it kept time, neither fast nor slow, steady. Her mother's hands going still over the sock. Her father at the table, both hands around his coffee, looking up at her with the face she was learning to read — and then the English word, her name, the one he had always known and had just now said again.

Zuhause.

She went to sleep.

input.content:
# The Addendum

The February log ran clean for seventeen days before anything happened worth noting, and even then what happened was routine: a dock cleat worked loose in the fourteenth's blow, and she spent an afternoon rethreading it through gusts that averaged thirty-eight knots and peaked at forty-one. That went in the log. Tide, barometer, wind direction — those went in every morning. The harbor radio gave her the European news at low volume and she let it run. The Third Army was at the Rhine. The Russians had crossed the Oder in force. She was aware of these things the way she was aware of the tide schedule: as facts she needed to know and that shaped what she could expect, not as events she was experiencing from the inside.

The inner cove had been locked under ice since mid-January. Two lobster boats were still working the outer bar — the *Maisie K.* and Farber's *June M.* — and they came to the dock every third day or so to unload and ice down, and she wrote their arrivals and departures in the log, and they went back out again, and the cove stayed still and gray-white under the overcast that had been sitting over the coast for most of the month. The mail boat came Tuesdays and Fridays. She was at the dock to log it and to take the harbor's share of the freight, which in February was modest.

The middle drawer was locked. The key was on the ring above the door, where it always was.

She had known since December what she was going to do. Not in the way of a decision — she had not sat down and decided. It had come in the way things come when they are correct: over a succession of ordinary mornings, arriving in segments, settling into place without ceremony. By January it was there, occupying the same part of her thinking as the seam she needed to re-pitch on the float's east fender plank: a thing that would be done. The ice-out came the same way. You did not wait for a moment. You felt the particular quality of the late-winter light and you looked at the cove, still as a plate of glass, and you understood that it was the last state, not the permanent one. You wrote the ice-over in the log and you got on with the work.

On a Wednesday morning in late February, the tide in from the southeast, the barometer holding at 30.2, the harbor with nothing on it that needed her right then, she got out the harbormaster's stationery.

---

The form was pale green stock, the port seal in the upper left corner. The heading lines were set for date, subject, and reference. She dated it February 28, 1945. She wrote *Supplementary Statement — Addendum to Record, Re: Incident of 12 October 1943* on the subject line and the reference to Lieutenant Ennis and the First District file below it. Then she wrote the body.

She did not draft it first. She had known what it would say since sometime in December. She wrote it once, in the harbormaster's hand she had been using in this office for nine years — the hand that was hers now in a way it had started out not being; she had consciously copied Owen's script in the first months, believing consistency in the log mattered enough to justify it, and had only gradually stopped.

---

*Supplementary Statement — Addendum to Record*
*Re: Incident of 12 October 1943, Coldwater Reach, Maine*
*Reference: Statement of 12 October 1943, USCG First District, Portland — Lt. R. Ennis, case officer*

*I, Eira J. Bowman, Harbormaster, Port of Coldwater Reach, Maine, submit the following supplementary material in addition to my statement of October 12, 1943, filed with the United States Coast Guard, First District, Portland.*

*On the night of October 11, 1943, at approximately 23:00 hours, I was present at the Coldwater Reach dock performing routine inspection of the F/V* Callie B. *(owner: R. Farber), moored at the second slip. During this inspection, I observed a small wooden motorboat, running without navigation lights, approach from the south and tie at the dock's eastern end, near the breakwater access. I observed a single occupant — male, of approximately middle age — who left the vessel on foot and proceeded in the direction of the breakwater. I did not engage with the individual. I observed him for less than one minute. I was unable to identify the individual or to determine the vessel's name or registration.*

*When I returned to the dock the following morning, October 12, 1943, the vessel was absent.*

*I did not include this observation in my statement of October 12, 1943, to Lieutenant R. Ennis. My reason for the omission: I judged the observation insufficiently documented and the identification of the individual uncertain.*

*I submit this account now as supplementary material to the above-referenced case file, for the record.*

*Eira J. Bowman*
*Harbormaster, Port of Coldwater Reach*
*February 28, 1945*

---

She set down the pen. She read it over once, from the heading to her name. Nothing to change.

The reason she had given for the omission was true. The observation had been at a distance, in the dark, for less than a minute. She had not been able to see his face. She had not known the man's name and did not know it now. She had judged it insufficiently documented and she had been right. These things were true. They were not everything. The official record would hold what it could hold.

---

The Yarmouth reply took less time. She had been composing it, off and on, for months. She wrote it to the Harbour Authority at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, in response to their inquiry dated March 19, 1944 — filed in the back of the middle drawer for eleven months. She directed them to the USCG First District case file in Portland, Maine, under the October 12, 1943 incident at Coldwater Reach. She noted that supplementary material bearing on the inquiry had been submitted to the same file that morning, February 28, 1945. She did not speculate about what the material might indicate. She did not name anyone.

She signed it, dated it February 28, 1945, and addressed the envelope.

Both documents went into a manila folder. She wrote the date on the tab and set it on the corner of the desk.

---

She put on Owen's peacoat and her hat and went up the hill.

It was a cold morning, overcast, temperature in the low twenties with no wind to speak of. The road from the dock to the main street was glazed from the overnight freeze, and she took the pace she always took on ice — heels down, weight back, steps shorter than usual. She had learned this pace from Owen, or from watching him; she had learned a great many physical habits in this job from watching him, and they had worn into her in the years since until she could not have said which were copied and which were simply hers. The hardware store was open. The diner's windows were fogged from the breakfast crowd, and from inside came the particular radio-noise of a morning when someone had turned it up louder than the room required. She passed both without stopping. Nine minutes to the auxiliary station.

The Coast Guard auxiliary station sat above the main street on a short rise, set back behind a parking apron with a flagpole. The flag was up and moving slightly in what wind there was off the harbor. She had been here four times in her eight-plus years as harbormaster: twice with emergency weather reports during the bad winters, once in her first year to register the dock's navigation-light upgrade under the blackout protocol, and once in November 1943, ten days after the October inquiry was closed, when she had come to give her formal statement to Ennis's district clerk. She had been here that time and said what she had said and signed where they told her to sign and come back down the hill and written the day's weather in the log. The visit was in the log as a notation. Everything was in the log.

The petty officer on duty was a young man she had seen twice but didn't know well — Kerrigan, she thought, transferred down from Bath in September. He was at the counter when she came in, working through a maintenance form, and he looked up.

She said she had documents to submit for forwarding to the First District office in Portland, relating to the October 1943 incident at Coldwater Reach.

He set down the form and held out a hand for the folder.

He opened it and read both documents through, working at a steady rate, starting with the addendum and then moving to the Yarmouth reply. She stood at the counter and waited. The station had a coal stove in the near corner and she felt the warmth of it through the peacoat after the cold outside. The harbor radio was running in the back room on the same frequency she kept the shack radio, and the correspondents were giving the morning news at higher volume, and it was the same news she'd had at low volume in the shack, which meant the same news had followed her up the hill and was now in the room with her.

He said he would log the receipt and forward both documents to Portland with the district courier. The addendum would go to the existing case file under the October 1943 incident reference number. The Yarmouth reply would go with it as associated correspondence. He gave her the copies — one each — and wrote the log entry. She watched him write it. He had small, neat handwriting, the kind that gets used to forms.

He pushed the copies across the counter. She folded them once and put them in her inside coat pocket.

He asked if there was anything else.

She said: has anything come in on the October 1943 inquiry. From the First District, or from anywhere. Any response on record.

He went to the logbooks behind the counter. He pulled 1944 and ran a finger down the index, turned to October, went through it. He turned forward to November and December. He pulled 1943 and worked backwards from December. Then he set both books back in place.

Nothing in the record from Portland, he said. No response on record from any source.

She said: thank you. She buttoned the coat and went back out into the cold.

---

She went down the hill at the same pace she had come up. The road still glazed. The diner windows still fogged. The harbor was where she had left it.

She went into the shack and sat down at the desk.

The manila folder was gone from the corner. That was how it felt — not lighter in the room, just accurate, the way a room feels when a thing that should not be on the desk is no longer on the desk. The middle drawer was still there. She sat for a moment and looked at the harbor through the window without opening it.

The breakwater ran out to its fixed red light. The inner cove was still locked, same as this morning, the same as yesterday and the day before. A single herring gull was working the water off the end of the dock float, circling and dipping and circling again, its pattern unchanged by what had or hadn't been submitted to the Coast Guard auxiliary station twenty minutes ago.

The Yarmouth letter was gone from the drawer. The addendum was filed. What remained: the wallet, still wrapped in Farber's tarp in the back of the middle section. And inside the wallet, compressed between the seam and the stiff fold of card stock, the partial script that Marcus Klein had read under the lamp in January and returned to her before eight o'clock the following morning, carrying it up the hill in his briefcase in the cold. She had put it back in the wallet and put the wallet back in the drawer and locked the drawer and said nothing to anyone.

She had not submitted these objects because they were physical property — they belonged to the dead man or to his estate, such as it was, wherever it was — and they belonged in the official file, and she was not ready to give them up.

She was not sure why. Not exactly.

She put the submission copies in the front section of the drawer's ordinary papers and locked the drawer again and hung the key on the ring on the nail above the door. The ring was heavier than it needed to be — four keys on it, the drawer key and the dock locker and the supply cabinet and the shack's main door, and she had never taken any of them off because the ring had been that way since Owen had it and it had stayed that way.

The harbor was outside the window. Late February. The overcast sat flat and high over the cove. Somewhere off the breakwater's east face the number-four bell buoy was ringing in the long swell — its clapper worn, the tone a half-step flat from its rated note, a thing she had stopped noticing years ago except when she made herself notice it. She had logged it three times for service and service had been twice deferred and the buoy was still half a step flat and it rang in the swell the same as always.

She did not feel better. She did not feel worse. What she felt — if it was a feeling and not simply a state — was something she did not try to name. It was in the category of: done. The thing that was to be done had been done. From where she stood, in this office, with the information she had been carrying for sixteen months, she had done what she could do. This was not the same as having done everything, and it was not the same as having done nothing, and it occupied a place she had been in before, when she had made a decision she could not unmake and then lived inside the consequences of it and found the consequences livable. She knew that place. She had been harbormaster long enough to know that place well.

The harbor did not need the rest of it.

---

She opened the log and wrote the day's conditions.

*Feb. 28. Overcast. Temp. 22°F at 0800, rising slowly. Wind NW at 8 kts. Barometer 30.2, steady. Tide: high 0643, low 1301. Inner cove: ice holds. No arrivals. Buoy no. 4 clapper: third request for service, log this date.*

Below the weather entry, in the same column and the same hand and the same black ink:

*Supplementary statement re: incident of 12 October 1943 submitted this date to USCG Aux. Station, Coldwater Reach, for forwarding to First District, Portland. Concurrent reply to Yarmouth NS inquiry (received April 1944) submitted. Copies held.*

She closed the log. She was still harbormaster. The harbor was there outside the window. She went back to work.

input.text:
Supplementary Statement — Addendum to Record
Re: Incident of 12 October 1943, Coldwater Reach, Maine
Reference: Statement of 12 October 1943, USCG First District, Portland — Lt. R. Ennis, case officer

I, Eira J. Bowman, Harbormaster, Port of Coldwater Reach, Maine, submit the following supplementary material in addition to my statement of October 12, 1943, filed with the United States Coast Guard, First District, Portland.

On the night of October 11, 1943, at approximately 23:00 hours, I was present at the Coldwater Reach dock performing routine inspection of the F/V Callie B. (owner: R. Farber), moored at the second slip. During this inspection, I observed a small wooden motorboat, running without navigation lights, approach from the south and tie at the dock's eastern end, near the breakwater access. I observed a single occupant — male, of approximately middle age — who left the vessel on foot and proceeded in the direction of the breakwater. I did not engage with the individual. I observed him for less than one minute. I was unable to identify the individual or to determine the vessel's name or registration.

When I returned to the dock the following morning, October 12, 1943, the vessel was absent.

I did not include this observation in my statement of October 12, 1943, to Lieutenant R. Ennis. My reason for the omission: I judged the observation insufficiently documented and the identification of the individual uncertain.

I submit this account now as supplementary material to the above-referenced case file, for the record.

Eira J. Bowman
Harbormaster, Port of Coldwater Reach
February 28, 1945

input.content:
# March

The frost went out of the ground in stages, which meant the farm got worse before it got better. The barn lane turned to mud first — knee-deep over frozen sub-soil, the upper layer thawing while the ground beneath stayed hard. You came back from the morning milking with your boots caked to the calf and the cows' hooves thick with it and the whole yard smelling of what came up when the earth loosened. The fence posts heaved. They did this every year, the same posts in the same corners, lifted half an inch or more out of true by the freeze and what came after it. She knocked them back down with the mallet and drove new staples into the wire and they would heave again the following year. That was mud season. It had been mud season before she could name it and it would be mud season after.

The east pasture wall had pushed out a corner stone that her father reset on a March morning before anyone was up. She found it back in place when she came out for the milking — the mud around the base still disturbed, the stone sitting level the way it had sat for twenty years. She did not mention it to him and he would not have said anything either. He was out there in the dark yard before the milking, and that was enough to know.

The radio ran most mornings. It had run through the whole war, kitchen radio and then the parlor radio too during the worst of the Bulge, but the way her father sat with it had changed. She had noticed this over the last few weeks without being able to say exactly when it shifted. Through the Bulge he had sat at the radio the way you sit at a thing you cannot put down and cannot bear to hold. Now he sat the way you sit beside something you have decided to witness. In early March — a Tuesday, she was in the middle of the milking — she had heard through the window he had cracked despite the cold that the Third Army had crossed the Rhine at Remagen, and she had understood without needing him to tell her what it meant. The end was approaching. Not here. Somewhere behind all the silence the war had made.

Some evenings he sat for the German-language broadcast. He sat for it the way he would sit for a letter from a person he had given up expecting a letter from.

The icehouse had been occupied since April 1943. Twenty-three months, now in its twenty-fourth. She had stopped counting somewhere in the fall.

Lonzo Reed had come out on a Thursday with papers from Camp Houlton — the directive from the War Department about the repatriation process, forwarded through the duty officer at the primary facility. She had watched him explain it to her father in the yard: Lonzo with his sheaf of forms, using the patient over-loud English he used when he thought he was being understood, her father nodding slowly with no expression. After Lonzo left her father stood in the yard for a moment and looked at the icehouse and then at the barn and then at the house. Then he went inside. She had the milk pails to scrub and she went back to them.

She knew what the papers said. When Germany surrendered, the satellite details would reassemble at Camp Houlton for processing and then be staged for transport back to Germany in phases. Timing unspecified. Weeks, maybe. Not months.

The end of this arrangement — which had become ordinary in the way that extraordinary things become ordinary when you live inside them long enough — was now approaching with an end date no one could name but everyone on the farm could feel.

---

Lonzo Reed's obligations to the war effort were, on Saturdays, his own business. He came at eight-thirty with the four of them for the barn work, and he was present and responsible through the first hour and a half, and then by mid-morning his presence became theoretical. The equipment shed. The supply room behind the icehouse. The kitchen, where her mother fed him bread without conversation. Wherever his Saturday attention required him, it required him somewhere other than where the prisoners were, because he had learned over twenty-three months that Karl and the others were not going anywhere, and because the end of the war was visible enough from where he stood that his boots and his Springfield rifle had adopted the posture of conclusion.

Hannah was alone at the north-pasture fence with the mallet and a coffee can of staples and the wire stretcher. The second post in from the corner. It had heaved last November and last February and now it had heaved again — the same six-inch lift, the same wire gone slack between it and its neighbor, the same ground doing what ground does, which is push up what it has not quite decided to accept as permanent.

She had knocked it back down and was setting the first staple when she heard him.

"Du weißt, dass wir gehen."

Not a question.

She set the staple first. Two strokes of the mallet, the wire seated, and then she straightened and looked at him across the fence.

He was standing on the pasture side with his hands in his coat pockets, not close to the wire, not leaning on it. The same wool coat he had come in with, re-stitched at the collar where it had separated sometime in the second winter. He had been nineteen when he arrived. He was twenty now. She could see it — something settled in the way he held himself that had not been there at the start, or maybe it was just that she had learned how to read his face and what she was seeing was simply familiar.

She said: "Ich hab's gehört."

He nodded. He said: a month, maybe. Maybe two. No one knows the exact date. But it's coming.

She turned back to the fence. She worked the wire stretcher on the next section and felt the wire tighten against the cold wood. Behind him across the field the icehouse was visible — the south corner, the stovepipe, the thin column of woodsmoke that bent east in the wind off the pasture. She moved her hands along the wire to the next staple position.

He crossed to the fence and picked up the piece of fencing wire she had set down on the post rail and held it against the staple position, without her asking him to.

She looked at his hands on the wire. She looked at the post.

She said: "Hast du Angst zurückzugehen?"

He was quiet for a while. Long enough that she drove the staple and moved to the next section before he answered. The field behind him was still brown from winter, the grass flat and pale, the mud season not yet reached here at the pasture's edge where the drainage was better.

He said: I don't know what I'm going back to.

She said: you know what you're going back to. She caught her own English and left it.

He said: a village and a farm and my mother. Yes. He said it the way you say a thing you have tested many times and found accurate and still insufficient. And then: but not what the village is now. Not what the country is now. I was — he stopped. He started again. I was nineteen twenty-three months ago. I'm twenty now. He stopped there.

She waited. He didn't continue.

She moved to the next staple position and he moved the wire with her, holding it against the post, his hands on one side of the fence, her hands on the other.

She said: "Wir sind noch hier."

He said: "Du bist."

They worked the last stretch without talking. She set the staples and he held the wire and she drove each one home. Two strokes, clean. The same motion — the wire against the post, her hand with the mallet — but she did not point that out and she did not look at his face to see whether he had noticed it. She watched the work and thought about nothing in particular and the cold was in her hands and it was March and he was leaving.

Then Lonzo came around the icehouse corner with his collar turned up, heading toward the barn, and he saw them at the fence and nodded the nod he used for everything he had decided to accept without comment. Karl stepped back from the wire.

She said: "Auf Wiedersehen."

He said: "Ja." And then he walked back across the brown field and met Lonzo at the barn door and that was that.

She picked up the coffee can and the wire stretcher and the mallet and carried them back toward the barn.

---

That evening her mother went to bed at eight, the same as most evenings since October. Her father sat with the kitchen radio until past nine, the volume low enough that she could not hear the words from the table, only the shape of the broadcast — the rhythm and register of German, the particular cadence of a voice reading prepared text in that language in 1945. Then he turned it off and set it back on the shelf and went upstairs. The house around her went quiet in the way a farmhouse in March goes quiet: the barn settling, the cows moving in their sleep, the wind off the east field, and the stove ticking as it cooled.

Hannah was at the kitchen table with her school notebook. She had carried it down thinking she would get through the Latin — three weeks of declension exercises she had been meaning to do since January — but instead she opened it to the Whitman annotation section, which was where she kept the work that was not Latin.

Between the last annotation page and the notebook's back cover. Folded in thirds. She had put it there in February of the previous year.

She took it out and set it on the table. She did not unfold it right away. She looked at the kitchen instead: the clock above the stove, the shelf where the radio had been until her father moved it toward the table and then moved it back again, the jar of wooden spoons her mother had placed in the empty space. The hanging lamp put a circle of warm light over the table and the notebook. Outside the window, the yard was dark.

She unfolded the letter.

The paper had changed from being held often — not worn through, just altered at the creases, the fold lines soft now in a way they had not been when she found it in the hay in February 1944. Fourteen months ago. The paper had taken on the quality of something carried, something kept rather than stored. She smoothed it against the table.

The handwriting ran in close lines. She had looked at it often enough to know its shapes: the way the G opened at the top, the r that crossed almost into an n, the period pressed hard into the paper at each sentence's end, as if to make the finality felt.

*die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.*

She read it. Those words on that paper in this kitchen with the stove going cool. The phrase was the same phrase it had always been. Marcus had given her what it said in English, in January of last year, and she had known most of it before then — her father's German at the supper table had been reaching her for seventeen years. Those who tried to go are gone. We pray for them.

She had held this letter for fourteen months. She had taken it from the hay by accident and then continued taking it by choice, which was a different thing — she had known that much in February 1944 and she knew it now. She had told Marcus she had it. She had not told her father. She had not told Karl.

But Karl was going. A month, maybe. Two.

She was going to give it back to him before the truck came. She had not known until tonight, sitting here with the letter on the table, that this was already the decision — she had thought, in the way you think when you are not quite ready to think clearly about something, that she was still in the process of deciding. She had been wrong about that. The decision was already made. It had been made somewhere in the fence field that afternoon, or maybe weeks before that, and she was only now arriving at it.

She didn't know what she would say when she handed it to him. She would find out. Maybe she would say only: this is yours. She thought that might be the right amount.

She folded the letter along its old lines — the paper fell into them without resistance — and put it back between the annotation pages and closed the notebook.

The clock ticked. The stove had gone cold enough to bank for the night. She should get up and do that. She sat for a moment longer.

Outside the window: the yard, the barn's dark shape, and past the barn's near edge the icehouse roof — just the south corner visible from where she sat, if she leaned toward the glass. She did not get up to look. She stayed at the table and the icehouse was across the yard and the lights were out in there already and Karl's last weeks here were finite and she had something that belonged to him and she was going to give it back.

She didn't know when.

She knew she would.

He enumerates — a village, a farm, his mother — then admits not what the village is now, not what the country is now; he was nineteen twenty-three months ago, he's twenty now, and he doesn't know what that means for home. She says Wir sind noch hier. He says Du bist. Karl holds the fence wire while Hannah drives the staple — a motion echoing their first fence exchange in December 1943. When Lonzo reappears, Karl returns to the work detail. Parting: Auf Wiedersehen. Ja. (3) That night. Her father listens to the German-language broadcast until past nine, then goes upstairs. She unfolds it and reads the phrase: die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie. She understands now, with Karl's departure finitely approaching, that she has already decided to return it before the truck comes. She folds it back, closes the notebook, sits with the lamp and the dark yard and the icehouse — lights already out — and the chapter closes on the unfinished action and its approaching deadline.

# April

The paper came in the school's Wednesday mail. He picked it up from the front office table on his way through — the Rockland Courier, folded once lengthwise as the secretary always left it — and tucked it under his arm. The announcement had already come through the school hallway's radio by nine that morning. He had been at the corridor's edge, between his classroom and the Latin room, when the broadcast ran through. He had stood and listened to the announcer's careful American voice for three or four minutes and then he had walked into his classroom and written *prima declinatio* on the board and taught the lesson.

He carried the paper home under his arm and set it on the desk without opening it.

He graded the Latin exercises. He did this with the paper beside the exercise books, visible but unread, and one part of his mind went through the work — the genitive plural errors, the margin notes, which of the three students had understood the principle and which had guessed correctly without understanding it — and the other part of his mind was somewhere he declined to follow it. He put the exercise books in the pile for morning and set down the pen.

He went downstairs. Lillian had left food in the kitchen. He ate at the small table alone — Henry was still at the school, something with the boiler — and when Henry came in, washing his hands at the sink, they exchanged two or three sentences about the cold for April and then Henry heated what was in the pot and sat down, and they finished the evening together without talking further. This was not unusual. Marcus had stopped noticing it as an accommodation sometime around the second winter, which he understood, when he noticed the stopping, for what it was.

He went upstairs.

He turned on the lamp and sat down at the desk. The Rockland Courier was where he had set it. He picked it up and opened it to the front page. He read the headline and the first three paragraphs of the dispatch. He turned to page two. He looked at page two. He turned to page three.

There were photographs on page three.

He looked at the photographs for perhaps four seconds before he folded the paper closed. He set it face-down on the desk. He sat in the chair for a moment with his hands in his lap.

He had known. This was the thing that required sitting with, in this room, in this chair: he had known. Not in the way of the photographs — not with that specificity, not at that scale, not in the form of the specific architecture the photographs were now showing — but in the form available to a man who had watched Vienna change in 1937 and 1938 and then left it. He had understood the direction. He had followed the logic as far as it went before he chose to stop following it, because the thing you construct in your mind when you follow that logic to its conclusion is a thing you cannot allow to be true, and so you manage the logic at a certain distance, you hold it in the form of structure rather than completion, the way you can know the shape of a building from its foundation plan without having to stand inside it.

The photographs were inside it.

He did not open the paper again.

He thought about the people he knew. Not as a category — specifically, in the way a man thinks about the specific texture of specific encounters across seventeen years in a Viennese academic institution and two years in Paris. Jakob R., who had been his closest colleague in the philology department, who had a particular habit in seminar of beginning his disagreements with a question rather than a rebuttal — arms crossed, leaning back, the question arriving before he had finished forming it — a habit Marcus could still reproduce exactly if he was working to fall asleep and needed something to hold in his mind. They had exchanged letters in 1939, three in 1940, and then the letters stopped. The last one, in November of 1940, had carried a Berlin address. Marcus had not written to a Berlin address after 1941. He had arranged the reasons for this in a form that did not require him to name them.

Grete H., who had been his department's German-language assistant for seven years, whose administrative precision he had depended on in the way one depends on a function that works correctly without one's attention, and who had been in Vienna in 1938 when he left it, and from whom he had received nothing since. He had asked once through the Emergency Committee, in late 1942, and received a letter that said the committee had no current documentation for that name. He had understood, at the time, what current documentation meant, and he had done what he always did with the things he understood in this way, which was to hold them in the form of probably but not confirmed, which was the form available to him, and move on to the next thing that required moving on to.

Two others — names he permitted himself in his mind without writing them anywhere — whose last known addresses had been in Paris in 1940. He had not found them through the Emergency Committee's Paris contacts, who were themselves mostly gone from Paris by the time he was writing letters in 1942 and 1943. He had not let himself complete a thought about them in over two years. He let himself complete one now, briefly, sitting at the desk in the April dark with the folded paper in front of him, and the thought arrived at a conclusion that the photographs supported.

Then he thought about Felix K.

This had a different quality. He had been thinking about Felix K. since January — since the Thursday evening he came back from the harbormaster's shack and spent two hours in this room with the Feld letter and a sheet of working paper before he opened the German notebook and wrote the entry — in a specific register of probability that was not certainty and was not the same as comfort and was not the same as what he was now sitting with about Jakob R. and Grete H. and the others.

Felix K. had tried to go. That was what the evidence said. He had been documented in Yarmouth in September of 1943, heading south by sea, and the sea had brought him as far as Coldwater, and there he had run out of road.

He had not been in one of the camps.

Marcus turned this over in his mind. He had turned it over before — in January, after he assembled the theory, and in February, and in March, on evenings when the European news on the school hallway radio made the structure more visible — and he had not arrived at an answer, and he did not arrive at one now. There was a line of reasoning that said: he died in the Atlantic coast dark, in October, alone in an unlighted boat in cold water, and that was its own fact. There was no architecture behind it, no system, no list on which his name would appear. He had died in the specific and local way, which was the way of weather and the harbor and chance, and no one had done it to him, or it had been done to him by the full weight of what Europe had become for people who needed to leave it and ran out of time, which was a different thing from the same thing, and Marcus had not resolved this distinction and suspected he would not.

He went, Marcus thought. He tried.

After a while he picked up the newspaper and took it downstairs.

---

Henry and Lillian were in the parlor. The Zenith console was on — the same cabinet, the same chairs they had sat in on the evening of June 6 last year when the D-Day news came through and Marcus had translated BBC fragments in a low voice and afterward on the back-street porch neither of them had spoken for twenty minutes. Tonight no translation was needed or useful. The Zenith was carrying the same American voice, or another American voice with the same quality: the calibrated evenness of a man delivering copy that was not written to be delivered, because no one had written this kind of copy before. Lillian had her knitting in her lap. Her hands were very still.

Marcus set the newspaper on the sofa cushion beside him, face-down, and sat.

The Zenith was reporting on Bergen-Belsen tonight. The correspondent described, in the careful language of a wire dispatch, what British soldiers had found at the camp when they arrived. He read numbers. He described the camp's geography — the compound, the structures, the numbers of people found alive and the numbers not. The language grew more careful the more specific it became, in the way of a man who has been asked to describe something he does not have words for and is constructing the words as he goes, with insufficient material.

Marcus listened. He had been in the structure of this knowledge for seven years — since Vienna, since the winter of 1937 when the first changes were visible in the institution and in the streets — and now the structure had a form that the language could reach, barely, in insufficient words read by a correspondent in a careful voice on the Zenith in the Crow house parlor. He sat on the sofa and did not move.

He did not translate. He had enough English for this. He had enough of every language he possessed for this. Language was not the problem tonight.

After a while — he had stopped tracking time — Lillian said, quietly: "I'm going to bed."

She set her knitting in the basket beside the chair and stood. Before she went she looked at Marcus once, and in that look was something she was measuring against something else, deciding not to try to name. He met her eyes and nodded slightly. She went upstairs. Her footsteps crossed the ceiling above their heads and then stopped.

Henry was in his chair. Marcus was on the sofa.

The Zenith was still on.

---

Henry said: "Is there anyone you're trying to find out about?"

Marcus said: "Several. I don't know how to find out."

Henry said: "There will be lists."

Marcus said: "Yes."

Henry said: "That will take time."

Marcus said: "Yes."

They sat with the Zenith. The broadcast moved from the correspondent's copy to a recorded voice — a soldier, one of the soldiers who had been among the first to enter the camp — describing what he had seen. His voice was not calibrated. It started and found its direction and then lost it and started again. Marcus listened to the difficulty of what the soldier was doing — assembling, in real time, in front of a microphone, a language for something that no language had been built to describe in advance — and understood this from the other direction, because he had been working at this problem from the other direction since 1938. There was no adequate vocabulary. You used the words that existed and they were not sufficient and you kept going.

Henry got up at some point and went to the kitchen. He came back with two cups of coffee, set one down on the low table beside the sofa, and resumed his chair without anything being said. The Crow house coffee was better than anything else available in Coldwater, which Marcus had thought about at various points over three years without ever having remarked on it. He held the cup in both hands. The warmth was specific and useful.

The front-hall clock struck eleven.

Henry reached over and turned the volume down — not off, only down to the register where the Zenith voices were present in the room without demanding it. A small adjustment. He made it without looking at Marcus, who was looking at the floor in front of the sofa.

The clock struck twelve.

Henry stood. He said: "I'll be up."

Marcus said: "I know."

Henry went to the stairs. The third step from the top creaked, the same as it always did — that step in that house in that particular way, which Marcus had known for three years, the same as he knew the specific frequency of the harbor bell on foggy mornings and the boiler's low cycle at the school. Henry's footsteps crossed the upper floor and stopped.

Marcus turned off the Zenith. He sat for a moment in the quiet with the newspaper still face-down on the cushion beside him. Then he picked it up and went upstairs.

---

The lamp on. He pulled the chain and the light came on over the desk, the east window black above it, and he sat down.

The German notebook was on the shelf above the desk, between the English journal and the grammar workbook, the spine written in his English hand. He had last opened it in January — the Thursday evening he came back from the harbormaster's shack, the evening of the fragment and what the fragment said about the letters, the probable name. He had spent two hours working out the arithmetic on a separate sheet first and then he had transcribed the conclusion into the notebook because the notebook was where he kept things that needed to remain true when he looked at them again.

He took it down.

He opened it to the last page of writing. The January entry was there, in his German handwriting, which was not as clear as it had been. His English handwriting had become better than his German handwriting without his having done anything to cause this, which still surprised him when he noticed it, because the tools of his formation were not supposed to rearrange themselves without his knowledge.

*Fe—?—x. Felix K. Yarmouth, September 1943. Coldwater, Oktober 1943. Innenbar, Dezember 1944 geborgen.*

He read it.

He took his pen from the desk tray. He uncapped it.

Below the entry, on the next line, he wrote:

*Die die versucht haben zu gehen.*

He capped the pen. He closed the notebook. He set it back on the shelf.

---

He turned off the lamp.

The room in the dark was the same room it had been in every darkness for thirty-eight months: the east window a shade less dark than the walls surrounding it, the desk a shape he knew, the radiator on the south wall quiet for the night, the slanted ceiling on the north wall where the roofline came down to the plaster. He had arrived in this room in March of 1942 with a cardboard case, two books, and a suit with the shoulders gone loose from a year of ill fitting. He had sat at this desk and looked out this east window in August of that year and in November and in the first winter and in the winter after that and in the spring and the summer and the autumn that followed, through the mornings when Lillian knocked twice on the door frame and through the evenings when Henry's footsteps went past his door and the third step from the top announced him going to bed.

He did not open the shortwave.

He thought, briefly, about what the Europe across the east window consisted of now: what would be in it, who might be in it, what the street he had lived on for fourteen years looked like in April 1945. He had not allowed himself this thought often. He allowed it now for two or three minutes, sitting in the chair in the dark, and the thought did not arrive anywhere comforting and it did not arrive anywhere devastating. It arrived somewhere he did not have a word for, which was accurate, because there was no word for the specific state of a person who has held something at a manageable distance for seven years and can no longer hold it at that distance and is not yet sure what the shorter distance requires of him.

He would find out. That was all he had.

The notebook was on the shelf. What he had written in it was what it was.

The harbor was somewhere below the hill to the east, which he knew without seeing it. The ice was out of the inner cove by now. The boats were back on their moorings, the buoys rocking in the April chop, the tide coming in or going out according to its own arithmetic, which had nothing to say about what was happening in Europe and did not need to. He had been in this town for thirty-eight months. He had made it to this room in this house with this specific east-facing window. That was where he was.

He sat in the dark for a while. Then he went to bed.

# Spring Log

The tide gauge read four feet nine inches when she checked it at six forty-five. High water at nine fourteen; the published table had it at five feet two inches and the morning was confirming it. The inner cove was already full.

The lobster boats had been going out since before first light — she had heard the first engine on her walk down from home at quarter past six, one of the Beaumonts or Devereux, running early the way the early-season men did when the weather held. By the time she reached the dock end the channel was busy, the lobster boats moving through in the gray, their running lights off now that it was light enough to read the water. She counted them from the dock end as they cleared the harbor mouth. Seven, with Farber's June M. making the last one out at six fifty-two.

She stood at the dock end a moment before the rest of the morning claimed her. The air off the water in late April had a quality that was not available in any other month — not the salt and cold of October alone, not the freezing fog of January, but something that was both of those with warmth beginning to work through them. Diesel from the morning departures. Herring bait from the bait house where the lobstermen had provisioned since before her time at this dock. Cold water at the beginning of warming. The smell of the harbor coming back to itself from the winter.

Both draggers were running. Seven lobster boats were out. The season was fully open.

She went to the shack and got the log and turned on the NNW channel.

The harbor radio was carrying the European news between the marine traffic. It had been carrying it all week, since the Soviet forces moved through the outskirts of Berlin, since the dispatches had taken on the particular quality she had learned to recognize over four and a half years: the careful evenness of language at the end of something. This morning the correspondent was reporting on the street fighting still going in the German capital, and then, in a slightly different register, on a second report: American and Soviet troops meeting at a river somewhere in Germany, the two armies shaking hands across a bridge in what had been the center of the German state. The river's name came through the static and she caught a syllable of it and lost the rest.

The Beaumont brothers checked in from the outer bar at seven-oh-four — position, conditions, normal traffic. She logged them and responded. Then Devereux's boat, then two more by hull number from the outer bar, then the coast-service check at seven-twenty.

The marine traffic she logged. The European news she did not log.

The two draggers — Lily B. and Mackerel Sky — were both running full season. She could see the Mackerel Sky's boom swung wide as it cleared the harbor mouth at seven-ten; she knew from the empty mooring that the Lily B. had gone out before her morning rounds. Both draggers active. She noted it in the log and set the log aside until the freight manifests came in.

---

The first manifest was the Bangor order: hardware and dry goods on the seven-thirty schooner out of Rockland. She went through the bill of lading crate by crate. Two items short — the same two items from February, the same backlog, the third consecutive month Bangor had not cleared the order. She noted the shortage and pulled a fresh form for the Goulding memo.

The second manifest was fuel oil, direct delivery to the south pier storage tank. She countersigned the driver's paper and stood through the transfer without incident.

The mooring dispute came between the second manifest and the third.

Reg Farber appeared at the shack door at eight forty-five with the two Pelletier brothers directly behind him. All three men came through the door together, which filled the fourteen-foot shack considerably. The dispute was the third float on the east side — the commercial float, held by the two draggers under seasonal assignment from May through October. In the winter layup, when both draggers were pulled, Farber had been mooring the June M. there on Tuesdays for the outside berth because the float was empty and the habit was convenient. The Pelletiers had done the same thing on their own Tuesdays. Two weeks ago they had come in on the same Tuesday, both reaching for the outside mooring, and the collision of dock lines had put a gash in the June M.'s bow rubbing strip, which was the sum of Farber's complaint.

She let both parties say what they needed to say.

Then she opened the dock register to the float assignments and laid it on the counter flat where they could both see it.

The third float listed the Lily B. and the Mackerel Sky under seasonal commercial assignment, May through October, registered at the start of each season. The winter field was blank. The Pelletier boat appeared nowhere in the third float's history. Neither did the June M. Both boats had been mooring there since the winter layup without a registration of any kind, and the only thing that had changed was that both had tried to do it on the same Tuesday.

Farber said he had been there since March.

She asked him to point out in the register where that gave him the assignment.

He stood with his finger on the page for a moment and then took it away.

She assigned the June M. the second float's inside mooring for the season and the Pelletier boat the second float's outside mooring for the season. Both in ink. Both signed and dated. She closed the register. The second float, inside and outside, both boats side by side — which was not what either man had wanted and was the only arrangement that treated both registrations the same way.

Farber started to say something about Tuesday departures.

She told him to work it out with the Pelletiers.

Neither man argued. All three filed out in the order they had come in, and she could hear the conversation continuing on the dock for another minute before it dispersed. Both parties equally inconvenienced. That was the point of it.

She worked through the rest of the morning: the third manifest, the coast-service log update from the buoy tender visit last week, the carryover ledger entries. By eleven she was at the dock when the Heron came in.

Three bags: two mail, one package cargo for Goulding's store. She tallied the bags in the dock log and sent the cargo up the hill with the store runner.

No yellow envelopes in the Tuesday delivery.

She noted this in the margin of the dock log in the same compressed hand she used for the rest of it and went back to the shack.

---

The afternoon quieted early. The Heron was gone by twelve-thirty and the lobster boats would not start coming back until three at the earliest. The shack was warm — the south-facing window taking the April afternoon sun, the stove banked low, the room holding whatever heat the season offered. She worked through the remaining paperwork: the Bangor shortage memo, the second float entries transferred to the seasonal ledger, the Heron's cargo receipt.

At half past two she put down the pen.

Outside the window: the empty floats in the afternoon low, the lobster buoys marking the outer channel, the breakwater running east to where the red fixed light would come on when the evening reached it. It wasn't on yet. She knew where it was.

She had twenty minutes before the four o'clock radio check.

She opened the log ledger to the current date. Then, without precisely planning to, she turned back.

The log ledger she was writing in now had been in use since January of last year — it was the fourth book in the harbor record since 1891, the first three on the shelf above the desk, the oldest book from June of that year in a different hand entirely, the harbor's record before any living harbormaster. She had re-covered the 1935 book two years after she started, when the spine cracked; she had done the 1923 book the year after that. She knew the pages by their weight and their smell. Her thumb found the pages for the fall of 1944, the winter, and then she was through that year and into the 1935 book and she was turning through the autumn and into November before she had decided to.

Owen's handwriting came in at November 1.

His hand had a slight backward lean, the letters large and clear, the ink faded to brown at the older dates but still entirely legible in the afternoon light. He had been a careful log-keeper. She had been his deputy for six years before he died and had read his entries through all of them, and she could still anticipate the shape of each letter before it arrived — the *r* with its small curl at the tip, the *s* that ran slightly compressed, the *barometer* where the final letters crowded a little as if his pen moved faster than his hand.

November 3: fog all day, two vessels anchored overnight in the cove. November 7: mail boat delayed, seas at the outer bar. November 10: barometer 29.8 and falling, wind northwest and freshening. November 11: wind NNW at twenty-two knots, sea state four to five, all vessels secured.

November 12.

*November 12, 1935. Weather deteriorating, wind NNW increasing, barometer 29.1 and falling. Putting out additional mooring lines on —*

The sentence ended mid-line. The pen had come up from the page and not returned. The rest of the November 12 page was blank, and after it the next page in her own hand with a different date — the date she had taken over.

She read it.

She had read it many times. She had read it in the first winter after, when she was still rebuilding the hours around the storm. She had read it in 1939, when the war started in Europe and she had found herself in the shack on a September evening with the log open for no reason she could fully name. She had read it in October 1943, the night before the body came in, sitting at this desk until midnight with a particular quality of attention she would not have called grief and was not sure what else to call.

This time was not those times. She was reading it as someone who had finished what it was in the middle of.

He had stopped mid-entry to go put out the mooring lines. The weather had been moving faster than the barometer showed and he had set down the pen to go do what the weather required. The sentence broke off there because that was the last moment he had been at this desk.

She had finished what he had not. That was what the nine and a half years came to, in the kind of accounting that the log kept.

She closed the November 1935 page. She turned back to April 25, 1945.

---

She wrote the day.

*April 25, 1945. Weather: clear. Temperature 52°F. Wind SE, 6 knots. Barometer 30.2, rising. Visibility: unlimited.*

*Tide: high water 0914, 5 feet 2 inches. Low water expected 1527.*

*Vessels: seven lobster boats out; return expected by 1700. Both draggers active — Lily B., Mackerel Sky. Mail boat Heron, Tuesday arrival 1140, departed 1230. Three freight manifests received and signed: hardware/dry goods, Bangor order, partial, backlog, Goulding notified; fuel oil, south pier; Goulding parcel cargo, received and receipted.*

*Dock register action: seasonal berth resolution, Farber (June M.)–Pelletier, float 3 conflict. Farber assigned float 2 inside, Pelletier assigned float 2 outside. Entered and signed.*

*Mail boat Tuesday notification: none.*

She set the pen down and read it back. There was nothing to change.

She picked up the pen again.

Below the formal entry, in the same compressed exact hand she had been using in this log for nine years:

*Harbor in order. Nine years, five months. All boats accounted for.*

She put the pen down and looked at what she had written.

It was accurate. The harbor had been in order when she arrived at six forty-five and would be in order when she left tonight. Nine years and five months was what the calendar said, from November 1935 to April 1945. All seven lobster boats were registered and out and coming back. Both draggers were registered and running. The Heron was logged. The freight was receipted. The mooring assignments were in ink.

She closed the log.

---

The tide clock: she checked it. Four minutes fast. She had set it Monday and it had gained its four minutes since, which was what it did. She reached up and moved the hand back.

At four o'clock she called the NNW channel. The Beaumont brothers checked in from the outer bar — position and ETA, conditions normal. She logged them. Two more boats checked in before four-fifteen; she logged them both and gave the harbor conditions and signed off.

She banked the stove draft further. She locked the desk drawer. She took Owen's key ring from the nail by the door — four keys, unchanged since Owen had carried them — and used the shack key to lock the door behind her.

The red fixed light on the breakwater was on. She had seen it come on from the window, the first light of the evening, the harbor mouth marked. The lobster boats were coming in; she could hear the engines cutting as they found their moorings in the early dusk. Seven out, seven coming back.

She walked up the hill toward home.
