input.content:
# Komm Rein

The barn in late April was the same barn it had been in every October of the last three years and every month between them: the same smell of hay and cattle and morning damp in the boards, the same gray light through the high eastern windows coming in at an angle that moved six inches across the floor between the first milking and the second, the same sounds of the cows pulling at the water troughs and shifting in the stanchions before full light. Outside it was April, the field mud beginning to firm and the maples at the south bend of the road putting on leaves, but in here it was the same barn it had been in October 1943 when the icehouse was new and the arrangement was new and everything about it was new. Three years and the barn had absorbed all of it into its ordinary sounds. There were four mornings left.

The spring light on the hay in the loft was different from November — not the blue-white of January, not the flat gray of mud season, but a yellow that reached the far wall and made the dust visible in it. The smell of the barn in April was the smell of a winter's enclosure not yet fully aired: the cows inside all winter, the spring cleaning not done, the high windows still latched against the last cold. In another week she would open them properly. In another week the four men would be gone.

The morning routine had been what it always was: the six o'clock milking, the clean-up, the first feeding, the water troughs. She had done these things alongside the four prisoners and Lonzo Reed for thirty months and they had all learned the barn's particular sequence so well that nobody had to say which task came next; you simply arrived at the next thing and did it. This morning was the same, except that it was the last one.

She gave Karl the letter on the morning before the truck was due.

Lonzo Reed stepped outside through the side door for his cigarette at the same point in the early routine he always did — for the cigarette, or because thirty months of the same hours had made one minute out of the barn's particular air necessary. The door shut and she heard his boots on the gravel and then nothing.

She had carried the letter in her coat pocket since March, since Karl told her through the fence that repatriation would begin in weeks. She had known since then what she was going to do with it and had not done it, and now there was one morning left.

She crossed the barn to where Karl was at the far stanchion.

She said: Ich habe das gefunden. In der Scheune. Im Februar, letztes Jahr.

She held out the envelope. He looked at it before he took it — the look you give a thing you had stopped expecting to see again. The paper had gone soft at the crease lines from handling, and the upper left corner where the return address had been was stained pale brown from the hay it had lain in. His mother's name on the front in the postal officer's hand. He took the envelope from her and turned it over once.

He said: Ich hab mich gefragt, wo es hingegangen ist.

She said: Es tut mir leid.

He said: Nein. Without sharpness. As if the apology were the thing he was declining.

He held the envelope a moment without opening it. Then: Du konntest es lesen. Not a question.

She said: Ja.

He nodded once and put the letter in the inside pocket of his jacket, the pocket over his chest, and pressed it flat with his palm.

He said: Deine Mutter — beginning the sentence slowly, feeling for the path through the words. He stopped there.

She said: Wir beten für sie.

He looked at her. His face was the face it had been for thirty months — different from October 1943 in the ways that farm work and two winters make a face different, the jaw steadier, the skin rougher, the eyes accustomed. He said: Ich glaube, es geht ihr gut. Ich hoffe es.

She said: I hope so too.

He turned back to the stanchion. Lonzo's boots sounded on the gravel outside and the side door opened and the barn returned to itself.

---

The truck came at mid-morning. She heard the engine on the road before it turned in through the gate — the camp administration truck from Houlton, olive drab, the same model that had come with supply deliveries occasionally in the past two years. Two camp soldiers got down from the cab without hurry, one carrying a brown folder with the transfer paperwork.

Lonzo Reed was in the yard with his Springfield at his side and his winter coat on, the collar turned up against the April wind — the same coat he had worn all winter, the loose button on the left front still loose the way it had been since January. He walked over and took the folder and read the paperwork the way he read all paperwork: steadily, without hurry, nodding at the relevant parts. He signed with the pencil stub from his shirt pocket and handed the folder back.

The four prisoners came out of the icehouse with their things. There was not much — thirty months had accumulated some quantity of objects for each man but not much: a bag or a folded parcel, some letters, whatever the camp stores had issued over two winters. One of the three men Hannah had never learned to say right carried a folded blanket under his arm. Karl came out third. He had his jacket buttoned, his bag in one hand, and the inside pocket of his jacket lay flat against his chest where the letter was.

When they came out he did not look toward the porch.

Then, once, he did. She looked back. His face did not change and hers did not either, and then his head turned to follow the motion of the tailgate going down, and that was all. The four men loaded into the truck bed. The tailgate went up.

Lonzo shook hands with one of the camp soldiers — brief, two pumps, the handshake of strangers finishing the same piece of work. He stepped back to the yard's edge. The second soldier got in the cab. The engine turned over.

---

She was on the porch. She did not remember going up the steps. Her father was beside her at the railing, both hands around his coffee cup, already there the way he was sometimes simply there when something was starting in the yard without him. She had not heard him come out. Her mother had not come to the door.

They stood at the rail and watched the truck maneuver. The yard was not large and the turn was tight for the loaded truck and the engine labored while the front wheels found their angle. Beside her her father was breathing — she could hear him in the quiet of the yard — and he had not spoken since they came to the porch. He stood the way he stood at the icehouse window in the evenings, or at the edge of the south field when the weather was coming in from the northwest, weight settled into his feet, watching something he had no way to change.

The truck found the lane and moved forward. It went slowly down toward the road, the ruts filling with pale water behind the tires as the weight passed over them. At the end of the lane it turned south.

It went past the fence line along the south field. Past the heaved second post, the staple she had driven while Karl held the wire. Into the maple stand at the south bend and gone.

She counted without intending to. Under thirty seconds and the engine sound was gone south too, toward the highway, toward Houlton.

Lonzo Reed was still in the yard. He stood looking at where the truck had been, the Springfield at his side, his coat hem loose in the wind. Then he looked toward the porch. He lifted his chin once — the acknowledgment — and turned and walked down the lane. He went around the south bend.

The yard was empty.

Her father had not moved beside her. The tire tracks of the truck were filling slowly with the pale water that rose through this clay when you pressed it. The icehouse door was standing open at the back of the yard — left open when the four men came out and no one had gone back to close it. She could see the dark opening from the porch, the empty room inside, the rough walls the renovation had put up three years ago. The first time the icehouse had stood empty since April of 1943. The door open to the cold April air for the first time in two years.

From inside the barn came the ordinary sounds of the cows in the stanchions, indifferent to the hour. Sixteen cows. The south field across the fence, too soft to turn yet — another week, maybe two. The mud of the yard going still in the mid-morning light.

---

Her father put his hand on her shoulder.

The weight of his hand was specific — the farmer's hand, wide and dry and heavy, the hand that had been milking cows and turning hay and holding fence posts on this farm for twenty-two years. She could feel it through the wool of her coat. He did not grip or press. He set his hand on her shoulder the way you set something down carefully on a surface you want to stay level.

He said two words. She heard them in both languages he had. Komm rein.

She looked at the south bend of the road where the maple stand closed over it. The leaves were not yet full — late April and the canopy still thin enough for the light to come through in pieces. The road was empty.

Then she turned.

---

The kitchen was warm. The stove was going with the draft set low for the middle of the day, the room holding the warmth of the morning's bread and the coffee already on the table in three cups. Her mother had heard them on the porch and poured three cups and set them out before they came through the door. Magda was at the stove with her back to them, setting the pot back on the burner. She did not turn around.

Hannah sat down.

Her father sat across from her.

The table held what it always held: the cups, the pot, the sugar bowl with the chip on the rim that had been there as long as Hannah could remember, the dish her mother set the stirring spoon on. The window over the counter with the view of the barn roof and past it the south field and the maple stand at the south bend where the road disappeared.

She put her hands around her cup and let the warmth come through. The coffee was what it always was. Through the window the late-morning light was the thin April light that made everything look like it could become something else in a week, the fields not yet what they would be and already past what they had been.

The radio on the counter was off. She had not turned it on this morning and her father had not turned it on and the kitchen held its own quiet — not the silence of the last two years, not her mother's closed silence and her father's German and the icehouse full at the back of the yard, but the ordinary quiet of a room with the stove going and the coffee on the table. In the radio, if she turned it on, she would find the war in the quality it had had all spring: the careful evenness of the announcer's voice, the names of places in Germany spoken in a changed tense, the armies moving through a country that was finishing itself place by place. She could reach out and turn the dial.

She did not.

Her mother came from the stove and set the pot on the table. She put her hand flat on the surface once — her gesture for something she had observed and found sufficient, the gesture Hannah had been reading for two years as the closest thing to language her mother permitted herself. Then she sat down.

The three of them were at the table.

Her father drank his coffee. Her mother held her cup with both hands. Outside the window the barn roof was the same barn roof it had always been. The south field would tell her when it was ready — she would look at it this afternoon and the soil would give her what she needed to know. The icehouse door was still open at the back of the yard; she could not see it from this window but she knew it was open, the darkness inside it now the darkness of a room no longer in use.

The man on the breakwater would stay in the supplementary file in Portland, without a name.

Somewhere on a road south, the truck.

Her father set his cup down. Her mother refilled it from the pot, without being asked, without looking up. The farm was what it was and required what it required: the south field in another week, the sixteen cows waiting for the afternoon milking, the spring work ahead of all of it. The icehouse empty.

The war was in the radio. It was not yet over. It would be.

The farm was here.

## What the chapter does

The novel's final chapter is Hannah's, and it holds three distinct movements:

**1. The letter returned** (barn, morning before the truck). The exchange is eleven lines — quick, physical, done. She says she found it in the hay in February of last year. He says he wondered where it went. She says she's sorry. He says *nein* — declining the apology, not accepting it. She confirms she read it. He puts it in the inside pocket of his jacket and asks about his mother; she says *wir beten für sie*. He says he thinks she's all right, he hopes so. She says she hopes so too. He turns back to the stanchion. Lonzo comes back in. The barn returns to itself.

**2. The truck** (mid-morning). Lonzo signs the transfer forms. The four prisoners come out with their few things. Karl does not look at Hannah when they come out — then once he does, she looks back, his face does not change, hers does not either, and then the tailgate goes up. Lonzo shakes hands with the camp soldier and steps back. The truck goes slowly down the lane, turns south, disappears into the maple stand at the south bend. Under thirty seconds and the engine is gone. Lonzo lifts his chin at the porch and walks after the truck.

**3. Komm rein / the kitchen** (porch, then inside). Albrecht is already at the railing when Hannah arrives on the porch — coffee cup in both hands, Magda not coming to the door. They watch together. When the yard is empty, Albrecht puts his hand on Hannah's shoulder — the specific weight of the farmer's hand through her wool coat. He says two words. She hears them in both languages he has: *Komm rein*. She looks at the empty road and turns. Inside: Magda has poured three cups. The radio is off. The war is in the radio; she doesn't turn it on. The three of them sit. One subordinate clause for the man on the breakwater: *The man on the breakwater would stay in the supplementary file in Portland, without a name.* Somewhere on a road south, the truck. The farm is here.

Magda's resolution is entirely in gesture: three cups poured, hand flat on the table once. The breakwater arrives and departs in a single subordinate clause with no weight applied. The closing movement accumulates ordinary farm-future (the south field, sixteen cows, the afternoon milking ahead) before landing on "The farm was here" — four words, declarative, present tense, nothing after it.

# The Icehouse in October

The alarm was the four-fifteen, which she had moved back in September because the dark came earlier now and earlier meant harder. When it went she lay for a moment adding up the warmth she had against the warmth she would need: the cold of the kitchen floor, the cold of the yard, the barn and its better warmth that smelled of forty-five cows and hay and the steam of animals who had been working through their own slow processes since midnight. She added these in order and then she got up.

Her boots were by the door, laces already loosened from the night before. She dressed in the kitchen without lighting a lamp — she knew every nail and hook in her own kitchen in the dark — and took the lantern off the shelf and went out.

The yard in October. The dark was total until the lantern made it particular: the pump handle, the corner of the silo, the low fence of the kitchen garden with its dead stalks. The hayfield to the east gave off cold in a way the harbor-cold didn't, a cold from the earth rather than the water, dense and close to the ground. She was halfway to the barn before she could hear the cows clearly over the wind. Forty-five animals telling her what she already knew.

Inside she hung the lantern on the iron hook by the door and the light went orange in the warmth. The smell hit before the warmth did: hay and manure, the sweet-sharp smell of milk, the wet-wood smell of the stalls that had been wet since October and wouldn't dry until May. Above everything the animal steam, the breath and bodies of forty-five cows giving off heat into an enclosed space. She had breathed this smell every morning of her life. She did not think of it as a smell anymore; it was just where she was.

She started at the near end. Heide shifted left when she heard the bucket and had to be corrected — not hard, just redirected. Brunhild was easy. The red one they called Rote was easy. She worked down the stalls in the order her father had taught her when she was small enough that the cows had seemed very large, and her hands did it while the rest of her was still waking up, and the barn was warm and loud in the particular way of barns at four-thirty in the morning, which is not warm the way a room is warm, not loud the way a room is loud, but warm and loud in the way of forty-five large animals being specific about what they needed.

She was on the third bucket when the far door opened and her father came in.

He went directly to the east side, which was his, and he spoke to the first stall cow without stopping — die Kühe and their names and what he needed them to do, in the barn German that was older than the other German and didn't belong to the war. She had heard it her whole life. It was a different instrument than the German he used in the kitchen now, or the German she heard in the evenings through the wall. The barn German was working language, specific, not addressed to anyone she could hear.

He came along the aisle behind her toward the center where their rows met. She was reaching forward to adjust the bucket when he passed.

He said: Morgen.

He said it the way he had always said *good morning* — flatly, without looking up, a fact already established that required only acknowledgment. He had stopped saying *good morning* in the kitchen, at the table, when he stopped speaking English at home, but in the barn he had kept *good morning* and then at some point it became *Morgen*. She was not certain when. She hadn't been paying close enough attention to mark the exact day.

She said: Morgen.

She had started saying it back in August. She hadn't decided to. It was simply the response that required the least choosing, when the alternative was standing on the English side of it and making something of that. She didn't want to make something of it. He had always said good morning; she had always said good morning back.

He moved on without responding to her response, which she hadn't expected. Beyond her, toward his side, and his German came back in fragments down the length of the stalls — a cow's name, an instruction. The cows responded in their own register, which was not interested in the language being used.

---

At half past eight she heard the truck.

Lonzo Reed came through the gate with his Springfield over his right shoulder and his collar turned up against a cold that was October cold, not yet November cold, but Lonzo addressed all inconveniences at the level of their theoretical maximum. He had been a fisherman before the war and he moved with a fisherman's deliberateness — not slow, simply finished with haste as a method. He walked to the icehouse, knocked twice on the door, and pulled the latch.

The four men came out.

There was no drama in it. They had done this every morning since April: they emerged, they put their coats on in the yard, they separated to their assigned tasks without conference or complaint. Ernst — she thought his name was Ernst, she'd heard it once in June and had not confirmed it — came first. Then the heavyset one whose name she had never caught. Then the quiet one who favored his right shoulder but never mentioned it to Lonzo, because mentioning it to Lonzo would have required language neither of them had. Karl came last.

He came out pulling his jacket sleeve over his right wrist and saying something to the heavyset one in German that made the heavyset one tilt his head slightly. Then he saw that Lonzo was already making his perimeter check and he stopped saying it and looked at what needed doing.

He was nineteen. Lonzo had said so in July, in the tone of a man grateful the situation wasn't worse: *the youngest one's just nineteen.* As if the age were a mitigating factor in some calculation Hannah had not been asked to perform. Karl was from somewhere in Bavaria, fifty kilometers from where her father was born, which she had thought about more than once since they arrived in April.

He moved the way boys moved — not clumsily but with something in reserve, energy not yet fully organized into efficiency. There was still something in his movements that showed the learning. She noticed this the way she noticed whether the cows were favoring one side or the other: not as a judgment, as a reading.

Lonzo said his three German words and the four men spread to their tasks.

Karl went to the woodpile. He picked up the maul and turned it once in his hands before he set the first round on the block — this was always his habit, measuring first, then splitting. She'd watched it enough times to know. He'd been good at it since June and was better now. The quarter-round came off clean on the first stroke, the log falling to both sides evenly, and she turned away before he could notice her watching.

In front of Lonzo, Karl and her father were simply two people in the same yard. They didn't look at each other any differently than either of them looked at the fence or the barn. She understood why. There was something between them worth protecting and you protected things by not making them visible during the hours when they had to be invisible.

Lonzo stamped his feet and watched his breath go white and disperse. The morning kept on being the morning.

---

The feed store closed at five on Wednesdays. She took the Ford after school let out and drove the three miles of unpaved inland road — the truck pulling right the way it always did, the heater requiring the knob held at an angle slightly left of center, the Bangor station coming in on the radio with enough static that she kept it on anyway because it was better than the absence of it.

From the ridge above town the harbor was visible for a moment through the October haze: a strip of gray water, the breakwater a thin dark line extending from the dock, the fixed red light at its seaward end. She didn't look at it for longer than the road allowed.

She had heard it before she saw the water. Ellis Carver, in the hall outside Klein's classroom Tuesday morning: a man on the breakwater, the Coast Guard there and gone by ten, no one from Coldwater missing, no name and no papers and Reg Farber's youngest had found him before breakfast. She'd heard it again at lunch, from two other girls, with different details. She'd heard it from the Dunham boy in Latin class, who'd added additional details that contradicted Ellis Carver's details without either of them seeming to notice.

The general store was also the post office, which meant it was where information arrived without anyone needing to carry it. Mabel Trask was behind the counter and the Morrissette brothers were in the seed display for reasons that had nothing to do with seeds. They were there because Mabel knew.

What Mabel knew: not a fisherman, not anyone from around here. The Farber boy had thought he was sleeping. He was not sleeping. The Coast Guard took the body and took the log pages with it, which Mabel found notable and said so. The man had no identification. No one was looking for anyone from Coldwater.

The Morrissette brothers added commentary about a man they had once seen in Rockland who had struck them as the type, though they acknowledged it might not be the same man. Hannah listened. She bought her four bags of dairy meal — the good kind, not the cut kind, because the cows had been producing well and her father's rule was that good cows got good meal — and she heaved them over the tailgate one at a time with her left hip against the lip, the method her father had taught her, which left the small of the back out of it. Four bags, four thumps. She tied the tailgate and drove home.

The heater knob at its angle. The radio in fragments. The man was in her mind — not sharply, just present — his absence of name, the city shoes that Mabel had mentioned in passing. She had seen men in city shoes in Rockland, men who had not dressed for the coast. The shoes alone said something, though she could not have said precisely what.

She drove the inland road with the harbor behind her and the farmland opening up on both sides, the shadow of the silo already stretched halfway across the yard when she turned up the farm road. The light had gone orange on the eastern fields. The cows would be wanting their evening feed.

---

After supper she heard her father's voice through the kitchen wall.

The east side of the house shared its partition with the narrow yard hallway, and from the window above the dry sink she could hear things in the yard that would not be audible from anywhere else in the house. She had found this out by accident years ago and had used it since as one of the farm's small unremarkable facts, the way all old houses have their acoustics.

Magda was at the table with the hip seam in Albrecht's work pants. The right hip seam opened every October when he pulled the heavier work from the trunk — it had opened so reliably for so many years that she thought of it as a fall event, like the first hard frost, like the leaves off the maple by the kitchen door. Her mother's needle moved at the pace she worked at everything: exactly as fast as the thing required. She had not spoken in six months. The doctor in Rockland had a word for it that Hannah had not written down, a long word, functional at the beginning, meaning: not injury, not illness, but something the body had decided. Hannah's own theory was different and she kept it to herself.

The kitchen was quiet enough that she heard her father's voice through the wall — not the words, just the low movement of it — and she went to the window.

The icehouse window was lit. The kerosene lamp, which Lonzo had authorized in June when the wood stove started drawing properly: yellow and steady from outside, the window cracked its two or three inches that she had come to associate with the evenings since August. Her father stood in the yard with his back to her. She could see his work coat, the white of his breath.

Karl's voice came through the window. He was asking something. Then her father's voice: lower, going on past where a simple answer would have stopped.

She couldn't hear the words. She had never been close enough in the evenings to hear the words, and she had not gone closer on purpose. What she could hear was the quality of it — the rhythm of two people talking about something that warranted the talking. The barn German was not this. The barn German was a tool, transactional, used for specific animals in a specific order. This moved through the air differently. It had the cadence of things being described or asked about in earnest, of a question that expected a real answer.

Her father's shoulders in his work coat were not the shoulders she had been watching for two years. The particular set they'd had — since the telegram, she thought, or before the telegram, since December 1941 when the radio news came in and he had sat very still for a long time and she had been sixteen and had not known what she was seeing — that set was not there now. He was not relaxed; he was standing in the cold at an icehouse window and relaxed was not the situation. But he was in the moment. Present in one place, not carrying the elsewhere that had been in him for so long she had almost forgotten what his shoulders looked like without it.

The lamp inside shifted — someone moving near it — and the window brightened briefly and settled. Her father said something. Karl answered.

She stepped back from the window.

Her mother's needle moved in the hip seam. In the kitchen the only sound was the creak of the chair and the pull of thread and her own breathing, which she had not noticed until now.

---

She went upstairs.

The man on the breakwater was still with her — no name, city shoes, not from anywhere local — and she found she could hold it the way she held most things that didn't have conclusions yet. She turned it over: Reg Farber's youngest finding him in the fog. The Coast Guard coming and going before the town was properly awake. Someone with no name and no one looking for him from anywhere that had come forward yet. She did not know what to do with it, in the specific sense of what to do, and so she held it without doing anything.

She took off her boots and lay flat in the dark.

Underneath the man on the breakwater was the sound of her father's voice at the window. The length of it. Karl on the other side of the glass, Karl's question receiving an answer that was longer than the question. She did not know what they had been talking about. She had not decided to try to find out.

The house made its sounds around her — the pipes settling, the boards in the corner of her room that spoke once every night, the cold working at the seams of the window glass. She lay in the dark and did not try to make anything of it, and the dark of thinking and the dark before sleep had no clear boundary between them, and eventually she was on the far side of that boundary without having crossed it.

# The Crow House

The passage on the board was Lessing — the opening scene of *Minna von Barnhelm*, Act One, which he had chosen because it was military and therefore timely and had the further advantage of containing enough grammatical difficulty in the first page to occupy two students for the duration of the period without leaving them time to consider what they were actually translating. He had written it out in his German hand — the one that was smaller than his English hand and still leaned rightward in the way he had been taught at eight years old — and now he stood with his back to the room and looked at what he'd written while the two girls worked.

He could hear Doris Hatch on the second sentence by her breathing. She was the kind of student who held her breath when reading in a second language, as though the effort of comprehension required the body to suspend its ordinary functions until it could be resolved. Louise Pelletier had moved through the second sentence and arrived at the third, which contained a dative of purpose he had not glossed in the notes he had put on their desks, and he was waiting, without appearing to wait, to see what she would do with it.

The third chair — at the left-hand desk, second row from the window — was empty.

Pfeiffer. The information had not arrived as a deliberate perception but as an alteration in the room's ordinary texture, the way a room registers an absence not because one has looked for it but because the space that is usually occupied is not: a gap that does not announce itself but is there. Hannah Pfeiffer was the only one of the three who came to a German passage knowing, in some preliminary way, what the words contained before she construed them. She had her father's Bavarian dialect in her phrasing — recognizable even in the small German she produced in class, a particular shaping of the back vowels, a rhythm to the subordinate clause that was distinct from anything she might have learned here — and this told him things about the household she came from that he had not asked her to tell him and that she had not, so far, offered. She arrived at the page with knowledge she had absorbed before she knew she was absorbing it. He found this, as a professional matter, genuinely interesting.

"Hatch," he said.

Doris looked up with the expression of a student hoping to remain unnoticed a moment longer. She read the second sentence aloud. The German was accurate; the accent was northern American in the particular way that Maine is northern American, a distinct phonological territory, and the meaning came through intact, which was the purpose of translation class and sufficient. He corrected the long *u* once, without comment, and moved to Louise Pelletier, who had navigated the dative independently and correctly, a small specific satisfaction — the kind that belongs to teaching rather than scholarship, less clean but present in its way — and he told her so. He wrote the dative construction on the board and noted to himself to set it again in two weeks to see whether the lesson held.

Below the Lessing, he wrote: *Wohin?*

Beneath it, in English: *Where to?*

He left both on the board without explaining them. The word was in the passage; he had no other reason to put it there that he would have been able to articulate in terms the girls would find useful. Doris Hatch looked at the board and then at her notebook. Louise Pelletier looked at the board and then out the window, where the October trees had gone to the plain brown of late October, the last week before November reduced them further. The room smelled of chalk and damp wool and the coal furnace's particular brand of inadequacy, which he had been smelling since March and had accepted as characteristic. 

He stood with the chalk in his hand and the chalked German of a playwright dead a hundred and sixty years on the board behind him, and through the east window the afternoon light came in at the angle it came in at in mid-October at this latitude, low and already beginning its withdrawal, and the chair at the left-hand desk stayed empty, and he set them both to the fourth sentence and waited.

---

He heard his name not said.

The supply room at the end of the second-floor hall had a door that did not close flush with the frame, and over a year and a half he had learned to stand slightly back from it when he was collecting chalk or examination paper, because from that position he could hear, or could not hear, what was happening in the hallway in a way that was occasionally informative. This was not a habit he would have thought to develop in Vienna. It had developed, in stages, through Paris and London and afterward, the way certain habits develop under certain conditions without one's having chosen them.

He was putting chalk in his coat pocket when Hendricks from mathematics — and the woman whose name he had not yet retained, who taught something in the girls' physical program and something else he could not recall — came around the corner from the stairs. He heard them come to the particular pause that conversations came to when he entered a range. He walked at the pace he had learned, which was the pace of a man with nothing in particular he was doing or listening for, and came out of the supply room and went along the hall.

He heard: *no papers. No name.* He heard: *Coast Guard took the log pages, which Mabel thought was notable.* He heard: *not from Coldwater, not from anywhere anyone can—* and then he was past the point where it carried.

This was sufficient. He had been a philologist for twenty-three years; the practice of extracting meaning from fragmentary texts was not incidental to his training but central to it, and the habit persisted across genres. The body on the breakwater: no papers, no name, not from here. A man without documentation, found at the edge of the sea, in clothing that suggested somewhere else. He put the fragment where he put things he had not yet finished examining, and went down the stairs into the afternoon.

---

The walk from the school to the Crow house took nine minutes at his ordinary pace. Where the road bent upward at the ridge, before the elms closed in above it, the harbor was briefly visible through the October-stripped trees: a strip of gray water, the breakwater a dark granite line extending from the dock's end, the fixed red light at its seaward terminus not yet lit in the afternoon. He stopped for a moment — not for any reason that required stopping, but because the view had precise edges and he had discovered, in his months here, that he found a particular comfort in things with precise edges. Then he went on.

The Crow house was white clapboard, second-from-the-end on Elm Street, with a modest front yard and a porch that in warmer months Henry occupied in the last of the afternoon light. This was not a habit anyone had pointed out to Marcus; it was something he had understood, early in his time here, as the portion of the day Henry reserved for his own thinking, and he had taken some care not to arrive at that hour in a way that required Henry to acknowledge him. In October the porch was not useful. Henry was inside.

Marcus let himself in with his key.

The hallway was warm, not aggressively but sufficiently — the warmth of a house that had been maintained with care over a long time. He heard the Rockland paper's particular rustle from the kitchen, which meant Henry at the table. From the back of the house, coffee: the real kind, not the grain substitute, which had a flavor he had become too well acquainted with in his first months here before he understood that the Crow house was somehow an exception to this. He had arrived at the correct position about this fact, which was that it was not his to investigate and that the correct response to it was gratitude without commentary.

He hung his coat on the peg.

In the kitchen Lillian was at the stove with her back to him. She said, without turning: "Marcus. Coat."

"Already," he said.

She glanced back briefly — a look that was not a look of doubt but the kind of look one gives to confirm what one already knew. Henry was at the table with the Rockland paper and looked up from it in his way, which was not all the way up but enough: a look that meant *sit down*, and Marcus sat.

The kitchen table had three chairs. His was the one that faced the east window, through which the back yard was visible, and past the yard the hillside, and above the hillside the gray sky of October pressing down in a way that was not unpleasant but was entirely earnest. Henry's chair faced the door. Lillian's could see both. This arrangement had established itself in the first week of March and had not been discussed.

There was a quality to this kitchen that the rest of Coldwater, in general, did not have in his presence — a quality he had spent some months attempting to name and had eventually settled for calling the absence of management. Elsewhere in town he was, in some ongoing functional sense, a matter that required decisions: the credentials requiring periodic validation, the provenance requiring explanation when it came up, the presence requiring an account of itself in a community that had not anticipated it and had made what room it had made in the spirit of pragmatic necessity rather than affirmative welcome. He had learned to live within this without complaint, which was easier than it sounded and also harder than it sounded, the two things being simultaneously true. Here the management was absent. Lillian had written, in her letter through the school board the previous winter, that he was welcome, and the word had meant what it said.

He folded his hands on the table and then unfolded them, because folded hands was a classroom posture and he was not in the classroom.

"There was a man found on the breakwater," Marcus said. "Tuesday morning. I understand he had no papers and no name."

Henry did not respond immediately. He set the paper down, flat, without marking his place — he kept the page in his head — and turned the sentence over with the unhurried attention of a man who had decided that responses given before they were ready had a quality of incompleteness that was not worth the saved time. Then he said: "Found him Tuesday?"

"That is what I have been given to understand."

Henry nodded once, picked up the paper, and returned his attention to it. This gesture, which Marcus had initially read incorrectly in his first weeks here, meant that the information was received and placed and required no further handling at this moment — that there were categories of information which arrived complete and which adding to served nothing. It was not incuriosity; it was the practiced discipline of a man who had learned precisely which things warranted a response and which things warranted only acknowledgment, and who did not waste the one on occasions that called for the other. This was, Marcus had concluded sometime in the spring, among the most genuinely unusual habits he had encountered in his forty-seven years. He was still in the process of learning it.

Lillian set the cups down and sat and poured. She asked after the school furnace, which had been running cold on the second floor since September and which the building staff had so far addressed without result, and Marcus told her what he knew, and Henry's expression did not change, and Lillian said she would have a word.

They drank their coffee. The Rockland paper reported what it reported. Outside, Elm Street darkened toward five o'clock in the way October darkened it: not gradually but in steps, the light changing its angle and then abandoning the angle entirely and leaving only the flat gray that preceded the dark. They sat in it, in the kitchen, and Marcus held the fragment — no papers, no name, not from around here — at the edge of his attention where he had put it, and where it stayed.

---

His room was on the second floor, east-facing, with a slanted ceiling on the north wall where the roofline came down to meet the plaster, which gave it the shape of a room in which one moved with a working knowledge of the available space. He had acquired this knowledge in the first days of March and had arranged the room accordingly: the desk under the east window, the single wooden chair beside the bookcase, the narrow bed along the south wall near the radiator, about which he had not yet asked Henry, understanding the asking to require a confidence in his own domestic standing that he was still, in certain particulars, assembling, a year and a half on.

The shortwave was on the desk: a Zenith portable, not the console that sat in the Crows' parlor, but a smaller set he had acquired in Bangor in the spring of his arrival with money he had needed for other things and had spent on this instead. The reasoning had been straightforward enough: there were things happening in Europe that he required to know about, and the distance between him and Europe was now such that knowing about them required a particular kind of machinery and persistence. The dial glowed amber when the set was warm and the tuning knob required a light touch and something he had too much time to develop, which was patience.

He switched it on and waited.

The BBC World Service came in on 9.41 megacycles, or had come in there last Thursday; the frequencies shifted and he had to find them freshly each time, which was an inconvenience he had come to regard as appropriate, or at least as not inappropriate. He tuned.

Static. Through it, something: a woman's voice reading figures he couldn't resolve before the signal dropped. He tuned past. A military frequency in English, procedural, not meant for him. Past. At 9.38 the BBC identification signal arrived — four notes, the motif that had acquired, over three years of hearing it in conditions of varying comfort and uncertainty, a significance he would not have been able to reduce to mere preference or habit — and then the signal faltered and faded before the bulletin began.

He sat with the dial and waited.

It came back. The Italian campaign: not going quickly, but going. The Pacific: performing better than the assessments of late 1942 had suggested. The convoy situation in the North Atlantic: improved, the broadcaster said, in the careful syntax of someone managing what could not be entirely managed, and Marcus listened with the full attention he gave to news from Europe — noting what was said and what was not said with equal precision, the gaps in a broadcast being, in his professional experience, as informative as the content, sometimes more.

The man on the breakwater was there at the edge of his attention, where he had put the fragment.

No papers. No name. Not from around here.

He did not write in his German notebook tonight. He had taken it out and set it on the desk, which had been his intention, and the intention had not carried through.

The BBC signal faded. He tuned along the dial slowly — a quarter-degree at a time, the method that had a better yield than the broader sweeps he had tried in the early months — and found, in order: a fragment of French, gone before he could determine the source; something that might have been Brazilian, the geography of radio being less intuitive than one assumed; a clear voice in American English for thirty seconds on the subject of soybean prices in the Midwest; and then the static, full and thorough.

He sat with the static.

He had known, during the period before he came south, a physicist from Frankfurt — a compact, deliberate man whose name he required a moment now to recover, which was a thing that had begun happening with names from before 1941 — who held a theory about the interval between radio signals. The theory was that the interval was not silence but a different kind of information: denser, less formed, carrying what the broadcast could not carry. Marcus had thought this was nonsense at the time, and he maintained the position that it was probably nonsense, and he also found, sitting with the static in the dark of his room in October, that his confidence in the position had declined from where it had been.

No papers. No name. A man dressed carefully for something and arrived at the wrong end of it, at the edge of a sea he had apparently tried to cross. 

He held the fragment the way one holds a word at the edge of recall — not pressing on it, because pressure did not help.

He had possessed, in August of 1941, a suit that did not fit him. The chest had been correct; the shoulders had gone loose in the way garments go loose when the body inside them has reduced, over some months, to less than the garment expected. He had possessed, in August of 1941, a document describing him in English as a resident alien enemy — *enemy* the substantive noun, *alien* and *resident* the qualifying adjectives that determined what could legally be done with him — and this had been the document he had when he stepped off the train in Boston with his cardboard case and the two books he had been allowed to bring with him when he left. The man who stepped off the train did not correspond, in any precise sense, to the man who had boarded one in Vienna three years earlier. He had spent the months following the arrival determining the nature of the correspondence, and the question had not been fully resolved, though he had made progress.

He did not know why the man on the breakwater interested him with this particular quality of attention. He was aware of not knowing. He turned the tuning dial a quarter-degree and found static of a slightly different texture and went on sitting with the thought he was not quite pursuing, because the pursuit would not help, which was a thing he had also learned.

The BBC came back for a moment — shipyards, the Pacific, a name he didn't catch — and dissolved again into the static.

On the shelf above the desk, in the amber dial-glow, his notebooks stood in the order he maintained: the English journal, the grammar workbook from his first months at the school, the current German one. He could see, from his chair, that the spine of the German notebook was written in his English hand.

This had been happening for some months. When he needed to write something quickly — a word, a heading, a note in the margin of something — his English hand came first, without direction. Not because his German hand had failed him; when he turned to it deliberately it was there, the *Kurrent* script and the Roman print both intact, present and correct. But the English arrived first, without the interval of retrieval that German now required. The English was, in some working sense, more available. It was the closer thing.

He had not expected this. He had expected, if anything, the reverse to be permanent: that German would remain primary in the way a native language remains primary, the English always a skill rather than a reflex, the boundary maintained even when other things were not. The boundary had not maintained itself. He still noticed it when he noticed it, the way one notices a change that has been gradual enough to arrive without announcement.

He reached over and switched off the set.

---

The room without the radio found its other sounds: the north wall settling, cold working at the seams of the window glass, the boards making their adjustments with the night temperature. The harbor was somewhere down the hill in the dark beyond the east windows, not visible, present in the way of things one knows to be there without seeing them. In whatever building across town contained the information — whatever file or desk or locked cabinet — a dead man's absence of papers and name continued to be a fact that waited for whatever facts waited for.

Marcus took off his glasses and set them on the desk. The room went soft at its edges: the desk, the chair, the bookcase with its spines, the shelf above the desk with the notebooks — shapes he knew and knew where they were, imprecise now but present. The east window, dark. The harbor's direction.

The room was dark and cold and was, for the moment, where he lived.

# Across the Fence

The ground had frozen in the first week of December and stayed frozen. Not the way mud froze at night and softened by midmorning — a freeze that went deep, that changed the sound underfoot from the clinging pull of October into something brittle and fractured, the top layer of earth heaved into plates by the cold, glittering where the morning light caught it. It made the barn yard alien in a way Hannah had not expected. Eight months ago the paddock had looked like the paddock. Now it looked like something that had been broken and set back down in the shape of itself.

She noticed it every morning on the way out and she noticed it again now, coming on ten o'clock, her breath going gray in front of her, the post-driver heavy under her arm. She had known for two weeks that the southeast corner of the paddock fence had shifted. She could see it from the yard: the post leaning maybe three inches off plumb, the wire sagging with it. But there had been the south field and the window stuffing and three days where the temperature had not come above freezing even at noon. She had not gotten to it. Her father had not said anything about it. He would not. The fence was the fence and the fence required attention and she would give it attention when she could and when she did it would be done.

She hauled the post-driver out from behind the stacked straw and carried it into the paddock. The cows were still in the barn with the morning's hay going; the outer yard was empty. From around the south side of the barn she could hear the sound of splitting wood — the prisoners' work this time of year, the cold driving the field labor out and the barnyard chores in — and once in a while Lonzo Reed's voice carrying a direction in the three German words he had accumulated over six months, none of which she had confirmed for certain.

She set the driver over the post and began.

---

December had changed the work. Not only the ground — the whole farm had shifted with the season the way it always did, the way she had watched it shift every year of her life. The prisoners had been at the farm since April, which meant she had watched them go through summer and into October and now into the cold, and she had watched how the work changed and they changed with it. Less field work now. More of what the barn required: wood-splitting, repairs to the siding on the east wall, the work of keeping the icehouse warm enough and the barn functional. They had become competent at it in a way she could see from across the yard — not performing the work but doing it, a difference that was visible in the back.

Karl had picked up more English than the other three. That was clear by October and clearer now. She had not been close enough to hear much of it directly, but she had heard enough through the barn wall or at the yard's edge to know that what he was working with was a strange inheritance. Lonzo Reed's English was the English of a man who had been on lobster boats for thirty years before the war gave him this particular assignment, and what had passed from Lonzo to Karl had come with all of that still attached. She had heard Karl say something to the quiet prisoner — the one who favored his right shoulder — that had the rhythm and the clipped command of a man giving orders over engine noise, but with the consonants reassembled around a different mouth. Lonzo's vocabulary through a Bavarian throat. She had not said anything about this to anyone.

Lonzo Reed wore two coats now, a canvas work coat over what looked like his old fishing coat, and he had taken to standing with his back against the south barn wall when the wind came off the water, the wall that held afternoon warmth the longest. The Springfield rifle was on a shoulder sling that he had rigged to not interfere with the second coat. He did his work, which was standing there, and the prisoners did their work, which was everything else. He was not unkind. He was in his late fifties and the barn had a woodstove.

Hannah worked the driver down and stopped to feel the resistance. Still loose. The frost heave had pushed the post up a good two inches; she had to get it seated past where the frost had taken it or it would just come back. She lifted the driver and set it again.

---

She did not know which day it had started — Lonzo going into the barn for something in the late mornings. She had seen it happen before this, three or four times over the fall, and it did not surprise her. He was gone seven minutes, maybe ten. The barn had the stove and the stove was the warmest thing within a hundred yards and Lonzo Reed was in his late fifties. The prisoners went on with the woodpile or whatever they had when he went in, and when he came back out they were where he had left them.

So when she looked up from the post and found the yard on the far side of the fence empty of a guard, she did not make anything of it. She fitted the driver over the post again.

She heard him before she saw him — the sound of boots on frozen ground, and then the sound of two pieces of split wood being set on the fence rail. She looked up.

Karl had a piece of split wood in each hand, the way you might carry something if you were crossing toward where a person was working and wanted a reason for the crossing. He set one piece on the top rail. He kept the other.

He looked at the post. He said, in English: "The post, it is—"

He made a gesture with his free hand: palm tilting over, the motion of something going off plumb.

"Frost heave," she said. "Happens every December."

He looked at her a moment and then said it back: "*Frost heave.*" Not mechanically. More the way you repeat something to get its measure before you put it away.

"The ground freezes hard and it pushes everything up," she said. "You drive the post back down past where it was heaved to, tamp it good, it'll hold till spring."

He looked at the ground beside the post. Then he crouched down and set his piece of split wood against the post at the base, bracing it from the outside. She had not asked him to. There was not exactly a need — you could drive the post without it — but the wood would give it something to seat against on the way down, and that was not nothing.

She lifted the driver and brought it down.

He held the brace and she drove it three more times. The post went solid. She checked it with her hand — no give, not even a suggestion of one. She reached into her coat pocket for the staple gun.

He stood and held the second piece of wood and looked out across the frozen paddock while she reattached the wire: three staples, check the tension, check it again. The wire held. The fence was done.

She didn't say thank you. He didn't wait for her to say it. He was already picking up the first piece of wood from the rail when the sound of boots on the barn threshold came from behind her.

Lonzo Reed crossed the yard with his hands in his coat pockets and the rifle sling over his shoulder. His eyes went to the woodpile — the other three were there, the work going — and he came back to his place against the south wall and pulled his collar up.

Karl carried both pieces of wood back to the woodpile and set them on the split stack.

He did not hurry. He did not look back.

---

She went in at noon with the post-driver. Set it in the corner. Washed her hands at the sink and stood at the counter and made herself a plate with bread and the last of the headcheese and ate it looking at the yard through the kitchen window.

The woodpile was where it was. The prisoner detail was working. Lonzo had his back to the barn wall in the afternoon light.

It had been ninety seconds. Less. She did not know why she was thinking about it in units of time. She put her plate in the sink and went to get her school books.

---

That evening she was at the kitchen table with her algebra when her father came through from the back of the house. He didn't go to the table. He went to the window.

She had seen this enough times to know it without looking up. The particular tread, the small sound of the kitchen window being worked up an inch — it gave a line of sight toward the icehouse from the east corner of the frame. She kept her pencil on the page.

From outside, after a moment, came Karl's voice: low, careful. Her father answered. It was the German he used for these conversations — she had been hearing it since August and had not confused it with any other register he had. Not the barn German, die Kühe and the short working instructions, the language of cattle and what needed doing today. Not the supper German either, the brief declaratives about the south field or the feed schedule. This was different. This had the pace of two people finding what they shared, turning it in their hands, and she could hear in her father's voice something she had not heard from him in the direction of another person in two years: a quality of attention that was present rather than elsewhere.

She worked through the algebra. Page thirty-four, the right column. The equations had a quality she did not usually think about — everything came to a result, and the result was either right or wrong, and you could check it. She moved through the column and filled in the last answer and checked it.

Her father's voice went on, a sentence and then a pause, and Karl's voice answering, the words indistinct through the window and the cold and the twenty yards between the house and the icehouse. She was not trying to hear the words. She was hearing the quality of her father's voice the way you heard the quality of a sound you had learned to read for what it meant rather than what it said: the barn sounds at four-thirty a.m., the cows telling her what they were going to need before she reached them. Her father's voice telling her something she did not have a word for yet.

She put down her pencil and looked at the page.

She had been on the same farm as Karl Reinmar since April. Eight months. Before this morning he had said perhaps eight or ten words to her total — things addressed to the work, or to Lonzo, or to the yard in general, that she happened to be in earshot of. Today he had said perhaps thirty words. Thirty-two. *The post, it is—*. The tilting hand. *Frost heave*, the way he said it back, picking it up the way he picked things up, with the attention he gave to things that were useful.

She was aware of it the way she was aware of changes in the farm's arrangements — the kind of awareness that was not the same as deciding something about what had changed. When the morning order shifted and the quiet prisoner came out third one day instead of second she had noticed and filed it and not named it. That was how the farm worked. You read it accurately and you did not reach ahead of what you could see.

She was not sure what she had been watching for in eight months. She was not sure she had been watching for anything. She had been watching Karl Reinmar the way she watched everything on this farm: with the accuracy of someone who grew up reading a complicated environment, without putting a name to what the accuracy was in service of.

He had held the fence post. That was all.

The kitchen radio was off. Her mother had gone upstairs before eight. Her father's voice at the window, low and going on, the German in the dark.

She closed the algebra textbook.

The fence post would hold until spring. She had seated it past the frost line, tamped the ground around it with her heel, checked it twice. If February came in unusually hard it might heave again, but probably not. It was solid work and it would hold.

She stacked her books and carried them to the bottom of the stairs.

What she had resolved — if that was the word for something that had not felt like a resolution when it arrived, that had arrived more the way the farm's conclusions arrived, simply, without announcement — was to keep noticing what she noticed. Without deciding in advance what it meant. It was not a dramatic position. It was the kind of position that didn't announce itself as one. She had been arriving at it for eight months without knowing that was what she was doing.

She went upstairs. The cedar from her mother's linen chest reached her in the hall. She went into her room and wound the alarm to four-fifteen and got into bed.

Her father's voice was still going when she closed her eyes. She couldn't hear Karl's answers from up here. # A Letter from New York

The second line of the examination instructions had given him trouble since Sunday evening.

He had written it out in his room the night before — three attempts in the margin of his notebook page, each crossed — and then again this morning on the classroom board before the first class came up the east stair. He stood at the board with the chalk and read back what he had written: *When you do not know a word, consult the sense of the sentence.* The problem was *consult*, which required the student to have an intuition about what consulting a sentence meant, and it was exactly this intuition that he could not assume. He wiped the line.

He tried: *If you do not know a word, work from what the sentence needs it to mean.*

He stood back.

The German classroom occupied the second floor's east end, and in December it received the morning light in a way that was briefly pleasant before the cold coming off the north sill reasserted itself — the cold was better now, since Henry had planed the casement, but there was still a way the December light looked through those windows that was more like winter light pressing against glass than like light in a room. The examination sheets waited on the corner of his desk: three copies, typed himself on the school typewriter, which did not have the characters for *ü* or *ä*, requiring small substitutions he had worked out to preserve the sense if not the precision.

He read the second instruction line back. That would do. He had been a philologist for twenty years and had spent two days writing a sentence for the back of an examination sheet, which said something about either the importance of language or the particular liability of a mind that could not stop attending to it. He turned to lay the sheets on the desks and the bell from the floor below rang for the first class.

---

Parsons appeared during the interval between classes.

She came with the mail binder under her arm, the Tuesday delivery from the general store, which was also the post office, the mail sorted before school and walked up the hill in the binder. Marcus had Latin in twenty minutes. He knew, in the abstract, that nothing requiring an immediate response was likely to be in the binder, and he opened it anyway, as he always did, with the specific attention that he applied to anything arriving from outside Coldwater: the possibility that it was news.

The envelope from Dr. Feld was fourth from the top.

*Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars.* The letterhead on the envelope was the letterhead he had been receiving, in one form or another, since autumn 1940 — placement confirmation, credential documentation, quarterly notices about the wider network of displaced scholars the Committee maintained. Feld's own letters had been less frequent: two in 1941, one each in 1942 and the early part of 1943. Marcus had sent two postcards in the spring of this year, brief, reporting that his position continued and his address remained the same.

The envelope was thicker than a practical letter.

He opened it and read it standing. He had to sit down and read it again.

Feld was writing about a problem the Committee had encountered in tracking scholars who had been in transit during 1942 and into 1943. Some had arrived at their placements and failed to notify the office; this was not uncommon, and the Committee had means for re-establishing contact in most of those cases. Others were in Europe, unreachable for reasons that Feld described with a care that Marcus read as the careful prose of someone who did not yet know how to describe what was happening in Europe and was not going to guess. The third category was the one Feld lingered on: scholars who appeared to have been in transit and then ceased to be in transit, with no subsequent documentation and no record at any receiving institution.

Marcus knew that phrase. *Keine nachfolgende Dokumentation.* No subsequent documentation. The Emergency Committee used it the way a port authority used *vessel not arrived* — accurately, without affect. The period between his release from the camp and his arrival in Boston in August 1941 had been several weeks in which Marcus Klein existed in no file. The Committee had an address for him — the camp — that was no longer his address, and no forwarding address until he made contact from Boston. For those weeks, he had been a man of whom it could be written: *last documented at.* And then the next address.

The specific case was in the third page of the letter. Feld was careful with surnames, citing Committee privacy practice; he used initials where he could. A Dr. Felix K., he wrote — a linguist of German-Jewish origin, formerly of the University of Leipzig, who had been corresponding with the Committee from somewhere in Canada since early in 1943. His last letter to the office had been postmarked Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, September 22, 1943. In it he had told the Committee of his intention to travel south by sea, to reach Boston by late October; he had a contact in Boston. He had not written since. The Boston contact had heard nothing. The Committee had no other channel.

Feld was writing to Marcus partly because Marcus was placed in Maine — geographically relevant to a route running south from the Nova Scotia coast — and partly because he knew Marcus had been long enough on the Committee's rolls to have some reach into the network. Did Marcus know anything of a Dr. Felix K., Leipzig, a linguist?

Marcus read the letter through twice more.

He had a partial recollection — not a name, but something adjacent to a name, the way a word hovered at the edge of retrieval before either arriving or failing to arrive. A man at a philology conference in Vienna in 1936. Something at the intersection of Germanic philology and historical linguistics; he recalled a corridor in the Anatomiegebäude, the cold institutional light the building always had, two men talking in the specific Leipzig-accented German he had always found recognizable at a distance. He had been introduced. He had not spoken with the man at any length.

The name would not come. He might be constructing the memory from Feld's description rather than from the conference itself. A philologist could not always be trusted to distinguish reconstruction from recollection; it was one of the discipline's hazards he had never found a way around.

He set the letter on his desk.

Latin was beginning.

---

The German examination was the following Tuesday.

He read through Hannah Pfeiffer's paper first, which was not his usual order — he customarily worked alphabetically, which put Doris Hatch first and Hannah last — but which he found himself doing anyway. She had translated the passage from Goethe's correspondence correctly, which was not surprising; what stopped him was the word order. The passage was a letter Goethe had written to Schiller in October 1798 about the difficulty of rendering a natural scene in language without losing what had made the scene worth rendering. In the key sentence, the verb fell at the end, as German required. Most students, encountering this, pulled the verb forward; English demanded it, and the instinct was not wrong. Hannah Pfeiffer had left the verb where Goethe had placed it. The English she had produced was technically awkward and philologically correct, a sentence translated in the grammatical sense rather than the idiomatic one — you could see the German inside the English the way you could sometimes see the structure of a building inside the material it was built from.

He marked it correct and moved on to Doris Hatch.

He had not said anything. It was not the examination's occasion, and it was not entirely the German's occasion either; what she had given him told him something about where and how she had learned to read, which was not a conversation he was equipped to have in December with three weeks until Christmas break. He wrote *Good work* on her sheet and the same on Doris's and *This is improving* on Louise Pelletier's and meant all three, which was not always the case.

Latin was going well. Caesar's *De Bello Gallico*, the organization of the camp and the construction of the fortifications, twelve students working through the ablative absolutes with the patient incomprehension of people who found something merely difficult. After three students who found German faintly shameful, merely difficult was a relief he had not expected to feel as strongly as he did.

He encountered Henry Crow on Thursday afternoon in the second-floor hallway, Henry moving past with the supply cart.

"The window," Marcus said, which was not a complete sentence but arrived that way.

Henry looked at him.

"The north sill," Marcus said. "The cold isn't coming through the way it was."

"Block plane," Henry said. "And new caulk on the outside. It'll hold as long as the temperature stays above ten degrees. Below ten, the frame tightens." He added: "Might stick closed."

Marcus said he appreciated it.

Henry said it was his job and pushed the cart toward the supply closet at the hallway's end.

---

The school thinned in the last two weeks before Christmas break, the way it thinned every year — boys finding reasons to be on the water or in the timber, girls finding reasons to be needed at home, the teachers accepting these reasons with less scrutiny than they would have applied before the war. The building was quiet in the afternoons. Marcus finished the examination corrections and began preparing the January syllabus, working in the classroom for an hour after four o'clock because his room was colder than the classroom and the classroom had the east light for another forty minutes.

He had read Feld's letter three more times over the week. He had not replied.

---

He read it again that evening in his room, the lamp on, the letter flat on his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark that had been in place since half past four. There was no moon he could see and the cold pressed against the glass. The radiator on the south wall was running well, which it did not always do this early in December, and the room was warm enough that he could work at his desk without his coat.

He set the letter down. He took the German notebook from the shelf above his desk — more than half-full now, the compressed German hand running through its pages from April — and turned to the first blank leaf.

He wrote, in German, what he had:

*Felix K. Linguist. Leipzig. Zuletzt belegt in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, 22. September 1943. Beabsichtigte, Boston auf dem Seeweg zu erreichen, Ende Oktober.*

He looked at what he had written for a moment and then wrote below it:

*Ich glaube, ihn nicht zu kennen.*

He set down the pen. The 1936 Vienna corridor was still where it had been all week — present, the quality of the light available, the Leipzig-accented German available — and the name was still not there. He had searched the memory in the way you searched difficult German when you couldn't bring up a word: working around it, approaching from the surrounding context, trying the company the word had been in. It did not produce the name. He might be wrong about the conference. He might have assembled the memory from the description and mistaken the assembly for recollection.

He picked up the pen. Below the previous lines he wrote:

*Yarmouth nach Boston. Die Küste von Maine liegt dazwischen.*

He read the three lines back.

Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. He had not been there. He knew it as a port town on the southwestern coast, a transit point on the sea routes between the Atlantic provinces and New England — knew it in the way he knew most Maritime geography: from a map he had studied when he was trying to understand his own route south, the autumn of 1941. He could bring the coastline's shape from the map. He could not bring the harbor, the town's character, what it looked like from the water in late September. He had a place that was a location on a line rather than a place.

September 22, 1943. That was barely three weeks before the first heavy weather of the fall. A small vessel could make the run in favorable conditions in two to three days, or longer if the weather turned, or much longer, or not at all if the weather turned badly enough. It was a route that could be done. He did not know whether it had been.

He sat with the notebook open and the lamp on and thought about the phrase *zuletzt belegt in*.

Last documented in. The Emergency Committee's vocabulary for the point on the record where the thread ended. It was precise language; Feld was a precise man. He used the passive construction deliberately — *last documented in* rather than *last seen in* or *last known to be in* — because the documentation was what the Committee could stand behind, and he would not claim more certainty than the record gave him. The documentation ended at Yarmouth on September 22, 1943. What the documentation had been attached to continued, or did not continue, beyond that point, and the file had no way to say which.

He had been *last documented in* a place himself, in the summer of 1941. The documentation had said the camp; the camp had released him; for some weeks after that he had moved south without an address any file could reach him at. He had arrived in Boston, eventually, and written to the Emergency Committee from a boarding house on Commonwealth Avenue, and his file had been updated: Marcus Klein, Coldwater Reach, Maine, March 1942. Everything after that date was documented. Everything before August 1941, going back through Sherbrooke and London and Paris to Vienna, was documented also, in one archive or another. The gap between them was the condition Feld's phrase described, and Marcus had lived inside that condition and knew its particular quality: the sense of being in motion without leaving any trace of the motion, which was sometimes practical and sometimes something else.

Dr. Felix K. had been last documented in Yarmouth.

He did not write any of this in the notebook.

He put the pen down and opened the shortwave.

The BBC was not finding him tonight — 9.41 megacycles produced static and the fringe of something that might have been German, or might have been Dutch, sliding in and out at the edge of resolution. He moved the dial through the Brazilian Portuguese that appeared reliably above eleven megacycles, found a French signal that wavered between clarity and interference, found nothing else worth resting on. He moved down and found an American broadcast, clear and even, a news signal from somewhere in the domestic network. The Pacific: the Marshall Islands, conditions described with the precise optimism of someone who had been given permission to transmit and was being careful with it. He listened to the names of islands he had not known before the war and would not have had occasion to know. Maloelap. Wotje. He did not know where these were on a chart with any precision; he was assembling the Pacific the way he had assembled the Maine coast, location by location, from a distance, the geography of a war he was not in.

At nine-thirty he turned off the shortwave.

He took the Emergency Committee folder from the shelf between the English journal and the Stifter he had been reading since September. The folder held twelve letters now, going back to 1940, a paper record of his placement and its history. He put Feld's letter in the folder and put the folder back on the shelf.

He closed the German notebook and set it on the shelf above his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark, undiminished. He thought about Yarmouth, which he had not been to and did not know. He thought about the phrase *last documented in* and what came after it in the Committee's language: nothing, and then a date, and then the passive construction that meant someone had stopped being accountable to any record. He had been that. He knew the inside of it. The file noted the absence accurately and without editorial comment, which was the correct approach, and the absence itself remained — somewhere, in the space between the last documentation and whatever had come after — as a gap in the record that the record could acknowledge but not fill.

He turned off the lamp.

The room was dark and cold and smelled of woodsmoke from the furnace two floors below and of the particular density of cold books in a New England December, which he had come to know over the past two years without having been able to decide what he thought of it. He did not write anything more. The notebook was on the shelf, the folder was on the shelf, the shortwave sat silent on his desk. He did not move for a while. Outside the window the dark had the quality December dark always had at this latitude: complete, and cold, and indifferent to what was or wasn't documented in it.

Chapter 16 later demonstrates this pattern by referring to the internment only as "a place." I need to apply both fixes in one clean write.
