The BBC was not finding him tonight — 9.41 megacycles produced static and the fringe of something that might have been German, or might have been Dutch, sliding in and out at the edge of resolution. He moved the dial through the Brazilian Portuguese that appeared reliably above eleven megacycles, found a French signal that wavered between clarity and interference, found nothing else worth resting on. He moved down and found an American broadcast, clear and even, a news signal from somewhere in the domestic network. The Pacific: the Marshall Islands, conditions described with the precise optimism of someone who had been given permission to transmit and was being careful with it. He listened to the names of islands he had not known before the war and would not have had occasion to know. Maloelap. Wotje. He did not know where these were on a chart with any precision; he was assembling the Pacific the way he had assembled the Maine coast, location by location, from a distance, the geography of a war he was not in.

At nine-thirty he turned off the shortwave.

He took the Emergency Committee folder from the shelf between the English journal and the Stifter he had been reading since September. The folder held twelve letters now, going back to 1940, a paper record of his placement and its history. He put Feld's letter in the folder and put the folder back on the shelf.

He closed the German notebook and set it on the shelf above his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark, undiminished. He thought about Yarmouth, which he had not been to and did not know. He thought about the phrase *last documented in* and what came after it in the Committee's language: nothing, and then a date, and then the passive construction that meant someone had stopped being accountable to any record. He had been that. He knew the inside of it. The file noted the absence accurately and without editorial comment, which was the correct approach, and the absence itself remained — somewhere, in the space between the last documentation and whatever had come after — as a gap in the record that the record could acknowledge but not fill.

He turned off the lamp.

The room was dark and cold and smelled of woodsmoke from the furnace two floors below and of the particular density of cold books in a New England December, which he had come to know over the past two years without having been able to decide what he thought of it. He did not write anything more. The notebook was on the shelf, the folder was on the shelf, the shortwave sat silent on his desk. He did not move for a while. Outside the window the dark had the quality December dark always had at this latitude: complete, and cold, and indifferent to what was or wasn't documented in it.

# January Harbor

The inner cove had been icing since the second week of January — a thin skin at first, gray at the margins where the fresh water off the Reach mixed with the salt, then thickening toward the center until by the twenty-second it was opaque white ice that would not hold a man and would not let a boat through. It was not hard winter; the outer approach stayed open. The two draggers — the Callie B. and the Margaret Rose, Pelletier's — were tied at the outer dock and had been for nine days. The lobster boats were on their trailers at Farber's yard and at the Pelletier place up the road. The mail boat came Tuesdays and Fridays, worked the outer approach, tied at the deep-water slip, and was gone within the hour.

January harbor. Fewer reasons to be on the dock.

She did her rounds in the mornings. In summer the rounds took forty minutes: log, bilge checks, dock inspection, radio at 0800. In January they took twenty-five, with the fleet reduced and the radio check running once daily and the bilge pumps demanding less attention than they did in active season. She had learned, in her second winter at the post, not to stretch the rounds to fill the time. Owen had said something close to this before the fact, though she had arrived at it herself before she remembered that he had said it, and she was no longer certain whether she had arrived at it or remembered it, and she did not pursue the question.

She walked the outer dock each morning and noted the ice line in the log. January 22: inner cove ice approximately four inches, opaque. Outer approach clear. Callie B. and Margaret Rose, outer dock, checked and secure. Wind NNW at eleven knots. Barometer 30.14, steady. She checked the Callie B.'s bilge pump — running clean, had been since the boat was tied up — and noted it and went on.

The Callie B.'s bilge pump was what she had gone to check on the night of October 11. It had been running clean then too. She had made her note and left the dock at 2330. She had told Ennis this, and it was accurate.

She did not think about this on the dock. It presented itself and she noted it and moved on.

Back in the shack she ran the 0800 check on the BC-1206 — weather, traffic conditions, the harbor operations she monitored on the coast — and logged the result. Then she turned to the ledger.

She had been opening it to October since November. Not every morning; some mornings she skipped it. But she had opened it enough that it was a part of the mornings, and she had stopped asking herself why, the same way she had stopped asking herself why she rechecked the Callie B.'s bilge pump when she knew perfectly well it was running clean.

The gap was on the right-hand page, midway through the ledger. Pages 114 through 119: Ennis had taken them at 1008 on October 12, folded them into his document envelope with the efficiency of a man for whom this was ordinary procedure. What remained was a faint unevenness in the binding — not something you would notice if you weren't looking, but a different weight when you held the spread open. The stitching showed at the spine, pale thread where the section had gone.

The entry before the gap was October 8. Weather, tide, traffic, nothing unusual. Her handwriting, quick and competent. The entry after the gap was October 13: the body, the Coast Guard, the departure of the district lieutenant at 1008. Her handwriting again, abbreviated.

She held the spread open and looked at both sides of what wasn't there.

Then she closed the ledger and left it on the desk.

---

On Wednesdays she went to Merrill's for coffee. Owen had gone every morning; she had made it once a week, not from economy alone — once a week gave it something mornings would have worn smooth. In January, Merrill's had a particular quality: warm in a way the shack was never warm, and occupied in the particular way that the working middle generation occupied things in January, which was with a settled patience, people who had made their arrangements with winter and found a diner a reasonable place to sit with them.

She was on her second cup when Reg Farber came in.

She knew him as she knew most of the fishermen: by his boats first. Eight years of the Callie B. — the bilge pump, a mooring chain in '41, a registration discrepancy the fall before last — had given them a specific and sufficient acquaintance. Since October they had another kind: the kind produced by proximity to the same event. When they ran into each other at the dock or on the road, the body was there without being mentioned. This was common enough in a town of Coldwater's size. Most things that had happened were there without being mentioned.

Farber sat two stools down from her. The counterman brought him coffee without being asked. He looked into his cup.

He said: "I've been thinking about that fellow since October."

Eira said: "I expect most people have."

"My boy." He stopped. "He doesn't say much about it. Hard to tell what kids carry."

"No," she said.

He drank his coffee. She held her cup. Outside the front window the road was frozen and empty, the empty that Wednesday afternoon in January produced with particular thoroughness.

He said: "I was up late on the eleventh. Night before."

She set down her cup.

"Couldn't sleep." He said it without particular weight; insomnia in January was ordinary. "I was on the porch around eleven, eleven-thirty. I saw a boat come in." He paused. "Small wooden thing. No lights."

She waited.

"It tied up at the far end of the dock — past the dock extension, where you can't see from the road. I watched it for a few minutes. I've gone without navigation lights myself, close in, when I've been out later than I planned and I know the water. Didn't think much of it." He shook his head slowly. "Went back inside around midnight. It was gone by morning."

"When did it connect?" she said.

"Few weeks after. I was thinking about who the man could have been and I remembered seeing the boat and thought — I don't know." He looked at her. "I don't know that it's connected. I just had it sitting with me and didn't know where to put it."

"Did you report it to the Coast Guard?"

He turned his coffee cup on the counter. "No. Didn't think to. Should I?"

She said: "I'll mention it if it's relevant."

He said: "Probably isn't." He looked up at the counterman. "You have apple pie today?"

---

She walked home in the cold.

The road was frozen, the ruts from the last mud period locked into the surface now until spring. She kept to the margin where the ground was flat. January light at two-thirty had maybe ninety minutes in it before the sky gave up. She could feel it going.

What Farber didn't know: she had been on the dock. In the shadow of the Callie B.'s wheelhouse, twenty feet from the dock extension, close enough to hear the engine cut. She had seen the boat come in and she had watched it tie up. She had seen the man step off and stand at the foot of the dock for a moment, getting his bearings — the dark overcoat, the shoes that were wrong for the dock in the way they turned out to be wrong for everything. Twenty seconds, maybe less. Then he had turned and walked toward the breakwater. She had watched him go.

She had gone home and gone to bed. She had told Ennis she had checked the bilge pump, found it running clean, and left the dock at 2330. All of that was true. The truth as she had told it contained all of it except the boat and the man and those twenty seconds, which were not in the account she gave and not in the pages Ennis took and not anywhere except in her.

She had run the other version in October. Thoroughly, carefully, arriving at her conclusions the same way she arrived at conclusions about weather: by looking at the available information from each angle until the picture was clear. The conclusions held. She had not changed them.

What was different now was Farber.

He had been on his porch. He had seen the boat come in from the same direction she had seen it. He had watched it for a few minutes — his words — which meant he had stood in the cold in the dark doing his own version of what she had done from the shadow of the Callie B., and then he had gone inside and not thought much of it until he had, and he had carried it for three months because he didn't know where to put it, and he had put it down at Merrill's on a Wednesday in January because the occasion was there and the Wednesday was long.

He didn't connect the boat to the body with certainty. He had said so.

The road turned uphill past the Congregational church. The church windows held the last of the afternoon light for a moment and then let it go. The sky above the tree line was pale gray, moving toward the blue that came before dark.

She had been the only person who knew about the boat for three months. She had not thought about it in those terms — had not told herself each morning, *I am the only person who knows the boat was there.* But she had known it the way she knew the tide tables: as a condition, a baseline, reliable because it had been reliable yesterday and the day before and the month before that. She had counted on it without knowing she was counting on it.

Farber had put a second point of knowledge into the world. He had done it the way people did things without knowing what they were doing — honestly, without urgency, because he had been meaning to go through that drawer and the occasion presented itself.

She was not the only witness now. She was the witness who knew the most. Farber had seen the boat. She had the boat and the man: the twenty seconds on the dock, the overcoat, the shoes, the direction he walked. Farber was missing those twenty seconds and he would not know to look for them.

The short road to her house. The maple in the front yard was bare, the branches black against a sky that was almost dark now.

She went inside.

She took off Owen's peacoat and hung it on the peg. The kitchen was cold; she had banked the stove before leaving and it needed tending. She put wood on and adjusted the draft and waited until the flame took before she closed the stove door.

She did not go to the log. She had thought, walking home, that there might be a form for Farber's account — some way of putting it into the record where it could exist separate from what she chose to do with it. She stood at the kitchen table. She did not go to the log.

She made supper. She ate. She cleaned up.

The barometer at four-thirty was 30.18 and rising. Clear weather coming, and cold with it.

Reg Farber's information was somewhere in her now, without a ledger to put it in. She did not know what she would do with it. She had not done anything yet.

She went to bed.

# A Report from Portland

By the last week of March the ice was going from the inner cove — pulling back from the edges first, a dark rim of open water widening an inch a day, the granite shelf of the shore returning in the mornings like something remembered. The center still held: opaque where it had been clear, four inches where it had been five, the surface pale and slightly sunken where the melt had come through and refrozen in February. She had been watching this progress for three weeks.

The Callie B. and the Margaret Rose had moved back to their slips on the twentieth. Farber first, because Farber was like that about weather and tide, and the Pelletiers a day behind. The lobster boats were still on trailers at Pelletier's yard — Kincaid's four, the two from the Dunbar brothers — waiting on the ice and on permits that came out of Portland at their own pace. She had six boats on the waiting list for the first week of April. The radio had been busy for two weeks: weather checks, supply questions, the kind of talk that accumulated when men had been on shore since January and the season was getting close.

She did her rounds at half past seven. Dock cleats, the drain at the float ramp, the fuel line, the BC-1206's daily check. The tide clock had gained a minute since she last reset it. She wound it, adjusted it, made a note. The spring smelled different from the other seasons — not better, she had stopped that mistake years ago — but specific: salt and diesel and the cold mud coming up where the dock skirting had held ice all winter, and underneath both, something opened that had been shut.

In the afternoon she wrote the permits. Six boats, six sets of documentation, the spring registration forms that had to be filed with Portland by April 15. She had been harbormaster for more than eight years and the forms had not changed. She worked through them from top to bottom, the same order every year.

---

The letter came in Friday's mail.

It arrived with the February billings from the fuel cooperative — they were always late — a parts catalog from Portland Chandlery, and a Coastal Patrol circular about spring procedure. She took the stack back to the desk and dealt with them in order: bills, catalog, circular. The envelope from Boston was last.

Standard government stock, cream-colored, slightly heavy. Return address: First Coast Guard District, Headquarters, Boston, Massachusetts. Redirected through the Portland auxiliary, which had added a date stamp in blue ink, March 28 — nine days in transit.

She opened it and read it through.

---

The letter was a page and a half. Dated March 19. An administrative lieutenant she didn't know. At the bottom, a notation in smaller type indicating the original inquiry had been received from the Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, port authority and was being distributed to relevant coastal stations for information and response.

The substance: a party in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, had received no word from a man to whom they had either lent or rented a small wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet. The man had departed Yarmouth approximately September 28, 1943, reportedly heading south by sea, with the stated intention of making landfall in Massachusetts. He had not returned the boat. The owner had assumed, initially, that the occupant and the boat had reached their destination and that the boat had been sold or left somewhere. The missing-persons report had not been filed until February 1944, the letter noted, because the owner had been uncertain whether the report was his to make.

The description of the occupant: male, middle-aged, of continental European appearance, with limited English. No further identifying details available from the Yarmouth party.

The inquiry was being routed to coastal stations, the letter explained, because a body fitting some elements of the description — middle-aged male, civilian, no identification — had been recovered on the Maine coast in October 1943. The District was asking affected ports to provide any relevant information.

She set the letter on the desk. She read it again. Then she sat for a while with the radio on the south wall and the tide charts above it and the April light coming through the shack's east window.

---

What the letter had: a wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet. A single male occupant. Continental European appearance. Limited English. Departed Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, approximately September 28, 1943. Destination: Massachusetts, loosely.

What she had: a wooden boat, no lights, tied at the dock extension on the night of October 11, 1943. Gone before morning. A man stepping off the boat and standing at the foot of the dock extension before walking toward the breakwater. Dark overcoat, city cut. Leather shoes that had never been made for a dock. She had been in the shadow of the Callie B.'s wheelhouse, twenty feet away. She had watched him for twenty, thirty seconds. She had not seen his face.

She turned slightly and looked at the chart above the radio.

Yarmouth to Coldwater Reach. She had never made the crossing herself, but she knew the coast by chart and radio contact and the general arithmetic of small-boat passage. Yarmouth was in the southwest of Nova Scotia — a harbor town, working, the kind of place where you could rent a boat from someone who had one to rent. Once you cleared Cape Sable and came south along the outer coast you were in open water: the Atlantic running hard in autumn, the Bay of Fundy's tides working the approaches, no shelter until you reached the outer islands and could begin to work your way inshore. The crossing from Yarmouth to the midcoast of Maine was not impossible in a well-found boat with a good engine. In an eighteen-foot wooden motorboat, alone, in the last days of September — it was something you would undertake carefully, or not at all.

The end of September 1943 had closed badly on this coast. She had the record. Four days of northeast blow beginning the 27th, moderate on the 30th, another two days of wind and rain before it cleared around October 4. If he had departed on the 28th and run into the blow — and he would have run into it, there was no way not to, it had run from the Maritimes to Cape Ann — he would have had to find shelter somewhere and wait it out. An eighteen-foot wooden boat could have done this: put in behind an island, anchor in a cove, wait for the weather to settle. Then come out again and make what time he could.

September 28 to October 11 was thirteen days. Portland to Yarmouth by sea was roughly 200 miles along the coast. At that distance, with four days of bad weather in the middle, a small boat making eight or ten miles a day in the open and thirty or forty in a good stretch — thirteen days was not an impossible time. It was a long time. It was the arithmetic of someone who was being very careful, or very slow, or who had run into trouble more than once and recovered from it and continued south anyway.

She looked at the letter. Middle-aged. Continental European appearance. Limited English.

The man she had seen at the dock extension: a dark overcoat, city cut. Leather shoes. He had stood at the foot of the dock for thirty seconds before he moved. He had walked with the deliberate care of a man who was very tired or not well — she had noticed this and stored it in November and had not returned to it since. He had not spoken. He had not known she was there.

No papers. The Coast Guard had searched the body on October 12 and found nothing: pockets empty, no identification, nothing to give him a name or an address or a record of where he had come from. She had been present when Ennis conducted the search. She had watched him go through the coat and the trouser pockets — exterior, breast, inside — and come up with nothing.

A man traveling from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, in a borrowed boat, at the end of September, heading south toward Massachusetts, without papers. With limited English. With continental European appearance, which was the letter's language and not hers, but which was the right kind of language for what she had seen at the dock.

The letter did not contain a name.

---

The desk drawer stuck in the way it always did — the wood had swollen in February's wet and had not recovered fully — and she pressed it open and laid the letter at the back, behind the January freight manifests, which were thick and which she would not need again until the end-of-year accounting.

She should respond. The letter asked specifically for any relevant information; she had the authority to write a response and direct it through the Portland auxiliary to the District's administrative office. She would do this.

She closed the drawer. She opened the log and wrote the afternoon's conditions: wind NNW at ten knots, barometer 30.24 and rising, inner cove northwest corner open approximately one-third, outer dock in good order, registration forms filed for six vessels pending April permits. Tide times for the evening. She closed the log.

At three-thirty she did her afternoon rounds. Dock, drain, radio check. The cove had opened another half inch since morning.

---

She made supper and ate it at the table. She had done this every evening for more than eight years, since there was no one else to do it and no one in the house who would eat it with her. The kitchen was Owen's kitchen: his shelf heights, his arrangement of the cups on the left side of the cabinet, the window latch he had repaired in September of 1935 and which she had not replaced because it worked. She sat with her plate and then with her tea and with what the letter had put in the room.

The man had come from Yarmouth. He had left on approximately September 28, heading south, in a small wooden boat. He had no papers and limited English and the kind of appearance that was described by phrases like continental European, which was what you wrote when you meant something more specific but did not have the specifics. He had arrived at Coldwater Reach on the night of October 11 after thirteen days of bad-weather passage and she had watched him walk to the breakwater.

He had been heading somewhere. This was what the letter had put into the room and would not take back. He had borrowed a boat in Yarmouth and gone south, and Yarmouth was not where you ended up — it was where you passed through on your way to somewhere else, somewhere with a wharf and a street address and a person who was expecting you. Massachusetts, loosely. Boston, probably. He had had a destination and a reason for the destination and people at the destination who had expected his arrival.

They had received instead the kind of silence that comes when someone does not arrive and cannot be found. The owner in Yarmouth had waited five months to file his report, uncertain whether it was his to file. There might be other people who had waited longer, who were more certain that it was not theirs to file, who had no way to report anything because reporting would require them to explain why they had been waiting for him.

She sat with this for some time. The March dark had come down on the cove and the harbor and the breakwater's red light was running at the end of its two hundred yards of granite. Five miles visible offshore. The same as always.

She did not write anything in the log.

She went to bed.

# Ice Out

The ice had been pulling back from the northwest corner since the last week of March. Each morning she had checked it from the dock end before opening the shack — the strip of ice shelf along the cove's north wall narrowing by degrees, turning gray and porous, the color of something ceding ground. She logged the observations without commentary, the way she logged the barometer and the bilge on the Callie B. and the angle of the breakwater light at first dark: not expecting any particular morning's measurement to matter on its own, but keeping the increment because the day the increment did not come was a day that needed marking.

May 3, 1944. She opened the shack door at five-thirty-five and the inner cove was open water.

She stood in the doorway for a moment with her hand on the frame. The salt came in off the water the way it did in working season — not the thin cold salt of winter, which arrived only on high wind off the open bay, but the full harbor salt: diesel underneath it, the particular smell of the tide flat at low water and the channel bottom's specific mud and something above all of it that was specifically this harbor, this reach. It had been five months. She had not been keeping track of that, or had not let herself keep track, and standing in the door she noticed she had been keeping track.

She wrote in the log: *Ice out, inner cove, full extent. May 3, 1944. 0535 hours.*

She checked the tide clock. She had reset it Monday, as she always did on Monday mornings, and it was running true. She made the notation in the maintenance column.

She ran the radio: primary check, backup frequency, Coast Guard channel at Group Southwest Harbor, the weather broadcast from the Rockland station. Northeast, light and variable, high overcast, no precipitation through Sunday. She wrote it in the weather column.

Before the lobster boats went out she walked down to the second slip to check the Callie B.'s bilge pump. The pump had been running on slow-leak monitor since November — the port quarter taking water at its old rate, never more than expected, twice-weekly checks through the winter, one spike in January when the hard freeze put tension on the hull and the pump managed six inches over three days before things equalized. She had notified Farber in January; she had continued the checks. Now she ran the pump through its test cycle: float switch responding, intake clear, discharge running clean. She wrote it in the maintenance log. The pump was running clean.

The lobster boats went out before six. She counted them from the dock end: nine, which was the full complement for the harbor. The permits had been backed up in Portland — a classification question on the renewed forms that had to be resolved in writing — and had not cleared until the last day of April, but all nine boats had their papers and the nine boats went. Burgess first, as he had been first every season she could recall, leading out with the particular certainty of a man who was not waiting on anyone. Then the two brothers from the far end of the village, then the others in loose sequence, each one pushing through the channel mouth and picking up speed in the open water beyond the bar.

She watched them clear the breakwater.

At seven-sixteen the Callie B. went out, the Margaret Rose ten minutes behind it. She logged their departures. Reg Farber at the Callie B.'s wheel, standing slightly off-center in his usual way, raised a hand as he cleared the dock without looking toward it.

The radio was busy after eight. The weekly freight traffic from Rockland, a fishing advisory from Group Southwest Harbor, two exchanges on the lobster frequency that she monitored in case one of them was going to become a buoy-line dispute — one of them was, and she noted it. She ran the correction forms for the six seasonal mooring permits that had been in error since April: each one reviewed against the tonnage classification table, corrected, re-signed. Six minutes per form. She sealed the Portland envelope.

It happened every year — the harbor going from winter's compression back to its working configuration in the space of a single week. She was aware it should not still catch her slightly, after nine seasons, and every year it caught her slightly. How quickly it became itself again.

---

Reg Farber came to the shack on the Friday after ice-out.

He was a large man and the shack was not a large room and he had developed, over years, the practice of stopping at the threshold rather than coming in. This kept things workable. She had never named it aloud and did not name it now. He stopped in the threshold with his cap in both hands and said he had a question about the June M.

The June M. was his lobster boat, a thirty-two-foot wooden trap hauler he had been running for eleven years. She waited.

He laid it out the way he laid things out: in order, without additions. The June M.'s seasonal dock fee came due at the end of the month. He was behind on it. The mooring line had snapped in the hard January freeze — the temperature dropping faster than the almanac had called for, the line under more tension than it was designed to carry before he got to the dock to ease it. When it let go it took dock cleat number seven with it, midpoint starboard of the outer float. The cleat had been in questionable condition before the failure. He had not wanted a dispute about whose responsibility the replacement was, so he had paid for it himself: forty-two dollars for the hardware and the installation labor. He had also had a winter where the trawl catch was down and the fuel cost was up, but he mentioned these in the way of context rather than argument and moved past them.

He was asking if she could defer the June M.'s seasonal fee to July.

The light in the shack was the flat morning light that came through the south-facing window over the radio. She could hear the radio cycling through its scan in the background, the low static between intervals.

The fee schedule was fixed by the District office. She did not have formal discretion to defer a seasonal boat fee. The hardship fund was administered through Portland with an application process and a result that came in August when it came at all, and August was not July and July was not May. Farber was not a man in financial distress — he had been running two boats from this harbor for fifteen years — but forty-two dollars onto a low season was forty-two dollars, and she was not going to name the hardship fund as an answer to his question.

She pulled the spring maintenance folder from the back of the desk.

She had kept the maintenance log in calendar quarters since she took the desk over in 1936. One page per quarter, each dock fitting and installation numbered and noted by location. She found the October 1943 page. She ran her finger down the entries until she found what she had noted on the evening of October 11: *Outer dock, east float hardware survey. Cleat #7, midpoint starboard: bracket wear evident, seating slightly loose. Recommend assessment spring 1944.*

She had written that entry in the fall and filed it and it had been on her spring list. She had not gotten to it. The spring list had four items ahead of it.

She looked at the entry.

She said: "I'll need to look at the cleat."

"It's been replaced," Farber said. "New hardware, good installation."

"The condition of the original fitting is a maintenance question. It was flagged in my fall survey for spring assessment." She set the folder on the desk. "A fee review pending that inspection is within the standard process."

He said nothing for a moment. He was working the cap slightly with both hands, not nervousness, the physical version of waiting.

She wrote in the log: *June M. seasonal fee under review pending dock maintenance inspection — cleat #7, outer float, east of midpoint starboard. Per fall 1943 survey notation. Review to be completed prior to end of month.*

She dated it. She said: "Can you be at the dock Thursday morning?"

"Seven o'clock," he said. "I'll be there."

She said: "I'll write it up as I find it."

He held his cap for a moment. He said: "I appreciate that, Eira."

She didn't answer to that. He left.

She looked at the entry. The maintenance note from October was in the quarterly record, dated, in her handwriting. The spring inspection was overdue by her own log. Her authority to hold a seasonal fee pending a maintenance question was in the harbormaster's charter. The July timeline would follow from the inspection timeline without requiring the log to carry anything the log would not carry. The entry was accurate. It was complete.

She picked up the mooring permit form she had set aside when he knocked. The radio gave her the eleven o'clock weather update. She wrote it in the weather column and went back to the form.

---

Thursday morning at seven o'clock she was at the outer float.

Farber was already there. He was a man who arrived on time in the way that people who respected their own word arrived — without ostentation, just there. She acknowledged him with a nod. She knelt at cleat number seven.

The replacement hardware was in good condition: galvanized steel, properly bedded in the float decking, the seating solid. She checked the surrounding plank for movement; none. She checked the adjacent cleats on either side for comparison; both showed similar surface weathering, both solid. She stood up and made the notation in the inspection log she had brought: *Cleat #7, replacement hardware, installation sound. Base deck condition within acceptable range. Pre-existing bracket wear at original fitting location consistent with fall 1943 survey notation. Failure mode: line-tension overload, not fitting failure.* She initialed it and dated it.

She said: "The cleat's in order. The original fitting was fair wear."

Farber said: "I know that."

"The inspection supports the fee schedule adjustment. The review is closed."

He nodded. That was all. He went back to the June M., which was in the slip behind them, lines checked, ready for the day's run. She watched him go aboard and wrote the final notation in the inspection log.

The morning was overcast, the temperature forty-two degrees, the harbor in its first full working week. She walked back to the shack.

---

The Heron came in on Tuesdays and Fridays from Rockland — mail, packaged freight, occasionally a passenger traveling one direction or the other. She used the outermost slip, the longest approach in the harbor. Eira had assigned it in 1942.

The second Friday in May. She was working through the monthly mooring-line inspection — outer dock, section by section, each line lifted and checked for chafe at the attachment fitting and surface rust on the hardware — when she heard the Heron's horn off the breakwater. She was at section eleven. She kept working. The Heron needed twelve minutes from the breakwater to the dock and she had seven sections remaining.

She was coming down the outer dock when she saw Marcus Klein standing at the end of it.

He was there for the mail, or for the same kind of parcel the Emergency Committee sent up through the Rockland freight — she had seen him once before on a mail-boat Friday, waiting for a box addressed in a Manhattan hand. He stood at the end of the dock the way he stood everywhere he stood: upright, coat buttoned regardless of the temperature, looking at the harbor with an attention that was not a harbor person's attention. She could not have said, exactly, what the difference was. He was watching the water. He was not reading it.

She kept moving.

He said: "Warmer."

She said: "Finally."

He moved in the direction of the Heron's slip, which was the direction she was moving. She kept her eye on the approach line.

He said: "The boats are back."

She said: "They are."

The Heron was throttling back at the right distance, coming in at the slight angle Ayers always corrected in the last fifty feet. She watched the approach.

He said: "Any word —"

She said: "Nothing from Portland."

He nodded. She was at the slip. The bow line came across and she held it while the Heron came alongside, then cleated it and checked the fender placement. Ayers said, "Morning, Eira." She said, "Morning." She went to check the stern line while the freight hatch opened.

She did not look back at Klein. She heard the hatch open and the shift of boxes. By the time she finished the stern line he had moved to the hatch, collecting whatever was addressed to him. She went back to section twelve.

The line at section twelve showed surface weathering on the starboard fitting — not structural, worth monitoring. She wrote it in the inspection log. She finished the remaining sections. The afternoon sea fog was beginning to come in off the bar, the familiar mid-May pattern, the visibility softening at the channel mouth without obscuring the breakwater light.

She walked back to the shack.

---

She wrote the day's entries at six in the evening.

Weather: overcast, high cirrus by early afternoon. Wind northeast seven to twelve knots, backing southwest by eighteen hundred hours. Sea fog, harbor approach, fifteen-thirty to seventeen hundred. No precipitation. Visibility unlimited otherwise.

Traffic: nine lobsters out, nine in. Callie B. out 0716, in 1638. Margaret Rose out 0724, in 1503. Heron arrived 1050, departed 1116. Two freight deliveries, afternoon, invoices attached.

*June M. seasonal fee review — closed. Cleat #7 dock inspection completed May 11. Replacement hardware satisfactory, installation sound. Pre-existing wear condition per fall 1943 survey confirmed; line failure attributed to tension overload, not fitting defect. Review complete. June M. seasonal fee rescheduled: due July 31, 1944.*

She blotted the entry and dated it.

She wrote the barometer reading — 30.09 inches, falling slowly — and the morning and evening tide observations. She wrote the mooring-line inspection summary: thirty-one sections inspected over two days, one notation for monitoring, no replacements required.

The shack had gone quiet around her. The radio was on the evening scan, low, cycling through the empty frequencies. Owen's log ledger was on the bottom shelf of the cabinet to her left, where she had moved it in February 1936 when she'd taken the desk over — his handwriting running from June 1891 through the last entry in November 1935, where it stopped. She had not moved it since. The current ledger, her third volume, was on the desk.

She had a quarter of the page left below the day's entries.

She wrote: *May. Ice out. Harbor open. All boats accounted for.*

She put the pen down. She blotted it. She looked at it for a moment.

Then she closed the log.

# June Radio

Four-thirty in June was different from any other four-thirty. The dark was shorter and thinner — already a gray line at the east edge of the fields when she opened the barn door, the horizon somewhere between night and something. The cows were already up. June made them impatient, all that summer weight on them, and they came to the stanchions without needing to be pressed. The hay was warm and dry and the barn's smell this month was not the closed winter smell but something looser, the boards having breathed themselves out all through May.

She moved through the milking the way she always did, can to can, one end of the row to the other. The light over the door came on automatically when she switched the barn circuit; she had not needed the kerosene lamp since April. By the time she finished the second row the gray outside had become something almost blue. By the time she was done and washing down the stanchions a quarter past six, the fields were fully lit.

She came out of the barn. The south field was high and green, the hay cutting maybe a week out. The silo, the icehouse, the farmhouse: the yard in the morning quiet, everything where it was.

Lonzo arrived at eight with the prisoners. He came through the front gate in his patient way with the Springfield on his shoulder and the four of them behind him: Fischer first, then Brandt, then Walther, then Karl last, looking at the fence posts or the middle distance the way he usually did. Lonzo said good morning toward the barn where she was standing. She nodded. They went to the south field for the morning's work and the day looked like a Tuesday in June.

---

The kitchen radio was on at breakfast, as it was every morning now. The habit had formed somewhere in the spring; she couldn't have named the day. Her father held the Rockland paper without reading it. Her mother stood at the stove with her back to the room. The radio cycled through its programs in the ordinary way.

She was pouring coffee into her cup.

The radio said: *Allied forces have landed on the coast of Normandy. The operation is underway.*

She set the coffee pot down. The cup was beside it, she had not poured, she did not remember stopping.

The radio kept talking.

Her father pushed back from the table. He crossed to the radio and turned it louder, both hands on the knob, and came back and sat down. He had his coat on from the morning barn check and he did not take it off. He sat at the table with his coat on.

The radio said: *A massive amphibious operation. Airborne divisions in the early morning hours. The Allies on French soil.*

She sat down. She had her coffee cup in front of her now, somehow; she didn't remember pouring. She picked it up and held it.

Her mother came in from the garden at quarter past nine and sat down at the table between them and stayed. The three of them in the kitchen with the radio going, eating and not eating. Hannah ate a piece of bread, then set the second piece down. Her father's food sat where her mother had put it. Her mother had her hands folded in front of her and her attention pointed somewhere ahead of herself, all the way into the radio, the way her silence collected itself when it had somewhere to go.

The CBS correspondent said: *Casualties are reported to be significant. The fighting continues at several points along the beachhead.*

The BBC faded in through static at ten-fifteen when the kitchen set picked up the signal — it did this some mornings, caught the BBC clear and others got nothing — and the BBC voice was more formal than CBS but said similar things: *Operation Overlord. The largest amphibious operation in history. Allied forces establishing positions.* She tried to hold the two accounts in sequence and could not. Two voices from two studios in London both saying Normandy, saying beaches, saying dawn.

Her father's hands were flat on the table.

Through the window over the sink she could see the south field.

Four figures out there, far enough that she could not read their faces, not even which one had stopped moving. At the northeast corner, one of them stood briefly apart from the others — she could tell it was Karl by his build, the particular width of his shoulders, the size of him she had been looking at across fences and through glass for more than a year. Then he bent down and went back to the row and he was not distinguishable from the others at that distance.

Camp operations would have told them. She did not know in what form or at what hour — roll call, a guard with a statement, something. But it would be strange if they hadn't known by now.

She took her plate to the counter and washed it and put it in the rack. Her father was still at the table. The radio was still talking.

---

She heated soup at noon and set it beside him. He ate it, which she noticed without looking at him directly, the bowl emptying while she ate her own soup standing at the counter. The radio had not been turned off. It said: *The Prime Minister addressed the House of Commons this morning. The King has spoken to the nation.* It said: *Fighting continues at the beachhead.* It said the names of the beaches and she could not retain them in order.

She went out at one o'clock. The north barn needed the afternoon hay brought down from the loft, and the east-pasture gate needed checking after the spring flooding had shifted the post on the hinge side. The farm did not stop for this. She pulled her jacket from the hook by the door and went out.

Outside the day was warm and cloudless and knew nothing about any of it. The fields were the fields. The sky was a June sky. She went to the north barn and spent the better part of an hour on the hay and the gate, and when she came out and crossed the south end of the yard she was taking the shorter way back to the kitchen, which meant passing along the fence line of the south field.

Karl was at the northeast corner, thirty yards from the fence. He was bent at the waist, working along the row, his head down. She could see his face clearly from this distance. It was his working face, the same one every day, and she could not read anything in it from here.

She did not stop.

There was nothing to say today and no place to say it — not with Lonzo twenty-five yards away eating his lunch off the tailgate, not with all of them visible from the farmhouse window, not with the morning still in her head and the radio going in the kitchen and no German that was the right German for the gap between the fence and the row and what this day was. She went back to the kitchen.

Her father was still at the table. He had turned the newspaper face-down at some point, which she had not seen him do.

---

By four o'clock he had moved to the parlor.

The parlor radio was the better set, the signal cleaner and the BBC coming in without the kitchen static. He was in the chair he used only in winter — the corner chair by the window, the one with the gray slipcover her mother put on every November and took off every April. The coat was off now, folded over the arm. He had not called her in.

She passed the doorway twice on errands and saw him there each time in the same position: hands in his lap, the radio on the side table. The quality of his stillness was the same one she had seen in December 1941, that Sunday, when she had been fifteen and had stood in the kitchen doorway not knowing whether to go in. Something very large was being absorbed very slowly and there was nothing left over for the surface of his face.

She went in and sat in the straight chair by the door. He did not look at her. The BBC correspondent was saying that additional forces were moving to reinforce the initial landings, that the situation continued to develop, that the casualties could not yet be fully accounted for. She sat for a while and then stood and went back to the kitchen.

Her mother came through a few minutes later with a cup of coffee and went into the parlor and set it on the side table next to the radio, next to his hand. She said nothing. He reached for the cup without looking up and drank from it and set it back down. Her mother came back to the kitchen.

Hannah watched her come back and turned to the stove and put the kettle on.

---

The prisoners came in from the field at five. She heard them through the open kitchen window — Lonzo's voice carrying across the yard without the words, and then the four of them moving through the yard to the icehouse, and then the icehouse door. Then quiet from that direction.

She made supper. By six her father had come in from the parlor and sat at the table and eaten, which surprised her — she had expected him to carry the day's stillness through to tonight unchanged. But he ate all of his supper, carefully, the way he did everything carefully. When he finished he set his fork down and sat for a moment and went back to the parlor.

Hannah washed the dishes. Her mother dried them and put them away. They had been doing this without talking all spring, longer than that, and tonight was the same except that the quiet in the kitchen had the weight of the day behind it. Her mother folded the dish towel and hung it on the hook. She looked at Hannah for a moment — not speaking, never speaking, but something in the look — and then went to bed.

Hannah dried her hands and went to the table.

She had *The Selected Poems of Robert Frost* open in front of her. She'd been working through it since the term ended, not because Marcus had assigned it but because she kept returning to it, kept finding the same pages. She was not reading now. She had the book open and the lamp on and the radio coming low from the parlor, where her father had turned it down after supper — she could hear it the way she heard rain, as a sound that was always there but was not a voice.

He came into the kitchen at half past eight.

She heard him before she saw him, his footsteps crossing the parlor floor. He came through the doorway and crossed the kitchen and stood at the window over the sink. He did not acknowledge her. He stood at the window the way you stand at a window when you are not trying to see something but cannot leave the glass.

Through the window: the yard, half-lit by the kitchen lamp. The icehouse at the far edge of the lamplight, its window dark.

He stood there for a long moment.

He said, to the window, to himself, to no one in the room: "Nun ist es fertig."

He did not explain it. He turned from the window and went upstairs. She heard his footsteps on the stairs, even and slow, the familiar weight of him on the second step that always creaked. The door at the top of the stairs opened and then closed.

The house was quiet.

The radio was still on in the parlor, very low, a program that had nothing to do with France — some orchestra in a studio somewhere, the sound barely carrying. She could hear it the way she heard the pump.

She did not move.

The kitchen lamp was on. Through the window the icehouse held no light. Karl was in the icehouse with Fischer and Brandt and Walther, in the dark across the yard, and whatever this day had been for them was behind the dark window and she had no way into it and it was not the night to try.

Her father had said: Nun ist es fertig.

She sat at the table. The fields were moving outside the open window, the long summer grass at the field edge, the nighthawks somewhere over the south field making the sound they made in June. She had heard it every June of her life. She heard it now.

The radio on low from the parlor. Karl in the dark across the yard.

What came next, she did not know.

# The Zenith

The Crow house was quiet when Marcus turned onto the back street at twenty minutes past four, the same time he always turned onto it on a Tuesday in June. He had stayed after the last Latin class to review a student's Cicero translation — the girl had mistaken a subjunctive for an indicative and the meaning had shifted in a way that was grammatically precise and entirely wrong — and he had marked it with a note instead of a mark, because at a certain level of wrongness the mark would not tell her anything useful about what she had misread and the note might. He was still thinking about this, about the difference between correcting a mistake and explaining its interior logic, when he heard it.

The parlor window was open two inches and through it the Zenith's voice reached him across the front yard and the porch: not music, but a man speaking carefully and without pause, in the register that radio voices took on when the news was large. He had learned this register since December 1941 — the slight slowing, the particular economy between phrases, as if the voice understood what it was carrying and was choosing to carry it with a certain care.

He came up the porch steps. He could hear the words now.

*Allied forces have landed on the coast of France. Units of the American, British, and Canadian armies, under the supreme command of General Dwight Eisenhower, have this morning begun the liberation of Western Europe.*

He opened the door and stood in the hall.

Through the parlor doorway: Henry was in his chair, still in his work clothes, his cap on the side table beside him. Lillian was in the doorway between the kitchen and the parlor with a dish towel held in both hands in front of her in the manner of something forgotten — she had picked it up for a reason and the reason had stopped mattering.

Neither of them looked at him.

Marcus set his briefcase on the floor beside the umbrella stand. He crossed the hall. He sat on the parlor sofa without taking off his coat.

---

The CBS broadcast ran through five and into six. At some point Marcus stood and turned the dial, past a farm report from Portland and two stations of static, until the BBC came in — clear and precise, the presenter carrying his characteristic quality of British reserve in the service of very large information. He went back to the sofa. From here he could manage the dial with a single step; he reached over several times during the six o'clock hour to correct for drift, the BBC signal restless on its frequency.

Lillian brought supper at half past six. She had made a pot roast with carrots and there were biscuits, and she carried everything in on a tray and set it on the low parlor table without asking whether anyone wanted to eat in the parlor. She had moved the table from its usual position against the wall and put two chairs alongside the sofa, so all three of them could sit without being far from the radio. This seemed to Marcus an act of considerable domestic intelligence — the recognition that the kitchen was, tonight, the wrong room.

He ate without being particularly aware of it. The food was warm and substantial and he was grateful in the simple way you are grateful for simple things when you cannot manage anything more complex.

They ate at the parlor table, the Zenith between them and the wall, the broadcasters alternating their accounts of the morning in France. The CBS man had a tendency toward summary; the BBC presenter organized by geography, moving from beach to beach along the coast in a way that Marcus found he could almost follow on the map he held in his head, though the map had gaps. He had never been to Normandy. He knew the coastline by its name and its latitude and the general shape of it on paper, but he could not place himself in it, could not see the particular quality of the sand or the height of the sea cliffs or the angle of the morning light coming in from the east.

He tried to imagine it and got only the radio's language.

Lillian refilled his coffee cup at seven o'clock without asking — real coffee, not the substitute that the ration book pushed you toward, the kind she made on evenings when something required it. He accepted it and set it on the table and forgot about it until it was cold and drank it cold. It was still good.

---

He found it by accident at nine o'clock, turning the dial during a CBS break.

He was looking for the BBC — it had drifted during the eight o'clock hour and he had been tracking it incrementally, degree by degree of the dial — when he passed through a frequency and heard something under the English signal. Not alongside it. Under it, as if two broadcasts occupied nearly the same position and one of them was losing ground.

German.

He rotated the dial back slowly until both were audible: the English on top, the German below it, the two signals in an involuntary conversation. The BBC European service — or something like it — the transmission aimed east, toward the occupied territories, designed for listeners with clandestine receivers hidden in farmhouse cellars and back-room closets, who were listening in a way that had consequences if they were caught listening. The German was formal and deliberate, the register of a language designed to be received once by someone in a dangerous position and understood immediately.

He listened.

The sentences were complete, clear, not overlapped by the English signal in any way that made them inaudible to someone who knew the language.

Henry said, "What's that other voice?"

"A German broadcast," Marcus said. "The BBC. For occupied Europe."

Lillian had come back from the kitchen with a dish towel, which she set on the arm of Henry's chair. She said nothing, but she was listening.

The German ran alongside the English for another thirty seconds — close enough on the dial that moving away from one would lose the other — and then the English signal gathered itself and the German reduced to something barely present. In the time it was clear:

Henry said, "What are they saying?"

Marcus translated without looking away from the radio. "They are saying the Allied landing was conducted at multiple points along the coast in the early morning hours, before the German commanders understood what was happening. They are saying the initial German assessment was that the landing was a diversion, not the primary operation." He stopped, listening. "They are saying the element of surprise —"

The broadcast shifted. The CBS signal reasserted itself and the German was gone; what remained was the American presenter saying something about airborne divisions and the pre-dawn hours and the fields behind the beaches. Marcus released the dial. He sat back on the sofa.

Lillian sat down in the armchair by the lamp, which she had turned low at seven when the evening had settled into itself. Henry was in his chair, his hands in his lap, his expression the one Marcus had come to understand as Henry's form of total attention — it was not demonstrative and could be read, by someone who didn't know him, as merely neutral; it was the furthest thing from neutral.

The three of them sat in the low lamplight with the Zenith speaking at the wall.

---

He had not been trying to think about Paris.

His job in this room was to track the dial, to translate if there was anything that needed translating, to be present to what was happening on the radio in the way that this household had decided to be present to it together rather than alone. He was not trying to think about Paris. But Paris was present in the way that certain things were present on such evenings: not summoned, not avoidable, simply there.

He had been in Paris for twenty-four months, from the spring of 1938 until May 1940. He had left before the Germans came — made the calculation in May and acted on it, not knowing at the time whether the calculation was right, not knowing it was right until several weeks afterward when the information began arriving about the people who had not made the same calculation. So Paris for him was not June 1940. He had not seen the flags in the Place de la Concorde or the soldiers coming down the Champs-Élysées. He had not seen any of that. He had the twenty-four months before it: the reading room at the Bibliothèque nationale, where a reader's card was the only requirement and a man could sit from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon and the staff required nothing further. The Sainte-Chapelle in November. A café near the Odéon where he had spent several evenings working on a chapter about Klopstock, the coffee good and the other patrons uninterested in him, which was its own form of grace.

The Louvre. He had been to the Louvre more times in twenty-four months than he had been to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in ten years in Vienna — something he had not anticipated of himself, that temporary residence in a city made him attend to it more carefully than permanent residence, as if the known deadline of departure organized the seeing.

German soldiers had been in the Louvre for four years.

He was hearing, on the Zenith, that this might be beginning to change — that the soldiers might leave the streets of Paris if the battle at Normandy moved in the direction the announcer's careful optimism implied. He listened to the optimism as a document: the radio presenter knew, tonight, which things he was authorized to say and which he was not, and so the shape of the optimism told you something about the shape of the uncertainty. The optimism was real but measured. The uncertainty was real and larger.

A colleague from the École pratique des hautes études who had gone to London in the spring of 1940, whose current address Marcus did not have and had not had for three years. A street that someone's cousin had known, the name of which Marcus had written on a piece of paper once and then lost. The apartment in Vienna that had been taken over by whoever took over such apartments, where a monograph on Klopstock sat in a drawer, or had been turned to other uses, or had been thrown away.

He had been not-knowing about the colleagues for four years. The not-knowing had accumulated a specific gravity over that time — different from the not-knowing of the early months, when not-knowing still felt like a condition that would resolve. It had not resolved. It had become the form in which he held the people he had known before 1938: probable but unverifiable, present in the room as a weight rather than as a fact.

He turned the dial. Found the BBC. Left it there.

Henry reached forward and adjusted the lamp. The room settled.

---

At ten o'clock the news became a different kind of news.

In the first hours, information had been arriving as it was established — each fact landing with the specific weight of something genuinely new, the picture building in real time, the uncertainty alive. At ten o'clock the uncertainty had not resolved but the shape of the day had solidified, and what the radio was doing now was the work of assembly: the same facts fitted into a chronology, the event having happened, the urgency dropping slightly and in its place something more like record. Still important. Not the same kind of important.

Lillian gathered the cups and the last of the supper things and took them to the kitchen. She came back and stood in the parlor doorway for a moment.

"I'm going up," she said.

"All right," Henry said.

She looked at Marcus in the particular way she looked at him on evenings when she was concerned — not with alarm but with care, direct and without gloss. "Get some sleep, Marcus," she said.

"I will," he said. "Thank you, Lillian."

She went upstairs. They listened to the sounds of her on the second floor: the hallway, the bathroom, the bedroom door, the familiar sequence of the house settling itself.

Henry reached over and turned the Zenith down to just above silence. The announcer continued at that volume without mass, a presence in the room rather than an account. The lamp was still on but low. The chairs were in something near their usual positions. The supper things were gone.

They sat.

---

Henry said, "I'm going to sit out on the porch a while."

He stood and went to the door. Marcus got his coat from the sofa arm and followed.

The night was warm in the way that June nights in Maine were rarely warm — warm meaning simply that it did not require defending against, that the air lay around you without urgency. The back street ran dark between the houses under the elm canopy; above it the sky held its midsummer blue even at this hour, more blue than black, some reserve of daylight still in the horizon to the north that the season refused to entirely give up.

Mrs. Pelletier's lamp was on across the way. Otherwise the street was quiet.

Henry sat in the left chair. Marcus sat in the right. It was the arrangement they had, established without discussion, in the way that specific chairs over enough evenings become your chairs without anyone having decided. He had been in this house for two years and three months and this porch was one of the things in Coldwater that had become, in a precise and undramatic way, his.

The elm leaves were still. Down the block a screen door opened and closed.

They were quiet for some time.

Henry said: "You have people there?"

Marcus considered this. He said: "I did. I don't know."

Henry nodded. He didn't follow it with another question.

The screen door was quiet. In the elm's upper branches, some movement of air too light to reach the porch shifted the leaves briefly and then stopped.

Marcus said, after a while: "It's a long way to go."

Henry said: "It is."

He was talking about the invasion — the distance the soldiers had crossed in the dark before dawn, the Channel, the boats, the beach they had crossed on foot. Marcus was talking about that too. He was also talking about his particular relation to the distance between here and France, between this porch and a city he had lived in and left before it became something other than itself. And he was aware, as he said the words, that Henry's relationship to the distance between here and somewhere else was not the same as his — that Norfolk, Virginia, and the distance between Coldwater Reach and there, and whatever lay in the country between those two coordinates, was a different distance from Marcus's distance even when they arrived at similar things: the not-knowing about people, the specific quality of being somewhere that required managing, the particular alertness you developed in a town that was yours only within certain limits.

Both of them understood this — that their versions of the distance were not the same distance — without its needing to be said. The porch held both versions in the same silence.

Another quarter-hour. The elm leaves. The street quiet under the midsummer sky.

---

He went back inside at midnight.

The Zenith was still on in the parlor, turned to its lowest setting, the announcer's voice carrying across the room without weight. Marcus turned it off on his way through. It seemed wrong to leave it talking to an empty room when what it had to say tonight had already been said and what remained was only the saying of it again.

The house was dark. Henry had come in a few minutes before him and the downstairs was settled.

He went upstairs.

His room was the way he had left it in the morning: the chair by the east window, the books on the desk arranged in the order he had put them in March and not disturbed since, the shortwave on the corner table with its dial dark. He had not turned it on all evening. What would it find that the Zenith had not already given him — what frequency between here and Europe would carry something the CBS presenter had not already said, that the BBC hadn't organized into its careful English, that the German signal, briefly audible under the English, had not already delivered in the register designed for people in danger?

He sat in the chair by the window without turning on the lamp.

Through the glass: the back street below, the elm canopy, and above it the sky, which even at this hour was holding its blue. He had not expected this of Maine when he arrived — that the sky refused its full dark for most of June, that the light had a longer argument to make than it did in Vienna or Paris or London, though London was different because of the blackout, because the dark in London had been enforced rather than natural, a different kind of dark altogether.

The window faced east.

He was aware of this in a way he was not usually aware of it: east across the town and east across the harbor and east across the Atlantic was France, and the men on the beach at Normandy, and the German soldiers withdrawing from certain positions, and somewhere beyond that, Paris — the reading room, the café near the Odéon, the colleagues whose current situations he did not know. He had been not-knowing about them for four years, and the quality of the not-knowing had changed as it accumulated, had become something he carried differently than he had carried it in 1940 or 1941 or 1942. He was not sure if the hearing that this might be ending would change the quality of the not-knowing, or whether it would only change the shape of what he did not know, which was not the same as knowing.

He did not open the notebook.

What was in the notebook was already there — the entries in shorthand, the arithmetic, the question at the page's bottom that had been there since April and was not going to answer itself tonight. Tonight was its own thing. He did not think it was necessary to open the notebook tonight.

He sat in the chair until the cold came in through the old window frame — June cold, not significant, but enough at two in the morning to make itself present. He stood. He went to the bed and lay down in the room's dark without the lamp, without the shortwave, without the notebook.

The window faced east. The dark outside it was the direction of everything he had come from: the libraries and reading rooms and cafés, the colleagues whose faces he could still reconstruct in certain lights, the monograph in a drawer in Vienna, the man on the Coldwater breakwater who had tried to cross from the far side of the same distance and had run out of road. The apartment that someone else lived in now, in the city the soldiers might be beginning to leave.

The lamp was off. Outside, the elm leaves moved against what remained of the sky's blue.

He closed his eyes.
