# School Hours

The back door of the Coldwater school used a skeleton key and required a lift on the handle before the lock would turn. Henry had learned this in his first week and it was still true eleven years later. He came through it at five-twenty and pulled the light chain at the bottom of the basement stairs.

The furnace was a Vulcan No. 6, coal-fired, installed 1921. In cold weather below twenty degrees it ran lean on the right side near the upper draft plate. Not a defect. A characteristic. He adjusted for it the same way every time: two scoops from the left bunker, one from the right, the draft plate turned clockwise a half-turn from where he'd left it Friday. He stood and listened. The furnace settled the way it should. He replaced the scuttle and went upstairs.

Before anyone arrived the building made its own sounds. The pipes coming up with the heat. The windows ticking in their frames. The particular creak of the second-floor hallway where the building had settled eastward over the years, the floorboards riding the angle. Henry had heard these sounds enough times that they weren't sounds anymore. They were the building telling him it was all right.

He had been in this building eleven years. He knew it in November: which windows swelled in their frames overnight, which stair nosings worked loose before Christmas, how much heat the east corridor lost between seven and noon when the wind came off the water from the north. He had a route, the same every day, adjusted for what the building needed.

The enrollment was down since spring. About fifteen students now, where there had been twenty-two. The lockers in the east bank had keys no one had come to collect in September. Henry kept them tagged in the supply closet. He'd asked Parsons in October what the protocol was for unclaimed lockers; she said she'd look into it. She hadn't looked into it yet. He swept past them every morning.

By seven-thirty he had the hallways swept. The chalk dust came off Marcus Klein's end of the hall in considerable measure — the man wrote everything twice on the board, the original text and then the English below it, all of it in a small precise hand that required more erasing than you might expect. Henry cleared the ledges and went downstairs and had the supply closet in order before the students arrived at eight.

They came through the front doors at eight. About fifteen of them. He heard them without needing to see them.

The building's social weather he read the same way he read the physical building — its pressures, what moved and what didn't. Mrs. Morse and Miss Tatum said good morning when they came by him in the hall. Mr. Reedy did not, which had been the case since September 1932, and Henry didn't expect it to change. He held the mop and let Reedy pass.

---

Mid-morning, carrying the repair kit from the supply closet to the east stairwell, Henry came around the corner as Marcus turned out of the German room. Marcus had a roll of papers under one arm — the Latin texts, from the look of them.

"The window," Marcus said.

"Still sticking?"

"The cold comes in on the north side."

"I'll get to it this afternoon," Henry said.

Marcus said that was fine and went left down the hall toward Latin. Henry watched him go — the slight figure, the coat a little wrong for the Maine weather, the careful step — and then went downstairs to put the kit away.

---

Around two o'clock he went to the teachers' room to collect the recycled paper. Mrs. Morse and Miss Tatum were there. He heard the word "breakwater" and then something about what a shame and whether the Coast Guard had ever found anything out.

He took the paper box and went.

The body had come in off the water five weeks ago. The Coast Guard had come and gone. The town had not stopped talking about it. He heard it most days, coming through rooms with the mop and the repair kit — the breakwater, the body, what the Coast Guard might or might not know. He expected to keep hearing it until something replaced it, and nothing had.

---

At three-thirty he stopped at the school office about the supply order. The chalk stock was running low and the coal bunker needed a second delivery before December. Parsons had the forms ready and they went through them. When they were done she kept him a moment.

"Mr. Crow," she said. She stopped. Started again. "There was a letter, early October. From a parent." Her eyes were on the wall beside his shoulder. "They wrote to the board — asking whether the school had properly considered Dr. Klein's background. Whether a German teacher was appropriate, given the times."

Henry waited.

"I wrote back myself. That his credentials were confirmed by the Emergency Committee and that the board had reviewed the matter thoroughly before his hire." She straightened the folder she was holding. "Nothing formal came of it. I kept the letter in the file. I thought you should know."

"I appreciate you telling me," Henry said.

She nodded and went back to her desk.

He went upstairs.

The German classroom was empty. Marcus had left at four, the way Marcus left every day at four. Henry opened the repair kit on the windowsill and took out the block plane. The casement had swollen in the frame — the putty on the north side gone brittle in October, the wood moving with the temperature. He shaved a quarter-inch off the casement edge, worked the sash until it seated right, and checked that the latch caught. Cold would still come in on the north side in any real wind. There was a limit to what a block plane could do about November.

He tested the window twice and closed the classroom door behind him. The hallway was empty.

He walked home.

---

Lillian had soup on the stove. Henry hung his coat on the peg by the kitchen door and washed his hands at the sink. The bowls were already out.

"How was today?" she asked.

"Fine," he said.

She set the bread on the table. They ate. After a while she said: "Is Marcus still running the shortwave every night?"

"I expect so," Henry said.

She got up and refilled his bowl without asking. He thanked her. They ate the rest of it and she washed the dishes and he dried them and put them away, and then she went upstairs. He heard her on the stairs — the third step from the top, the one that always spoke — and then the floor above him and then nothing.

He sat down at the kitchen table with the Rockland paper.

---

He had already read most of it. He opened it to the shipping notices anyway.

The furnace was running below. The window over the sink showed nothing but the dark outside and his own dim shape when he looked up. The house settled in the cold — the boards in the west wall moved once, then a second time, then stopped.

He didn't read the notices.

Parsons had the letter in her file. Nothing formal had come of it, and if something formal did come, he would know before it reached anywhere that could do damage. In eleven years he had become the person in this building that people told things to when they needed to set something down — Parsons tonight, others before her, others probably still to come. He had it now. He had fixed the window. The window was fixed.

He folded the paper and turned off the kitchen lamp and went upstairs in the dark. He knew each stair. He got into bed without waking Lillian and lay still until he was warm.

# Across the Fence

The ground had frozen in the first week of December and stayed frozen. Not the way mud froze at night and softened by midmorning — a freeze that went deep, that changed the sound underfoot from the clinging pull of October into something brittle and fractured, the top layer of earth heaved into plates by the cold, glittering where the morning light caught it. It made the barn yard alien in a way Hannah had not expected. Eight months ago the paddock had looked like the paddock. Now it looked like something that had been broken and set back down in the shape of itself.

She noticed it every morning on the way out and she noticed it again now, coming on ten o'clock, her breath going gray in front of her, the post-driver heavy under her arm. She had known for two weeks that the southeast corner of the paddock fence had shifted. She could see it from the yard: the post leaning maybe three inches off plumb, the wire sagging with it. But there had been the south field and the window stuffing and three days where the temperature had not come above freezing even at noon. She had not gotten to it. Her father had not said anything about it. He would not. The fence was the fence and the fence required attention and she would give it attention when she could and when she did it would be done.

She hauled the post-driver out from behind the stacked straw and carried it into the paddock. The cows were still in the barn with the morning's hay going; the outer yard was empty. From around the south side of the barn she could hear the sound of splitting wood — the prisoners' work this time of year, the cold driving the field labor out and the barnyard chores in — and once in a while Lonzo Reed's voice carrying a direction in the three German words he had accumulated over six months, none of which she had confirmed for certain.

She set the driver over the post and began.

---

December had changed the work. Not only the ground — the whole farm had shifted with the season the way it always did, the way she had watched it shift every year of her life. The prisoners had been at the farm since April, which meant she had watched them go through summer and into October and now into the cold, and she had watched how the work changed and they changed with it. Less field work now. More of what the barn required: wood-splitting, repairs to the siding on the east wall, the work of keeping the icehouse warm enough and the barn functional. They had become competent at it in a way she could see from across the yard — not performing the work but doing it, a difference that was visible in the back.

Karl had picked up more English than the other three. That was clear by October and clearer now. She had not been close enough to hear much of it directly, but she had heard enough through the barn wall or at the yard's edge to know that what he was working with was a strange inheritance. Lonzo Reed's English was the English of a man who had been on lobster boats for thirty years before the war gave him this particular assignment, and what had passed from Lonzo to Karl had come with all of that still attached. She had heard Karl say something to the quiet prisoner — the one who favored his right shoulder — that had the rhythm and the clipped command of a man giving orders over engine noise, but with the consonants reassembled around a different mouth. Lonzo's vocabulary through a Bavarian throat. She had not said anything about this to anyone.

Lonzo Reed wore two coats now, a canvas work coat over what looked like his old fishing coat, and he had taken to standing with his back against the south barn wall when the wind came off the water, the wall that held afternoon warmth the longest. The Springfield rifle was on a shoulder sling that he had rigged to not interfere with the second coat. He did his work, which was standing there, and the prisoners did their work, which was everything else. He was not unkind. He was in his late fifties and the barn had a woodstove.

Hannah worked the driver down and stopped to feel the resistance. Still loose. The frost heave had pushed the post up a good two inches; she had to get it seated past where the frost had taken it or it would just come back. She lifted the driver and set it again.

---

She did not know which day it had started — Lonzo going into the barn for something in the late mornings. She had seen it happen before this, three or four times over the fall, and it did not surprise her. He was gone seven minutes, maybe ten. The barn had the stove and the stove was the warmest thing within a hundred yards and Lonzo Reed was in his late fifties. The prisoners went on with the woodpile or whatever they had when he went in, and when he came back out they were where he had left them.

So when she looked up from the post and found the yard on the far side of the fence empty of a guard, she did not make anything of it. She fitted the driver over the post again.

She heard him before she saw him — the sound of boots on frozen ground, and then the sound of two pieces of split wood being set on the fence rail. She looked up.

Karl had a piece of split wood in each hand, the way you might carry something if you were crossing toward where a person was working and wanted a reason for the crossing. He set one piece on the top rail. He kept the other.

He looked at the post. He said, in English: "The post, it is—"

He made a gesture with his free hand: palm tilting over, the motion of something going off plumb.

"Frost heave," she said. "Happens every December."

He looked at her a moment and then said it back: "*Frost heave.*" Not mechanically. More the way you repeat something to get its measure before you put it away.

"The ground freezes hard and it pushes everything up," she said. "You drive the post back down past where it was heaved to, tamp it good, it'll hold till spring."

He looked at the ground beside the post. Then he crouched down and set his piece of split wood against the post at the base, bracing it from the outside. She had not asked him to. There was not exactly a need — you could drive the post without it — but the wood would give it something to seat against on the way down, and that was not nothing.

She lifted the driver and brought it down.

He held the brace and she drove it three more times. The post went solid. She checked it with her hand — no give, not even a suggestion of one. She reached into her coat pocket for the staple gun.

He stood and held the second piece of wood and looked out across the frozen paddock while she reattached the wire: three staples, check the tension, check it again. The wire held. The fence was done.

She didn't say thank you. He didn't wait for her to say it. He was already picking up the first piece of wood from the rail when the sound of boots on the barn threshold came from behind her.

Lonzo Reed crossed the yard with his hands in his coat pockets and the rifle sling over his shoulder. His eyes went to the woodpile — the other three were there, the work going — and he came back to his place against the south wall and pulled his collar up.

Karl carried both pieces of wood back to the woodpile and set them on the split stack.

He did not hurry. He did not look back.

---

She went in at noon with the post-driver. Set it in the corner. Washed her hands at the sink and stood at the counter and made herself a plate with bread and the last of the headcheese and ate it looking at the yard through the kitchen window.

The woodpile was where it was. The prisoner detail was working. Lonzo had his back to the barn wall in the afternoon light.

It had been ninety seconds. Less. She put her plate in the sink and went to get her school books.

---

That evening she was at the kitchen table with her algebra when her father came through from the back of the house. He didn't go to the table. He went to the window.

She had seen this enough times to know it without looking up. The particular tread, the small sound of the kitchen window being worked up an inch — it gave a line of sight toward the icehouse from the east corner of the frame. She kept her pencil on the page.

From outside, after a moment, came Karl's voice: low, careful. Her father answered. It was the German he used for these conversations — she had been hearing it since August and had not confused it with any other register he had. Not the barn German, die Kühe and the short working instructions, the language of cattle and what needed doing today. Not the supper German either, the brief declaratives about the south field or the feed schedule. This was different. This had the pace of two people finding what they shared, turning it in their hands, and she could hear in her father's voice something she had not heard from him in the direction of another person in two years: a quality of attention that was present rather than elsewhere.

She worked through the algebra. Page thirty-four, the right column. The equations had a quality she did not usually think about — everything came to a result, and the result was either right or wrong, and you could check it. She moved through the column and filled in the last answer and checked it.

Her father's voice went on, a sentence and then a pause, and Karl's voice answering, the words indistinct through the window and the cold and the twenty yards between the house and the icehouse. She was not trying to hear the words. She was hearing the quality of her father's voice the way you heard the quality of a sound you had learned to read for what it meant rather than what it said: the barn sounds at four-thirty a.m., the cows telling her what they were going to need before she reached them. Her father's voice telling her something she did not have a word for yet.

She put down her pencil and looked at the page.

She had been on the same farm as Karl Reinmar since April. Eight months. Before this morning he had said perhaps eight or ten words to her total — things addressed to the work, or to Lonzo, or to the yard in general, that she happened to be in earshot of. Today he had said perhaps thirty words. Thirty-two. *The post, it is—*. The tilting hand. *Frost heave*, the way he said it back, picking it up the way he picked things up, with the attention he gave to things that were useful.

She was aware of it the way she was aware of changes in the farm's arrangements. When the morning order shifted and the quiet prisoner came out third one day instead of second she had noticed and filed it and not named it. That was how the farm worked. You read it accurately and you did not reach ahead of what you could see.

She was not sure what she had been watching for in eight months. She was not sure she had been watching for anything. She had been watching Karl Reinmar the way she watched everything on this farm: with the accuracy of someone who grew up reading a complicated environment.

He had held the fence post. That was all.

The kitchen radio was off. Her mother had gone upstairs before eight. Her father's voice at the window, low and going on, the German in the dark.

She closed the algebra textbook.

The fence post would hold until spring. She had seated it past the frost line, tamped the ground around it with her heel, checked it twice. If February came in unusually hard it might heave again, but probably not. It was solid work and it would hold.

She stacked her books and carried them to the bottom of the stairs.

What she had resolved — if that was the word for something that had not felt like a resolution when it arrived, that had arrived more the way the farm's conclusions arrived, simply, without announcement — was to keep noticing what she noticed. Without deciding in advance what it meant.

She went upstairs. The cedar from her mother's linen chest reached her in the hall. She went into her room and wound the alarm to four-fifteen and got into bed.

Her father's voice was still going when she closed her eyes. She couldn't hear Karl's answers from up here. She could hear her father's voice, low and present and in the language she had grown up inside, talking to the person across the wall who was not her, and then she was in the morning and the dark and the alarm doing what it always did.

### Meta-commentary on cognition

**Cut:** "She did not know why she was thinking about it in units of time."

> Original context: "It had been ninety seconds. Less. She did not know why she was thinking about it in units of time. She put her plate in the sink and went to get her school books."

When the morning order shifted and the quiet prisoner came out third one day instead of second she had noticed and filed it and not named it. That was how the farm worked. You read it accurately and you did not reach ahead of what you could see."

> Original context: "She had been watching Karl Reinmar the way she watched everything on this farm: with the accuracy of someone who grew up reading a complicated environment, without putting a name to what the accuracy was in service of."

Without deciding in advance what it meant. It was not a dramatic position. It was the kind of position that didn't announce itself as one. She had been arriving at it for eight months without knowing that was what she was doing."

Three sentences of escalating structural analysis: the first labels the kind of position it is; the second restates the label; the third names the chapter's implicit arc ("eight months" arriving at "this"). All three describe the architecture of a resolution the preceding prose already conveyed. The final sentence is pure post-scene subtext naming — it tells the reader what to conclude from the chapter. Cut leaves the resolution itself and moves directly to the physical close (stairs, cedar, alarm).

Two sentences later, *He had held the fence post. That was all.* delivers the same thing without saying it. The clause was pre-glossing the payoff.

**4. Emotional structural analysis + post-scene subtext naming** — `"It was not a dramatic position. It was the kind of position that didn't announce itself as one. She had been arriving at it for eight months without knowing that was what she was doing."` Three sentences of escalating structural commentary on a resolution the preceding prose had already rendered. The last sentence names the chapter's arc for the reader. Cut leaves the resolution itself and drops straight into the physical close — stairs, cedar, alarm — which is the right ending beat.

# A Letter from New York

The second line of the examination instructions had given him trouble since Sunday evening.

He had written it out in his room the night before — three attempts in the margin of his notebook page, each crossed — and then again this morning on the classroom board before the first class came up the east stair. He stood at the board with the chalk and read back what he had written: *When you do not know a word, consult the sense of the sentence.* The problem was *consult*, which required the student to have an intuition about what consulting a sentence meant, and it was exactly this intuition that he could not assume. He wiped the line.

He tried: *If you do not know a word, work from what the sentence needs it to mean.*

He stood back.

The German classroom occupied the second floor's east end, and in December it received the morning light in a way that was briefly pleasant before the cold coming off the north sill reasserted itself — the cold was better now, since Henry had planed the casement, but there was still a way the December light looked through those windows that was more like winter light pressing against glass than like light in a room. The examination sheets waited on the corner of his desk: three copies, typed himself on the school typewriter, which did not have the characters for *ü* or *ä*, requiring small substitutions he had worked out to preserve the sense if not the precision.

He read the second instruction line back. That would do. He turned to lay the sheets on the desks and the bell from the floor below rang for the first class.

---

Parsons appeared during the interval between classes.

She came with the mail binder under her arm, the Tuesday delivery from the general store, which was also the post office, the mail sorted before school and walked up the hill in the binder. Marcus had Latin in twenty minutes. He knew, in the abstract, that nothing requiring an immediate response was likely to be in the binder, and he opened it anyway, as he always did, with the specific attention that he applied to anything arriving from outside Coldwater: the possibility that it was news.

The envelope from Dr. Feld was fourth from the top.

*Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars.* The letterhead on the envelope was the letterhead he had been receiving, in one form or another, since autumn 1940 — placement confirmation, credential documentation, quarterly notices about the wider network of displaced scholars the Committee maintained. Feld's own letters had been less frequent: two in 1941, one each in 1942 and the early part of 1943. Marcus had sent two postcards in the spring of this year, brief, reporting that his position continued and his address remained the same.

The envelope was thicker than a practical letter.

He opened it and read it standing. He had to sit down and read it again.

Feld was writing about a problem the Committee had encountered in tracking scholars who had been in transit during 1942 and into 1943. Some had arrived at their placements and failed to notify the office; this was not uncommon, and the Committee had means for re-establishing contact in most of those cases. Others were in Europe, unreachable for reasons that Feld described with a care that Marcus read as the careful prose of someone who did not yet know how to describe what was happening in Europe and was not going to guess. The third category was the one Feld lingered on: scholars who appeared to have been in transit and then ceased to be in transit, with no subsequent documentation and no record at any receiving institution.

Marcus knew that phrase. *Keine nachfolgende Dokumentation.* No subsequent documentation. The Emergency Committee used it the way a port authority used *vessel not arrived* — accurately, without affect. The period between his release from the camp and his arrival in Boston in August 1941 had been several weeks in which Marcus Klein existed in no file. The Committee had an address for him — the camp — that was no longer his address, and no forwarding address until he made contact from Boston. For those weeks, he had been a man of whom it could be written: *last documented at.* And then the next address.

The specific case was in the third page of the letter. Feld was careful with surnames, citing Committee privacy practice; he used initials where he could. A Dr. Felix K., he wrote — a linguist of German-Jewish origin, formerly of the University of Leipzig, who had been corresponding with the Committee from somewhere in Canada since early in 1943. His last letter to the office had been postmarked Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, September 22, 1943. In it he had told the Committee of his intention to travel south by sea, to reach Boston by late October; he had a contact in Boston. He had not written since. The Boston contact had heard nothing. The Committee had no other channel.

Feld was writing to Marcus partly because Marcus was placed in Maine — geographically relevant to a route running south from the Nova Scotia coast — and partly because he knew Marcus had been long enough on the Committee's rolls to have some reach into the network. Did Marcus know anything of a Dr. Felix K., Leipzig, a linguist?

Marcus read the letter through twice more.

He had a partial recollection — not a name, but something adjacent to a name, the way a word hovered at the edge of retrieval before either arriving or failing to arrive. A man at a philology conference in Vienna in 1936. Something at the intersection of Germanic philology and historical linguistics; he recalled a corridor in the Anatomiegebäude, the cold institutional light the building always had, two men talking in the specific Leipzig-accented German he had always found recognizable at a distance. He had been introduced. He had not spoken with the man at any length.

The name would not come. He might be constructing the memory from Feld's description rather than from the conference itself.

He set the letter on his desk.

Latin was beginning.

---

The German examination was the following Tuesday.

He read through Hannah Pfeiffer's paper first, which was not his usual order — he customarily worked alphabetically, which put Doris Hatch first and Hannah last — but which he found himself doing anyway. She had translated the passage from Goethe's correspondence correctly, which was not surprising; what stopped him was the word order. The passage was a letter Goethe had written to Schiller in October 1798 about the difficulty of rendering a natural scene in language without losing what had made the scene worth rendering. In the key sentence, the verb fell at the end, as German required. Most students, encountering this, pulled the verb forward; English demanded it, and the instinct was not wrong. Hannah Pfeiffer had left the verb where Goethe had placed it. The English she had produced was technically awkward and philologically correct, a sentence translated in the grammatical sense rather than the idiomatic one — you could see the German inside the English the way you could sometimes see the structure of a building inside the material it was built from.

He marked it correct and moved on to Doris Hatch.

He had not said anything. It was not the examination's occasion, and it was not entirely the German's occasion either — not a conversation he was equipped to have in December with three weeks until Christmas break. He wrote *Good work* on her sheet and the same on Doris's and *This is improving* on Louise Pelletier's and meant all three.

Latin was going well. Caesar's *De Bello Gallico*, the organization of the camp and the construction of the fortifications, twelve students working through the ablative absolutes with the patient incomprehension of people who found something merely difficult.

He encountered Henry Crow on Thursday afternoon in the second-floor hallway, Henry moving past with the supply cart.

"The window," Marcus said.

Henry looked at him.

"The north sill," Marcus said. "The cold isn't coming through the way it was."

"Block plane," Henry said. "And new caulk on the outside. It'll hold as long as the temperature stays above ten degrees. Below ten, the frame tightens." He added: "Might stick closed."

Marcus said he appreciated it.

Henry said it was his job and pushed the cart toward the supply closet at the hallway's end.

---

The school thinned in the last two weeks before Christmas break, the way it thinned every year — boys finding reasons to be on the water or in the timber, girls finding reasons to be needed at home, the teachers accepting these reasons with less scrutiny than they would have applied before the war. The building was quiet in the afternoons. Marcus finished the examination corrections and began preparing the January syllabus, working in the classroom for an hour after four o'clock because his room was colder than the classroom and the classroom had the east light for another forty minutes.

He had read Feld's letter three more times over the week. He had not replied.

---

He read it again that evening in his room, the lamp on, the letter flat on his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark that had been in place since half past four. There was no moon he could see and the cold pressed against the glass. The radiator on the south wall was running well, which it did not always do this early in December, and the room was warm enough that he could work at his desk without his coat.

He set the letter down. He took the German notebook from the shelf above his desk — more than half-full now, the compressed German hand running through its pages from April — and turned to the first blank leaf.

He wrote, in German, what he had:

*Felix K. Linguist. Leipzig. Zuletzt belegt in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, 22. September 1943. Beabsichtigte, Boston auf dem Seeweg zu erreichen, Ende Oktober.*

He looked at what he had written for a moment and then wrote below it:

*Ich glaube, ihn nicht zu kennen.*

He set down the pen. The 1936 Vienna corridor was still where it had been all week — present, the quality of the light available, the Leipzig-accented German available — and the name was still not there. He might be wrong about the conference. He might have assembled the memory from the description and mistaken the assembly for recollection.

He picked up the pen. Below the previous lines he wrote:

*Yarmouth nach Boston. Die Küste von Maine liegt dazwischen.*

He read the three lines back.

Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. He had not been there. He knew it as a port town on the southwestern coast, a transit point on the sea routes between the Atlantic provinces and New England — knew it in the way he knew most Maritime geography: from a map he had studied when he was trying to understand his own route south, the autumn of 1941. He could bring the coastline's shape from the map. He could not bring the harbor, the town's character, what it looked like from the water in late September.

September 22, 1943. That was barely three weeks before the first heavy weather of the fall. A small vessel could make the run in favorable conditions in two to three days, or longer if the weather turned, or much longer, or not at all if the weather turned badly enough. It was a route that could be done. He did not know whether it had been.

He sat with the notebook open and the lamp on and thought about the phrase *zuletzt belegt in*.

Last documented in. The Emergency Committee's vocabulary for the point on the record where the thread ended. It was precise language; Feld was a precise man. He used the passive construction deliberately — *last documented in* rather than *last seen in* or *last known to be in* — because the documentation was what the Committee could stand behind, and he would not claim more certainty than the record gave him. The documentation ended at Yarmouth on September 22, 1943. What the documentation had been attached to continued, or did not continue, beyond that point, and the file had no way to say which.

He had been *last documented in* a place himself, in the summer of 1941. The documentation had said the camp; the camp had released him; for some weeks after that he had moved south without an address any file could reach him at. He had arrived in Boston, eventually, and written to the Emergency Committee from a boarding house on Commonwealth Avenue, and his file had been updated: Marcus Klein, Coldwater Reach, Maine, March 1942. Everything after that date was documented. Everything before August 1941, going back through the camp and London and Paris to Vienna, was documented also, in one archive or another.

Dr. Felix K. had been last documented in Yarmouth.

He did not write any of this in the notebook.

He put the pen down and opened the shortwave.

The BBC was not finding him tonight — 9.41 megacycles produced static and the fringe of something that might have been German, or might have been Dutch, sliding in and out at the edge of resolution. He moved the dial through the Brazilian Portuguese that appeared reliably above eleven megacycles, found a French signal that wavered between clarity and interference, found nothing else worth resting on. He moved down and found an American broadcast, clear and even, a news signal from somewhere in the domestic network. The Pacific: the Marshall Islands, conditions described with the precise optimism of someone who had been given permission to transmit and was being careful with it. He listened to the names of islands he had not known before the war and would not have had occasion to know. Maloelap. Wotje. He did not know where these were on a chart with any precision; he was assembling the Pacific the way he had assembled the Maine coast, location by location, from a distance.

At nine-thirty he turned off the shortwave.

He took the Emergency Committee folder from the shelf between the English journal and the Stifter he had been reading since September. The folder held twelve letters now, going back to 1940, a paper record of his placement and its history. He put Feld's letter in the folder and put the folder back on the shelf.

He closed the German notebook and set it on the shelf above his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark, undiminished. He thought about Yarmouth, which he had not been to and did not know. He thought about the phrase *last documented in* and what came after it in the Committee's language: nothing, and then a date, and then the passive construction that meant someone had stopped being accountable to any record. He had been that. He knew the inside of it.

He turned off the lamp.

The room was dark and cold and smelled of woodsmoke from the furnace two floors below and of the particular density of cold books in a New England December. He did not write anything more. The notebook was on the shelf, the folder was on the shelf, the shortwave sat silent on his desk. He did not move for a while. Outside the window the dark had the quality December dark always had at this latitude: complete, and cold.

## 10-a-letter-from-new-york

### Thesis restatement

- **Cut:** "He had been a philologist for twenty years and had spent two days writing a sentence for the back of an examination sheet, which said something about either the importance of language or the particular liability of a mind that could not stop attending to it."
  — Scene already showed the two days of labor; this sentence names "the importance of language" and "the particular liability of a mind that could not stop attending to it" as abstract themes. Reader has the scene; the annotation is dead weight.

- **Cut:** "and indifferent to what was or wasn't documented in it" from the chapter's final sentence.
  — Appended to the closing image ("complete, and cold"), this phrase names the chapter's central preoccupation explicitly at the moment the image should be doing that work alone. Chapter now ends: "complete, and cold."

### Post-scene subtext naming

- **Cut:** "The file noted the absence accurately and without editorial comment, which was the correct approach, and the absence itself remained — somewhere, in the space between the last documentation and whatever had come after — as a gap in the record that the record could acknowledge but not fill."
  — This sentence follows "He had been that. He knew the inside of it." — the landing is already clean. The cut sentence names and architectures what the two preceding sentences already convey. Removed entirely; chapter proceeds directly to "He turned off the lamp."

### Emotional structural analysis

- **Cut:** "After three students who found German faintly shameful, merely difficult was a relief he had not expected to feel as strongly as he did."
  — The Latin passage already shows "the patient incomprehension of people who found something merely difficult." This sentence converts that image into a named feeling with a quantified intensity. The image was the thing; the feeling-diagram is redundant.

- **Cut (partial merge):** "The gap between them was the condition Feld's phrase described, and Marcus had lived inside that condition and knew its particular quality: the sense of being in motion without leaving any trace of the motion, which was sometimes practical and sometimes something else."
  — Follows "Everything before August 1941 ... was documented also, in one archive or another." The gap between the two documented periods is already visible; this sentence names it, architectures it ("its particular quality"), and annotates it ("sometimes practical and sometimes something else"). Removed entirely.

### Meta-commentary on cognition

- **Cut:** "A philologist could not always be trusted to distinguish reconstruction from recollection; it was one of the discipline's hazards he had never found a way around."
  — Follows "He might be constructing the memory from Feld's description rather than from the conference itself." That prior sentence is the observation; this sentence labels it as a disciplinary category. The label is redundant.

- **Cut:** "which he had come to know over the past two years without having been able to decide what he thought of it" from the final paragraph's sensory sentence.
  — "the particular density of cold books in a New England December" is the complete image. The appended clause annotates Marcus's cognitive relationship to it rather than letting it be sensory.

### Redundant transition / re-summary

- **Cut:** "He had searched the memory in the way you searched difficult German when you couldn't bring up a word: working around it, approaching from the surrounding context, trying the company the word had been in. It did not produce the name."
  — The linguistic-retrieval analogy was already established earlier in the chapter ("not a name, but something adjacent to a name, the way a word hovered at the edge of retrieval before either arriving or failing to arrive"). This passage in section 6 repeats the same analogy. "He might be wrong about the conference. He might have assembled the memory…" follows directly and reads cleanly.

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

- **Cut:** "He had a place that was a location on a line rather than a place."
  — Follows "He could bring the coastline's shape from the map. He could not bring the harbor, the town's character, what it looked like from the water in late September." Those two sentences already make the contrast; this closing line re-states it as a formulation.

- **Cut:** "the geography of a war he was not in" from the Pacific/shortwave passage.
  — Appended to "he was assembling the Pacific the way he had assembled the Maine coast, location by location, from a distance," this phrase names the thematic significance (his relationship to the war as a non-combatant displaced person). The analogy is kept; the thesis tag is cut.

- **Cut:** "which was not always the case" from "He wrote *Good work* on her sheet … and meant all three, which was not always the case."
  — "Meant all three" already implies the contrast (he doesn't always mean it). The tag makes explicit what the word "meant" already carried.

### Dialogue gloss

- **Cut:** "which was not a complete sentence but arrived that way" from "'The window,' Marcus said, which was not a complete sentence but arrived that way."
  — The reader sees that "The window" is not a complete sentence. The annotation is textbook dialogue-gloss.

- **Merged:** "It was not the examination's occasion, and it was not entirely the German's occasion either; what she had given him told him something about where and how she had learned to read, which was not a conversation he was equipped to have in December with three weeks until Christmas break."
  → "It was not the examination's occasion, and it was not entirely the German's occasion either — not a conversation he was equipped to have in December with three weeks until Christmas break."
  — "what she had given him told him something about where and how she had learned to read" is meta-commentary on the examination paper's significance. The paper itself showed what it showed; the clause labels the inference. Removed; the preceding and following clauses merge cleanly.

# January Harbor

The inner cove had been icing since the second week of January — a thin skin at first, gray at the margins where the fresh water off the Reach mixed with the salt, then thickening toward the center until by the twenty-second it was opaque white ice that would not hold a man and would not let a boat through. It was not hard winter; the outer approach stayed open. The two draggers — the Callie B. and the Margaret Rose, Pelletier's — were tied at the outer dock and had been for nine days. The lobster boats were on their trailers at Farber's yard and at the Pelletier place up the road. The mail boat came Tuesdays and Fridays, worked the outer approach, tied at the deep-water slip, and was gone within the hour.

January harbor. Fewer reasons to be on the dock.

She did her rounds in the mornings. In summer the rounds took forty minutes: log, bilge checks, dock inspection, radio at 0800. In January they took twenty-five, with the fleet reduced and the radio check running once daily and the bilge pumps demanding less attention than they did in active season. She had learned, in her second winter at the post, not to stretch the rounds to fill the time. Owen had said something close to this before the fact, though she had arrived at it herself before she remembered that he had said it, and she was no longer certain whether she had arrived at it or remembered it.

She walked the outer dock each morning and noted the ice line in the log. January 22: inner cove ice approximately four inches, opaque. Outer approach clear. Callie B. and Margaret Rose, outer dock, checked and secure. Wind NNW at eleven knots. Barometer 30.14, steady. She checked the Callie B.'s bilge pump — running clean, had been since the boat was tied up — and noted it and went on.

The Callie B.'s bilge pump was what she had gone to check on the night of October 11. It had been running clean then too. She had made her note and left the dock at 2330. She had told Ennis this, and it was accurate.

Back in the shack she ran the 0800 check on the BC-1206 — weather, traffic conditions, the harbor operations she monitored on the coast — and logged the result. Then she turned to the ledger.

She had been opening it to October since November. Not every morning; some mornings she skipped it. But she had opened it enough that it was a part of the mornings, and she had stopped asking herself why, the same way she had stopped asking herself why she rechecked the Callie B.'s bilge pump when she knew perfectly well it was running clean.

The gap was on the right-hand page, midway through the ledger. Pages 114 through 119: Ennis had taken them at 1008 on October 12, folded them into his document envelope with the efficiency of a man for whom this was ordinary procedure. What remained was a faint unevenness in the binding — not something you would notice if you weren't looking, but a different weight when you held the spread open. The stitching showed at the spine, pale thread where the section had gone.

The entry before the gap was October 8. Weather, tide, traffic, nothing unusual. Her handwriting, quick and competent. The entry after the gap was October 13: the body, the Coast Guard, the departure of the district lieutenant at 1008. Her handwriting again, abbreviated.

She held the spread open and looked at both sides of what wasn't there.

Then she closed the ledger and left it on the desk.

---

On Wednesdays she went to Merrill's for coffee. Owen had gone every morning; she had made it once a week, not from economy alone — once a week gave it something mornings would have worn smooth. In January, Merrill's had a particular quality: warm in a way the shack was never warm, and occupied in the particular way that the working middle generation occupied things in January, which was with a settled patience, people who had made their arrangements with winter and found a diner a reasonable place to sit with them.

She was on her second cup when Reg Farber came in.

She knew him as she knew most of the fishermen: by his boats first. Eight years of the Callie B. — the bilge pump, a mooring chain in '41, a registration discrepancy the fall before last — had given them a specific and sufficient acquaintance. Since October they had another kind: the kind produced by proximity to the same event. When they ran into each other at the dock or on the road, the body was there without being mentioned. This was common enough in a town of Coldwater's size. Most things that had happened were there without being mentioned.

Farber sat two stools down from her. The counterman brought him coffee without being asked. He looked into his cup.

He said: "I've been thinking about that fellow since October."

Eira said: "I expect most people have."

"My boy." He stopped. "He doesn't say much about it. Hard to tell what kids carry."

"No," she said.

He drank his coffee. She held her cup. Outside the front window the road was frozen and empty, the empty that Wednesday afternoon in January produced with particular thoroughness.

He said: "I was up late on the eleventh. Night before."

She set down her cup.

"Couldn't sleep." He said it without particular weight; insomnia in January was ordinary. "I was on the porch around eleven, eleven-thirty. I saw a boat come in." He paused. "Small wooden thing. No lights."

She waited.

"It tied up at the far end of the dock — past the dock extension, where you can't see from the road. I watched it for a few minutes. I've gone without navigation lights myself, close in, when I've been out later than I planned and I know the water. Didn't think much of it." He shook his head slowly. "Went back inside around midnight. It was gone by morning."

"When did it connect?" she said.

"Few weeks after. I was thinking about who the man could have been and I remembered seeing the boat and thought — I don't know." He looked at her. "I don't know that it's connected. I just had it sitting with me and didn't know where to put it."

"Did you report it to the Coast Guard?"

He turned his coffee cup on the counter. "No. Didn't think to. Should I?"

She said: "I'll mention it if it's relevant."

He said: "Probably isn't." He looked up at the counterman. "You have apple pie today?"

---

She walked home in the cold.

The road was frozen, the ruts from the last mud period locked into the surface now until spring. She kept to the margin where the ground was flat. January light at two-thirty had maybe ninety minutes in it before the sky gave up. She could feel it going.

What Farber didn't know: she had been on the dock. In the shadow of the Callie B.'s wheelhouse, twenty feet from the dock extension, close enough to hear the engine cut. She had seen the boat come in and she had watched it tie up. She had seen the man step off and stand at the foot of the dock for a moment, getting his bearings — the dark overcoat, the shoes that were wrong for the dock in the way they turned out to be wrong for everything. Twenty seconds, maybe less. Then he had turned and walked toward the breakwater. She had watched him go.

She had gone home and gone to bed. She had told Ennis she had checked the bilge pump, found it running clean, and left the dock at 2330. All of that was true. The truth as she had told it contained all of it except the boat and the man and those twenty seconds, which were not in the account she gave and not in the pages Ennis took and not anywhere except in her.

She had run the other version in October. Thoroughly, carefully, arriving at her conclusions the same way she arrived at conclusions about weather: by looking at the available information from each angle until the picture was clear. The conclusions held.

What was different now was Farber.

He had been on his porch. He had seen the boat come in from the same direction she had seen it. He had watched it for a few minutes — his words — which meant he had stood in the cold in the dark doing his own version of what she had done from the shadow of the Callie B., and then he had gone inside and not thought much of it until he had, and he had carried it for three months because he didn't know where to put it, and he had put it down at Merrill's on a Wednesday in January because the occasion was there and the Wednesday was long.

He didn't connect the boat to the body with certainty. He had said so.

The road turned uphill past the Congregational church. The church windows held the last of the afternoon light for a moment and then let it go. The sky above the tree line was pale gray, moving toward the blue that came before dark.

She had been the only person who knew about the boat for three months. She had not thought about it in those terms — had not told herself each morning, *I am the only person who knows the boat was there.* But she had known it the way she knew the tide tables: as a condition, a baseline, reliable because it had been reliable yesterday and the day before and the month before that.

Farber had put a second point of knowledge into the world. He had done it honestly, without urgency, because he had been meaning to go through that drawer and the occasion presented itself.

She was not the only witness now. She was the witness who knew the most. Farber had seen the boat. She had the boat and the man: the twenty seconds on the dock, the overcoat, the shoes, the direction he walked. Farber was missing those twenty seconds and he would not know to look for them.

The short road to her house. The maple in the front yard was bare, the branches black against a sky that was almost dark now.

She went inside.

She took off Owen's peacoat and hung it on the peg. The kitchen was cold; she had banked the stove before leaving and it needed tending. She put wood on and adjusted the draft and waited until the flame took before she closed the stove door.

She did not go to the log. She had thought, walking home, that there might be a form for Farber's account — some way of putting it into the record where it could exist separate from what she chose to do with it. She stood at the kitchen table. She did not go to the log.

She made supper. She ate. She cleaned up.

The barometer at four-thirty was 30.18 and rising. Clear weather coming, and cold with it.

Reg Farber's information was somewhere in her now, without a ledger to put it in.

She went to bed.

# Found

The cows moved before she got the barn door open — a shifting, the soft thud of hooves on packed earth, a low sound one of them made to another in the dark. She had been hearing this for six years, since the first winter she was old enough to do the milking alone, and she still stopped for a moment when it happened: the sound of the herd gathering itself in the dark, the way they knew someone was at the door before the door opened.

February cold had drawn itself into the boards overnight. Her breath showed when she stepped through, and then the cows' breath showed too, a white fog rising from the near stalls in the lantern light, and she stood a moment in the smell of it — wet hay and grain, the close animal heat, the February cold that lived at shin level and in the beam joints and did not warm off entirely even when the herd had been standing in it for hours. The lantern made a small yellow circle on the earthen floor. Above it, darkness.

Four-thirty. She went to work.

Her section was the six Guernseys on the near side. She had been milking them, or cows like them, since she was eleven and her hands knew the work without asking her permission. The one who kicked left. The two who leaned into the pail. The last one, who needed settling before she would let you near her, who had been that way for two years and would probably always be that way. Hannah moved through them in the order she always moved through them, unhurried, the pail finding its place, her fingers working.

Her father was in the far stalls with his Holsteins, and she could hear the rhythm of his milking through the divider — pull and ring, pull and ring — as steady as it had been for as long as she had known what milking was. They had not spoken during morning milking in as long as she could remember. The barn had its own kind of quiet and they both kept it. This had been true before his English went away, which made it a barn thing and not a silence thing.

February dark outside the barn door was total. She had been standing on the back step before she came down, her coat half-buttoned, and the hill above the property had been just a darker shape against a dark sky and the fields were nothing at all. July dark wanted something from you; it had insects in it, motion, the rustling of things that had business to do. February dark had no business. It settled in and waited.

She finished her third Guernsey, moved to the fourth.

Somewhere around five, the wind came over the roof peak and she heard a nail pull free — a ping against one of the far boards — and she looked over at the dark end of the barn where the sound had been, and couldn't see anything that had changed. She would check it in daylight. There was always something in February that needed checking in daylight.

---

At six, Lonzo Reed came with the four men.

She heard the keys first, always. Then the footsteps crossing the barnyard, the particular sound of four people being walked somewhere at six in the morning in cold they had not chosen. Then the drag of the door against the ice that had been building at the sill for ten days. Lonzo came through first with the Springfield, and then Werner, and Gerd, and the quiet one whose name she could never remember even though she heard it every morning — some difficulty between the German and the Maine of it — and then Karl last.

Lonzo had fallen in the first week of the month. He'd gone down hard on the icy patch near the barn door, the Springfield striking the ground before he did, and after that he walked from the icehouse to the barn with the deliberateness of an old man testing ice, each step settled before the next. He was not old, exactly, but he walked old on ice now.

The prisoners had not fallen. Karl had learned to read the ice sometime in January; she had noticed it: the widening of his step on the gray patches, the way his weight shifted back. He was nineteen and his body took what the ground taught it quickly. The other three were older and slower to adjust.

She did not look up when they came in.

The February arrangement was the same as January: the prisoners took the far stalls for mucking and for the cleanup work while she and her father managed the milking, and then when the Guernseys were done Karl and Werner carried the cans to the cooling tank. Her father worked the Holstein end. Lonzo Reed stood near the center beam with his rifle and his cold, stamping his feet occasionally on the earthen floor.

She finished her fifth Guernsey and moved to the last.

Karl came across the barn with a can in each hand, moving at the pace she had watched him find over the winter — not rushing, not dawdling, the workman's pace that got things done. He was aimed for the door. The icy patch near the sill was the same patch Lonzo had gone down on: the temperature dropped overnight and the melt off their boots refroze by morning and the ash she spread kept being absorbed into the gray surface and needing spreading again. She saw Karl hit the edge of it. His right foot went sideways, the can in his left hand knocked outward, and he caught himself in a single half-step — no drama in it, the body's fast knowledge — and set his feet right and kept going through the door.

The right can sloshed. He had not dropped it.

She was back at the last Guernsey, moving the pail, when she saw the paper on the floor.

---

It lay near the icy patch, close to where his foot had turned. A folded page, doubled twice. She could see from where she stood the wear at the folds — the paper darkened there, soft with handling, the kind of wear that came from something carried and taken out and folded back again, many times.

She looked at the door. It was closed.

She went to the page and picked it up.

There was a wooden ledge beside the door post, where people set things down when their hands were full — a glove, a harness strap. She could put the page there, where Karl would see it when he came back for the second pass on the cans. She held the page.

She looked at the far stalls. Werner and the others working, the sound of it regular. Her father's voice, once, in German, to one of his Holsteins. Lonzo Reed had gone out with Karl.

She unfolded the page.

A woman's handwriting — that was what she understood first, before the language sorted itself. Careful, narrow, slightly formal, the kind of handwriting that was tidy from intention and not from ease. The kind of handwriting that had been drilled into a girl and had stayed. The page had been folded and unfolded enough times that the creases held their shape even flat.

German. She understood this a moment after the handwriting, the way you caught the voice before you caught the words. And then, inside the German: Bavarian. Her ear for it was her father's ear — she had not learned it, had not been taught it, had absorbed it the way she had absorbed the sound of cows at four-thirty, from before she was old enough to know what learning was. This was not Dr. Klein's classroom German and not the German she had found in books. It was the German of home, some home she had never seen, the same dialect she had been hearing through the floor and through the icehouse window since April.

She read.

A neighbor's fence, replaced that autumn. Some difficulty with the materials, a delay, but it was finished and holding now, better than the old one. Potatoes more expensive than last year, as everything was. A cousin — her name appeared to be Els — had married in October: a small gathering, quietly done, the family had been there, the weather better than you would expect for October. The writer hadn't been able to come but had sent something with Els's sister. The cellar was holding better this winter than the winter before. The dog — a name she couldn't parse from the cursive — had been sick in December, something in the stomach, but had come back to himself; he was back to his old habits.

She read slowly.

Then, at the end of the paragraph about the cousin's wedding, this:

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.

She read it again.

Those who tried to go are gone. We pray for them.

The sentence was between a line about the October weather and a line about the cellar and it did not explain itself. The writer moved on after it to something about firewood. The war was not named in the letter, not once in the whole page, and yet versucht haben zu gehen was not a sentence about the cellar. Sind weg was not the dog being sick in December.

She didn't know who the people were. She had enough German to know that the sentence was specific — a real attempt, past tense, over; particular people this woman knew; a prayer for them by name, or rather for them in the place of their names, which were not given. She did not know where they had tried to go or what had become of them when they went.

The door scraped.

She folded the page on its creases and put it in her coat pocket and went back to the last Guernsey.

---

Karl came in again with Werner for the second pass on the cans. Lonzo Reed came through behind them, saying something about the ash and whether she had more of it. She told him where the bucket was.

She finished the last cow and carried her pail to the cooling tank. Her father came out of the far stalls and they moved the last of the milk across the barnyard to the cellar, two trips, without speaking. The cold that early in February cut straight down through the collar. The sky above the hill was just starting to separate itself from the darkness, gray coming up from the east.

She heard Lonzo lock the barn behind them.

---

That afternoon she sat at the kitchen table with her school notebook open.

She took the letter out of her coat pocket and unfolded it.

The handwriting first, again. Careful and narrow. In the kitchen light — the wood stove going, the gray February afternoon outside the window above the sink — the handwriting looked like someone who had sat down to write this with an intention to do it well, to send her son something careful. The page had been read smooth. He had been carrying it in his jacket pocket since whenever it arrived, October maybe or November, through the ice and the cold and the early mornings and the icy patch near the barn door, through whatever November and December and January were like in an icehouse in Maine.

She read it from the beginning.

The fence. The potatoes. Cousin Els. The cellar. The dog.

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.

She sat with it.

She could ask Dr. Klein. She had thought of him by name in the barn. He was the only person in Coldwater who would know both the German and enough of the world beyond Coldwater to know what a sentence like that was the end of. But asking Dr. Klein meant taking the letter out of her pocket in front of someone, meant explaining where it had come from, meant saying what she had done with it when she found it.

She had not decided to do that yet.

She put the letter between the pages of her English literature notes — a Whitman passage she had been annotating, the words barely visible through the folded page — and closed the notebook and set it in her school bag.

The fire in the stove was going. She could hear her mother in the back room moving about, the particular footstep that said she was sweeping, and outside the February light doing what it always did at three-thirty, which was give up.

She pulled her arithmetic toward her and began.

## 12-found

### Meta-commentary on cognition

**Cut 1:** `, though she did not separate them in her thinking`
> From: "…which made it a barn thing and not a silence thing, though she did not separate them in her thinking."
> The barn-silence distinction is shown by what precedes it; labeling that she doesn't analytically separate them adds nothing the prose hasn't already enacted.

**Cut 2:** `without deciding to notice it`
> From: "she had noticed it without deciding to notice it: the widening of his step on the gray patches…"
> The colon clause already renders the observation in full. The framing of how she noticed is a cognition label the text doesn't need.

**Cut 3:** `, the way you thought of someone when you had a question in the right subject`
> From: "She had thought of him by name in the barn, the way you thought of someone when you had a question in the right subject."
> Labels the mechanism of a recalled name. The next two sentences explain why she considered Dr. Klein; the gloss is redundant.

---

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

**Cut 4:** `Her German was her father's German and this woman wrote in her father's register, the long comfortable sentences that carried everything without stopping to set pieces down separately.`
> From: "She read slowly. Her German was her father's German and this woman wrote in her father's register…"
> Double infraction: (a) the letter we just read demonstrated its own register; glossing it afterward is a sentence-after-the-sentence. (b) "her father's German/ear" was established two paragraphs earlier — this is a near-verbatim repeat. Leaves "She read slowly." as the transition, which now carries more charge.

---

### Redundant transition / re-summary

**Cut 5:** `She had enough German for all of that and not enough for anything further.`
> From: "She did not know where they had tried to go or what had become of them when they went. She had enough German for all of that and not enough for anything further."
> The paragraph already showed, in precise detail, exactly what she could and couldn't parse. The closing sentence re-states the limits abstractly after the concrete work is done.

---

### Post-scene subtext naming

**Cut 6:** `She had taken something that did not belong to her and she knew that she had taken it and neither of these facts resolved the other.`
> From: "…which was give up. She had taken something that did not belong to her and she knew that she had taken it and neither of these facts resolved the other.\n\nShe pulled her arithmetic toward her and began."
> The chapter's action — pocketing the letter, holding it through the morning's work, re-reading it alone, hiding it in her notebook — already names the moral situation. The sentence closes the scene by stating what it was "really about." Its removal leaves the final beat ("She pulled her arithmetic toward her and began.") to land immediately after the atmospheric close, which is stronger.
