# April

The paper came in the school's Wednesday mail. He picked it up from the front office table on his way through — the Rockland Courier, folded once lengthwise as the secretary always left it — and tucked it under his arm. The announcement had already come through the school hallway's radio by nine that morning. He had been at the corridor's edge, between his classroom and the Latin room, when the broadcast ran through. He had stood and listened to the announcer's careful American voice for three or four minutes and then he had walked into his classroom and written *prima declinatio* on the board and taught the lesson.

He carried the paper home under his arm and set it on the desk without opening it.

He graded the Latin exercises. He did this with the paper beside the exercise books, visible but unread, and one part of his mind went through the work — the genitive plural errors, the margin notes, which of the three students had understood the principle and which had guessed correctly without understanding it — and the other part of his mind was somewhere he declined to follow it. He put the exercise books in the pile for morning and set down the pen.

He went downstairs. Lillian had left food in the kitchen. He ate at the small table alone — Henry was still at the school, something with the boiler — and when Henry came in, washing his hands at the sink, they exchanged two or three sentences about the cold for April and then Henry heated what was in the pot and sat down, and they finished the evening together without talking further. This was not unusual. Marcus had stopped noticing it as an accommodation sometime around the second winter, which he understood, when he noticed the stopping, for what it was.

He went upstairs.

He turned on the lamp and sat down at the desk. The Rockland Courier was where he had set it. He picked it up and opened it to the front page. He read the headline and the first three paragraphs of the dispatch. He turned to page two. He looked at page two. He turned to page three.

There were photographs on page three.

He looked at the photographs for perhaps four seconds before he folded the paper closed. He set it face-down on the desk. He sat in the chair for a moment with his hands in his lap.

He had known. This was the thing that required sitting with, in this room, in this chair: he had known. Not in the way of the photographs — not with that specificity, not at that scale, not in the form of the specific architecture the photographs were now showing — but in the form available to a man who had watched Vienna change in 1937 and 1938 and then left it. He had understood the direction. He had followed the logic as far as it went before he chose to stop following it, because the thing you construct in your mind when you follow that logic to its conclusion is a thing you cannot allow to be true, and so you manage the logic at a certain distance, you hold it in the form of structure rather than completion, the way you can know the shape of a building from its foundation plan without having to stand inside it.

The photographs were inside it.

He did not open the paper again.

He thought about the people he knew. Not as a category — specifically, in the way a man thinks about the specific texture of specific encounters across seventeen years in a Viennese academic institution and two years in Paris. Jakob R., who had been his closest colleague in the philology department, who had a particular habit in seminar of beginning his disagreements with a question rather than a rebuttal — arms crossed, leaning back, the question arriving before he had finished forming it — a habit Marcus could still reproduce exactly if he was working to fall asleep and needed something to hold in his mind. They had exchanged letters in 1939, three in 1940, and then the letters stopped. The last one, in November of 1940, had carried a Berlin address. Marcus had not written to a Berlin address after 1941. He had arranged the reasons for this in a form that did not require him to name them.

Grete H., who had been his department's German-language assistant for seven years, whose administrative precision he had depended on in the way one depends on a function that works correctly without one's attention, and who had been in Vienna in 1938 when he left it, and from whom he had received nothing since. He had asked once through the Emergency Committee, in late 1942, and received a letter that said the committee had no current documentation for that name. He had understood, at the time, what current documentation meant, and he had done what he always did with the things he understood in this way, which was to hold them in the form of probably but not confirmed, which was the form available to him, and move on to the next thing that required moving on to.

Two others — names he permitted himself in his mind without writing them anywhere — whose last known addresses had been in Paris in 1940. He had not found them through the Emergency Committee's Paris contacts, who were themselves mostly gone from Paris by the time he was writing letters in 1942 and 1943. He had not let himself complete a thought about them in over two years. He let himself complete one now, briefly, sitting at the desk in the April dark with the folded paper in front of him.

Then he thought about Felix K.

This had a different quality. He had been thinking about Felix K. since January — since the Thursday evening he came back from the harbormaster's shack and spent two hours in this room with the Feld letter and a sheet of working paper before he opened the German notebook and wrote the entry — in a specific register of probability that was not certainty and was not the same as comfort and was not the same as what he was now sitting with about Jakob R. and Grete H. and the others.

Felix K. had tried to go. That was what the evidence said. He had been documented in Yarmouth in September of 1943, heading south by sea, and the sea had brought him as far as Coldwater, and there he had run out of road.

He had not been in one of the camps.

Marcus turned this over in his mind. He had turned it over before — in January, after he assembled the theory, and in February, and in March, on evenings when the European news on the school hallway radio made the structure more visible — and he had not arrived at an answer, and he did not arrive at one now. There was a line of reasoning that said: he died in the Atlantic coast dark, in October, alone in an unlighted boat in cold water, and that was its own fact. There was no architecture behind it, no system, no list on which his name would appear. He had died in the specific and local way, which was the way of weather and the harbor and chance, and no one had done it to him, or it had been done to him by the full weight of what Europe had become for people who needed to leave it and ran out of time, which was a different thing from the same thing, and Marcus had not resolved this distinction and suspected he would not.

He went, Marcus thought. He tried.

After a while he picked up the newspaper and took it downstairs.

---

Henry and Lillian were in the parlor. The Zenith console was on — the same cabinet, the same chairs they had sat in on the evening of June 6 last year when the D-Day news came through and Marcus had translated BBC fragments in a low voice and afterward on the back-street porch neither of them had spoken for twenty minutes. Tonight no translation was needed or useful. The Zenith was carrying the same American voice, or another American voice with the same quality: the calibrated evenness of a man delivering copy that was not written to be delivered, because no one had written this kind of copy before. Lillian had her knitting in her lap. Her hands were very still.

Marcus set the newspaper on the sofa cushion beside him, face-down, and sat.

The Zenith was reporting on Bergen-Belsen tonight. The correspondent described, in the careful language of a wire dispatch, what British soldiers had found at the camp when they arrived. He read numbers. He described the camp's geography — the compound, the structures, the numbers of people found alive and the numbers not. The language grew more careful the more specific it became, in the way of a man who has been asked to describe something he does not have words for and is constructing the words as he goes, with insufficient material.

Marcus listened. He had been in the structure of this knowledge for seven years — since Vienna, since the winter of 1937 when the first changes were visible in the institution and in the streets — and now the structure had a form that the language could reach, barely, in insufficient words read by a correspondent in a careful voice on the Zenith in the Crow house parlor. He sat on the sofa and did not move.

He did not translate. He had enough English for this. He had enough of every language he possessed for this.

After a while — he had stopped tracking time — Lillian said, quietly: "I'm going to bed."

She set her knitting in the basket beside the chair and stood. Before she went she looked at Marcus once, and in that look was something she was measuring against something else, deciding not to try to name. He met her eyes and nodded slightly. She went upstairs. Her footsteps crossed the ceiling above their heads and then stopped.

Henry was in his chair. Marcus was on the sofa.

The Zenith was still on.

---

Henry said: "Is there anyone you're trying to find out about?"

Marcus said: "Several. I don't know how to find out."

Henry said: "There will be lists."

Marcus said: "Yes."

Henry said: "That will take time."

Marcus said: "Yes."

They sat with the Zenith. The broadcast moved from the correspondent's copy to a recorded voice — a soldier, one of the soldiers who had been among the first to enter the camp — describing what he had seen. His voice was not calibrated. It started and found its direction and then lost it and started again. Marcus listened to the difficulty of what the soldier was doing — assembling, in real time, in front of a microphone, a language for something that no language had been built to describe in advance — and understood this from the other direction, because he had been working at this problem from the other direction since 1938. There was no adequate vocabulary. You used the words that existed and they were not sufficient and you kept going.

Henry got up at some point and went to the kitchen. He came back with two cups of coffee, set one down on the low table beside the sofa, and resumed his chair without anything being said. The Crow house coffee was better than anything else available in Coldwater, which Marcus had thought about at various points over three years without ever having remarked on it. He held the cup in both hands. The warmth was specific and useful.

The front-hall clock struck eleven.

Henry reached over and turned the volume down — not off, only down to the register where the Zenith voices were present in the room without demanding it. A small adjustment. He made it without looking at Marcus, who was looking at the floor in front of the sofa.

The clock struck twelve.

Henry stood. He said: "I'll be up."

Marcus said: "I know."

Henry went to the stairs. The third step from the top creaked, the same as it always did — that step in that house in that particular way, which Marcus had known for three years, the same as he knew the specific frequency of the harbor bell on foggy mornings and the boiler's low cycle at the school. Henry's footsteps crossed the upper floor and stopped.

Marcus turned off the Zenith. He sat for a moment in the quiet with the newspaper still face-down on the cushion beside him. Then he picked it up and went upstairs.

---

The lamp on. He pulled the chain and the light came on over the desk, the east window black above it, and he sat down.

The German notebook was on the shelf above the desk, between the English journal and the grammar workbook, the spine written in his English hand. He had last opened it in January — the Thursday evening he came back from the harbormaster's shack, the evening of the fragment and what the fragment said about the letters, the probable name. He had spent two hours working out the arithmetic on a separate sheet first and then he had transcribed the conclusion into the notebook because the notebook was where he kept things that needed to remain true when he looked at them again.

He took it down.

He opened it to the last page of writing. The January entry was there, in his German handwriting, which was not as clear as it had been. His English handwriting had become better than his German handwriting without his having done anything to cause this, which still surprised him when he noticed it, because the tools of his formation were not supposed to rearrange themselves without his knowledge.

*Fe—?—x. Felix K. Yarmouth, September 1943. Coldwater, Oktober 1943. Innenbar, Dezember 1944 geborgen.*

He read it.

He took his pen from the desk tray. He uncapped it.

Below the entry, on the next line, he wrote:

*Die die versucht haben zu gehen.*

He capped the pen. He closed the notebook. He set it back on the shelf.

---

He turned off the lamp.

The room in the dark was the same room it had been in every darkness for thirty-eight months: the east window a shade less dark than the walls surrounding it, the desk a shape he knew, the radiator on the south wall quiet for the night, the slanted ceiling on the north wall where the roofline came down to the plaster. He had arrived in this room in March of 1942 with a cardboard case, two books, and a suit with the shoulders gone loose from a year of ill fitting. He had sat at this desk and looked out this east window in August of that year and in November and in the first winter and in the winter after that and in the spring and the summer and the autumn that followed, through the mornings when Lillian knocked twice on the door frame and through the evenings when Henry's footsteps went past his door and the third step from the top announced him going to bed.

He did not open the shortwave.

He thought, briefly, about what the Europe across the east window consisted of now: what would be in it, who might be in it, what the street he had lived on for fourteen years looked like in April 1945. He had not allowed himself this thought often. He allowed it now for two or three minutes, sitting in the chair in the dark, and the thought did not arrive anywhere comforting and it did not arrive anywhere devastating. It arrived somewhere he did not have a word for.

He would find out. That was all he had.

The notebook was on the shelf. What he had written in it was what it was.

The harbor was somewhere below the hill to the east, which he knew without seeing it. The ice was out of the inner cove by now. The boats were back on their moorings, the buoys rocking in the April chop, the tide coming in or going out according to its own arithmetic. He had been in this town for thirty-eight months. He had made it to this room in this house with this specific east-facing window. That was where he was.

He sat in the dark for a while. Then he went to bed.

# Spring Log

The tide gauge read four feet nine inches when she checked it at six forty-five. High water at nine fourteen; the published table had it at five feet two inches and the morning was confirming it. The inner cove was already full.

The lobster boats had been going out since before first light — she had heard the first engine on her walk down from home at quarter past six, one of the Beaumonts or Devereux, running early the way the early-season men did when the weather held. By the time she reached the dock end the channel was busy, the lobster boats moving through in the gray, their running lights off now that it was light enough to read the water. She counted them from the dock end as they cleared the harbor mouth. Seven, with Farber's June M. making the last one out at six fifty-two.

She stood at the dock end a moment before the rest of the morning claimed her. The air off the water in late April had a quality that was not available in any other month — not the salt and cold of October alone, not the freezing fog of January, but something that was both of those with warmth beginning to work through them. Diesel from the morning departures. Herring bait from the bait house where the lobstermen had provisioned since before her time at this dock. Cold water at the beginning of warming.

Both draggers were running. Seven lobster boats were out.

She went to the shack and got the log and turned on the NNW channel.

The harbor radio was carrying the European news between the marine traffic. It had been carrying it all week, since the Soviet forces moved through the outskirts of Berlin, since the dispatches had taken on the particular quality she had learned to recognize over four and a half years: the careful evenness of language at the end of something. This morning the correspondent was reporting on the street fighting still going in the German capital, and then, in a slightly different register, on a second report: American and Soviet troops meeting at a river somewhere in Germany, the two armies shaking hands across a bridge in what had been the center of the German state. The river's name came through the static and she caught a syllable of it and lost the rest.

The Beaumont brothers checked in from the outer bar at seven-oh-four — position, conditions, normal traffic. She logged them and responded. Then Devereux's boat, then two more by hull number from the outer bar, then the coast-service check at seven-twenty.

The marine traffic she logged. The European news she did not log.

The two draggers — Lily B. and Mackerel Sky — were both running full season. She could see the Mackerel Sky's boom swung wide as it cleared the harbor mouth at seven-ten; she knew from the empty mooring that the Lily B. had gone out before her morning rounds. Both draggers active. She noted it in the log and set the log aside until the freight manifests came in.

---

The first manifest was the Bangor order: hardware and dry goods on the seven-thirty schooner out of Rockland. She went through the bill of lading crate by crate. Two items short — the same two items from February, the same backlog, the third consecutive month Bangor had not cleared the order. She noted the shortage and pulled a fresh form for the Goulding memo.

The second manifest was fuel oil, direct delivery to the south pier storage tank. She countersigned the driver's paper and stood through the transfer without incident.

The mooring dispute came between the second manifest and the third.

Reg Farber appeared at the shack door at eight forty-five with the two Pelletier brothers directly behind him. All three men came through the door together, which filled the fourteen-foot shack considerably. The dispute was the third float on the east side — the commercial float, held by the two draggers under seasonal assignment from May through October. In the winter layup, when both draggers were pulled, Farber had been mooring the June M. there on Tuesdays for the outside berth because the float was empty and the habit was convenient. The Pelletiers had done the same thing on their own Tuesdays. Two weeks ago they had come in on the same Tuesday, both reaching for the outside mooring, and the collision of dock lines had put a gash in the June M.'s bow rubbing strip, which was the sum of Farber's complaint.

She let both parties say what they needed to say.

Then she opened the dock register to the float assignments and laid it on the counter flat where they could both see it.

The third float listed the Lily B. and the Mackerel Sky under seasonal commercial assignment, May through October, registered at the start of each season. The winter field was blank. The Pelletier boat appeared nowhere in the third float's history. Neither did the June M. Both boats had been mooring there since the winter layup without a registration of any kind, and the only thing that had changed was that both had tried to do it on the same Tuesday.

Farber said he had been there since March.

She asked him to point out in the register where that gave him the assignment.

He stood with his finger on the page for a moment and then took it away.

She assigned the June M. the second float's inside mooring for the season and the Pelletier boat the second float's outside mooring for the season. Both in ink. Both signed and dated. She closed the register. The second float, inside and outside, both boats side by side — which was not what either man had wanted and was the only arrangement that treated both registrations the same way.

Farber started to say something about Tuesday departures.

She told him to work it out with the Pelletiers.

Neither man argued. All three filed out in the order they had come in, and she could hear the conversation continuing on the dock for another minute before it dispersed. Both parties equally inconvenienced.

She worked through the rest of the morning: the third manifest, the coast-service log update from the buoy tender visit last week, the carryover ledger entries. By eleven she was at the dock when the Heron came in.

Three bags: two mail, one package cargo for Goulding's store. She tallied the bags in the dock log and sent the cargo up the hill with the store runner.

No yellow envelopes in the Tuesday delivery.

She noted this in the margin of the dock log in the same compressed hand she used for the rest of it and went back to the shack.

---

The afternoon quieted early. The Heron was gone by twelve-thirty and the lobster boats would not start coming back until three at the earliest. The shack was warm — the south-facing window taking the April afternoon sun, the stove banked low, the room holding whatever heat the season offered. She worked through the remaining paperwork: the Bangor shortage memo, the second float entries transferred to the seasonal ledger, the Heron's cargo receipt.

At half past three she put down the pen.

Outside the window: the empty floats in the afternoon low, the lobster buoys marking the outer channel, the breakwater running east to where the red fixed light would come on when the evening reached it. It wasn't on yet. She knew where it was.

She had twenty minutes before the four o'clock radio check.

She opened the log ledger to the current date. Then she turned back.

The log ledger she was writing in now had been in use since January of last year — it was the fourth book in the harbor record since 1891, the first three on the shelf above the desk, the oldest book from June of that year in a different hand entirely, the harbor's record before any living harbormaster. She had re-covered the 1935 book two years after she started, when the spine cracked; she had done the 1923 book the year after that. She knew the pages by their weight and their smell. Her thumb found the pages for the fall of 1944, the winter, and then she was through that year and into the 1935 book and she was turning through the autumn and into November.

Owen's handwriting came in at November 1.

His hand had a slight backward lean, the letters large and clear, the ink faded to brown at the older dates but still entirely legible in the afternoon light. He had been a careful log-keeper. She had been his deputy for six years before he died and had read his entries through all of them, and she could still anticipate the shape of each letter before it arrived — the *r* with its small curl at the tip, the *s* that ran slightly compressed, the *barometer* where the final letters crowded a little as if his pen moved faster than his hand.

November 3: fog all day, two vessels anchored overnight in the cove. November 7: mail boat delayed, seas at the outer bar. November 10: barometer 29.8 and falling, wind northwest and freshening. November 11: wind NNW at twenty-two knots, sea state four to five, all vessels secured.

November 12.

*November 12, 1935. Weather deteriorating, wind NNW increasing, barometer 29.1 and falling. Putting out additional mooring lines on —*

The sentence ended mid-line. The pen had come up from the page and not returned. The rest of the November 12 page was blank, and after it the next page in her own hand with a different date — the date she had taken over.

She read it.

She had read it many times. She had read it in the first winter after, when she was still rebuilding the hours around the storm. She had read it in 1939, when the war started in Europe and she had found herself in the shack on a September evening with the log open for no reason she could fully name. She had read it in October 1943, the night before the body came in, sitting at this desk until midnight with a particular quality of attention she would not have called grief.

This time was not those times. She was reading it as someone who had finished what it was in the middle of.

He had stopped mid-entry to go put out the mooring lines. The weather had been moving faster than the barometer showed.

She closed the November 1935 page. She turned back to April 25, 1945.

---

She wrote the day.

*April 25, 1945. Weather: clear. Temperature 52°F. Wind SE, 6 knots. Barometer 30.2, rising. Visibility: unlimited.*

*Tide: high water 0914, 5 feet 2 inches. Low water expected 1527.*

*Vessels: seven lobster boats out; return expected by 1700. Both draggers active — Lily B., Mackerel Sky. Mail boat Heron, Tuesday arrival 1140, departed 1230. Three freight manifests received and signed: hardware/dry goods, Bangor order, partial, backlog, Goulding notified; fuel oil, south pier; Goulding parcel cargo, received and receipted.*

*Dock register action: seasonal berth resolution, Farber (June M.)–Pelletier, float 3 conflict. Farber assigned float 2 inside, Pelletier assigned float 2 outside. Entered and signed.*

*Mail boat Tuesday notification: none.*

She set the pen down and read it back. There was nothing to change.

She picked up the pen again.

Below the formal entry, in the same compressed exact hand she had been using in this log for nine years:

*Harbor in order. Nine years, five months. All boats accounted for.*

She put the pen down and looked at what she had written.

It was accurate. The harbor had been in order when she arrived at six forty-five and would be in order when she left tonight. Nine years and five months was what the calendar said, from November 1935 to April 1945. All seven lobster boats were registered and out and coming back. Both draggers were registered and running. The Heron was logged. The freight was receipted. The mooring assignments were in ink.

She closed the log.

---

The tide clock: she checked it. Four minutes fast. She had set it Monday and it had gained its four minutes since, which was what it did. She reached up and moved the hand back.

At four o'clock she called the NNW channel. The Beaumont brothers checked in from the outer bar — position and ETA, conditions normal. She logged them. Two more boats checked in before four-fifteen; she logged them both and gave the harbor conditions and signed off.

She banked the stove draft further. She locked the desk drawer. She took Owen's key ring from the nail by the door — four keys, unchanged since Owen had carried them — and used the shack key to lock the door behind her.

The red fixed light on the breakwater was on. She had seen it come on from the window, the first light of the evening, the harbor mouth marked. The lobster boats were coming in; she could hear the engines cutting as they found their moorings in the early dusk. Seven out, seven coming back.

She walked up the hill toward home.

# Komm Rein

The barn in late April was the same barn it had been in every October of the last two years and every month between them: the same smell of hay and cattle and morning damp in the boards, the same gray light through the high eastern windows coming in at an angle that moved six inches across the floor between the first milking and the second, the same sounds of the cows pulling at the water troughs and shifting in the stanchions before full light. Outside it was April, the field mud beginning to firm and the maples at the south bend of the road putting on leaves, but in here it was the same barn it had been in October 1943 when the icehouse was new and the arrangement was new and everything about it was new. Two years and the barn had absorbed all of it into its ordinary sounds. There were four mornings left.

The spring light on the hay in the loft was different from November — not the blue-white of January, not the flat gray of mud season, but a yellow that reached the far wall and made the dust visible in it. The smell of the barn in April was the smell of a winter's enclosure not yet fully aired: the cows inside all winter, the spring cleaning not done, the high windows still latched against the last cold. In another week she would open them properly. In another week the four men would be gone.

The morning routine had been what it always was: the six o'clock milking, the clean-up, the first feeding, the water troughs. She had done these things alongside the four prisoners and Lonzo Reed for twenty-four months and they had all learned the barn's particular sequence so well that nobody had to say which task came next; you simply arrived at the next thing and did it. This morning was the same, except that it was the last one.

She gave Karl the letter on the morning before the truck was due.

Lonzo Reed stepped outside through the side door for his cigarette at the same point in the early routine he always did — for the cigarette, or because twenty-four months of the same hours had made one minute out of the barn's particular air necessary. The door shut and she heard his boots on the gravel and then nothing.

She had carried the letter in her coat pocket since March, since Karl told her through the fence that repatriation would begin in weeks. She had known since then what she was going to do with it and had not done it, and now there was one morning left.

She crossed the barn to where Karl was at the far stanchion.

She said: Ich habe das gefunden. In der Scheune. Im Februar, letztes Jahr.

She held out the envelope. He looked at it before he took it — the look you give a thing you had stopped expecting to see again. The paper had gone soft at the crease lines from handling, and the upper left corner where the return address had been was stained pale brown from the hay it had lain in. His mother's name on the front in the postal officer's hand. He took the envelope from her and turned it over once.

He said: Ich hab mich gefragt, wo es hingegangen ist.

She said: Es tut mir leid.

He said: Nein. Without sharpness.

He held the envelope a moment without opening it. Then: Du konntest es lesen. Not a question.

She said: Ja.

He nodded once and put the letter in the inside pocket of his jacket, the pocket over his chest, and pressed it flat with his palm.

He said: Deine Mutter — beginning the sentence slowly, feeling for the path through the words. He stopped there.

She said: Wir beten für sie.

He looked at her. His face was the face it had been for twenty-four months — different from October 1943 in the ways that farm work and two winters make a face different, the jaw steadier, the skin rougher, the eyes accustomed. He said: Ich glaube, es geht ihr gut. Ich hoffe es.

She said: I hope so too.

He turned back to the stanchion. Lonzo's boots sounded on the gravel outside and the side door opened and the barn returned to itself.

---

The truck came at mid-morning. She heard the engine on the road before it turned in through the gate — the camp administration truck from Houlton, olive drab, the same model that had come with supply deliveries occasionally in the past two years. Two camp soldiers got down from the cab without hurry, one carrying a brown folder with the transfer paperwork.

Lonzo Reed was in the yard with his Springfield at his side and his winter coat on, the collar turned up against the April wind — the same coat he had worn all winter, the loose button on the left front still loose the way it had been since January. He walked over and took the folder and read the paperwork the way he read all paperwork: steadily, without hurry, nodding at the relevant parts. He signed with the pencil stub from his shirt pocket and handed the folder back.

The four prisoners came out of the icehouse with their things. There was not much — twenty-four months had accumulated some quantity of objects for each man but not much: a bag or a folded parcel, some letters, whatever the camp stores had issued over two winters. One of the three men Hannah had never learned to say right carried a folded blanket under his arm. Karl came out third. He had his jacket buttoned, his bag in one hand, and the inside pocket of his jacket lay flat against his chest where the letter was.

When they came out he did not look toward the porch.

Then, once, he did. She looked back. His face did not change and hers did not either, and then his head turned to follow the motion of the tailgate going down, and that was all. The four men loaded into the truck bed. The tailgate went up.

Lonzo shook hands with one of the camp soldiers — brief, two pumps, the handshake of strangers finishing the same piece of work. He stepped back to the yard's edge. The second soldier got in the cab. The engine turned over.

---

She was on the porch. She did not remember going up the steps. Her father was beside her at the railing, both hands around his coffee cup, already there the way he was sometimes simply there when something was starting in the yard without him. She had not heard him come out. Her mother had not come to the door.

They stood at the rail and watched the truck maneuver. The yard was not large and the turn was tight for the loaded truck and the engine labored while the front wheels found their angle. Beside her her father was breathing — she could hear him in the quiet of the yard — and he had not spoken since they came to the porch. He stood the way he stood at the icehouse window in the evenings, or at the edge of the south field when the weather was coming in from the northwest, weight settled into his feet, watching something he had no way to change.

The truck found the lane and moved forward. It went slowly down toward the road, the ruts filling with pale water behind the tires as the weight passed over them. At the end of the lane it turned south.

It went past the fence line along the south field. Past the heaved second post, the staple she had driven while Karl held the wire. Into the maple stand at the south bend and gone.

She counted without intending to. Under thirty seconds and the engine sound was gone south too, toward the highway, toward Houlton.

Lonzo Reed was still in the yard. He stood looking at where the truck had been, the Springfield at his side, his coat hem loose in the wind. Then he looked toward the porch. He lifted his chin once and turned and walked down the lane. He went around the south bend.

The yard was empty.

Her father had not moved beside her. The tire tracks of the truck were filling slowly with the pale water that rose through this clay when you pressed it. The icehouse door was standing open at the back of the yard — left open when the four men came out and no one had gone back to close it. She could see the dark opening from the porch, the empty room inside, the rough walls the renovation had put up two years ago. The first time the icehouse had stood empty since April of 1943. The door open to the cold April air for the first time in two years.

From inside the barn came the ordinary sounds of the cows in the stanchions, indifferent to the hour. Forty-five cows. The south field across the fence, too soft to turn yet — another week, maybe two. The mud of the yard going still in the mid-morning light.

---

Her father put his hand on her shoulder.

The weight of his hand was specific — the farmer's hand, wide and dry and heavy, the hand that had been milking cows and turning hay and holding fence posts on this farm for twenty-two years. She could feel it through the wool of her coat. He did not grip or press. He set his hand on her shoulder the way you set something down carefully on a surface you want to stay level.

He said two words. She heard them in both languages he had. Komm rein.

She looked at the south bend of the road where the maple stand closed over it. The leaves were not yet full — late April and the canopy still thin enough for the light to come through in pieces. The road was empty.

Then she turned.

---

The kitchen was warm. The stove was going with the draft set low for the middle of the day, the room holding the warmth of the morning's bread and the coffee already on the table in three cups. Magda was at the stove with her back to them, setting the pot back on the burner. She did not turn around.

Hannah sat down.

Her father sat across from her.

The table held what it always held: the cups, the pot, the sugar bowl with the chip on the rim that had been there as long as Hannah could remember, the dish her mother set the stirring spoon on. The window over the counter with the view of the barn roof and past it the south field and the maple stand at the south bend where the road disappeared.

She put her hands around her cup and let the warmth come through. The coffee was what it always was. Through the window the late-morning light was the thin April light that made everything look like it could become something else in a week, the fields not yet what they would be and already past what they had been.

The radio on the counter was off. She had not turned it on this morning and her father had not turned it on and the kitchen held its own quiet — not the silence of the last two years, not her mother's closed silence and her father's German and the icehouse full at the back of the yard, but the ordinary quiet of a room with the stove going and the coffee on the table. In the radio, if she turned it on, she would find the war in the quality it had had all spring: the careful evenness of the announcer's voice, the names of places in Germany spoken in a changed tense, the armies moving through a country that was finishing itself place by place. She could reach out and turn the dial.

She did not.

Her mother came from the stove and set the pot on the table. She put her hand flat on the surface once — the gesture Hannah had been reading for two years as the closest thing to language her mother permitted herself. Then she sat down.

The three of them were at the table.

Her father drank his coffee. Her mother held her cup with both hands. Outside the window the barn roof was the same barn roof it had always been. The south field would tell her when it was ready — she would look at it this afternoon and the soil would give her what she needed to know. The icehouse door was still open at the back of the yard; she could not see it from this window but she knew it was open, the darkness inside it now the darkness of a room no longer in use.

The man on the breakwater would stay in the supplementary file in Portland, without a name.

Somewhere on a road south, the truck.

Her father set his cup down. Her mother refilled it from the pot, without being asked, without looking up. The farm was what it was and required what it required: the south field in another week, the forty-five cows waiting for the afternoon milking, the spring work ahead of all of it. The icehouse empty.

The war was in the radio. It was not yet over. It would be.

The farm was here.

## 30-komm-rein

### Dialogue gloss

**Cut:** "As if the apology were the thing he was declining."
After Karl says "Nein. Without sharpness." — the next sentence names what the refusal was refusing. This is the construction the style guide explicitly forbids ("as if to say," "which meant"). "Nein" and "Without sharpness" together are complete. The reader hears the line.

---

### Sentence-after-the-sentence (gesture gloss)

**Cut:** "— the acknowledgment —" from "He lifted his chin once — the acknowledgment — and turned and walked down the lane."
The chin-lift is the gesture. Bracketing it with its own label ("the acknowledgment") is the sentence-after-the-sentence pattern applied within a single sentence. After cut: "He lifted his chin once and turned and walked down the lane."

---

### Redundant transition / re-summary

**Cut:** "Her mother had heard them on the porch and poured three cups and set them out before they came through the door."
The preceding sentence already places the coffee on the table in three cups. This sentence explains the logistics of an image the reader already holds. The next sentence (Magda at the stove, back turned) is the image; the cut sentence is setup-explanation between two images that don't need it.

---

### Post-scene subtext naming (emotional structural analysis)

**Cut:** "her gesture for something she had observed and found sufficient, " from Magda's gesture sentence.
Original: "She put her hand flat on the surface once — her gesture for something she had observed and found sufficient, the gesture Hannah had been reading for two years as the closest thing to language her mother permitted herself."
The dash-clause contained two interpretive layers. The second ("the gesture Hannah had been reading for two years as the closest thing to language her mother permitted herself") is the earned payoff and is kept per the "leave one" rule. The first ("her gesture for something she had observed and found sufficient") explained the content of the gesture before the more resonant clause named its relational significance — and glossed the hand-flat image before the reader could receive it. Cut the first; kept the second.

---

### Not cut (noted for record)

- "watching something he had no way to change" (Albrecht at the porch railing): borderline — it interprets his stance, but it's a participial within the same sentence as the described image, not a following sentence. Left in per strict reading of "sentence-after-the-sentence" as a cross-sentence pattern.
- "Not a question" after "Du konntest es lesen": a delivery note on ambiguous German syntax (statement vs. question intonation is indeterminate on the page), not a content gloss; retained.
- The final four declaratives ("The war was in the radio. It was not yet over. It would be. / The farm was here."): all concrete statements, not abstract thesis restatement; retained.

## Macro arc assessment

### Arc shape — overall

*Coldwater Reach* has a clean four-phase plan (Setup 1–8 / Development 9–16 / Turn 17–23 / Resolution 24–30) and the structural bones are sound. The opening eight chapters do efficient work introducing three POVs plus Henry Crow, and the resolution phase (Chs 24–30) is the book's best-woven section: threads resolve in staggered sequence, the mystery protection holds, and the final two chapters (29, 30) earn their weight. The main problems are in the middle: a real midbook sag in the mystery threads, one risky consecutive-chapter pair, and an ending-mode pattern that could flatten the development escalation curve.

---

### Midbook sag — Chapters 17–22 (the mystery goes quiet)

The central spine of Threads 1 and 2 (What Eira Knows / Who Was the Dead Man) makes no meaningful forward movement for six consecutive chapters — Chs 17 through 22, covering May through November 1944. The weave check marks Thread 1 advancing at Ch 17 (twelve words between Eira and Marcus: "Nothing from Portland") and again at Ch 20 (a brief dock exchange), but the story-arc summaries confirm both are gestures rather than advances. Thread 2 marks nothing in this stretch at all.

Six chapters — roughly a fifth of the novel — carry the book on Hannah/Karl, Hannah/father, and Marcus/Henry threads only. That's legitimate dramatic material, but the mystery's engine having gone entirely cold for that span creates a low-pressure corridor precisely where accumulation should be building toward the December wallet revelation (Ch 23). The risk is that when the wallet arrives, readers who remember the mystery primarily as "what Eira knows" will feel the six-chapter gap as the book having moved on — and the cliffhanger mode at Ch 23 will land softer than intended.

**Flag:** Chapters 17–22 need at least one additional mystery-thread beat somewhere in the run. Ch 20 (Mail Boat) is the natural host — it already has an Eira/Marcus exchange; extending that contact toward the proximity of the mystery (without prematurely surfacing it) could sustain the thread without disrupting structure. The fix is a single paragraph of deepened interiority or a withheld detail, not a new scene.

---

### D-Day pair — Chapters 18–19 (identical emotional shape)

Chapters 18 (June Radio) and 19 (The Zenith) cover the same event — June 6, 1944 — from Hannah's POV and Marcus's. Both are high-concept ideas executed individually. The problem is that they land on nearly the same emotional note: in both, the POV character is near a radio, the war is arriving as sound, and the chapter closes on something that cannot be said (Hannah's father's single German sentence to no one; the four sentences across twenty minutes of silence on the porch). Both end in the "silence is the thing" mode — Ch 18 elliptical, Ch 19 literary fade. The content differs, but the emotional gesture is cognate.

Consecutive chapters should not register as emotional echoes of each other. One of the two needs a distinct texture at its close. Ch 18's closing image (the father's single German sentence) is the more surprising and should probably be preserved. Ch 19 has more latitude — Marcus's chapter could close on action, information, or even the briefest forward implication, rather than the porch-silence fade. This is a low-word fix, not a restructure.

---

### Ending-mode clustering in the Development phase

Of the nine resolved-beat closings across the novel, five fall in Chs 9–17 (the Development phase and early Turn): Chs 9, 13, 15, 17, and then Ch 20. The run 13 → 15 → 17 is three resolved beats in five chapters (with one elliptical in between). For a novel working in restraint throughout, this could feel like the book repeatedly arriving at the same small clearing before walking back into the forest. Escalation should be visible even in a quiet novel — each chapter's closing beat should feel *further along* than the last, not equivalently settled.

Chapters 15 (Sprechen) and 17 (Ice Out) are the two most likely candidates for mode adjustment if an edit is warranted. Ch 15's resolved beat (Hannah and Karl are now in each other's language — something shifts) is a genuine advance and should stay. Ch 17's resolved beat (dock dispute resolved, twelve words with Marcus) is the weakest close in the Development phase — the chapter is doing Eira-thread maintenance and its resolution is administrative. If Ch 17 closed elliptically instead — leaving the harbor's ordinary-on-the-surface texture slightly open — it would not repeat the same mode across Chs 13/15/17 and would hold more tension before the D-Day pair.

---

### Thread 6 scaffolding risk

Henry Crow's two chapters (Ch 8, 1,500 words; Ch 22, 1,500 words) are separated by fourteen chapters and roughly eleven story-months. Thread 6 is meant to accumulate through the margins of Marcus's chapters in between, but those margins depend on the reader tracking a friendship that has only two named anchors in the entire novel. The Ch 28 resolution moment — Henry staying until midnight after the liberation news, and the two sentences that mean what they mean — is the most emotionally compact resolution in the book. If the friendship hasn't accumulated enough visible weight across the Marcus chapters, that moment won't carry what it's meant to.

No structural change needed, but the per-chapter pass on Chs 19, 22, and 28 should verify that the friendship's texture is present — not explained but *felt* — in the Marcus POV. The craft log shows Ch 19 (The Zenith) carries the friendship well. Ch 22 (Henry's chapter) and Ch 28 are the checkpoints.

---

### Climax/coda balance — sound

The resolution phase (Chs 24–30) is properly weighted. Threads resolve across seven chapters in different registers — fragment/identification (Ch 24), daughter/father (Ch 25), the addendum (Ch 26), repatriation foretold (Ch 27), liberation/recognition (Ch 28), spring log (Ch 29), departure (Ch 30). The two deliberately unresolved threads (Thread 2 and Thread 6) are held with discipline. Ch 30's coda mode is the right close. The only small concern is that Eira's thread resolves formally at Ch 26 but she appears again substantively at Ch 29 — that's appropriate (the spring log as emotional aftermath), not padding, provided Ch 29 doesn't re-settle what Ch 26 already settled. The story-arc summary suggests it doesn't: Ch 29 gives Eira Owen, not the addendum, as its center.

---

### Summary priority list

1. **(High)** Chs 17–22: mystery sag; find one beat in this run, probably Ch 20, to keep Thread 1/2 warm without resolving.
2. **(Medium)** Chs 18–19: D-Day pair's closing notes are too cognate; Ch 19's porch-silence fade could be varied.
3. **(Medium)** Ch 17: resolved-beat ending in the weakest-close spot of the arc; consider elliptical.
4. **(Low)** Thread 6: verify the friendship's texture lands in Marcus's Chs 19, 24, and 28 before the per-chapter pass closes.

# The Icehouse in October

The alarm was the four-fifteen, which she had moved back in September because the dark came earlier now and earlier meant harder. When it went she lay for a moment adding up the warmth she had against the warmth she would need: the cold of the kitchen floor, the cold of the yard, the barn and its better warmth that smelled of forty-five cows and hay and the steam of animals who had been working through their own slow processes since midnight. She added these in order and then she got up.

Her boots were by the door, laces already loosened from the night before. She dressed in the kitchen without lighting a lamp — she knew every nail and hook in her own kitchen in the dark — and took the lantern off the shelf and went out.

The yard in October. The dark was total until the lantern made it particular: the pump handle, the corner of the silo, the low fence of the kitchen garden with its dead stalks. The hayfield to the east gave off cold in a way the harbor-cold didn't, a cold from the earth rather than the water, dense and close to the ground. She was halfway to the barn before she could hear the cows clearly over the wind. Forty-five animals telling her what she already knew.

Inside she hung the lantern on the iron hook by the door and the light went orange in the warmth. The smell hit before the warmth did: hay and manure, the sweet-sharp smell of milk, the wet-wood smell of the stalls that had been wet since October and wouldn't dry until May. Above everything the animal steam, the breath and bodies of forty-five cows giving off heat into an enclosed space. She had breathed this smell every morning of her life.

She started at the near end. Heide shifted left when she heard the bucket and had to be corrected — not hard, just redirected. Brunhild was easy. The red one they called Rote was easy. She worked down the stalls in the order her father had taught her when she was small enough that the cows had seemed very large, and her hands did it while the rest of her was still waking up, and the barn was warm and loud in the particular way of barns at four-thirty in the morning, which is not warm the way a room is warm, not loud the way a room is loud, but warm and loud in the way of forty-five large animals being specific about what they needed.

She was on the third bucket when the far door opened and her father came in.

He went directly to the east side, which was his, and he spoke to the first stall cow without stopping — die Kühe and their names and what he needed them to do, in the barn German that was older than the other German and didn't belong to the war. She had heard it her whole life. It was a different instrument than the German he used in the kitchen now, or the German she heard in the evenings through the wall. The barn German was working language, specific, not addressed to anyone she could hear.

He came along the aisle behind her toward the center where their rows met. She was reaching forward to adjust the bucket when he passed.

He said: Morgen.

He said it the way he had always said *good morning* — flatly, without looking up, a fact already established that required only acknowledgment. He had stopped saying *good morning* in the kitchen, at the table, when he stopped speaking English at home, but in the barn he had kept *good morning* and then at some point it became *Morgen*. She was not certain when. She hadn't been paying close enough attention to mark the exact day.

She said: Morgen.

She had started saying it back in August. She hadn't decided to. It was simply the response that required the least choosing, when the alternative was standing on the English side of it and making something of that. He had always said good morning; she had always said good morning back.

He moved on without responding to her response, which she hadn't expected. Beyond her, toward his side, and his German came back in fragments down the length of the stalls — a cow's name, an instruction. The cows responded in their own register, which was not interested in the language being used.

---

At half past eight she heard the truck.

Lonzo Reed came through the gate with his Springfield over his right shoulder and his collar turned up against a cold that was October cold, not yet November cold, but Lonzo addressed all inconveniences at the level of their theoretical maximum. He had been a fisherman before the war and he moved with a fisherman's deliberateness — not slow, simply finished with haste as a method. He walked to the icehouse, knocked twice on the door, and pulled the latch.

The four men came out.

There was no drama in it. They had done this every morning since April: they emerged, they put their coats on in the yard, they separated to their assigned tasks without conference or complaint. Ernst — she thought his name was Ernst, she'd heard it once in June and had not confirmed it — came first. Then the heavyset one whose name she had never caught. Then the quiet one who favored his right shoulder but never mentioned it to Lonzo, because mentioning it to Lonzo would have required language neither of them had. Karl came last.

He came out pulling his jacket sleeve over his right wrist and saying something to the heavyset one in German that made the heavyset one tilt his head slightly. Then he saw that Lonzo was already making his perimeter check and he stopped saying it and looked at what needed doing.

He was nineteen. Lonzo had said so in July, in the tone of a man grateful the situation wasn't worse: *the youngest one's just nineteen.* As if the age were a mitigating factor in some calculation Hannah had not been asked to perform. Karl was from somewhere in Bavaria, fifty kilometers from where her father was born, which she had thought about more than once since they arrived in April.

He moved the way boys moved — not clumsily but with something in reserve, energy not yet fully organized into efficiency. She noticed this the way she noticed whether the cows were favoring one side or the other: not as a judgment, as a reading.

Lonzo said his three German words and the four men spread to their tasks.

Karl went to the woodpile. He picked up the maul and turned it once in his hands before he set the first round on the block — this was always his habit, measuring first, then splitting. She'd watched it enough times to know. He'd been good at it since June and was better now. The quarter-round came off clean on the first stroke, the log falling to both sides evenly, and she turned away before he could notice her watching.

In front of Lonzo, Karl and her father were simply two people in the same yard. They didn't look at each other any differently than either of them looked at the fence or the barn.

Lonzo stamped his feet and watched his breath go white and disperse. The morning kept on being the morning.

---

The feed store closed at five on Wednesdays. She took the Ford after school let out and drove the three miles of unpaved inland road — the truck pulling right the way it always did, the heater requiring the knob held at an angle slightly left of center, the Bangor station coming in on the radio with enough static that she kept it on anyway because it was better than the absence of it.

From the ridge above town the harbor was visible for a moment through the October haze: a strip of gray water, the breakwater a thin dark line extending from the dock, the fixed red light at its seaward end. She didn't look at it for longer than the road allowed.

She had heard it before she saw the water. Ellis Carver, in the hall outside Klein's classroom Tuesday morning: a man on the breakwater, the Coast Guard there and gone by ten, no one from Coldwater missing, no name and no papers and Reg Farber's youngest had found him before breakfast. She'd heard it again at lunch, from two other girls, with different details. She'd heard it from the Dunham boy in Latin class, who'd added additional details that contradicted Ellis Carver's details without either of them seeming to notice.

The general store was also the post office, which meant it was where information arrived without anyone needing to carry it. Mabel Trask was behind the counter and the Morrissette brothers were in the seed display for reasons that had nothing to do with seeds. They were there because Mabel knew.

What Mabel knew: not a fisherman, not anyone from around here. The Farber boy had thought he was sleeping. He was not sleeping. The Coast Guard took the body and took the log pages with it, which Mabel found notable and said so. The man had no identification. No one was looking for anyone from Coldwater.

The Morrissette brothers added commentary about a man they had once seen in Rockland who had struck them as the type, though they acknowledged it might not be the same man. Hannah listened. She bought her four bags of dairy meal — the good kind, not the cut kind, because the cows had been producing well and her father's rule was that good cows got good meal — and she heaved them over the tailgate one at a time with her left hip against the lip, the method her father had taught her, which left the small of the back out of it. Four bags, four thumps. She tied the tailgate and drove home.

The heater knob at its angle. The radio in fragments. The man was in her mind — not sharply, just present — his absence of name, the city shoes that Mabel had mentioned in passing. She had seen men in city shoes in Rockland, men who had not dressed for the coast. The shoes alone said something.

She drove the inland road with the harbor behind her and the farmland opening up on both sides, the shadow of the silo already stretched halfway across the yard when she turned up the farm road. The light had gone orange on the eastern fields. The cows would be wanting their evening feed.

---

After supper she heard her father's voice through the kitchen wall.

The east side of the house shared its partition with the narrow yard hallway, and from the window above the dry sink she could hear things in the yard that would not be audible from anywhere else in the house. She had found this out by accident years ago and had used it since.

Magda was at the table with the hip seam in Albrecht's work pants. The right hip seam opened every October when he pulled the heavier work from the trunk — it had opened so reliably for so many years that she thought of it as a fall event, like the first hard frost, like the leaves off the maple by the kitchen door. Her mother's needle moved at the pace she worked at everything: exactly as fast as the thing required. She had not spoken in six months. The doctor in Rockland had a word for it that Hannah had not written down, a long word, functional at the beginning, meaning: not injury, not illness, but something the body had decided. Hannah's own theory was different and she kept it to herself.

The kitchen was quiet enough that she heard her father's voice through the wall — not the words, just the low movement of it — and she went to the window.

The icehouse window was lit. The kerosene lamp, which Lonzo had authorized in June when the wood stove started drawing properly: yellow and steady from outside, the window cracked its two or three inches that she had come to associate with the evenings since August. Her father stood in the yard with his back to her. She could see his work coat, the white of his breath.

Karl's voice came through the window. He was asking something. Then her father's voice: lower, going on past where a simple answer would have stopped.

She had never been close enough in the evenings to hear the words, and she had not gone closer on purpose. What she could hear was the quality of it — the rhythm of two people talking about something that warranted the talking. The barn German was not this. The barn German was a tool, transactional, used for specific animals in a specific order. This moved through the air differently. It had the cadence of things being described or asked about in earnest, of a question that expected a real answer.

Her father's shoulders in his work coat were not the shoulders she had been watching for two years. The particular set they'd had — since the telegram, she thought, or before the telegram, since December 1941 when the radio news came in and he had sat very still for a long time and she had been sixteen and had not known what she was seeing — that set was not there now. He was not relaxed; he was standing in the cold at an icehouse window and relaxed was not the situation. Present in one place, not carrying the elsewhere that had been in him for so long she had almost forgotten what his shoulders looked like without it.

The lamp inside shifted — someone moving near it — and the window brightened briefly and settled. Her father said something. Karl answered.

She stepped back from the window.

Her mother's needle moved in the hip seam. In the kitchen the only sound was the creak of the chair and the pull of thread and her own breathing, which she had not noticed until now.

---

She went upstairs.

The man on the breakwater was still with her — no name, city shoes, not from anywhere local.

Underneath the man on the breakwater was the sound of her father's voice at the window. The length of it. Karl on the other side of the glass, Karl's question receiving an answer that was longer than the question. She did not know what they had been talking about. She had not decided to try to find out.

The house made its sounds around her — the pipes settling, the boards in the corner of her room that spoke once every night, the cold working at the seams of the window glass. She lay in the dark and the dark of thinking and the dark before sleep had no clear boundary between them, and eventually she was on the far side of that boundary without having crossed it.
