# A Letter from New York

The second line of the examination instructions had given him trouble since Sunday evening.

He had written it out in his room the night before — three attempts in the margin of his notebook page, each crossed — and then again this morning on the classroom board before the first class came up the east stair. He stood at the board with the chalk and read back what he had written: *When you do not know a word, consult the sense of the sentence.* The problem was *consult*, which required the student to have an intuition about what consulting a sentence meant, and it was exactly this intuition that he could not assume. He wiped the line.

He tried: *If you do not know a word, work from what the sentence needs it to mean.*

He stood back.

The German classroom occupied the second floor's east end, and in December it received the morning light in a way that was briefly pleasant before the cold coming off the north sill reasserted itself — the cold was better now, since Henry had planed the casement, but there was still a way the December light looked through those windows that was more like winter light pressing against glass than like light in a room. The examination sheets waited on the corner of his desk: three copies, typed himself on the school typewriter, which did not have the characters for *ü* or *ä*, requiring small substitutions he had worked out to preserve the sense if not the precision.

He read the second instruction line back. That would do. He turned to lay the sheets on the desks and the bell from the floor below rang for the first class.

---

Parsons appeared during the interval between classes.

She came with the mail binder under her arm, the Tuesday delivery from the general store, which was also the post office, the mail sorted before school and walked up the hill in the binder. Marcus had Latin in twenty minutes. He knew, in the abstract, that nothing requiring an immediate response was likely to be in the binder, and he opened it anyway, as he always did, with the specific attention that he applied to anything arriving from outside Coldwater: the possibility that it was news.

The envelope from Dr. Feld was fourth from the top.

*Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars.* The letterhead on the envelope was the letterhead he had been receiving, in one form or another, since autumn 1940 — placement confirmation, credential documentation, quarterly notices about the wider network of displaced scholars the Committee maintained. Feld's own letters had been less frequent: two in 1941, one each in 1942 and the early part of 1943. Marcus had sent two postcards in the spring of this year, brief, reporting that his position continued and his address remained the same.

The envelope was thicker than a practical letter.

He opened it and read it standing. He had to sit down and read it again.

Feld was writing about a problem the Committee had encountered in tracking scholars who had been in transit during 1942 and into 1943. Some had arrived at their placements and failed to notify the office; this was not uncommon, and the Committee had means for re-establishing contact in most of those cases. Others were in Europe, unreachable for reasons that Feld described with a care that Marcus read as the careful prose of someone who did not yet know how to describe what was happening in Europe and was not going to guess. The third category was the one Feld lingered on: scholars who appeared to have been in transit and then ceased to be in transit, with no subsequent documentation and no record at any receiving institution.

Marcus knew that phrase. *Keine nachfolgende Dokumentation.* No subsequent documentation. The Emergency Committee used it the way a port authority used *vessel not arrived* — accurately, without affect. The period between his release from the camp and his arrival in Boston in August 1941 had been several weeks in which Marcus Klein existed in no file. The Committee had an address for him — the camp — that was no longer his address, and no forwarding address until he made contact from Boston. For those weeks, he had been a man of whom it could be written: *last documented at.* And then the next address.

The specific case was in the third page of the letter. Feld was careful with surnames, citing Committee privacy practice; he used initials where he could. A Dr. Felix K., he wrote — a linguist of German-Jewish origin, formerly of the University of Leipzig, who had been corresponding with the Committee from somewhere in Canada since early in 1943. His last letter to the office had been postmarked Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, September 22, 1943. In it he had told the Committee of his intention to travel south by sea, to reach Boston by late October; he had a contact in Boston. He had not written since. The Boston contact had heard nothing. The Committee had no other channel.

Feld was writing to Marcus partly because Marcus was placed in Maine — geographically relevant to a route running south from the Nova Scotia coast — and partly because he knew Marcus had been long enough on the Committee's rolls to have some reach into the network. Did Marcus know anything of a Dr. Felix K., Leipzig, a linguist?

Marcus read the letter through twice more.

He had a partial recollection — not a name, but something adjacent to a name, the way a word hovered at the edge of retrieval before either arriving or failing to arrive. A man at a philology conference in Vienna in 1936. Something at the intersection of Germanic philology and historical linguistics; he recalled a corridor in the Anatomiegebäude, the cold institutional light the building always had, two men talking in the specific Leipzig-accented German he had always found recognizable at a distance. He had been introduced. He had not spoken with the man at any length.

The name would not come. He might be constructing the memory from Feld's description rather than from the conference itself.

He set the letter on his desk.

Latin was beginning.

---

The German examination was the following Tuesday.

He read through Hannah Pfeiffer's paper first, which was not his usual order — he customarily worked alphabetically, which put Doris Hatch first and Hannah last — but which he found himself doing anyway. She had translated the passage from Goethe's correspondence correctly, which was not surprising; what stopped him was the word order. The passage was a letter Goethe had written to Schiller in October 1798 about the difficulty of rendering a natural scene in language without losing what had made the scene worth rendering. In the key sentence, the verb fell at the end, as German required. Most students, encountering this, pulled the verb forward; English demanded it, and the instinct was not wrong. Hannah Pfeiffer had left the verb where Goethe had placed it. The English she had produced was technically awkward and philologically correct, a sentence translated in the grammatical sense rather than the idiomatic one — you could see the German inside the English the way you could sometimes see the structure of a building inside the material it was built from.

He marked it correct and moved on to Doris Hatch.

He had not said anything. It was not the examination's occasion, and it was not entirely the German's occasion either — not a conversation he was equipped to have in December with three weeks until Christmas break. He wrote *Good work* on her sheet and the same on Doris's and *This is improving* on Louise Pelletier's and meant all three.

Latin was going well. Caesar's *De Bello Gallico*, the organization of the camp and the construction of the fortifications, twelve students working through the ablative absolutes with the patient incomprehension of people who found something merely difficult.

He encountered Henry Crow on Thursday afternoon in the second-floor hallway, Henry moving past with the supply cart.

"The window," Marcus said.

Henry looked at him.

"The north sill," Marcus said. "The cold isn't coming through the way it was."

"Block plane," Henry said. "And new caulk on the outside. It'll hold as long as the temperature stays above ten degrees. Below ten, the frame tightens." He added: "Might stick closed."

Marcus said he appreciated it.

Henry said it was his job and pushed the cart toward the supply closet at the hallway's end.

---

The school thinned in the last two weeks before Christmas break, the way it thinned every year — boys finding reasons to be on the water or in the timber, girls finding reasons to be needed at home, the teachers accepting these reasons with less scrutiny than they would have applied before the war. The building was quiet in the afternoons. Marcus finished the examination corrections and began preparing the January syllabus, working in the classroom for an hour after four o'clock because his room was colder than the classroom and the classroom had the east light for another forty minutes.

He had read Feld's letter three more times over the week. He had not replied.

---

He read it again that evening in his room, the lamp on, the letter flat on his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark that had been in place since half past four. There was no moon he could see and the cold pressed against the glass. The radiator on the south wall was running well, which it did not always do this early in December, and the room was warm enough that he could work at his desk without his coat.

He set the letter down. He took the German notebook from the shelf above his desk — more than half-full now, the compressed German hand running through its pages from April — and turned to the first blank leaf.

He wrote, in German, what he had:

*Felix K. Linguist. Leipzig. Zuletzt belegt in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, 22. September 1943. Beabsichtigte, Boston auf dem Seeweg zu erreichen, Ende Oktober.*

He looked at what he had written for a moment and then wrote below it:

*Ich glaube, ihn nicht zu kennen.*

He set down the pen. The 1936 Vienna corridor was still where it had been all week — present, the quality of the light available, the Leipzig-accented German available — and the name was still not there. He might be wrong about the conference. He might have assembled the memory from the description and mistaken the assembly for recollection.

He picked up the pen. Below the previous lines he wrote:

*Yarmouth nach Boston. Die Küste von Maine liegt dazwischen.*

He read the three lines back.

Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. He had not been there. He knew it as a port town on the southwestern coast, a transit point on the sea routes between the Atlantic provinces and New England — knew it in the way he knew most Maritime geography: from a map he had studied when he was trying to understand his own route south, the autumn of 1941. He could bring the coastline's shape from the map. He could not bring the harbor, the town's character, what it looked like from the water in late September.

September 22, 1943. That was barely three weeks before the first heavy weather of the fall. A small vessel could make the run in favorable conditions in two to three days, or longer if the weather turned, or much longer, or not at all if the weather turned badly enough. It was a route that could be done. He did not know whether it had been.

He sat with the notebook open and the lamp on and thought about the phrase *zuletzt belegt in*.

Last documented in. The Emergency Committee's vocabulary for the point on the record where the thread ended. It was precise language; Feld was a precise man. He used the passive construction deliberately — *last documented in* rather than *last seen in* or *last known to be in* — because the documentation was what the Committee could stand behind, and he would not claim more certainty than the record gave him. The documentation ended at Yarmouth on September 22, 1943. What the documentation had been attached to continued, or did not continue, beyond that point, and the file had no way to say which.

He had been *last documented in* a place himself, in the summer of 1941. The documentation had said the camp; the camp had released him; for some weeks after that he had moved south without an address any file could reach him at. He had arrived in Boston, eventually, and written to the Emergency Committee from a boarding house on Commonwealth Avenue, and his file had been updated: Marcus Klein, Coldwater Reach, Maine, March 1942. Everything after that date was documented. Everything before August 1941, going back through the camp and London and Paris to Vienna, was documented also, in one archive or another.

Dr. Felix K. had been last documented in Yarmouth.

He did not write any of this in the notebook.

He put the pen down and opened the shortwave.

The BBC was not finding him tonight — static and the fringe of something that might have been German, or might have been Dutch, sliding in and out at the edge of resolution. He moved down and found an American broadcast, clear and even, a news signal from somewhere in the domestic network. The Pacific: the Marshall Islands, conditions described with the precise optimism of someone who had been given permission to transmit and was being careful with it. He listened to the names of islands he had not known before the war and would not have had occasion to know. Maloelap. Wotje. He did not know where these were on a chart with any precision; he was assembling the Pacific the way he had assembled the Maine coast, location by location, from a distance.

At nine-thirty he turned off the shortwave.

He took the Emergency Committee folder from the shelf between the English journal and the Stifter he had been reading since September. The folder held twelve letters now, going back to 1940, a paper record of his placement and its history. He put Feld's letter in the folder and put the folder back on the shelf.

He closed the German notebook and set it on the shelf above his desk.

Outside the east window: December dark, undiminished. He thought about Yarmouth, which he had not been to and did not know. He thought about the phrase *last documented in* and what came after it in the Committee's language: nothing, and then a date, and then the passive construction that meant someone had stopped being accountable to any record. He had been that. He knew the inside of it.

He turned off the lamp.

The room was dark and cold and smelled of woodsmoke from the furnace two floors below and of the particular density of cold books in a New England December. He did not write anything more. The notebook was on the shelf, the folder was on the shelf, the shortwave sat silent on his desk. He did not move for a while. Outside the window the dark had the quality December dark always had at this latitude: complete, and cold.

# What the Letter Said

Doris and Louise went past the desk in the current of coat-buttoning and the momentum of girls who have decided the afternoon is elsewhere. He heard Louise's laugh in the hallway — specific, uncontainable, the kind of laugh that was a fact about a person rather than a response to anything — and then the stair door, and the building's afternoon quiet.

Three forms of werden remained on the board. The future auxiliary, arranged in a column: wird, werden, werdet. He had written them with more care than the lesson warranted, the chalk letters spaced as though for a class of thirty rather than three, and he went to the board now and took the eraser.

Hannah Pfeiffer had not moved. She was at the middle desk, coat already on, her school bag on the desk before her but not yet buckled. She had stayed after before — once to ask about an irregular verb, and once for a question about the subjunctive in indirect questions that had lengthened into the most useful grammatical conversation he had managed in Coldwater — and she had always had a reason when she stayed, which was not universally true of students who lingered.

He tapped the eraser against the chalk rail and set it down. He went to his desk and opened his lesson folder.

She said: "There's something I don't entirely understand."

He said: "In what?"

She opened not her German grammar but her English literature notebook — the one he had seen her annotating through several weeks of Latin period, which was not his — and she took from between the pages a folded sheet of paper and set it on the front edge of her desk. "German," she said. "A phrase I follow partly."

He came around the desk to look.

---

He picked up the page. The wear at its folds registered before anything else — the paper softened there, the surface slightly fibrous from being taken out and refolded many times.

He had not asked where it came from. He would not ask.

A woman's hand. He understood this from the first line, and then from the particular use of wegen in the subordinate clause — Bavarian, or near enough; a formation that standard written German handled differently, a regional habit — and then from the letterforms themselves: the closing loops, the formation of the capitals, a schoolroom standard drilled in and retained without effort for forty or fifty years. He had been identifying regional written hands for twenty years. This one was not difficult.

He read from the beginning. She had asked about a phrase; he could not read a phrase. The letters on either side of it mattered for what it meant, and the letter's occasion mattered, and the whole domestic organization surrounding whatever had to be said mattered as much as what was said.

A neighbor's fence, replaced in autumn. Some difficulty with the materials, but holding now, better than the old one. Potato prices up. A cousin — Els — who had married in October: a small gathering, family present, weather better than October usually offered. The writer hadn't been able to attend but had sent something with Els's sister. The cellar better than last winter. A dog — the name blurred in the cursive — sick in December, something in the stomach, but recovered and back to his old habits.

He had been reading letters like this all his life — the domestic inventory that organized a world by its surfaces because the surfaces were what held. You said the fence, you said the cousin, you said the dog, and in saying them you maintained the world at its edges, kept the frame. He had received letters like this from Vienna, from Paris, from friends in places he would never return to. The inventory was a kind of loyalty: I am telling you the fence and the cousin and the dog because these things are still here. And sometimes, embedded in the inventory, between a wedding and firewood —

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. Wir beten für sie.

He read the sentence. He read it again. He continued to the end of the page, which closed in the middle of a paragraph about the cellar and ended there, no signature.

He looked up.

She had underlined die versucht haben zu gehen. He had read through the underlining without registering it.

He folded the page on its existing creases and set it on the edge of the desk between them.

She said: "Versucht — tried. And zu gehen — to go. But I don't have the whole phrase."

He said: "Those who tried to go are gone."

She was very quiet.

"Wir beten für sie," he said. "We pray for them."

"People who left Germany?" she said.

"People who tried to leave. Germany, or Austria, or Czechoslovakia. In the years before the war made it impossible — 1939, 1940, 1941 — there were people who attempted to emigrate and did not succeed. Who started and were stopped. Or who started and were not heard from again." The coal furnace behind the wall made its sound — something in the metal, a faint contraction against the February cold. "Some of the people who tried to go arrived in places like this. Some of them didn't arrive anywhere."

She said: "She knows particular people."

"Yes. The double relative — die die — gives you a specific group. A real group she knows. The names aren't in the sentence. Just the category: those who tried." He looked at the line. "The placement tells you the rest. Between a cousin's October wedding and the firewood. Past tense — the past perfective. This is something she knows and is passing on. It is already over. The prayer confirms it."

Hannah looked at her hands for a moment. Then: "And the people who tried to go — they were from the same community?"

"From her community. Yes." He paused. "She writes tried, not went. Not left. They attempted and did not complete. That is what the sentence contains."

She sat with it. She had an adolescent's capacity for absorbing a sentence without immediately producing a response to it, which he had noticed before in this room.

He did not say: I can date this letter to autumn 1943. A letter that mentions an October cousin's wedding and the onset of winter was written in late 1943, which meant that the people from their community who had tried to go in '39 or '40 or '41 had been gone for two years or more before she wrote this sentence, and the writing of it was not news but acknowledgment — telling her son in his POW camp in America what had become of the world he had come from. He did not say: the header is missing from this page, and I know what it means when a header is missing, and it tells me something about the path this page traveled to reach this room. He did not say: Yarmouth. He did not say the name from Feld's letter — the German-Jewish philologist, Leipzig, last documented Yarmouth Nova Scotia, September 1943 — and he did not say the coast of Maine between Yarmouth and Boston, and he did not say October.

He was close to saying these things to himself.

He handed the letter back to her.

---

She took it. She held it without immediately folding it, looking at the underlined phrase.

Then she looked up at him with the face that was not her classroom face. The classroom face was attentive and careful and gave nothing away. The other one, which appeared less often, was a girl thinking something and deciding whether to say it.

She said: "Were you one of them? The ones who tried to go?"

He was quiet for a moment.

"I am one of the ones who arrived," he said.

She received that.

"Vienna," he said. "Then Paris. London. Then Canada. Then here."

"Canada," she said.

"Briefly."

She did not ask about briefly. He had said the word with the register of a door that is shut, and she heard the register and left the door where it was. She had developed this particular skill somewhere. He knew where: the same place a girl would develop the skill of hearing her father through a floor, of reading the difference between a word that led somewhere and a word that was simply present in the room.

He said: "The leaving is not the hard part."

He had not intended to say this. He had known it was true for five or six years and had kept it in the notebook rather than giving it to rooms.

She looked at him.

"What is?" she said.

"The arriving," he said.

Which was a simplified version of the truth, close enough to the truth for a classroom in February, and as close as he had managed in language so far — the fuller version remained in the notebook, where he had been working on it since approximately Paris, and he had not yet found the sentence.

She was quiet for a moment. Then she said: "Yes."

Not I understand or I see. Just yes. Which was the right word, because it didn't claim more than she had.

She put the letter back between the annotation pages in the English literature notebook, closed it, buckled her school bag, and stood.

He said: "Good afternoon, Miss Pfeiffer."

She said: "Good afternoon." Then, at the door: "Thank you, Dr. Klein."

The door. The hallway. The stair door below. The building settling around its quiet.

---

He sat down at his desk.

The classroom arranged itself without him: the erased board, the three desks at their slight angles from the day's use, the chalk dust in the late February light. The coal furnace pressing its inadequate heat against the cold of the room, which absorbed it and remained cold. The east windows held February — condensation on the oldest frames, where the glass was thinnest and the fit loosest, the pines on the upper hill with their snow, the road below going toward four o'clock's early gray.

He reached for the letter from the edge of his desk and then stopped, because the letter was not there. She had taken it in her bag.

He put his hand flat on the surface.

Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg. He held the construction. In German — in the Bavarian formation, specifically — the double relative enacted the group before naming what happened to the group. Who they were first, before the fact of their going. The past perfective: had tried. Had been in the act of trying, had continued trying, had completed the trying, and it had not been enough. Sind weg: are gone. Not fled, not departed. Gone. Three words. Bavarian restraint doing the work of whatever the full account would require.

He thought about the woman who had written it. At a kitchen table somewhere, in a village whose letterforms he could place to within thirty or forty kilometers on the evidence of her handwriting — a village that lay within fifty kilometers of where a girl in his German class had grown up hearing her father's language, the dialect this woman wrote in, the register Hannah Pfeiffer's ear had been trained to by means she had never chosen. The world had a size. He had been learning this size since 1938, the same lesson in different rooms, in different languages, arriving each time as if for the first time. A mother at a table in Bavaria writing to her son in a POW icehouse in Maine, and the sentence she put between the cousin's wedding and the firewood, and the page separated from its header traveling from that table to this desk, and the girl who brought it to him, who carried in her speech the same dialect the letter was written in without knowing it — or without having said it.

He had told her the truth. What the phrase contained, what the construction meant, what kind of people the prayer was for. He had told her as much as was his to give from the letter she had given him, which was not the same as everything he had heard.

He held these things alongside each other and did not yet move them into sequence. They were adjacencies: real, probably connected, not yet proven. He had a habit of not closing adjacencies too quickly, a habit he had developed in the years when closing them too quickly had led to bad decisions in train stations and border offices. You looked at what you had; you wrote it down; you saw what it was.

Tonight he would write something in the notebook. He would look at what it looked like written down and decide from there.

He picked up his lesson folder and put it in his bag. His hat from the chair beside the desk. One of the student desks had drifted slightly from its usual position — the middle one, where she sat — and he moved it back, more carefully than necessary.

The world was a particular size. He had been learning this for six years.

He went out and closed the door.

# A Report from Portland

By the last week of March the ice was going from the inner cove — pulling back from the edges first, a dark rim of open water widening an inch a day, the granite shelf of the shore returning in the mornings like something remembered. The center still held: opaque where it had been clear, four inches where it had been five, the surface pale and slightly sunken where the melt had come through and refrozen in February. She had been watching this progress for three weeks.

The Callie B. and the Margaret Rose had moved back to their slips on the twentieth. Farber first, because Farber was like that about weather and tide, and the Pelletiers a day behind. The lobster boats were still on trailers at Pelletier's yard — Kincaid's four, the two from the Dunbar brothers — waiting on the ice and on permits that came out of Portland at their own pace. She had six boats on the waiting list for the first week of April. The radio had been busy for two weeks: weather checks, supply questions, the kind of talk that accumulated when men had been on shore since January and the season was getting close.

She did her rounds at half past seven. Dock cleats, the drain at the float ramp, the fuel line, the BC-1206's daily check. The tide clock had gained a minute since she last reset it. She wound it, adjusted it, made a note. The spring smelled different from the other seasons — not better, she had stopped that mistake years ago — but specific: salt and diesel and the cold mud coming up where the dock skirting had held ice all winter, and underneath both, something opened that had been shut.

In the afternoon she wrote the permits. Six boats, six sets of documentation, the spring registration forms that had to be filed with Portland by April 15. She had been harbormaster for more than eight years and the forms had not changed. She worked through them from top to bottom, the same order every year.

---

The letter came in Friday's mail.

It arrived with the February billings from the fuel cooperative — they were always late — a parts catalog from Portland Chandlery, and a Coastal Patrol circular about spring procedure. She took the stack back to the desk and dealt with them in order: bills, catalog, circular. The envelope from Boston was last.

Standard government stock, cream-colored, slightly heavy. Return address: First Coast Guard District, Headquarters, Boston, Massachusetts. Redirected through the Portland auxiliary, which had added a date stamp in blue ink, March 28 — nine days in transit.

She opened it and read it through.

---

The letter was a page and a half. Dated March 19. An administrative lieutenant she didn't know. At the bottom, a notation in smaller type indicating the original inquiry had been received from the Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, port authority and was being distributed to relevant coastal stations for information and response.

The substance: a party in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, had received no word from a man to whom they had either lent or rented a small wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet. The man had departed Yarmouth approximately September 28, 1943, reportedly heading south by sea, with the stated intention of making landfall in Massachusetts. He had not returned the boat. The owner had assumed, initially, that the occupant and the boat had reached their destination and that the boat had been sold or left somewhere. The missing-persons report had not been filed until February 1944, the letter noted, because the owner had been uncertain whether the report was his to make.

The description of the occupant: male, middle-aged, of continental European appearance, with limited English. No further identifying details available from the Yarmouth party.

The inquiry was being routed to coastal stations, the letter explained, because a body fitting some elements of the description — middle-aged male, civilian, no identification — had been recovered on the Maine coast in October 1943. The District was asking affected ports to provide any relevant information.

She set the letter on the desk. She read it again. Then she sat for a while with the radio on the south wall and the tide charts above it and the April light coming through the shack's east window.

---

What the letter had: a wooden motorboat, approximately eighteen feet. A single male occupant. Continental European appearance. Limited English. Departed Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, approximately September 28, 1943. Destination: Massachusetts, loosely.

What she had: a wooden boat, no lights, tied at the dock extension on the night of October 11, 1943. Gone before morning. A man stepping off the boat and standing at the foot of the dock extension before walking toward the breakwater. Dark overcoat, city cut. Leather shoes that had never been made for a dock. She had been in the shadow of the Callie B.'s wheelhouse, twenty feet away. She had watched him for twenty, thirty seconds. She had not seen his face.

She turned slightly and looked at the chart above the radio.

Yarmouth to Coldwater Reach. She had never made the crossing herself, but she knew the coast by chart and radio contact and the general arithmetic of small-boat passage. Yarmouth was in the southwest of Nova Scotia — a harbor town, working, the kind of place where you could rent a boat from someone who had one to rent. Once you cleared Cape Sable and came south along the outer coast you were in open water: the Atlantic running hard in autumn, the Bay of Fundy's tides working the approaches, no shelter until you reached the outer islands and could begin to work your way inshore. The crossing from Yarmouth to the midcoast of Maine was not impossible in a well-found boat with a good engine. In an eighteen-foot wooden motorboat, alone, in the last days of September — it was something you would undertake carefully, or not at all.

The end of September 1943 had closed badly on this coast. She had the record. Four days of northeast blow beginning the 27th, moderate on the 30th, another two days of wind and rain before it cleared around October 4. If he had departed on the 28th and run into the blow — and he would have run into it, there was no way not to, it had run from the Maritimes to Cape Ann — he would have had to find shelter somewhere and wait it out. An eighteen-foot wooden boat could have done this: put in behind an island, anchor in a cove, wait for the weather to settle. Then come out again and make what time he could.

September 28 to October 11 was thirteen days. Portland to Yarmouth by sea was roughly 200 miles along the coast. At that distance, with four days of bad weather in the middle, a small boat making eight or ten miles a day in the open and thirty or forty in a good stretch — thirteen days was not an impossible time. It was a long time. It was the arithmetic of someone who was being very careful, or very slow, or who had run into trouble more than once and recovered from it and continued south anyway.

She looked at the letter. Middle-aged. Continental European appearance. Limited English.

The man she had seen at the dock extension: a dark overcoat, city cut. Leather shoes. He had stood at the foot of the dock for thirty seconds before he moved. He had walked with the deliberate care of a man who was very tired or not well. He had not spoken. He had not known she was there.

No papers. The Coast Guard had searched the body on October 12 and found nothing: pockets empty, no identification, nothing to give him a name or an address or a record of where he had come from. She had been present when Ennis conducted the search. She had watched him go through the coat and the trouser pockets — exterior, breast, inside — and come up with nothing.

A man traveling from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, in a borrowed boat, at the end of September, heading south toward Massachusetts, without papers. With limited English. With continental European appearance, which was the letter's language and not hers, but which was the right kind of language for what she had seen at the dock.

The letter did not contain a name.

---

The desk drawer stuck in the way it always did — the wood had swollen in February's wet and had not recovered fully — and she pressed it open and laid the letter at the back, behind the January freight manifests, which were thick and which she would not need again until the end-of-year accounting.

She should respond. The letter asked specifically for any relevant information; she had the authority to write a response and direct it through the Portland auxiliary to the District's administrative office. She would do this.

She closed the drawer. She opened the log and wrote the afternoon's conditions: wind NNW at ten knots, barometer 30.24 and rising, inner cove northwest corner open approximately one-third, outer dock in good order, registration forms filed for six vessels pending April permits. Tide times for the evening. She closed the log.

At three-thirty she did her afternoon rounds. Dock, drain, radio check. The cove had opened another half inch since morning.

---

She made supper and ate it at the table. She had done this every evening for more than eight years, since there was no one else to do it and no one in the house who would eat it with her. The kitchen was Owen's kitchen: his shelf heights, his arrangement of the cups on the left side of the cabinet, the window latch he had repaired in September of 1935 and which she had not replaced because it worked. She sat with her plate and then with her tea and with what the letter had put in the room.

He had been heading somewhere. He had borrowed a boat in Yarmouth and gone south, and Yarmouth was not where you ended up — it was where you passed through on your way to somewhere else, somewhere with a wharf and a street address and a person who was expecting you. Massachusetts, loosely. Boston, probably. He had had a destination and a reason for the destination and people at the destination who had expected his arrival.

They had received instead the kind of silence that comes when someone does not arrive and cannot be found. The owner in Yarmouth had waited five months to file his report, uncertain whether it was his to file. There might be other people who had waited longer, who were more certain that it was not theirs to file, who had no way to report anything because reporting would require them to explain why they had been waiting for him.

She sat with this for some time. The March dark had come down on the cove and the harbor and the breakwater's red light was running at the end of its two hundred yards of granite. Five miles visible offshore. The same as always.

She did not write anything in the log.

She went to bed.

# Sprechen

April came in wet. Not the clean wet of rain — the slow wet of thaw, the ground releasing what winter had put into it, the low fields going to mud first and the mud staying because more came from above every second day and the higher ground was only drier by comparison, not dry. The farm roads had been impassable for two weeks in March. Even now the ruts in the south drive were four inches deep in the mornings, filling again before her father had the manure spreader across them.

The work changed with it. In winter you moved inside: repair, preparation, the woodwork and the harness work and the ledger kept beside the stove. In spring you moved back out into ground that didn't want you yet, into the mud and the half-frozen furrows and the particular cold of April that was colder than March because you had stopped expecting it. Her father had been trying to get at the low corner of the north field for three weeks. The drainage ditch below the elbow had been frozen since November, was open now but choked — sediment, dead stems, the runoff from the upper pasture backing up in the bend — and the low corner itself was standing in two inches of water that would not move until the ditch moved. He had put the prisoners on it Monday morning: two of them with drainage spades working the choke from the outlet upstream, the other two on the sod itself, turning forks, breaking the strips where the ground was solid enough to turn.

Lonzo Reed walked the south fence line. He had his Springfield on his shoulder and his hands in the pockets of his coat and he walked one direction and then the other at the end of the field, doing the job that was achievable: watching when he could watch, being visible the rest of the time. The field was long and the four men were spread across most of its length. There was no position from which one man could hold all four in view. Hannah had understood this about the farm's arrangement since at least October. She thought Lonzo had understood it since before she did, and had found his accommodation — the walking, the visibility, the attention at the moments when attention was possible — and left the gap between that and the theoretical complete at the back of his mind, which was where it belonged.

She was at the north fence. Three posts needed resetting: frost had lifted them through February and March, tilting two of them noticeably and leaving the wire slack between the second and the third. She had the post driver, the tamping bar, a bucket of gravel from the drive apron. The work was not complicated. Pull the post, clean the base, repack the depth, tamp the gravel, check the plumb, move on. She had done it three years running now. Next spring she would do it again.

The north fence work put her at the far end of the field from Lonzo, and roughly thirty yards from where Karl Reinmar was turning sod.

She had not arranged this. The north fence needed the work it needed. The prisoners had been assigned to the north field. The farm's geometry put her where it put her, and she was not going to spend the morning deciding what it meant or didn't mean.

The letter was in her school notebook, in her coat pocket. She had been carrying it since February, between the Whitman annotation pages where nobody would open. She had read it perhaps fifteen times — not to learn anything new from it, her German was enough for most of it and she had Dr. Klein's English for the phrase that mattered — but because she had it and Karl Reinmar did not know she had it. She had not returned it. She had considered the ledge beside the barn door, where things were left for other people's hands; she had considered slipping it into the pocket of his canvas jacket during the milk-can work. She had looked at each option and put it down. The letter stayed in the notebook.

She thought about what Dr. Klein had said. *Die die versucht haben zu gehen, sind weg.* He had given her the English: *Those who tried to go are gone.* He had said it quietly, without ceremony, looking at the page more than at her. And then: *The leaving is not the hard part.* She had not followed everything after that — the part about arriving, the brief word he used for Canada, the way he stopped himself partway through a sentence — but she had taken that line home and it had been there since, in the kitchen and in the barn and in the evenings when she heard the two voices through the glass of the icehouse window.

She thought about December. The fence post on the east side of the paddock, lifted by the frost, loose in its hole. Karl had found it before she did, had both hands on it to test it, and they had stood on either side of the fence with the cold between them for ninety seconds. He had said thirty-two words in uncertain English — *Fence. Post. Is loose — frost, I think. I can — with the tool — if you want.* She had answered. She had gone home afterward and decided to keep noticing what she noticed without deciding what it meant, and she had done this for four months, and now it was April and the ground was waterlogged and she was thirty yards from him with a post driver and a tamping bar.

She pulled the second fence post and cleaned the base.

She was going to speak to him in German.

She had known this for some time, not as a plan she had made and timed but as a thing that had already become true and was only waiting for the occasion. She could not have told anyone when she had decided it. Maybe when she read the letter at the kitchen table and put it in her notebook. Maybe when Dr. Klein said *the leaving is not the hard part.* Maybe earlier. She did not know how to locate when she had started moving toward something. She knew where she was.

She tamped the gravel and set the plumb. The post was straight. She moved to the third one.

Karl was twenty yards from her now, working a strip of turned sod. He had not looked up.

---

The occasion came on a Wednesday.

By four o'clock the light was going gray in the west and the temperature dropping, and Lonzo gathered the men in his customary way: a short two-note whistle, an arm wave, the walk from the field across the farmyard to the milking barn. The full cans needed moving before the evening escort back to the icehouse. Same procedure every afternoon.

Hannah was already in the barn. She had finished her portion of the afternoon milking — the late shift, her father's Guernseys, twelve animals in the south stanchion row — and was at the stanchions with the rinse pail when she heard the outer door.

Lonzo came through first, the way he always did, moving through the near end of the barn before the prisoners entered. He passed her without a word — that was usual too — and made his check of the space. Then the four men came through the door.

The three older ones went immediately to the far end. Fischer, Brandt, Walther: the motion of men who had done this a hundred times, moving to their positions at the carrying frames with the ease of a practiced routine. Karl came in last and took up his position near the door, where the two empty cans were waiting to be moved to the cold room.

The barn in April had its specific smell: winter still in the wood — straw, old manure, the cold settled into the rafters — and over it the new warmth the cows had been building since the temperature turned, something almost sweet, the particular heat of twelve animals at the end of a full day. She had known this smell her whole life. In winter it was comfort and in summer it was almost too much and in April it was both at once.

Lonzo said, to nobody in particular, in the mild and slightly apologetic tone he used when he was really talking to himself: I believe I could use a minute of cold air.

His boots on the door planks. The cold outside coming in briefly, then the door.

She had perhaps three minutes.

She moved the rinse pail to the corner. She turned.

Karl had the first empty can in his hands. He looked at her directly — no fence between them, no width of field — and he was nineteen years old and very still, the kind of stillness that is attention, not surprise.

She said, in Bavarian German, her father's Bavarian German, the kitchen German, the words she had grown up on before she had any other words at all:

Bist du von nah an Rosenheim?

He stopped moving.

He said — not the halting English he had been absorbing from Lonzo, not the vocabulary of weather and farm tasks and Lonzo Reed's fisherman's Maine, but his own German, the German of someone who thinks in German, the German of someone for whom German is the place the words come from:

Ja. Nah an Rosenheim. Du sprichst Bayrisch.

She said: Mein Vater ist Bayer.

He said: Ich weiß. Er hat mir gesagt. Wir reden manchmal.

She said: Ich weiß.

A pause. He looked at her steadily. He said: Verstehst du uns?

She said: Einiges.

He settled the can against his hip, looking at the middle distance for a moment — at the carrying frame, at whatever he was about to say — and said:

Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören.

She said: Ich weiß.

Then Lonzo's boots on the door planks, the cold coming back in with him, and Karl moved toward the far end with the can. Fischer said something in German. Karl answered in two words. The carrying frames went up. The sound of boots and iron-wheeled carts on the stone floor.

The three minutes were over.

---

She finished the barn and walked up to the farmhouse. She went at her usual pace. She was carrying something and she did not want to drop it by moving too fast.

Her mother was at the stove. Her father's coat was on the hook — he was still in the south field, the manure spreader still to get through the ruts. The kitchen was warm after the barn's April cool, and it smelled of supper beginning: something on the back burner, the five-o'clock smell of the kitchen in every season she could remember.

She sat down at the table and held what she had.

She had spoken Bavarian German to Karl Reinmar in her father's milking barn. He had answered in it. They had been in the same language for approximately two minutes, for approximately forty words.

She went through them.

Her opening: Bist du von nah an Rosenheim. Then his: Ja. Nah an Rosenheim. Du sprichst Bayrisch. He had named it — the particular vowels, the particular verb placement, her father's dialect in her mouth.

Then hers: Mein Vater ist Bayer. Then his: Ich weiß. Er hat mir gesagt. Wir reden manchmal. She had already known this. She had been listening to the two voices through the icehouse window since at least October — her father's German, Karl's German, the back-and-forth of the exchange she could not fully follow but could read by its rhythm.

Then hers: Ich weiß. Then his: Verstehst du uns? Then hers: Einiges.

Then the last thing.

Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören.

She turned the sentence over in the way she did when a German word was doing more than she could immediately account for. Seltsam was a word she had from her father. He used it for things that were wrong in a way that was also right: the first warm day in March when you weren't prepared for it, the quality of the light after a storm, a calf in its first hour looking at the barn walls with its whole body. Seltsam. Strange and also true. Strange in a way that was not a complaint.

He had said es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören while he was looking at the middle distance — at the carrying frame, at whatever he was about to say — and she had heard the strangeness and she had heard the other thing in it too. Something she was not imagining.

Her mother moved the pot to the front burner. Hannah looked at her own hands, still cold from the barn, a faint smell of the rinse water still on them. Two minutes in the milking barn in April. It was the first time in her life she had spoken German to someone who was not her father, not Dr. Klein, not her own reflection testing phrases in the window glass before school.

She thought about the letter. She had thought, for the few seconds before Lonzo's boots on the door planks, that this might be the moment — that she could reach into her coat and pull the notebook out and set the page in his hands. She had not done it. She was not sure why. The letter was still between the Whitman pages. She sat with it in her pocket and with what she had said and what he had said and let the kitchen be what the kitchen was.

---

After supper her father went to the icehouse window.

She could hear them from the kitchen, where she was doing the clearing. The sound came through the old single-pane glass above the sink, not words but the quality of words — the rhythm of the exchange, the structure of turns. She had been listening to this for months. She could read it now the way she read the farm by its sounds: what the cows told you before anything else did, what the specific direction of wind in the north ridge meant in November against what it meant in April.

In the barn it had been different.

She stood at the sink with the clearing water and tried to hold what was different about it. In the barn Karl had been more level. Not equal — she did not have his twenty years of German and he knew this; Einiges was the honest answer — but not the younger-man-receiving-instruction either. Something between. The German of speaking across to someone unexpected. He had not expected her to come to him in that language. The surprise was in his stillness. The surprise was in the word seltsam.

She was not from the home he meant. She had never been to Bavaria. She had never been south of Portland. The Bavarian she had was her father's Bavarian, brought across the Atlantic in 1922 and passed down through the kitchen and the barn floor and the songs she learned without knowing she was learning them, and it was as much a part of her as the farm. She was from Coldwater. She would always be from Coldwater.

Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören.

Strange, to hear it here. She sat with the word seltsam the way she sat with things she wasn't finished with. Strange and also true. Strange and also, underneath the strangeness — she thought she had heard this in the word, in the way he looked at the carrying frame when he said it — not wrong at all. Not wrong in the way that strange things you haven't decided about yet are not wrong. The kind of strange that means: I did not know this was here. I did not know it could be here.

She thought he might also have meant: I am glad it is.

She did not know this. She had not imagined it.

---

She went to bed at half past nine.

She had done the thing she had been moving toward since she did not know when. The Wednesday had come and Lonzo had gone out for his three minutes of cold air and she had turned and said her father's words into the barn's April smell and Karl had answered in his own German, full and careful and from the same ground.

She did not know what it meant for the farm, for her parents, for the arrangement. She did not know whether Karl would carry it forward or whether the icehouse window would have a different quality now. She did not know whether the letter still in her notebook meant the same thing it had meant in February, or whether she should return it, or whether returning it was something entirely separate from what had happened in the barn.

She did not know how to locate when it had started: the fence post in December, the letter in February, Dr. Klein's classroom, the north fence in April and Karl thirty yards from her at the turning fork. Some combination of these and something underneath the combination she didn't have a name for.

Two minutes in the milking barn in April. Forty words in the language her father had brought from Bavaria to Coldwater, Maine. Es ist seltsam, das hier zu hören. She had said Ich weiß, and she had meant it.

She went to sleep.

# Ice Out

The ice had been pulling back from the northwest corner since the last week of March. Each morning she had checked it from the dock end before opening the shack — the strip of ice shelf along the cove's north wall narrowing by degrees, turning gray and porous, the color of something ceding ground. She logged the observations without commentary, the way she logged the barometer and the bilge on the Callie B. and the angle of the breakwater light at first dark: not expecting any particular morning's measurement to matter on its own, but keeping the increment because the day the increment did not come was a day that needed marking.

May 3, 1944. She opened the shack door at five-thirty-five and the inner cove was open water.

She stood in the doorway for a moment with her hand on the frame. The salt came in off the water the way it did in working season — not the thin cold salt of winter, which arrived only on high wind off the open bay, but the full harbor salt: diesel underneath it, the particular smell of the tide flat at low water and the channel bottom's specific mud and something above all of it that was specifically this harbor, this reach. It had been five months. She had not been keeping track of that, or had not let herself keep track, and standing in the door she noticed she had been keeping track.

She wrote in the log: *Ice out, inner cove, full extent. May 3, 1944. 0535 hours.*

She checked the tide clock. She had reset it Monday, as she always did on Monday mornings, and it was running true. She made the notation in the maintenance column.

She ran the radio: primary check, backup frequency, Coast Guard channel at Group Southwest Harbor, the weather broadcast from the Rockland station. Northeast, light and variable, high overcast, no precipitation through Sunday. She wrote it in the weather column.

Before the lobster boats went out she walked down to the second slip to check the Callie B.'s bilge pump. The pump had been running on slow-leak monitor since November — the port quarter taking water at its old rate, never more than expected, twice-weekly checks through the winter, one spike in January when the hard freeze put tension on the hull and the pump managed six inches over three days before things equalized. She had notified Farber in January; she had continued the checks. Now she ran the pump through its test cycle: float switch responding, intake clear, discharge running clean. She wrote it in the maintenance log. The pump was running clean.

The lobster boats went out before six. She counted them from the dock end: nine, which was the full complement for the harbor. The permits had been backed up in Portland — a classification question on the renewed forms that had to be resolved in writing — and had not cleared until the last day of April, but all nine boats had their papers and the nine boats went. Burgess first, as he had been first every season she could recall, leading out with the particular certainty of a man who was not waiting on anyone. Then the two brothers from the far end of the village, then the others in loose sequence, each one pushing through the channel mouth and picking up speed in the open water beyond the bar.

She watched them clear the breakwater.

At seven-sixteen the Callie B. went out, the Margaret Rose ten minutes behind it. She logged their departures. Reg Farber at the Callie B.'s wheel, standing slightly off-center in his usual way, raised a hand as he cleared the dock without looking toward it.

The radio was busy after eight. The weekly freight traffic from Rockland, a fishing advisory from Group Southwest Harbor, two exchanges on the lobster frequency that she monitored in case one of them was going to become a buoy-line dispute — one of them was, and she noted it. She ran the correction forms for the six seasonal mooring permits that had been in error since April: each one reviewed against the tonnage classification table, corrected, re-signed. Six minutes per form. She sealed the Portland envelope.

It happened every year — the harbor going from winter's compression back to its working configuration in the space of a single week.

---

Reg Farber came to the shack on the Friday after ice-out.

He was a large man and the shack was not a large room and he had developed, over years, the practice of stopping at the threshold rather than coming in. This kept things workable. She had never named it aloud and did not name it now. He stopped in the threshold with his cap in both hands and said he had a question about the June M.

The June M. was his lobster boat, a thirty-two-foot wooden trap hauler he had been running for eleven years. She waited.

He laid it out the way he laid things out: in order, without additions. The June M.'s seasonal dock fee came due at the end of the month. He was behind on it. The mooring line had snapped in the hard January freeze — the temperature dropping faster than the almanac had called for, the line under more tension than it was designed to carry before he got to the dock to ease it. When it let go it took dock cleat number seven with it, midpoint starboard of the outer float. The cleat had been in questionable condition before the failure. He had not wanted a dispute about whose responsibility the replacement was, so he had paid for it himself: forty-two dollars for the hardware and the installation labor. He had also had a winter where the trawl catch was down and the fuel cost was up, but he mentioned these in the way of context rather than argument and moved past them.

He was asking if she could defer the June M.'s seasonal fee to July.

The light in the shack was the flat morning light that came through the south-facing window over the radio. She could hear the radio cycling through its scan in the background, the low static between intervals.

The fee schedule was fixed by the District office. She did not have formal discretion to defer a seasonal boat fee. The hardship fund was administered through Portland with an application process and a result that came in August when it came at all, and August was not July and July was not May. Farber was not a man in financial distress — he had been running two boats from this harbor for fifteen years — but forty-two dollars onto a low season was forty-two dollars, and she was not going to name the hardship fund as an answer to his question.

She pulled the spring maintenance folder from the back of the desk.

She had kept the maintenance log in calendar quarters since she took the desk over in 1936. One page per quarter, each dock fitting and installation numbered and noted by location. She found the October 1943 page. She ran her finger down the entries until she found what she had noted on the evening of October 11: *Outer dock, east float hardware survey. Cleat #7, midpoint starboard: bracket wear evident, seating slightly loose. Recommend assessment spring 1944.*

She had written that entry in the fall and filed it and it had been on her spring list. She had not gotten to it. The spring list had four items ahead of it.

She looked at the entry.

She said: "I'll need to look at the cleat."

"It's been replaced," Farber said. "New hardware, good installation."

"The condition of the original fitting is a maintenance question. It was flagged in my fall survey for spring assessment." She set the folder on the desk. "A fee review pending that inspection is within the standard process."

He said nothing for a moment. He was working the cap slightly with both hands, not nervousness, the physical version of waiting.

She wrote in the log: *June M. seasonal fee under review pending dock maintenance inspection — cleat #7, outer float, east of midpoint starboard. Per fall 1943 survey notation. Review to be completed prior to end of month.*

She dated it. She said: "Can you be at the dock Thursday morning?"

"Seven o'clock," he said. "I'll be there."

She said: "I'll write it up as I find it."

He held his cap for a moment. He said: "I appreciate that, Eira."

She didn't answer to that. He left.

She looked at the entry. The maintenance note from October was in the quarterly record, dated, in her handwriting. The spring inspection was overdue by her own log. Her authority to hold a seasonal fee pending a maintenance question was in the harbormaster's charter. The July timeline would follow from the inspection timeline without requiring the log to carry anything the log would not carry. The entry was accurate. It was complete.

She picked up the mooring permit form she had set aside when he knocked. The radio gave her the eleven o'clock weather update. She wrote it in the weather column and went back to the form.

---

Thursday morning at seven o'clock she was at the outer float.

Farber was already there. He was a man who arrived on time in the way that people who respected their own word arrived — without ostentation, just there. She acknowledged him with a nod. She knelt at cleat number seven.

The replacement hardware was in good condition: galvanized steel, properly bedded in the float decking, the seating solid. She checked the surrounding plank for movement; none. She checked the adjacent cleats on either side for comparison; both showed similar surface weathering, both solid. She stood up and made the notation in the inspection log she had brought: *Cleat #7, replacement hardware, installation sound. Base deck condition within acceptable range. Pre-existing bracket wear at original fitting location consistent with fall 1943 survey notation. Failure mode: line-tension overload, not fitting failure.* She initialed it and dated it.

She said: "The cleat's in order. The original fitting was fair wear."

Farber said: "I know that."

"The inspection supports the fee schedule adjustment. The review is closed."

He nodded. That was all. He went back to the June M., which was in the slip behind them, lines checked, ready for the day's run. She watched him go aboard and wrote the final notation in the inspection log.

The morning was overcast, the temperature forty-two degrees, the harbor in its first full working week. She walked back to the shack.

---

The Heron came in on Tuesdays and Fridays from Rockland — mail, packaged freight, occasionally a passenger traveling one direction or the other. She used the outermost slip, the longest approach in the harbor. Eira had assigned it in 1942.

The second Friday in May. She was working through the monthly mooring-line inspection — outer dock, section by section, each line lifted and checked for chafe at the attachment fitting and surface rust on the hardware — when she heard the Heron's horn off the breakwater. She was at section eleven. She kept working. The Heron needed twelve minutes from the breakwater to the dock and she had seven sections remaining.

She was coming down the outer dock when she saw Marcus Klein standing at the end of it.

He was there for the mail, or for the same kind of parcel the Emergency Committee sent up through the Rockland freight — she had seen him once before on a mail-boat Friday, waiting for a box addressed in a Manhattan hand. He stood at the end of the dock the way he stood everywhere he stood: upright, coat buttoned regardless of the temperature, looking at the harbor with an attention that was not a harbor person's attention. He was watching the water. He was not reading it.

She kept moving.

He said: "Warmer."

She said: "Finally."

He moved in the direction of the Heron's slip, which was the direction she was moving. She kept her eye on the approach line.

He said: "The boats are back."

She said: "They are."

The Heron was throttling back at the right distance, coming in at the slight angle Ayers always corrected in the last fifty feet. She watched the approach.

He said: "Any word —"

She said: "Nothing from Portland."

He nodded. She was at the slip. The bow line came across and she held it while the Heron came alongside, then cleated it and checked the fender placement. Ayers said, "Morning, Eira." She said, "Morning." She went to check the stern line while the freight hatch opened.

She did not look back at Klein. She heard the hatch open and the shift of boxes. By the time she finished the stern line he had moved to the hatch, collecting whatever was addressed to him. She went back to section twelve.

The line at section twelve showed surface weathering on the starboard fitting — not structural, worth monitoring. She wrote it in the inspection log. She finished the remaining sections. The afternoon sea fog was beginning to come in off the bar, the familiar mid-May pattern, the visibility softening at the channel mouth without obscuring the breakwater light.

She walked back to the shack.

---

She wrote the day's entries at six in the evening.

Weather: overcast, high cirrus by early afternoon. Wind northeast seven to twelve knots, backing southwest by eighteen hundred hours. Sea fog, harbor approach, fifteen-thirty to seventeen hundred. No precipitation. Visibility unlimited otherwise.

Traffic: nine lobsters out, nine in. Callie B. out 0716, in 1638. Margaret Rose out 0724, in 1503. Heron arrived 1050, departed 1116. Two freight deliveries, afternoon, invoices attached.

*June M. seasonal fee review — closed. Cleat #7 dock inspection completed May 11. Replacement hardware satisfactory, installation sound. June M. seasonal fee rescheduled: due July 31, 1944.*

She blotted the entry and dated it.

She wrote the barometer reading — 30.09 inches, falling slowly — and the morning and evening tide observations. She wrote the mooring-line inspection summary: thirty-one sections inspected over two days, one notation for monitoring, no replacements required.

The shack had gone quiet around her. The radio was on the evening scan, low, cycling through the empty frequencies. Owen's log ledger was on the bottom shelf of the cabinet to her left, where she had moved it in February 1936 when she'd taken the desk over — his handwriting running from June 1891 through the last entry in November 1935, where it stopped. She had not moved it since. The current ledger, her third volume, was on the desk.

She had a quarter of the page left below the day's entries.

She wrote: *May. Ice out. Harbor open. All boats accounted for.*

She put the pen down. She blotted it. She looked at it for a moment.

# June Radio

Four-thirty in June was different from any other four-thirty. The dark was shorter and thinner — already a gray line at the east edge of the fields when she opened the barn door, the horizon somewhere between night and something. The cows were already up. June made them impatient, all that summer weight on them, and they came to the stanchions without needing to be pressed. The hay was warm and dry and the barn's smell this month was not the closed winter smell but something looser, the boards having breathed themselves out all through May.

She moved through the milking the way she always did, can to can, one end of the row to the other. The light over the door came on automatically when she switched the barn circuit; she had not needed the kerosene lamp since April. By the time she finished the second row the gray outside had become something almost blue. By the time she was done and washing down the stanchions a quarter past six, the fields were fully lit.

She came out of the barn. The south field was high and green, the hay cutting maybe a week out. The silo, the icehouse, the farmhouse: the yard in the morning quiet, everything where it was.

Lonzo arrived at eight with the prisoners. He came through the front gate in his patient way with the Springfield on his shoulder and the four of them behind him: Fischer first, then Brandt, then Walther, then Karl last, looking at the fence posts or the middle distance the way he usually did. Lonzo said good morning toward the barn where she was standing. She nodded. They went to the south field for the morning's work and the day looked like a Tuesday in June.

---

The kitchen radio was on at breakfast, as it was every morning now. The habit had formed somewhere in the spring; she couldn't have named the day. Her father held the Rockland paper without reading it. Her mother stood at the stove with her back to the room. The radio cycled through its programs in the ordinary way.

She was pouring coffee into her cup.

The radio said: *Allied forces have landed on the coast of Normandy. The operation is underway.*

She set the coffee pot down. The cup was beside it, she had not poured, she did not remember stopping.

The radio kept talking.

Her father pushed back from the table. He crossed to the radio and turned it louder, both hands on the knob, and came back and sat down. He had his coat on from the morning barn check and he did not take it off. He sat at the table with his coat on.

The radio said: *A massive amphibious operation. Airborne divisions in the early morning hours. The Allies on French soil.*

She sat down. She had her coffee cup in front of her now. She picked it up and held it.

Her mother came in from the garden at quarter past nine and sat down at the table between them and stayed. The three of them in the kitchen with the radio going, eating and not eating. Hannah ate a piece of bread, then set the second piece down. Her father's food sat where her mother had put it. Her mother had her hands folded in front of her and her attention pointed somewhere ahead of herself, all the way into the radio, the way her silence collected itself when it had somewhere to go.

The CBS correspondent said: *Casualties are reported to be significant. The fighting continues at several points along the beachhead.*

The BBC faded in through static at ten-fifteen when the kitchen set picked up the signal — it did this some mornings, caught the BBC clear and others got nothing — and the BBC voice was more formal than CBS but said similar things: *Operation Overlord. The largest amphibious operation in history. Allied forces establishing positions.* She tried to hold the two accounts in sequence and could not. Two voices from two studios in London both saying Normandy, saying beaches, saying dawn.

Her father's hands were flat on the table.

Through the window over the sink she could see the south field.

Four figures out there, far enough that she could not read their faces, not even which one had stopped moving. At the northeast corner, one of them stood briefly apart from the others — she could tell it was Karl by his build, the particular width of his shoulders, the size of him she had been looking at across fences and through glass for more than a year. Then he bent down and went back to the row and he was not distinguishable from the others at that distance.

Camp operations would have told them. She did not know in what form or at what hour — roll call, a guard with a statement, something. But it would be strange if they hadn't known by now.

She took her plate to the counter and washed it and put it in the rack. Her father was still at the table. The radio was still talking.

---

She heated soup at noon and set it beside him. He ate it, the bowl emptying while she ate her own soup standing at the counter. The radio had not been turned off. It said: *The Prime Minister addressed the House of Commons this morning. The King has spoken to the nation.* It said: *Fighting continues at the beachhead.* It said the names of the beaches and she could not retain them in order.

She went out at one o'clock. The north barn needed the afternoon hay brought down from the loft, and the east-pasture gate needed checking after the spring flooding had shifted the post on the hinge side. The farm did not stop for this. She pulled her jacket from the hook by the door and went out.

Outside the day was warm and cloudless and knew nothing about any of it. The fields were the fields. The sky was a June sky. She went to the north barn and spent the better part of an hour on the hay and the gate, and when she came out and crossed the south end of the yard she was taking the shorter way back to the kitchen.

Karl was at the northeast corner, thirty yards from the fence. He was bent at the waist, working along the row, his head down. She could see his face clearly from this distance. It was his working face, the same one every day, and she could not read anything in it from here.

She did not stop.

There was nothing to say today and no place to say it — not with Lonzo twenty-five yards away eating his lunch off the tailgate, not with all of them visible from the farmhouse window, not with the morning still in her head and the radio going in the kitchen and no German that was the right German for the gap between the fence and the row and what this day was. She went back to the kitchen.

Her father was still at the table. He had turned the newspaper face-down at some point, which she had not seen him do.

---

By four o'clock he had moved to the parlor.

The parlor radio was the better set, the signal cleaner and the BBC coming in without the kitchen static. He was in the chair he used only in winter — the corner chair by the window, the one with the gray slipcover her mother put on every November and took off every April. The coat was off now, folded over the arm. He had not called her in.

She passed the doorway twice on errands and saw him there each time in the same position: hands in his lap, the radio on the side table. The quality of his stillness was the same one she had seen in December 1941, that Sunday, when she had been fifteen and had stood in the kitchen doorway not knowing whether to go in.

She went in and sat in the straight chair by the door. He did not look at her. The BBC correspondent was saying that additional forces were moving to reinforce the initial landings, that the situation continued to develop, that the casualties could not yet be fully accounted for. She sat for a while and then stood and went back to the kitchen.

Her mother came through a few minutes later with a cup of coffee and went into the parlor and set it on the side table next to the radio, next to his hand. She said nothing. He reached for the cup without looking up and drank from it and set it back down. Her mother came back to the kitchen.

Hannah watched her come back and turned to the stove and put the kettle on.

---

The prisoners came in from the field at five. She heard them through the open kitchen window — Lonzo's voice carrying across the yard without the words, and then the four of them moving through the yard to the icehouse, and then the icehouse door. Then quiet from that direction.

She made supper. By six her father had come in from the parlor and sat at the table and eaten. He ate all of his supper, carefully, the way he did everything carefully. When he finished he set his fork down and sat for a moment and went back to the parlor.

Hannah washed the dishes. Her mother dried them and put them away. They had been doing this without talking all spring, longer than that, and tonight was the same except that the quiet in the kitchen had the weight of the day behind it. Her mother folded the dish towel and hung it on the hook. She looked at Hannah for a moment — not speaking, never speaking, but something in the look — and then went to bed.

Hannah dried her hands and went to the table.

She had *The Selected Poems of Robert Frost* open in front of her. She'd been working through it since the term ended, not because Marcus had assigned it but because she kept returning to it, kept finding the same pages. She was not reading now. She had the book open and the lamp on and the radio coming low from the parlor, where her father had turned it down after supper — she could hear it the way she heard rain, as a sound that was always there but was not a voice.

He came into the kitchen at half past eight.

She heard him before she saw him, his footsteps crossing the parlor floor. He came through the doorway and crossed the kitchen and stood at the window over the sink. He did not acknowledge her.

Through the window: the yard, half-lit by the kitchen lamp. The icehouse at the far edge of the lamplight, its window dark.

He stood there for a long moment.

He said, to the window, to himself, to no one in the room: "Nun ist es fertig."

He turned from the window and went upstairs. She heard his footsteps on the stairs, even and slow, the familiar weight of him on the second step that always creaked. The door at the top of the stairs opened and then closed.

The house was quiet.

The radio was still on in the parlor, very low, a program that had nothing to do with France — some orchestra in a studio somewhere, the sound barely carrying. She could hear it the way she heard the pump.

She did not move.

The kitchen lamp was on. Through the window the icehouse held no light. Karl was in the icehouse with Fischer and Brandt and Walther, in the dark across the yard, and whatever this day had been for them was behind the dark window and she had no way into it and it was not the night to try.

Her father had said: Nun ist es fertig.

She sat at the table. The fields were moving outside the open window, the long summer grass at the field edge, the nighthawks somewhere over the south field making the sound they made in June. She had heard it every June of her life. She heard it now.

The radio on low from the parlor. Karl in the dark across the yard.

What came next, she did not know.
