# The Zenith

The Crow house was quiet when Marcus turned onto the back street at twenty minutes past four, the same time he always turned onto it on a Tuesday in June. He had stayed after the last Latin class to review a student's Cicero translation — the girl had mistaken a subjunctive for an indicative and the meaning had shifted in a way that was grammatically precise and entirely wrong — and he had marked it with a note instead of a mark, because at a certain level of wrongness the mark would not tell her anything useful about what she had misread and the note might. He was still thinking about this, about the difference between correcting a mistake and explaining its interior logic, when he heard it.

The parlor window was open two inches and through it the Zenith's voice reached him across the front yard and the porch: not music, but a man speaking carefully and without pause, in the register that radio voices took on when the news was large. He had learned this register since December 1941 — the slight slowing, the particular economy between phrases, as if the voice understood what it was carrying and was choosing to carry it with a certain care.

He came up the porch steps. He could hear the words now.

*Allied forces have landed on the coast of France. Units of the American, British, and Canadian armies, under the supreme command of General Dwight Eisenhower, have this morning begun the liberation of Western Europe.*

He opened the door and stood in the hall.

Through the parlor doorway: Henry was in his chair, still in his work clothes, his cap on the side table beside him. Lillian was in the doorway between the kitchen and the parlor with a dish towel held in both hands in front of her in the manner of something forgotten.

Neither of them looked at him.

Marcus set his briefcase on the floor beside the umbrella stand. He crossed the hall. He sat on the parlor sofa without taking off his coat.

---

The CBS broadcast ran through five and into six. At some point Marcus stood and turned the dial, past a farm report from Portland and two stations of static, until the BBC came in — clear and precise, the presenter carrying his characteristic quality of British reserve in the service of very large information. He went back to the sofa. From here he could manage the dial with a single step; he reached over several times during the six o'clock hour to correct for drift, the BBC signal restless on its frequency.

Lillian brought supper at half past six. She had made a pot roast with carrots and there were biscuits, and she carried everything in on a tray and set it on the low parlor table without asking whether anyone wanted to eat in the parlor. She had moved the table from its usual position against the wall and put two chairs alongside the sofa, so all three of them could sit without being far from the radio. This seemed to Marcus an act of considerable domestic intelligence.

He ate without being particularly aware of it.

They ate at the parlor table, the Zenith between them and the wall, the broadcasters alternating their accounts of the morning in France. The CBS man had a tendency toward summary; the BBC presenter organized by geography, moving from beach to beach along the coast in a way that Marcus found he could almost follow on the map he held in his head, though the map had gaps. He had never been to Normandy. He knew the coastline by its name and its latitude and the general shape of it on paper, but he could not place himself in it, could not see the particular quality of the sand or the height of the sea cliffs or the angle of the morning light coming in from the east.

He tried to imagine it and got only the radio's language.

Lillian refilled his coffee cup at seven o'clock without asking — real coffee, not the substitute that the ration book pushed you toward, the kind she made on evenings when something required it. He accepted it and set it on the table and forgot about it until it was cold and drank it cold. It was still good.

---

He found it by accident at nine o'clock, turning the dial during a CBS break.

He was looking for the BBC — it had drifted during the eight o'clock hour and he had been tracking it incrementally, degree by degree of the dial — when he passed through a frequency and heard something under the English signal. Not alongside it. Under it, as if two broadcasts occupied nearly the same position and one of them was losing ground.

German.

He rotated the dial back slowly until both were audible: the English on top, the German below it, the two signals in an involuntary conversation. The BBC European service — or something like it — the transmission aimed east, toward the occupied territories, designed for listeners with clandestine receivers hidden in farmhouse cellars and back-room closets, who were listening in a way that had consequences if they were caught listening. The German was formal and deliberate, the register of a language designed to be received once by someone in a dangerous position and understood immediately.

He listened.

The sentences were complete, clear, not overlapped by the English signal in any way that made them inaudible to someone who knew the language.

Henry said, "What's that other voice?"

"A German broadcast," Marcus said. "The BBC. For occupied Europe."

Lillian had come back from the kitchen with a dish towel, which she set on the arm of Henry's chair. She said nothing.

The German ran alongside the English for another thirty seconds — close enough on the dial that moving away from one would lose the other — and then the English signal gathered itself and the German reduced to something barely present. In the time it was clear:

Henry said, "What are they saying?"

Marcus translated without looking away from the radio. "They are saying the Allied landing was conducted at multiple points along the coast in the early morning hours, before the German commanders understood what was happening. They are saying the initial German assessment was that the landing was a diversion, not the primary operation." He stopped, listening. "They are saying the element of surprise —"

The broadcast shifted. The CBS signal reasserted itself and the German was gone; what remained was the American presenter saying something about airborne divisions and the pre-dawn hours and the fields behind the beaches. Marcus released the dial. He sat back on the sofa.

Lillian sat down in the armchair by the lamp, which she had turned low at seven when the evening had settled into itself. Henry was in his chair, his hands in his lap, his expression the one Marcus had come to understand as Henry's form of total attention — it was not demonstrative and could be read, by someone who didn't know him, as merely neutral; it was the furthest thing from neutral.

The three of them sat in the low lamplight with the Zenith speaking at the wall.

---

He had not been trying to think about Paris.

His job in this room was to track the dial, to translate if there was anything that needed translating, to be present to what was happening on the radio in the way that this household had decided to be present to it together rather than alone. He was not trying to think about Paris. But Paris was present in the way that certain things were present on such evenings: not summoned, not avoidable, simply there.

He had been in Paris for twenty-four months, from the spring of 1938 until May 1940. He had left before the Germans came — made the calculation in May and acted on it, not knowing at the time whether the calculation was right, not knowing it was right until several weeks afterward when the information began arriving about the people who had not made the same calculation. So Paris for him was not June 1940. He had not seen the flags in the Place de la Concorde or the soldiers coming down the Champs-Élysées. He had the twenty-four months before it: the reading room at the Bibliothèque nationale, where a reader's card was the only requirement and a man could sit from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon and the staff required nothing further. The Sainte-Chapelle in November. A café near the Odéon where he had spent several evenings working on a chapter about Klopstock, the coffee good and the other patrons uninterested in him, which was its own form of grace.

The Louvre. He had been to the Louvre more times in twenty-four months than he had been to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in ten years in Vienna — something he had not anticipated of himself, that temporary residence in a city made him attend to it more carefully than permanent residence, as if the known deadline of departure organized the seeing.

German soldiers had been in the Louvre for four years.

He was hearing, on the Zenith, that this might be beginning to change — that the soldiers might leave the streets of Paris if the battle at Normandy moved in the direction the announcer's careful optimism implied. He listened to the optimism as a document: the radio presenter knew, tonight, which things he was authorized to say and which he was not, and so the shape of the optimism told you something about the shape of the uncertainty. The optimism was real but measured. The uncertainty was real and larger.

A colleague from the École pratique des hautes études who had gone to London in the spring of 1940, whose current address Marcus did not have and had not had for three years. A street that someone's cousin had known, the name of which Marcus had written on a piece of paper once and then lost. The apartment in Vienna that had been taken over by whoever took over such apartments, where a monograph on Klopstock sat in a drawer, or had been turned to other uses, or had been thrown away.

He had been not-knowing about the colleagues for four years. The not-knowing had accumulated a specific gravity over that time — different from the not-knowing of the early months, when not-knowing still felt like a condition that would resolve. It had not resolved. It had become the form in which he held the people he had known before 1938: probable but unverifiable, present in the room as a weight rather than as a fact.

He turned the dial. Found the BBC. Left it there.

Henry reached forward and adjusted the lamp. The room settled.

---

At ten o'clock the news became a different kind of news.

In the first hours, information had been arriving as it was established — each fact landing with the specific weight of something genuinely new, the picture building in real time, the uncertainty alive. At ten o'clock the uncertainty had not resolved but the shape of the day had solidified, and what the radio was doing now was the work of assembly: the same facts fitted into a chronology, the event having happened, the urgency dropping slightly and in its place something more like record. Still important. Not the same kind of important.

Lillian gathered the cups and the last of the supper things and took them to the kitchen. She came back and stood in the parlor doorway for a moment.

"I'm going up," she said.

"All right," Henry said.

She looked at Marcus in the particular way she looked at him on evenings when she was concerned. "Get some sleep, Marcus," she said.

"I will," he said. "Thank you, Lillian."

She went upstairs. They listened to the sounds of her on the second floor: the hallway, the bathroom, the bedroom door, the familiar sequence of the house settling itself.

Henry reached over and turned the Zenith down to just above silence. The announcer continued at that volume without mass, a presence in the room rather than an account. The lamp was still on but low. The chairs were in something near their usual positions. The supper things were gone.

They sat.

---

Henry said, "I'm going to sit out on the porch a while."

He stood and went to the door. Marcus got his coat from the sofa arm and followed.

The night was warm in the way that June nights in Maine were rarely warm — warm meaning simply that it did not require defending against, that the air lay around you without urgency. The back street ran dark between the houses under the elm canopy; above it the sky held its midsummer blue even at this hour, more blue than black, some reserve of daylight still in the horizon to the north that the season refused to entirely give up.

Mrs. Pelletier's lamp was on across the way. Otherwise the street was quiet.

Henry sat in the left chair. Marcus sat in the right. It was the arrangement they had, established without discussion. He had been in this house for two years and three months and this porch was one of the things in Coldwater that had become, in a precise and undramatic way, his.

The elm leaves were still. Down the block a screen door opened and closed.

They were quiet for some time.

Henry said: "You have people there?"

Marcus considered this. He said: "I did. I don't know."

Henry nodded. He didn't follow it with another question.

The screen door was quiet. In the elm's upper branches, some movement of air too light to reach the porch shifted the leaves briefly and then stopped.

Marcus said, after a while: "It's a long way to go."

Henry said: "It is."

He was talking about the invasion — the distance the soldiers had crossed in the dark before dawn, the Channel, the boats, the beach they had crossed on foot. Marcus was talking about that too. He was also talking about his particular relation to the distance between here and France, between this porch and a city he had lived in and left before it became something other than itself. And he was aware, as he said the words, that Henry's relationship to the distance between here and somewhere else was not the same as his — that Norfolk, Virginia, and the distance between Coldwater Reach and there, and whatever lay in the country between those two coordinates, was a different distance from Marcus's distance even when they arrived at similar things: the not-knowing about people, the specific quality of being somewhere that required managing, the particular alertness you developed in a town that was yours only within certain limits.

Another quarter-hour. The elm leaves. The street quiet under the midsummer sky.

---

He went back inside at midnight.

The Zenith was still on in the parlor, turned to its lowest setting, the announcer's voice carrying across the room without weight. Marcus turned it off on his way through. It seemed wrong to leave it talking to an empty room when what it had to say tonight had already been said and what remained was only the saying of it again.

The house was dark. Henry had come in a few minutes before him and the downstairs was settled.

He went upstairs.

His room was the way he had left it in the morning: the chair by the east window, the books on the desk arranged in the order he had put them in March and not disturbed since, the shortwave on the corner table with its dial dark. He had not turned it on all evening. What would it find that the Zenith had not already given him — what frequency between here and Europe would carry something the CBS presenter had not already said, that the BBC hadn't organized into its careful English, that the German signal, briefly audible under the English, had not already delivered in the register designed for people in danger?

He sat in the chair by the window without turning on the lamp.

Through the glass: the back street below, the elm canopy, and above it the sky, which even at this hour was holding its blue. He had not expected this of Maine when he arrived — that the sky refused its full dark for most of June, that the light had a longer argument to make than it did in Vienna or Paris or London, though London was different because of the blackout, because the dark in London had been enforced rather than natural, a different kind of dark altogether.

The window faced east.

He was aware of this in a way he was not usually aware of it: east across the town and east across the harbor and east across the Atlantic was France, and the men on the beach at Normandy, and the German soldiers withdrawing from certain positions, and somewhere beyond that, Paris — the reading room, the café near the Odéon, the colleagues whose current situations he did not know. He had been not-knowing about them for four years, and the quality of the not-knowing had changed as it accumulated, had become something he carried differently than he had carried it in 1940 or 1941 or 1942. He was not sure if the hearing that this might be ending would change the quality of the not-knowing, or whether it would only change the shape of what he did not know, which was not the same as knowing.

He did not open the notebook.

What was in the notebook was already there — the entries in shorthand, the arithmetic, the question at the page's bottom that had been there since April and was not going to answer itself tonight.

He sat in the chair until the cold came in through the old window frame — June cold, not significant, but enough at two in the morning to make itself present. He stood. He went to the bed and lay down in the room's dark without the lamp, without the shortwave, without the notebook.

# The Mail Boat

The mooring assignments were posted the first weekday after ice-out and then adjusted through June as the fleet returned. By the first full week of July the harbor had settled into itself: seven lobster boats, the Callie B. and the June M. on drag rotation, three pleasure craft from Portland. Plus a day sailer from Rockland whose owner, a man named Burnham, had appeared at the shack on a Thursday morning in late June to ask about temporary mooring fees and had been visibly startled to find a woman behind the desk.

She'd charged him the full summer rate. He'd paid it. He had come back twice since for the weekly renewal and was no longer startled, which was the trajectory these things followed.

The summer work was inventory rather than crisis: dock fees, mooring assignments, freight manifests for the twice-weekly Heron runs, radio checks at six in the morning and noon, the September mooring schedule already half-drafted in her mind by late July. She knew the harbor's summer logic as well as she knew its winter logic, which she knew well. Which boats would run to the western ground and which worked the inner reach. Which lobstermen were in by two and which ran long toward dark and needed her to hold their dock space. The particular compression note of Arsenault's hauler clearing the harbor mouth. The June M.'s starboard engine knock, audible at the third slip on a calm morning a minute before the boat came around the point.

She had been running this harbor for nearly nine years. Owen had done it for six, before November 1935. She had learned a great deal from what he left behind in the log: his method of weather notation, his system for the dock-fee ledger, the way he organized the mooring priority by boat size and gear type rather than by seniority, which was the logical system and which she had kept. She had also, in nine years, learned things he had not had time to learn. The way the southwest wind behaved differently in August than in June, coming off the warmer water with a different load. The relationship between the inner cove's ice and the timing of the outer breakwater pressure in a hard winter, which she could now read in the barometer two days before the event. The harbor she ran in July 1944 was his arrangement in its bones and her arrangement in its living parts.

Six years, then nearly nine.

---

The Heron was sixty feet, white-sided, out of Rockland. It ran Tuesdays and Fridays, arrived at the outer slip at half past two and turned back at four-thirty. She was at the dock for both runs: freight manifests to sign, dock lines to check, the general accounting of what came in. The freight manifest was her authority over the dock; she took it seriously.

The Heron's crew sorted the mail in the hold before docking. When the run was done and the boat secured, the mailman came up the gangway with the canvas pouch and handed it to whoever met the boat — in summer, usually Gladys at the post office, or her assistant on Fridays. The sorted mail went into the pouch in the hold and came out the same way, which meant what was on top coming out was what the crew had put on top when they sorted.

The yellow envelopes were a particular yellow. You could see their color through the canvas of the pouch when the afternoon light was at the right angle, which it often was in July. She had learned by late June to read the mailman's stance in the gangway before the pouch came off — a slight hesitation, or no hesitation, which told you the same thing the canvas told you.

---

The second Tuesday in July the Heron brought two.

She was on the far side of the freight stack when the mail went — she had three crates of canned goods and a drum of machine oil to sign for, and the drum's stenciling was partially obscured, which required a manifest annotation before she could file it. By the time she came around the stack the mail was sorted and the pouch gone. She did not need to have seen it. She had seen the canvas on the gangway.

By suppertime the word was around town. Doris Hatch's older brother — E.J. Hatch, Navy, two years ahead of Doris at school, gone to the Pacific in the spring of '42. And Albert Eaton's youngest, who had come in from the Eaton farm up the valley road every summer to help with the August freight unloading when Eira needed extra hands at the dock, and who had enlisted the November after Pearl Harbor.

The harbor did not stop for this. The fly was running and three of the lobster boats came in heavy at half past three and the loading dock was busy until nearly dark. The weather was good: wind SW at twelve knots, swell steady, visibility clear to the outer buoy and past it. She logged it all. It was all true.

She went home that evening and ate supper and came back to lock the shack at nine. The harbor was quiet. The outer light was doing its work. She stood in the door of the shack a moment with the key in her hand before she locked it.

The following Tuesday the Heron brought no yellow envelopes.

She saw it before the boat tied up. The crew on the gangway. The mailman's hands on the pouch. She kept her eyes on the freight manifest and made the amendment notation and stood aside for the dock crew.

She noticed there were five people at the dock head waiting for the Heron, which was two more than usual for a Tuesday in July. She noticed that when the mail went to Gladys and Gladys sorted it at the dock-end table and there were no yellow envelopes, the five people at the dock head left in stages — not quickly, not dramatically, simply in the ordinary way people leave a dock when there's no particular reason to stay. She did not write any of this in the log.

She wrote the weather and the vessel statuses and the freight manifest and she went home.

---

Marcus Klein was at the dock for the second Tuesday in August.

She saw him at the dock head when she turned onto the dock with the freight manifest. He was standing with his hands in the coat pockets, weight back, watching the Heron come in. His wool coat was wrong for August, though August in Maine was the least wrong month for it she could imagine given the places he had come from, which she knew about only in general terms.

The Emergency Committee parcels came through Rockland freight every few months. She hadn't expected him today. She went past him to the outer end.

Four crates of hardware for Donnelly's, a pallet of seed stock for the Peabody farm up the valley. The Heron's first mate had the manifest ready; she checked it and signed it and stood aside for the off-loading. Klein had come down past the freight stack and was signing a shipping receipt with the crew. Brown-paper parcel, flat, twine-wrapped, books from the look of it. He tucked it under his arm and turned toward the dock head.

She had been checking the mailman's hands through all of this. Gladys was at the dock-end table with the sorted mail. No yellow envelopes. She could see that clearly. She had kept the freight manifest in front of her and she knew it clearly.

Klein was heading back up the dock, his parcel under his arm, and she said — at the distance she would use for calling to a lobsterman about a dock line:

"Dr. Klein."

He turned.

She said: "No yellow envelopes today."

He looked at her for a moment. He said: "Good."

She said: "So far."

She went back to the manifest.

He went up the dock. She filed the amendment and waited for the Heron to complete off-loading and walked the dock lines and checked the freight cage lock. It took the remainder of the afternoon. The Heron turned at four-thirty, its usual time, and she watched it clear the outer slip and heard its engine change pitch as it came around to the Rockland heading, and then it was around the point and she went back to the shack.

---

She wrote the harbor log at seven in the evening with the shack door wedged open against the day's remaining heat.

Hot, clear. Wind SW, eight knots. Barometric pressure 30.04, steady. Swell eight to ten inches. Callie B. in, routine. June M. out, due back Thursday 0800 estimated. All seven lobster boats accounted for by 1800 hours. Freight received: four crates hardware (Donnelly's Hardware), one pallet seed stock (Peabody, valley road). Emergency Committee book parcel, one unit, received per manifest by Dr. Klein, Coldwater School. Manifest filed and signed.

She wrote the day's operational entries in their order. Twelve minutes. She was not hurried. The log was the record and the record was worth the twelve minutes.

When the operational entries were done she held the pen over the page.

Outside the shack's open door, the harbor at seven in a hot August evening was doing what the harbor did. Boats at their moorings in the last of the direct light. The water picking up the west sky and lying flat and particular with it. The outer light at the breakwater end beginning to assert itself as the ambient light dropped. Arsenault's trap hauler at the third float, dock line coiled on the cleat the right way — it had taken her two reminders at the start of the season and now he coiled it the right way without being reminded. The June M.'s empty slip, her mooring line looped at the head. Nothing wrong. Nothing outstanding.

She wrote one more line.

*Hatch, E.J. — no telegram this Tuesday. The harbor was full.*

She had done this twice before. The first time in late November 1943, after the Tuesday boat brought no yellow envelopes the week following the week it had brought one — there had been a name in November too, a Coldwater boy she had known since he was twelve and crewing on his father's boat. The second time in June, in the middle of a run of good Tuesdays. Both times the same kind of entry: a name, a fact, the harbor's condition.

There was no column in the harbor log's official charter for this kind of entry. The charter — the document governing the post she held — required tide records, weather, vessel status, dock activity, freight summaries, notable maritime events. What she wrote was not a maritime event. It was not notable in the sense the charter intended. It was not any of the things the charter authorized. It sat in the log's column in her regular compressed hand, in the same black ink, the same weight as the freight summary above it. She did not put these entries in the margin. She did not flag them with a notation. They were in the log because the log was the record, and if the record was going to be the record at all it was going to be complete, and complete meant what actually happened, not only what the charter had space for.

She was not certain, yet, what she was making. The harbor log since June 1891 had recorded the harbor's official business: what came in, what went out, what the weather did, what the vessels required. She was now recording something else in the same space, without separating it. The October 1943 entry that the Coast Guard had removed was pages 114 through 119. Those pages had held the official account of the official event, and they were in Portland now, in a file she had been told she could not request. But the log was still here. Her hand was still in it. She had kept writing in it through November and December and every month since and the harbor she ran was in those pages completely, including the things the charter did not have a form for.

She set the pen in the desk tray.

Outside: the harbor in the last of the day. The boats at their moorings. The breakwater light ticking in the dusk. In the still water at the dock's near end, the reflection of the dock boards and the sky above them, the doubled image clear enough that the reflection looked like the thing rather than the reflection.

She closed the log.

She sat with her hand on the closed log cover.

Then she stood and went to lock up the shack.

# The Second October

The Tuesday morning in the second week of October was cold before it was light. Hannah had been up since four-thirty, which was not different from any other morning except for the cold, which said plainly that the season had crossed into a different register in the night and would not go back. She milked with the kerosene lamp because there was not enough daylight yet. Steam came off the nearest cow's back in the lamplight. The barn was warm in the animal way and cold at the boards and at the high window where the October air pressed in.

She had known what date it was since she turned the calendar page in September and saw October laid out in its grid and counted forward to the twelfth. Not marked it anywhere. The twelfth was a Tuesday this year, and on her Tuesdays she walked the inland road to where it met the school road and down the hill, and at the foot of that hill the harbor was visible for approximately forty seconds of walking.

She had been carrying the date since early September, which was less like dread than like the awareness of a fence post that has shifted — not a problem yet, a thing to check on when you came to it. In October 1943 a man had washed up at the end of the breakwater after a three-day blow, and she had been seventeen and had heard about it as town rumor, and the rumor had settled into the year the way certain things settled: not gone, present in a particular way that was different from the presence of things that had been named.

She finished the near stalls and moved to the far side of the barn. The cows were in more often now, which was right for the season. From the far window she could see the icehouse, dark. Lonzo would come at eight.

---

On the Tuesday morning she walked her usual route. Cold, the road hard, the maples mostly bare, the fields gray in the early light, the inland air already different from August. She came down the school-road hill at her usual pace and at the bottom the harbor opened up on the left: the water flat and dark, the dock, the granite breakwater running two hundred yards out, the red light at the end off in the daylight.

She looked at the breakwater for three seconds while walking and then she was past the angle where it was visible and up the hill on the other side and the harbor was behind her.

She was eighteen. The birthday had come one week before the twelfth, and she found herself thinking of the two dates together even though they were not the same date and did not mark the same thing. Eighteen. Her mother had put a cake on the kitchen table without speaking, which was how Magda did everything now, and Hannah had stopped expecting anything different, and the cake had been good regardless because Magda made good cake regardless of what was happening in whatever interior space had gone quiet in her. Her father had come in from the barn and said Herzlichen Glückwunsch. She had said Danke, Vater. He had looked at her then with an expression she had been trying to place for two years: not the expression of a man who was pleased, exactly, and not the expression of a man who was displeased. Something more complicated than either, something that contained its own object and she could not identify the object.

She had answered him in German without deciding to. It had come out of her the way German came out when she was inside it — her father's accent and her father's cadence, the Bavarian vowels that Marcus had noticed in September 1943 in the classroom and had said yes to without saying more. She had been answering her father in the language he had used, which was the language of the house, which was the language inside her in the place where the house was.

He had looked at her, and then looked away, and cut the cake.

---

The prisoners had been on the Pfeiffer farm for eighteen months.

She had counted this in September when she was counting other things, and the number had come out to eighteen months without her having expected it to mean anything, and it had meant something anyway. Her parents had been in Bavaria for three years before they came to Maine — she knew this from her father's brief account, given years ago when she was eleven or twelve, the story of the village and the land prices in Maine and the crossing. Three years in Bavaria. Eighteen months in the icehouse. The arithmetic did not go anywhere useful. She turned it over once and set it aside.

Karl was twenty now. His birthday had been sometime in the summer — July, she thought, or possibly August; she had not asked and did not know. She had learned the date had passed because Fischer said something to Walther in the milking barn one afternoon in early August, something quick in German about the summer and Karl's twentieth, whether anything had been done. Nothing had been done. The farm did not observe German prisoners' birthdays and there was no reason it should, and she had been at the near stall when Fischer said it and had moved to the next stall without giving a sign that she had understood.

His English by October 1944 was serviceable in the way of anything absorbed from Lonzo Reed: practical, coastal, occasionally imprecise in ways that were Lonzo's imprecision rather than Karl's, passed through eighteen months of proximity into what Karl reached for when he needed English quickly. *That post wants setting.* *Come on, old girl, come on.* *Cold moving in, Lonzo says, from the northwest.* She had heard him say variations of each of these at various points since spring, and they were entirely accurate and entirely Lonzo's idiom in Karl's mouth. His German was still his German. When he used both languages in the same hour she could hear the seam between them, where one thing stopped and another started.

Since the barn in April — the three minutes while Lonzo was outside, the forty words in Bavarian German, the confirmation that the language between them was the language between them — their exchanges had settled into something she had not been expecting, though she had not expected anything. What it was: a sentence at the fence when Lonzo was occupied elsewhere. A question about the work or the weather, the kind of question that required an answer and no more than an answer. Wie viele Kühe? Sixteen. Dieselben wie letztes Jahr? The same sixteen as last year, yes. One year's worth of farm, one exchange at a time. The German was ordinary. The conversations were about the farm. Neither of them reached for more than the farm provided.

She had thought more than once about what word applied to what Karl was to her and had not found one that fit. This did not trouble her in the way she thought it might trouble someone who needed words for things. She was eighteen. She had decided she did not need to find the word yet, and she went on milking the cows and doing the fence work and handing Karl the extra wire staples when his supply ran short without having a word for the thing.

---

The second Saturday in October the work detail went to the north pasture's upper wall.

The wall was stone-and-mortar, her grandfather's or before her grandfather's, built sometime when walls like this were built, and it needed pointing before the ground froze or the winter would work the joints open and by spring you'd have a gap. Albrecht had told Lonzo at the start of the week. Lonzo had told the prisoners. Saturday morning: Karl and Fischer with a bucket of mortar and a trowel and a brush, Lonzo twenty feet behind with the Springfield and his bad knee, which had been troubling him since September and which he managed by finding a flat rock to sit on.

Hannah was at the lower fence on the south side of the north pasture, the wire fence that had gone slack over the summer and needed tightening before it became a problem. Her own work, not assigned. She had the wire stretcher and a spool of new wire for the section that had corroded through, and the work required attention because losing tension on a wire stretch meant starting over. She could see the upper wall from where she crouched: the stone line of it along the field's high edge, the work detail there, Karl at the near face with the trowel.

She had been at the fence forty minutes when she said something.

She was not certain afterward whether she had intended to. The wire work was going well and she was focused on it, and there was a long section of the upper wall where the mortar had failed between two large anchor stones, and Karl was packing that section carefully, the mortar pressed into the joint in the right way. Lonzo had shifted further up the field, sitting on a different rock. Fischer was around the wall's far end.

She said: Wird der Mörtel halten, wenn der Boden tief friert?

*Will the mortar hold if the ground freezes deep.*

She said it without raising her voice. She was twenty feet from the wall.

Karl looked up. He had mortar dust on his hands and on the sleeve of the jacket the prisoners wore. He looked at the section he had been working, not at her. He said: Wenn er richtig einzieht. Man muss ihn trocknen lassen.

*If it sets right. You have to let it cure.*

She said: Wie lange.

He said: Zehn Tage. Vielleicht zwei Wochen. Je nach Temperatur.

*Ten days. Maybe two weeks. Depending on the temperature.*

She looked at his work for a moment — the joint well-packed, the mortar even in the gap. He knew how to do this. He had known how to do most of the farm work from the beginning, which made sense given where he was from. She went back to the fence.

Two sentences each. The conversation was about the stone wall's mortar and the time it needed to cure before the ground froze, which was a reasonable thing to know about a wall you were repairing in October. She reached the next post and crouched to check the staples and looked up.

Her father was at the field's edge.

He was standing at the point where the north pasture's fence met the farm road — thirty feet from where she crouched, further from the wall and the work detail. He was not moving. He had his hands in the pockets of his coat and he was standing with the quality of someone who had been standing there for a while, not as if he had just arrived but as if he had been there long enough to have settled into the standing. He had come from the direction of the barn. The barn was behind him and the field was in front of him and he was standing at the boundary between.

His face was toward the field. Toward her and toward the upper wall and Karl and Fischer and Lonzo, though not settling on any one of them from what she could see at this distance. She could not read his expression at thirty feet with the October light behind him. She had been reading his face her whole life — in kitchen light, in barn light, in the particular gray light of a Maine October morning — and from this distance and in this light it was the quality of his stillness she could read rather than the expression itself.

It was the stillness of something working through him that he was not going to say. She had seen it at the kitchen radio in June when the news came in from Normandy. She had seen it in August in the yard when Karl had finished the icehouse roof cladding and Albrecht had come out and stood and looked at the work without saying whether it was good or not. That stillness: a man holding something, not yet released.

He looked at her once. She was certain of this because she was watching him and his gaze came from the wall and moved across the field and stopped at her for a moment before moving on. She did not look away. She did not know what her own face was doing. She held still in the same way he was holding still, each of them at their respective stations in the field.

Then he turned and went back toward the barn. His stride was his usual stride, deliberate, slightly favoring the right knee since early spring. He went around the corner of the barn and was gone.

She finished the section. Coiled the wire stretcher and gathered the remaining staples. On the upper wall the work detail was still going, Lonzo on his rock, Fischer visible at the wall's far end. She did not say anything else. She went in.

---

That evening Albrecht was at the icehouse window.

He was there most evenings when Lonzo had gone home and the farm was down to its nighttime arrangements. She heard it from the kitchen table: her father's voice, low and measured; then Karl's voice answering; then her father again. The German came through the icehouse wall and the kitchen wall between them at the pitch of ordinary conversation, and she could not make out the words from where she sat and had stopped trying months ago. What they said was between them. The making-out of words had never been the point, or it had not been her point, and she had accepted this at some particular moment and could not remember when.

The kitchen was where it had always been. The schoolwork in front of her was the schoolwork. The German through the walls was the German through the walls.

In October 1943 the icehouse had four German prisoners and her father spoke to Karl in the evenings and Lonzo came at eight o'clock and the cows were sixteen and the fence along the north pasture needed maintenance and the breakwater was where it was. She had been seventeen.

In October 1944 the icehouse had four German prisoners and her father spoke to Karl in the evenings and Lonzo came at eight o'clock and the cows were sixteen and the fence along the north pasture needed maintenance and the breakwater was where it was.

She was not the same person inside the list.

Her father had watched her and Karl at the fence. He had looked at her once and walked back to the barn. That evening he was at the icehouse window, as usual, and his voice came through the wall at its usual pitch. She did not know what he had seen when he looked across the field. She did not know what had been in his face at the field's edge — not anger, she thought, with reasonable confidence; not approval, which was its own complicated thing in her father's register. She could describe his face. She could describe the stillness and the hands in the coat pockets and the gaze that came to rest on her for one moment. She could not reach through the description to the thing inside it.

She closed the schoolwork and went upstairs.

The German was still coming through the walls. She did not stand on the stairs to listen. She went to her room and the question of what her father had seen, and what he was doing about it in whatever space behind his face was used for such questions, came with her, and it was still there when she lay down, and she did not reach for it again that night.

# December

The radio had been bringing the news since Saturday. German counteroffensive. Belgium. The Ardennes. Three gaps in the Allied line, the communiqué said, the front still moving west. The announcer read the communiqués with the practiced evenness the networks had developed — it gave the information without telling you how to hold it. She had been keeping the radio on since Saturday morning, the volume low, the way she had kept it on through the June weeks when the news was also continuous and also required management. There was nothing to do about the Ardennes from the harbormaster's shack in Coldwater, Maine. She did her work and kept the radio on.

December harbor: four lobster boats at the dock, the Callie B. laid up for her winter haul-out at the south end, two moorings occupied by day-sailers whose owners would not come until April. The mail boat Tuesdays and Fridays, Rockland to Coldwater and back. Since the weekend blow, which had cleared anything still out to tie up or stay out, nothing in or out. The harbor was quiet in the way it was quiet in December, which was different from the way it was quiet in October: in December the quiet was the shape of the season, not an interruption.

Ice: not yet on the inner cove. She had been noting the water temperature dropping faster than last year and had marked it in the weather column without drawing a conclusion she couldn't yet support. In 1943 the cove had iced in the third week of January. She thought it might come sooner this year.

She did the 0700 log entry — wind NNW ten knots, barometer 30.04 and rising, sky overcast, no precipitation — and kept the radio on.

The antenna check: the northwest frequency was crackling. Third consecutive Tuesday. That moved it from coincidence to the antenna wire and she put it on the maintenance list with a note: before January.

The 0900 communiqué ran for six minutes. Road junction in Belgium. German armor advancing on multiple axes. Air support impossible in current weather. She turned the volume down a half-step and went back to the freight manifests.

---

Farber came in around nine.

She heard him on the dock boards before the door: his footfall familiar, heavier on the left side, the right leg working harder than it should because of the knee he did not discuss. He had been running long lines off the inner bar since Thanksgiving week — winter lobstering, the water cold enough now that the lobster were moving deeper, but traps still out. He came in with his catch on the June M. and then he came up to the shack.

He had something tucked under his arm. A piece of tarp, folded over. He set it on her desk. He took his cap off and put it in his coat pocket. He said he had pulled it up in his net that morning, off the inner bar — maybe eighty yards out from the breakwater's cove-side base. It had come up in the trawl with a quarter-crate of rock crab and he had kept it separate. He was looking at the dock through the window while he said this.

She said: what is it.

He said: you should look.

She was not going to ask him why he had brought it to her rather than leaving it on the dock or throwing it back. He was Reg Farber, and this was December 1944, and the inner bar was eighty yards from where the breakwater met the cove bottom, and October 1943 was fourteen months ago in the calendar and not particularly distant in any other sense. He had brought it to the harbor authority because it had come out of the harbor's floor. He had brought it to her specifically because of October.

She unwrapped the tarp.

---

A wallet. Or what a wallet becomes in fourteen months of saltwater and tidal action: the leather warped and contracted, shrunk into itself, the color bleached and darkened until it was a gray-brown that told you nothing about what it had started as. The stitching on one long side was open, the two layers of leather parted and curling away from each other at the seam. She turned it over in her hands.

Fourteen months, approximately, if it had gone into the water on or near the night of October 11, 1943. The tidal set in the inner cove ran north-northwest on the ebb. The bar was where something would settle, given time and the particular geometry of the cove. Eighty yards was consistent.

She worked it with her hands carefully. The billfold pocket: gone, the seam failed and the pocket open and empty. Water and fourteen months were sufficient for that. The rear face pocket: same — the lower seam failed, nothing remaining. She turned the wallet in her hands and found the center divider pocket on the interior face.

That seam had held. The leather had been pressed into the leather by the compression and the drying, the two layers sealed against each other in something close to adhesion. She worked her thumbnail into the top edge of the seam, a quarter inch at a time, without tearing. She worked it open the full length.

Inside: a piece of paper, folded twice. The paper was heavy stock — heavier than ordinary writing paper, the weight of an envelope's back flap or the card at the front of a formal letter. It had been wet and compressed and partly dried and wet again, and it had come out the other side as something closer to thin board than paper: stiff along the fold lines, slightly bowed. She unfolded it flat on the desk blotter and smoothed the folds with two fingers.

Handwriting. She could see the shape of it before she could see the letters — the slant and press of a careful hand, the ink bled at the edges of each stroke into the paper's grain but held in the center of each line where the pen had pressed hardest. The lower half of the card was gone: a uniform gray-brown wash, the ink dispersed too completely to reconstruct. The upper third was partial — lines, possible shapes, nothing she could resolve into letters. But in the center third, where the outermost fold had held longest and the protected seam had given it the most shelter, three letters were readable. Possibly four; the right edge of the fold had not quite held, and what might have been a fourth letter was present as a partial form.

Handwritten, not printed. A formal script. The ascenders had the backward cant — right to left, the slope reversed from what English cursive did — that she had seen in the typed header on the Yarmouth letter. Two of the three clear letters had that cant. The third, which sat between the two ascenders and was a lower form, had a double-barred crosspiece she had seen Marcus Klein's students copying badly from the board on the two or three occasions she had passed through the school hallway long enough to see anything through the classroom door.

The letters were German. She was certain of that much. She could not read them.

She looked at them for a long time. The radio came on at the half-hour. She did not turn toward it.

---

She folded the card back along its original lines and wrapped the wallet in the tarp. She opened the middle drawer — log pages in their column on the left, freight files for October through December, and at the back behind the January manifests the Yarmouth letter still in its envelope, where she had put it in April — and pressed the bundle to the rear of the drawer, behind the Yarmouth envelope, against the back wall. She shut the drawer. She took the key from the ring and turned it in the lock. The key went back on the ring. The spare was at the house, on the hook inside the kitchen door. No other key.

She said to Farber: I'll look into it.

He said: I figured you would. He paused. He said: I wasn't going to say anything one way or the other.

She said: I know.

He put his cap back on and went back to the June M.

---

The rest of Tuesday was the day's work: the 1300 log entry, wind WNW nine knots, barometer holding, one vessel in from Rockland. The February dock assignments, which had to reach the District office before the last week of December. She ran the 1400 radio check; the northwest frequency was clear. She went out for the afternoon rounds at fifteen hundred and it took twenty-five minutes in the cold, the light already going, and everything was in order.

She did not open the middle drawer.

At five she locked the shack, locked the dock gate, and walked up the hill. December in Coldwater: the harbor smell off the water, herring and diesel and cold salt, the dock lights at their minimum. The inner cove dark and still at the ebb, the bar visible as a faint pale line at the water's surface. The breakwater's red light turning on and off at its interval in the distance.

She went home. She made supper — salt fish, potatoes — and ate standing at the stove because she was tired. She washed the dishes. She banked the coal stove and checked the back door and went to bed.

The wallet was in the drawer. The drawer was locked. She had the key on the ring on the nail by the door. In the morning she would take it and go down to the shack and do the 0700 log and keep the radio on.

She lay in the dark.

She did not tell anyone.

# The Fragment

The note was waiting for him at the school office on Tuesday morning, the first Tuesday of January, slipped through the door grid of his mail slot between the week's attendance forms and the District office circular about spring scheduling. He found it when he came for the day's mail before first period: a folded half-sheet, his name in ink on the front fold. The handwriting was compressed and exact.

*Dr. Klein — If it is not inconvenient, could you stop at the harbormaster's office at your convenience this week. I have a document in German I would like you to look at, briefly. — E. Bowman.*

He stood in the office doorway with the note in his hand. The morning bell had not yet rung. Through the window above the secretary's desk he could see the schoolyard: frost on the packed ground, the elm at the corner of Henry's lot bare against the January sky, two students moving quickly across the yard in the cold.

He read the note again. Then once more.

*A document in German.* He was not certain what to make of that, in this place, in this January, in the third full winter of his knowledge of Coldwater Reach and the harbormaster who ran it with the careful neutrality of a person working inside a chosen boundary. He was available Thursday afternoon; there was nothing after four o'clock, and the walk to the harbor shack was eight minutes from the school's back steps, or nine in January when the footing was uncertain. He put the note in his coat pocket. He picked up his attendance forms and went upstairs.

He came on Thursday.

---

The harbor in January was a different harbor than in any other month — not merely colder or emptier but quieter in a way that was more total, as if the season had removed something structural and left only the essential geometry. Three lobster boats at the east face of the dock, nothing moored, the Callie B. laid up at the south end, the water in the inner cove nearly still at the low tide and reflecting the sky's flat gray. Marcus came down the hill from the school's back street and onto the dock road with his collar up and his hands in his pockets and the cold finding the gaps at his wrists and behind his ears with the thoroughness he had come to expect of it. The dock boards were clear of ice; someone had sanded them. The shack at the dock's head had its light on inside.

He knocked twice.

She opened the door immediately. She said: come in and shut it.

He shut it. The interior: the radio set on the left wall, the tide clock on the right, the desk in the center with the log ledger open to the current week's entries. She had moved a chair from the corner and positioned it beside the desk's near edge. He sat. She sat. The cold he had brought in with him dispersed quickly in the shack's heat; the coal stove in the corner was burning low and steady. The harbor sound outside was muffled by the closed door and the winter-weight windows — or not muffled exactly, but held at a distance.

She did not speak at once. She pulled open the desk's middle drawer and lifted out something wrapped in a piece of dark tarp — a flat bundle the size of a wallet, which it became, a moment later, when she set it on the desk blotter and began folding the tarp back.

She said: it came out of Farber's net off the inner bar in December. Fourteen months in the water. She said: could you look at the paper inside.

The wallet: leather, badly deteriorated, warped to the shape of whatever it had settled against below the bar. One long seam was open, the leather parted and curling. She opened the wallet along its length and folded the front face back, and he could see the interior: the pocket seams failed, the compartments empty. But the center divider had held. She had already worked it open — her thumbnail along the seam's edge, he guessed, a quarter-inch at a time — and from the interior face she drew a folded piece of paper, stiff now as thin card, and laid it flat on the blotter.

He leaned forward.

He did not touch it yet. He looked at the handwriting first: a formal Continental script, the kind taught in German-language schools from the 1880s through to the 1920s and perhaps beyond, with the characteristic backward cant of the ascenders — the tall letters sloping right to left, opposite to the English habit. The ink had bled into the paper's grain at the stroke edges but held in the center of each mark where the pen's pressure had been greatest. The lower portion of the card was gone to a uniform gray-brown wash. The upper third was partial, lines visible in outline but not legible. In the center third, where the outermost fold had held longest against the shelter of the sealed divider, three letters were readable. Possibly the beginning of a fourth, at the fold's right edge, where the protection had been incomplete.

He looked at them for a long time.

The first two letters were clear. *F* and *e*. The *F* had the diagonal crossbar of the German formal hand; the *e* was open at its top in the continental manner. The third character was ambiguous: the ink's ghost suggested the loop of an *l* or the closed form of an *i*, but the damage at the stroke's center made certainty impossible. The fourth, if there was a fourth, was a partial arc at the edge of the fold's protection — the upper curve of something. It might be *x*. It might be *k*. It might be a letter he could not reconstruct from so partial a form.

He sat back.

He said: I can make out part of what may be a name. The first two letters are *F* and *e*. He said: the subsequent letters are damaged. He paused. He asked: where did you say this was found?

She said: Farber's net. The inner bar. He brought it in on the nineteenth of December.

He looked at the fragment again without touching it. He said: may I look at it more carefully this evening? Under better light. I would return it in the morning.

She looked at him, and it was not the look of someone suspicious of him so much as the look of someone who was deciding what kind of person he was — taking a measurement she had been in the process of taking for some time. He held the measurement. She said: yes. She refolded the card along its existing lines and wrapped the wallet in the tarp and held it across the desk. He took it.

She said: I'll expect it before school, then.

He said: before eight.

She pulled the middle drawer open and shut it again, the particular gesture of someone verifying that something remains where it has been put. He stood and put on his coat. The tarp bundle went into the breast pocket, where the note had been on Tuesday morning. He went out.

The cold came back immediately, specific and total.

---

His room at half past nine: the radiator on the south wall making its mid-winter noise — the metal's expansion against the heat, a ticking that was at first, when he arrived in Coldwater, an irritation, and was now something he rarely heard except in moments of particular attention. The desk lamp on. The tarp unwrapped and the wallet open on the blotter with the fragment flat on its surface, held at the top edge by two books pressed together so that they weighted the card without creasing it.

He found the Emergency Committee folder on the shelf above the desk, behind the Stifter volume and ahead of the District correspondence box. He had not opened it since spring. He opened it now and found Dr. Feld's December 1943 letter in the second section, filed deliberately behind his own New York correspondence, because that was where a letter that might require future action belonged. He drew it out and read it in full in his usual way — sequentially, not skipping to the part he was looking for, because skipping was a practice that caused him to miss things, and he did not want to miss anything tonight.

The paragraph was in the letter's third section. *Felix K., linguist, formerly of Leipzig. Last documented Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, September 22, 1943. Intended to travel south by sea. No further word as of this date.*

He set the letter on the blotter, to the left of the fragment, so that both were visible under the lamp at once.

*Fe.*

*Felix.*

He sat with the two objects in front of him and did not move for a little while.

The probability was very high — the fragment on the right, the letter on the left, the lamp between them casting the precise light of the thing. The first two letters matched. The ambiguous third was consistent with *l*. The incomplete fourth was consistent with *x*: the terminal letter of *Felix*, if you were reading from the German, if you were a linguist from Leipzig trained in the formal hand of the late century, if you had been last documented in Yarmouth on the twenty-second of September 1943 and had been intending, from there, to travel south by sea.

The inner bar lay eighty yards from the breakwater's cove-side base. She had said so. Fourteen months of tidal action in the inner cove: a body and its effects settling toward the bar on the ebb, shifting and settling again, small objects moving in the specific geometry of the Reach's bottom currents until they rested. He had not needed to work the arithmetic because he had already worked it, in a different form, in the notebook in April, with the autumn weather record and the crossing time for a small motorboat out of Yarmouth running south.

He got the notebook from its place between the English journal and the grammar workbook.

He wrote the date at the top of a fresh page. Then in the private shorthand he kept in the German, the notation stripped of its qualifying architecture — bare sequences of fact, the record pared to what resisted argument — he wrote:

*Fe — l or i — x or k. Fragment, wallet, inner bar. Recovered December 1944. Fourteen months in the water.*

*Felix K. Linguist, Leipzig. Yarmouth NS, September 22, 1943. Coldwater, October 1943.*

He drew a line.

*If this is correct: Felix K. is the man on the breakwater. No one has known his name for fourteen months.*

He drew another line.

*I do not know for certain. The fragment is not sufficient.*

He put the pen down. He looked at what he had written for a moment — at the last two lines in particular. They were accurate. They remained.

He put the fragment back in the tarp. He put the Feld letter in the folder and returned the folder to the shelf, to its position behind the Stifter volume. He closed the notebook and put it back in its place.

He would return the fragment before eight. He would tell her what he could honestly tell her: that the legible letters were *F* and *e*, consistent with the beginning of a German-language name; that the subsequent letters were too damaged for certain identification; that this was the limit of what the fragment permitted him to say.

He would not tell her about the Feld letter.

He turned the reasons over and they remained reasons. He had a theory, not a confirmed name. A theory offered to Eira Bowman — a probable name for the man on her breakwater, the man she had watched walk out of the dock's darkness fourteen months ago in October, whatever she had been carrying about that night — was not information she could use. A theory she could not verify was weight with no purchase. And if he was wrong, the wrong name in the mind of a woman already holding what she held was a harm he would not be able to undo.

This was the argument. He believed it.

He was not entirely certain it was the only reason.

He did not open the shortwave. He went to bed.

The name lay where he had put it, in the notebook, in the German, on the shelf under the Stifter volume, in the dark. *Felix K.* He looked at the ceiling's familiar shape — the north side's slant where the roofline came down to meet the plaster — and the question he had written in the notebook's margin that April evening in the empty classroom, *What do I intend to do with this?*, had finally obtained an answer of a kind: for now, nothing. Return the fragment. Say what the evidence permits. Hold the rest.

*For now* was a qualified phrase. He went to sleep with it in the sentence.

# Zuhause

The cows were restless through most of December. It was the dark, or the cold, or the particular quality of deep winter that animals seemed to register before people did and which manifested in the barn as a low-grade generalized unease — not sickness, nothing clinical, just the small signs of discomfort she had learned to read in the years she'd been doing the four-thirty milking. Hannah talked to them through the work the same as always: the low reassuring murmur that barn work required, not words exactly, just sound, the human voice as its own argument for calm. She had been doing this since she was old enough to carry a pail. She would probably do it when she was fifty.

The radio was on before she got back to the kitchen. It had been on since December sixteenth, which was the morning she'd heard the word Ardennes over breakfast and watched her father set down his coffee and not pick it up again. The Ardennes was a place she knew from Harton's atlas — a forest on the German border with Belgium, which had nothing to do with Maine, which was therefore precisely the place her father would listen to for twelve hours straight. The German army had pushed through it, or was still pushing, the news confused in the first days, the correspondents using a kind of controlled uncertainty that told you the situation on the ground was more uncertain than the broadcasts could sustain.

Her father was at the kitchen set in the mornings and the parlor set in the evenings, and on the twenty-second he had both going at once, a thing she had not seen since the summer of 1942 when the tankers were burning off Cape Cod. The Ardennes was different from that. The tankers were the war coming here — a thing to be frightened of in the specific way of physical nearness, the fire visible on the horizon, the smell of it. The Ardennes was the war going there: to the country he had left in 1922, to the fields that were not Maine fields, to whatever was or wasn't in the Bavarian farmland he had not heard from in two years, perhaps longer. She had lost count of when the letters had stopped and could not remember if he had ever told her exactly.

She made breakfast and brought him coffee. He said danke and went back to listening.

Karl came to the barn willingly, the same as always. He moved through the milking stalls with the economy of someone who had worked animals since before he could read. Hannah moved through them the same way, on the opposite side, and the work got done in the barn's usual quiet. They had not spoken much since October. No particular thing had been said to stop it — the winter had done it, the way cold does, slowing things to stillness and leaving them to start again when the air changed. She knew where it had been and she knew it was still there.

She went to school on the days she went, which in December was most of them and in January was four out of five — the road iced over on Tuesdays and Wednesdays of the second week, and she stayed to do the morning work and then the evening, and the school day was somewhere else, occurring without her. Marcus Klein would have set her the reading. He did not make a particular occasion of her absences, which she appreciated.

---

The Bulge resolved in the Allies' favor by the end of January. The papers said it and the radio said it and Harton's geography students moved the pins back across the map in the school hallway, east and east again until the line was approximately where it had been before December sixteenth. Hannah watched this happen over three mornings on her way to German class. The resolution was accurate. The satisfaction it produced in her was not equal to the relief she had expected and she did not know what to do with that, so she left it.

Her father was not better.

She had let herself believe that the Bulge resolving would move something in him the way the tides moved things. In and then out, the particular pressure going and the next thing arriving. But the Bulge going had left him quieter, not more open, and the quality of his stillness had changed in a way she had to look at carefully to name. He was not sad, or not only sad. He was the face of a man who had handed something away and was now in the absence of the thing. She did not have a German word for it. She did not have an English one either.

He sat at the radio less. Her mother moved through the kitchen with the efficiency she had maintained across two years of silence: bringing him coffee in the parlor without being asked, the way she communicated everything now, by action without word. Hannah had learned to read the quality of her mother's movements the same way she had learned to read her father's face — it had simply taken different practice.

What Hannah wanted to say to her father was not a question.

She had questions. She had accumulated them for three years of living inside a house that had reorganized itself around two different silences. Whether there was family still in Bavaria that she'd been told about too young to remember. What he heard when he listened to the radio and what it cost him to hear it. What the German word was for whatever had happened to him when the war started and then went on and then the letters stopped. These were questions and she had given up expecting answers to them — not in despair, just as a practical matter, the same way you gave up expecting a certain kind of weather in February and instead worked with what February brought.

What she wanted to say was not a question.

She wanted to say: she knew about him and Karl. The icehouse window, the evenings, the particular register she had heard in her father's voice — the third register, neither barn German nor supper German but something slower, with more room in it, the pace of two people finding shared ground. She had known since spring and had said nothing because she had not known how to say it without seeming to offer something she was not offering. She did not want to make it strange, the way saying the name of something ordinary can suddenly make it strange.

She wanted to say: she spoke German now. Not Morgen, not the supper-table yes-father words. She had spoken German to Karl in the barn in April, forty words, and he had answered, and she had understood, and she had not been afraid of the language. She had been afraid of other things — whether Lonzo would come in, what her father's face would do if he saw — but not of the language itself. She had been speaking it at the fence through the fall, the ordinary German of farm questions and weather, the language settling into her the same way the barn language had settled in when she was three and the cow language when she was four. It was hers now. It had always been hers.

She had not said this to anyone in the farmhouse. She had walked through this house for eight months with the language in her and had not brought it into the same room as her father's language, as if they were two things that should be kept separate, as if the fence that kept Karl in the paddock also ran through the kitchen. By mid-January she recognized this as a kind of cowardice she had dressed in the wrong name. She had been calling it caution. It was not caution.

---

On a Thursday evening in late January she came in from the barn and stopped in the mudroom. She still had her coat on. The lantern was in her left hand. Outside the mudroom window the cold was absolute, the temperature well below what it had been when she went out, the sky clear and indifferent. She had not planned Thursday. Thursday had simply arrived at the end of enough other Thursdays.

The kitchen was lit by the overhead and the stove's firebox glow. Her father was at the table. Not beside the radio — the radio was on the counter, its dial barely amber, turned so low it was barely registering, just the habit of having it on that he had not fully let go since December. He was sitting with both hands around his coffee cup. He was looking at the table's grain. She had seen this posture many times in the last year: turned inward toward whatever country existed behind his eyes. Not empty. He was never empty. Somewhere.

Her mother was at the far end of the table with her darning. The sock on the needle was Lonzo Reed's — she had been mending the farm socks since November when Lonzo held out a heel with a hole in it and Magda had taken it from him and nodded. The darning gave her hands something. Hannah thought of it as that, and perhaps her mother did too.

Hannah set the lantern on its peg. She came into the kitchen. She sat down across from her father.

She said, in German — his German, the Bavarian she had grown up hearing through the floor and at the supper table and in the barn when she was close enough to catch it: Papa. Ich muss dir was sagen.

Her father looked up.

He had not heard her speak German to him — deliberately, directly, aimed at him across a table — since before the war. Since she was fourteen at the oldest and it was still the house's ordinary language, before the ordinary had ended. He looked up and his face was the face she had been learning to read. She thought she was closer to it now than she had ever been, which was different from having it fully.

He said: Dann sag es.

She said: she knew about him and Karl. The window. The evenings. That Karl was from fifty kilometers from where he was born, that she knew that and had known it, and that she knew it was not nothing. She said: I speak German now. Not the words I grew up with. I speak it. I have been speaking it for eight months and I was afraid to say so to you, and I'm not afraid anymore.

He was quiet.

She let him be quiet. The stove worked. At the far end of the table her mother went on with the sock, the needle moving in the same small arc, steady. The clock on the shelf above the icebox ticked through the room — the clock with the white face and the brass pendulum that her father wound every Sunday morning the same time as the barn, the first task of the week. She could hear it clearly now.

He said, in German, more slowly than his German usually moved, as if he were finding each word before he let it into the sentence: Du hast das von mir.

She said: Ja.

He said: Ich weiß das.

A pause. She had learned, in three years of this house, that some pauses were meant to be filled and some were themselves the conversation — the space the other person needed to breathe in. She held this one.

Then, quietly — in English, the language he had not spoken to her, not once, not even in passing, in more than two years — he said: "Hannah."

Just her name.

Her mother did not look up from the darning. But her hands were still.

---

Hannah went to bed.

She lay in the dark and the farm settled around her the way it settled in deep winter: the boards in the cold, the cows in the barn making the low sustained sound they made at night, the clock sending its voice through two walls and a ceiling. She had been falling asleep in this room her whole life and had never heard the clock so clearly, and she could not say why tonight was different except that it was.

She did not know what her father's name in English meant. She knew too many things it might mean, and too many things it couldn't mean, and she could not sort the combinations in a single night. She did not try very hard. She was eighteen and tired from the barn and from what she had done at the kitchen table, and the tiredness was not unpleasant.

She knew this: he had said it. He had found the language he had set down two years ago and picked it back up long enough to say her name. He had not offered a reason or a gesture toward reason. He had just said her name, in English, at the kitchen table in January, and the English was real — not a slip — real and deliberate and directed at her specifically, which was the person it had always been for.

She thought about the word zuhause.

She had been trying for years to know what it meant in this house. Her father's German and her mother's silence and Karl through the icehouse window speaking to her father in the register of a young man learning from an older one, and the school German that was Hochdeutsch when she expected Bavarian, and the barn German that was in between, and the language at the fence with Karl that had gradually stopped being between anything and started being its own thing. She had been looking for the word that covered all of it and finding that no single word did, that what fit Bavaria didn't fit Maine and what fit Maine didn't fit the kitchen in the evenings when everything was German and she was standing at the edge of it.

Tonight it meant the kitchen in January. The stove's glow. The clock that her father wound every Sunday and which kept time the way it kept time, neither fast nor slow, steady. Her mother's hands going still over the sock. Her father at the table, both hands around his coffee, looking up at her with the face she was learning to read — and then the English word, her name, the one he had always known and had just now said again.

Zuhause.

She went to sleep.
