# The Crow House

The passage on the board was Lessing — the opening scene of *Minna von Barnhelm*, Act One, which he had chosen because it was military and therefore timely and had the further advantage of containing enough grammatical difficulty in the first page to occupy two students for the duration of the period without leaving them time to consider what they were actually translating. He had written it out in his German hand — the one that was smaller than his English hand and still leaned rightward in the way he had been taught at eight years old — and now he stood with his back to the room and looked at what he'd written while the two girls worked.

He could hear Doris Hatch on the second sentence by her breathing. She was the kind of student who held her breath when reading in a second language, as though the effort of comprehension required the body to suspend its ordinary functions until it could be resolved. Louise Pelletier had moved through the second sentence and arrived at the third, which contained a dative of purpose he had not glossed in the notes he had put on their desks, and he was waiting, without appearing to wait, to see what she would do with it.

The third chair — at the left-hand desk, second row from the window — was empty.

Pfeiffer. The information had not arrived as a deliberate perception but as an alteration in the room's ordinary texture, the way a room registers an absence not because one has looked for it but because the space that is usually occupied is not: a gap that does not announce itself but is there. Hannah Pfeiffer was the only one of the three who came to a German passage knowing, in some preliminary way, what the words contained before she construed them. She had her father's Bavarian dialect in her phrasing — recognizable even in the small German she produced in class, a particular shaping of the back vowels, a rhythm to the subordinate clause that was distinct from anything she might have learned here — and this told him things about the household she came from that he had not asked her to tell him and that she had not, so far, offered.

"Hatch," he said.

Doris looked up with the expression of a student hoping to remain unnoticed a moment longer. She read the second sentence aloud. The German was accurate; the accent was northern American in the particular way that Maine is northern American, a distinct phonological territory, and the meaning came through intact, which was the purpose of translation class and sufficient. He corrected the long *u* once, without comment, and moved to Louise Pelletier, who had navigated the dative independently and correctly, a small specific satisfaction — the kind that belongs to teaching rather than scholarship, less clean but present in its way — and he told her so. He wrote the dative construction on the board and would set it again in two weeks to see whether the lesson held.

Below the Lessing, he wrote: *Wohin?*

Beneath it, in English: *Where to?*

He left both on the board without explaining them. The word was in the passage; he had no other reason to put it there that he would have been able to articulate in terms the girls would find useful. Doris Hatch looked at the board and then at her notebook. Louise Pelletier looked at the board and then out the window, where the October trees had gone to the plain brown of late October, the last week before November reduced them further. The room smelled of chalk and damp wool and the coal furnace's particular brand of inadequacy, which he had been smelling since March and had accepted as characteristic. 

He stood with the chalk in his hand and the chalked German of a playwright dead a hundred and sixty years on the board behind him, and through the east window the afternoon light came in at the angle it came in at in mid-October at this latitude, low and already beginning its withdrawal, and the chair at the left-hand desk stayed empty, and he set them both to the fourth sentence and waited.

---

He heard his name not said.

The supply room at the end of the second-floor hall had a door that did not close flush with the frame, and over a year and a half he had learned to stand slightly back from it when he was collecting chalk or examination paper, because from that position he could hear, or could not hear, what was happening in the hallway in a way that was occasionally informative. This was not a habit he would have thought to develop in Vienna. It had developed, in stages, through Paris and London and afterward.

He was putting chalk in his coat pocket when Hendricks from mathematics — and the woman whose name he had not yet retained, who taught something in the girls' physical program and something else he could not recall — came around the corner from the stairs. He heard them come to the particular pause that conversations came to when he entered a range. He walked at the pace he had learned, which was the pace of a man with nothing in particular he was doing or listening for, and came out of the supply room and went along the hall.

He heard: *no papers. No name.* He heard: *Coast Guard took the log pages, which Mabel thought was notable.* He heard: *not from Coldwater, not from anywhere anyone can—* and then he was past the point where it carried.

This was sufficient. He had been a philologist for twenty-three years. The body on the breakwater: no papers, no name, not from here. A man without documentation, found at the edge of the sea, in clothing that suggested somewhere else. He put the fragment where he put things he had not yet finished examining, and went down the stairs into the afternoon.

---

The walk from the school to the Crow house took nine minutes at his ordinary pace. Where the road bent upward at the ridge, before the elms closed in above it, the harbor was briefly visible through the October-stripped trees: a strip of gray water, the breakwater a dark granite line extending from the dock's end, the fixed red light at its seaward terminus not yet lit in the afternoon. He stopped for a moment — not for any reason that required stopping, but because the view had precise edges and he had discovered, in his months here, that he found a particular comfort in things with precise edges. Then he went on.

The Crow house was white clapboard, second-from-the-end on Elm Street, with a modest front yard and a porch that in warmer months Henry occupied in the last of the afternoon light. This was not a habit anyone had pointed out to Marcus; it was something he had understood, early in his time here, as the portion of the day Henry reserved for his own thinking, and he had taken some care not to arrive at that hour in a way that required Henry to acknowledge him. In October the porch was not useful. Henry was inside.

Marcus let himself in with his key.

The hallway was warm, not aggressively but sufficiently — the warmth of a house that had been maintained with care over a long time. He heard the Rockland paper's particular rustle from the kitchen, which meant Henry at the table. From the back of the house, coffee: the real kind, not the grain substitute, which had a flavor he had become too well acquainted with in his first months here before he understood that the Crow house was somehow an exception to this. He had arrived at the correct position about this fact, which was that it was not his to investigate and that the correct response to it was gratitude without commentary.

He hung his coat on the peg.

In the kitchen Lillian was at the stove with her back to him. She said, without turning: "Marcus. Coat."

"Already," he said.

She glanced back briefly — a look that was not a look of doubt. Henry was at the table with the Rockland paper and looked up from it in his way, which was not all the way up but enough, and Marcus sat.

The kitchen table had three chairs. His was the one that faced the east window, through which the back yard was visible, and past the yard the hillside, and above the hillside the gray sky of October pressing down in a way that was not unpleasant but was entirely earnest. Henry's chair faced the door. Lillian's could see both. This arrangement had established itself in the first week of March and had not been discussed.

There was a quality to this kitchen that the rest of Coldwater, in general, did not have in his presence — a quality he had spent some months attempting to name and had eventually settled for calling the absence of management. Elsewhere in town he was, in some ongoing functional sense, a matter that required decisions: the credentials requiring periodic validation, the provenance requiring explanation when it came up, the presence requiring an account of itself in a community that had not anticipated it and had made what room it had made in the spirit of pragmatic necessity rather than affirmative welcome. He had learned to live within this without complaint, which was easier than it sounded and also harder than it sounded. Here the management was absent. Lillian had written, in her letter through the school board the previous winter, that he was welcome, and the word had meant what it said.

He folded his hands on the table and then unfolded them, because folded hands was a classroom posture and he was not in the classroom.

"There was a man found on the breakwater," Marcus said. "Tuesday morning. I understand he had no papers and no name."

Henry did not respond immediately. He set the paper down, flat, without marking his place — he kept the page in his head — and turned the sentence over with the unhurried attention of a man who had decided that responses given before they were ready had a quality of incompleteness that was not worth the saved time. Then he said: "Found him Tuesday?"

"That is what I have been given to understand."

Henry nodded once, picked up the paper, and returned his attention to it. This gesture, which Marcus had initially read incorrectly in his first weeks here, meant that the information was received and placed and required no further handling at this moment — that there were categories of information which arrived complete and which adding to served nothing. It was not incuriosity; it was the practiced discipline of a man who had learned precisely which things warranted a response and which things warranted only acknowledgment, and who did not waste the one on occasions that called for the other. He was still in the process of learning it.

Lillian set the cups down and sat and poured. She asked after the school furnace, which had been running cold on the second floor since September and which the building staff had so far addressed without result, and Marcus told her what he knew, and Henry's expression did not change, and Lillian said she would have a word.

They drank their coffee. The Rockland paper reported what it reported. Outside, Elm Street darkened toward five o'clock in the way October darkened it: not gradually but in steps, the light changing its angle and then abandoning the angle entirely and leaving only the flat gray that preceded the dark. They sat in it, in the kitchen, and Marcus held the fragment — no papers, no name, not from around here — at the edge of his attention where he had put it, and where it stayed.

---

His room was on the second floor, east-facing, with a slanted ceiling on the north wall where the roofline came down to meet the plaster, which gave it the shape of a room in which one moved with a working knowledge of the available space. He had acquired this knowledge in the first days of March and had arranged the room accordingly: the desk under the east window, the single wooden chair beside the bookcase, the narrow bed along the south wall near the radiator, about which he had not yet asked Henry, understanding the asking to require a confidence in his own domestic standing that he was still, in certain particulars, assembling, a year and a half on.

The shortwave was on the desk: a Zenith portable, not the console that sat in the Crows' parlor, but a smaller set he had acquired in Bangor in the spring of his arrival with money he had needed for other things and had spent on this instead. The dial glowed amber when the set was warm and the tuning knob required a light touch and something he had too much time to develop.

He switched it on and waited.

The BBC World Service came in on 9.41 megacycles, or had come in there last Thursday; the frequencies shifted and he had to find them freshly each time, which was an inconvenience he had come to regard as appropriate, or at least as not inappropriate. He tuned.

Static. Through it, something: a woman's voice reading figures he couldn't resolve before the signal dropped. He tuned past. A military frequency in English, procedural, not meant for him. Past. At 9.38 the BBC identification signal arrived — four notes, the motif that had acquired, over three years of hearing it in conditions of varying comfort and uncertainty, a significance — and then the signal faltered and faded before the bulletin began.

He sat with the dial and waited.

It came back. The Italian campaign: not going quickly, but going. The Pacific: performing better than the assessments of late 1942 had suggested. The convoy situation in the North Atlantic: improved, the broadcaster said, in the careful syntax of someone managing what could not be entirely managed, and Marcus listened with the full attention he gave to news from Europe.

The man on the breakwater was there at the edge of his attention, where he had put the fragment.

He did not write in his German notebook tonight. He had taken it out and set it on the desk, which had been his intention, and the intention had not carried through.

The BBC signal faded. He tuned along the dial slowly — a quarter-degree at a time, the method that had a better yield than the broader sweeps he had tried in the early months — and found, in order: a fragment of French, gone before he could determine the source; something that might have been Brazilian, the geography of radio being less intuitive than one assumed; a clear voice in American English for thirty seconds on the subject of soybean prices in the Midwest; and then the static, full and thorough.

He sat with the static.

No papers. No name. A man dressed carefully for something and arrived at the wrong end of it, at the edge of a sea he had apparently tried to cross. 

He held the fragment the way one holds a word at the edge of recall — not pressing on it, because pressure did not help.

He had possessed, in August of 1941, a suit that did not fit him. The chest had been correct; the shoulders had gone loose in the way garments go loose when the body inside them has reduced, over some months, to less than the garment expected. He had possessed, in August of 1941, a document describing him in English as a resident alien enemy — *enemy* the substantive noun, *alien* and *resident* the qualifying adjectives that determined what could legally be done with him — and this had been the document he had when he stepped off the train in Boston with his cardboard case and the two books he had been allowed to bring with him when he left. The man who stepped off the train did not correspond, in any precise sense, to the man who had boarded one in Vienna three years earlier. He had spent the months following the arrival determining the nature of the correspondence, and the question had not been fully resolved, though he had made progress.

He did not know why the man on the breakwater interested him with this particular quality of attention. He turned the tuning dial a quarter-degree and found static of a slightly different texture and went on sitting with the thought he was not quite pursuing, because the pursuit would not help.

The BBC came back for a moment — shipyards, the Pacific, a name he didn't catch — and dissolved again into the static.

On the shelf above the desk, in the amber dial-glow, his notebooks stood in the order he maintained: the English journal, the grammar workbook from his first months at the school, the current German one. He could see, from his chair, that the spine of the German notebook was written in his English hand.

This had been happening for some months. When he needed to write something quickly — a word, a heading, a note in the margin of something — his English hand came first, without direction. Not because his German hand had failed him; when he turned to it deliberately it was there, the *Kurrent* script and the Roman print both intact, present and correct. But the English arrived first, without the interval of retrieval that German now required. The English was, in some working sense, more available. It was the closer thing.

He had not expected this. He had expected, if anything, the reverse to be permanent: that German would remain primary in the way a native language remains primary, the English always a skill rather than a reflex, the boundary maintained even when other things were not. The boundary had not maintained itself. He still noticed it when he noticed it, the way one notices a change that has been gradual enough to arrive without announcement.

He reached over and switched off the set.

---

The room without the radio found its other sounds: the north wall settling, cold working at the seams of the window glass, the boards making their adjustments with the night temperature. The harbor was somewhere down the hill in the dark beyond the east windows, not visible, present in the way of things one knows to be there without seeing them. In whatever building across town contained the information — whatever file or desk or locked cabinet — a dead man's absence of papers and name continued to be a fact that waited for whatever facts waited for.

Marcus took off his glasses and set them on the desk. The room went soft at its edges: the desk, the chair, the bookcase with its spines, the shelf above the desk with the notebooks — shapes he knew and knew where they were, imprecise now but present. The east window, dark. The harbor's direction.

The room was dark and cold and was, for the moment, where he lived.

# Statement

The auxiliary station had left a note.

Lt. R. Ennis, USCG, would attend the harbormaster's station on Wednesday the twentieth at nine a.m., regarding the formal statement in the matter of the body found October 12. It was written in pencil on a half-sheet with the station address at the top. The signature at the bottom belonged to someone named Osgood.

She read it Monday morning when she came in and set it on the corner of the desk.

The radio check at eight came in clear. She logged the conditions — wind WNW eleven knots, barometer 30.1 rising, tide low at six-forty-two — and went out to walk the dock in Owen's peacoat, which was enough coat for October and only just. The fog hadn't lifted; the breakwater showed the first hundred yards and then grayed out, the fixed light not yet switched on for the day. She walked dock head to end, checked the line on Pellerin's lobster boat, which had been sitting since Thursday, and found it holding. The fenders needed adjusting; she adjusted them. Through the *Callie B.*'s wheelhouse window she read the fuel gauge at three-quarters and wrote it in the log. At the far end of the dock, in the shallows near the seine sheds, the inner cove had put down a skin of ice overnight — thin and gray, early for October, the kind that a shift in wind would break before noon. She checked the cleat at the dock's end, which had been working loose since the blow, and found it had tightened on its own. She wrote that too, and went back inside.

The *Mabel Lena*'s winter registration was due November fifteenth and Clarence Pelletier hadn't come in to sign. She wrote a reminder. There was a discrepancy in the September fuel-allocation figures she needed to correct before the Portland form arrived; she worked through the log and found the error and noted the correction in the margin. She ran the noon check. She went out to re-seat the anemometer mount at the dock's end, which had been reading low since the blow preceding the twelfth, and came back in and made the entry: *anemometer mount re-seated; estimated variance in readings Oct 10–17 not to exceed 1.5 knots.* She dated it.

The note sat on the corner of the desk.

On Tuesday, Farber appeared around eight-thirty, coming down to check on the *Callie B.* before the next weather system moved back in. He thought he might run out Thursday if it held. She told him the pump was running clean, that she'd checked it herself Monday. He stood with his hand on the rail and said he'd heard the Coast Guard was coming Wednesday for her statement, about that business on the breakwater. She said yes, Wednesday morning. He said it was a peculiar thing, a man like that, no name or nothing. She said yes. He waited a moment, and then nodded and went down to his boat.

She did the Tuesday items. Tide charts through the end of October. The freight manifest for Friday's mail boat. The second fuel-log discrepancy, different from Monday's, which she tracked back through three weeks of entries to find its source.

On Tuesday afternoon she glanced at the note on the corner of the desk.

Wednesday morning, before she cleared the papers, she glanced at it a second time.

---

Wednesday she was at the shack by seven. The morning was cold and clear, the fog gone overnight, the breakwater showing its full length against a gray sky with the fixed light off in the daylight, the granite dark with the tide. She ran the eight o'clock check and logged conditions — wind WNW eight knots, barometer 30.2 steady, tide high ten thirty-four — and noted that the skin ice on the inner cove had persisted through Tuesday and thickened slightly overnight. She cleared the papers from the desk and moved the harbor log to the windowsill.

At nine she heard boots on the planking.

Ennis came in with a yeoman — a young man of about twenty-two with a Remington portable in a case — and the shack became a different size than it had been. The yeoman set the Remington on the desk, which took the left half of the work surface, and there was no useful place for anything else on it, so the harbor log stayed on the windowsill. The yeoman sat in the chair near the radio set, put paper in the machine, and waited. Ennis stood near the window with his clipboard. Eira stood near the stove. The arrangement sorted itself without comment.

Ennis was in his mid-forties, clean-shaven, in uniform with the rank on his collar. He had the look of a man who had made the drive down from Portland and intended to complete the task and make the drive back. He was not hostile. He was, in the particular manner of a man from a larger office with a form to complete, correct. He explained the process: statement on the events of October eleventh and the morning of the twelfth, typed as they went, reviewed and signed before departure. He looked at the clipboard while he spoke.

She said that was fine.

---

He began at the beginning.

What time had she arrived at the dock the evening of October eleventh.

Twenty-two forty-five, approximately.

Her purpose for being at the dock at that hour.

She had come to check the bilge pump on the *Callie B.*, registered to Reg Farber, second slip. A slow leak at the port quarter since early October; she had been monitoring it. She had checked it on the eighth and again on the eleventh.

Had the pump been running.

Running clean.

How long had she remained at the dock.

Until twenty-three thirty, approximately.

What had she observed during that time on the dock or on the breakwater.

She had not observed any individual on the dock or on the breakwater.

Had she observed any vessel not previously seen in the harbor.

She had not.

The yeoman typed. Each answer went in, the carriage returned, and the shack was quiet again until Ennis found the next item on the form.

Had she logged the dock visit.

No. A bilge-pump check on a vessel already in the harbor log didn't require a separate entry.

Was there any entry in the harbor log for the evening of October eleventh indicating unusual activity.

No.

Had she observed any unusual activity in the harbor between approximately twenty-two hundred hours and midnight.

No.

Had any other personnel been present on the dock during that time, to her knowledge.

No.

Was the visibility sufficient, given the conditions that evening, to observe the full length of the dock.

The fog had been moderate and the dock lights were on. She could see to the head of the breakwater steps from the *Callie B.*'s position at the second slip.

Ennis made a note on the form and looked at the next section.

He asked whether the dock lighting at the far end — near the breakwater steps — would have made it difficult to observe activity in that area.

She said yes. The lights were kept low.

Was that standard practice.

Standard practice since the summer of 1942, she said, per First District guidance. The dock lights at the seaward end had been reduced to fifteen watts. The breakwater's fixed light was on its regular schedule.

He wrote something. He was not looking at her while he wrote — his attention was at the form, at the space allocated for the answer. She watched him make the check beside the item. She heard the tide clock on the shelf and she didn't need to look at it but she looked at it anyway. Nine-seventeen. He moved to the next section.

---

He said he wanted to share what the investigation had developed, as a matter of courtesy to the harbormaster's office.

She said to go ahead.

The man had no papers, Ennis said. No wallet. No identification of any kind — nothing military, nothing naval, nothing issued by any civilian authority they had been able to identify. His clothing was civilian: a dark wool overcoat, a dress shirt. Nothing to indicate a branch or a service. The overcoat was of a quality suggesting a city rather than a working coast; the shirt collar had been intact, which was notable given the overall condition. He appeared to be in his forties or older, medium build. He was not, by any information the Coast Guard or the local inquiry had produced, a man from Coldwater or from the neighboring towns. He had been in the water or in severe weather conditions for some considerable time before reaching the breakwater — the physical evidence was consistent with exposure over several days, corresponding to the storm pattern in the days preceding October twelfth. The investigation was not formally closed, but there was at present no identifying information sufficient to support active inquiry. The record would be held at Portland. If she came across any additional information in her capacity as harbormaster, she should contact the auxiliary station.

She said she understood.

She did not ask how far such a man might have come in three days of weather, or what was on this stretch of coast if you worked it backward from Coldwater. It was not her investigation. The record was in Portland.

---

The yeoman pulled the form from the typewriter — three carbons — and set the original and one copy on the edge of the desk. Ennis put his clipboard on the windowsill beside the harbor log.

She read the typed statement. Her name, her position, her years of appointment. Wednesday, October twentieth, nineteen forty-three. The events of October eleventh and twelfth as she had given them: the dock, the bilge pump, the time arrived, the time departed, nothing unusual observed. She read each line for correspondence between what was written and what was known to be true. There was no line that was inaccurate. Each statement was a statement she had made and each corresponded to an event that had occurred. She signed the original and the carbon and set the pen down.

Ennis thanked her. He shook her hand — the grip of a man who had processed a task — and nodded to the yeoman, who was already putting the Remington in its case.

She held the door.

Ennis went down the dock at the pace of a man with a drive ahead of him. The yeoman, slower with the typewriter case, went past her with a nod that meant nothing particular. She watched them reach the dock end and turn toward the road and go from sight around the corner of the seine sheds.

---

The shack was the shack again. The radio set on the south wall. The harbor log on the windowsill. The tide clock on the shelf, reading past where it should read — she hadn't reset it Monday, she saw now, and hadn't reset it the Monday before either; the clock had been gaining since October twelfth, since before October twelfth, since the Monday when Farber's boy had come at a run and the morning had become something else. It had been gaining since then and she had not stopped to set it.

She moved the harbor log back to the desk.

The time was nine forty-three. The interview had run forty-three minutes.

She looked out the east window. The breakwater ran its full two hundred yards in the gray morning, the fixed light off in the daylight, the granite dark at the waterline with the incoming tide. A lobster boat was coming in through the outer channel with its running lights still on, the green on the starboard bow, reducing speed for the harbor entrance. She recognized the boat. She watched it complete the turn and did not write it down.

The case was, officially, in Portland's hands. There was a form with her name on it, accurate in every particular, and what it would produce when filed was the record of a harbormaster who had come to check a bilge pump on the evening of October eleventh and had observed nothing unusual. That was the record.

She took out the log and found the next empty line after the morning entry.

She wrote:

*October 20, 1943. Interview conducted with Lt. R. Ennis, USCG, re: body found October 12. Formal statement submitted. No additional information at this time.*

She dated the entry and initialed it.

She looked at what she had written.

Then she stood and took the tide clock from the shelf. She set it back four minutes. The clock settled to where it should read for the time of day, or near enough — she hadn't calculated exactly how much it had gained, and near enough was what she had. She put it back on the shelf.

She sat back down and took out the fuel allocation forms that needed updating before the end of the week, and she worked until noon.

The interpretive clause "it became apparent there was no more to it" reads in Marcus's analytical-qualifying register, not Eira's. Eira observes behavior; she doesn't name the apparent social logic. Removed the clause; kept the observable action: "He waited a moment, and then nodded and went down to his boat."

---

**Flagged for writer judgment — two items:**

**1. Ennis description parenthetical (mid-chapter):**
> "He was, in the particular manner of a man from a larger office with a form to complete, correct."

The syntactic form — a heavily parenthetical mid-sentence qualifier — is Marcus's signature construction, not Eira's. Eira's complex observations extend "clause by clause, as if she is running a calculation," but this sits the qualifier *inside* the predicate rather than adding to it, which is Marcus's habit. The content (reading Ennis's institutional correctness with precision) is entirely Eira; the *form* is the issue. A writer-level call: if this sentence were restructured to Eira's more additive syntax — e.g., "He was not hostile. He was correct, in the way of men from larger offices with forms to complete." — it would land as Eira's voice without losing the precision. But the current version is borderline enough that it may be intentional.

**2. "the morning had become something else" (tide-clock paragraph near chapter end):**
> "…since the Monday when Farber's boy had come at a run and the morning had become something else."

The phrase "had become something else" is slightly literary for Eira's register. Her emotional life is meant to arrive through the precision of the object (the gaining tide clock), not through a softly evocative descriptor on the morning itself. "Something else" deliberately refuses to name the feeling — which is Eira-consistent — but "had become something else" is the kind of atmospheric clause that belongs more in Hannah's register (accumulative, atmospheric, unresolved). In Eira's voice, the sentence could end at "at a run" and the tide clock does all the work. However, "something else" *is* holding back rather than naming, so this may be within bounds. Writer's call.

# Tuesday German

The letter was from 1847, a botanist writing to his brother from somewhere in the foothills north of Munich. The coal furnace in the corner of the classroom had been running since first period and was making the sound it made when it was working at full effort without much result — a low rattle behind the draft plate, intermittent, like a man clearing his throat in another room. The east windows held whatever October afternoon light was available, which at three forty-five was pale and going. Three coats on the hook by the door. The room smelled of chalk and cold wool and the faint chemical undertone of the wax Henry Crow had put on the floor in September, which cold air kept releasing in small quantities.

Dr. Klein stood at the board with the mimeographed passage in his hand. Doris Hatch had her pencil laid flat on the desk in front of her. Louise Pelletier was watching the window, not the glass of it but the sky beyond — the strip of gray sky between the school roof and the maple, which still had most of its leaves.

He read the first line aloud and asked Doris to construe it.

Doris construed it carefully, the way she did everything in this class: accurately, with a quality of not wanting to give the language more of herself than the task required. The verb position was right. The case was right. The sentence came out in the correct English order, stripped of whatever the original sentence had been in its own mind, and Dr. Klein said good and moved to the next line.

Louise took the third line. Louise had a facility with French that she had been applying sideways to German since September, which produced results that were more elegant than Doris's and occasionally less accurate. This time they were accurate. Dr. Klein told her so. He wrote the construction on the board: the dependent clause, the verb at the end, the reason for it. He asked what they noticed. Louise said it reminded her of something in French. He said that was not accidental and they could return to it in a later session.

He found the next paragraph and asked Hannah.

She took the fourth line: the botanist describing the larch in the valley, the way the trees held their yellow through October until a hard frost came through and dropped it all at once, and the road between the two towns she had never been to but knew by another road's name, the way her father named them — a slightly different vowel, a verb placed one beat earlier in the sentence than the textbook would place it, which was how it sat in her head because it was how her father said it. The sentence arrived whole, the way German arrived for her, and she said it the way she had heard it since she was small enough that hearing it had not seemed like a particular thing.

She came to the end of the sentence. She looked up.

Dr. Klein was not writing on the board. There was a pause that had a shape to it — not long, but present, like a page that had turned differently than expected. He was looking at the mimeograph. Then he said, in German: *Ihr Akzent kommt aus dem Süden. Östlich von München.*

Your accent places you south, east of Munich.

She said, in English: My father is from Bavaria.

He said: Yes.

That was all. He looked down at the paper and found the next paragraph and asked Doris to take the construction at the top of it. Doris bent over her page and began working out the verb.

Hannah looked at her own paper. The larch trees in October. She had gotten them right.

---

After class Doris and Louise went ahead. Hannah stood at her desk until they were through the door, then took her grammar and came up to where Dr. Klein was erasing the board.

She said she had a question about a construction — the conditional clause in the second paragraph, whether the finite verb always moved to clause-end or whether there were exceptions in older texts.

It was a real question. She had noticed it in the letter. She was also standing at the front of the room because she wanted to know whether he would say anything further.

He set the eraser on the chalk tray and considered the question properly, which he always did — she had been in this class since September and had noticed that he treated even the simple questions as worth the full consideration. He said yes, the finite verb moved to the end in dependent clauses, conditional and relative and otherwise, with specific exceptions in some eighteenth-century texts, particularly in certain genres of correspondence. He said the exceptions were catalogued in the grammar, page forty-eight, margin note.

He did not say anything further about the vowels.

She said thank you and went and took her coat from the hook by the door and put it on.

---

She walked the long way, past the harbor.

The direct road turned at the bottom of the school hill and angled inland; the harbor route added ten minutes and she had the south field before school tomorrow and the evening milking still ahead. She took the harbor route. She had been taking it since the middle of October, since the morning Doris had come into first period saying she'd heard someone had found a body on the breakwater, which turned out to be true.

The afternoon was going gray. The road curved down around the shoulder of the hill and the harbor opened below — the dock's gray planking, the seine sheds, the Callie B. and two lobster boats in their slips. Past the dock's end the breakwater ran out two hundred yards across the inner cove, granite, dark at the waterline where the tide was coming in. At the far end the fixed red light had just come on. The first light of the evening, a clean red against the gray.

She was looking at the point at the seaward end. Nothing was different. The stone was stone, the water was the harbor, the light was the light. The body had come in on a Tuesday morning three weeks ago and had gone out again the same day, taken by the Coast Guard and the tide of things the Coast Guard managed, and the breakwater was now just the breakwater.

She looked at it for a few seconds. Then she kept walking.

The road bent inland and the harbor went behind the seine sheds and then behind the hill, and after that it was the inland road, the smell of mud and leaves, the farms in the distance.

---

Her father was already at the table. He had changed from his work clothes; the almanac was open in front of him. Magda was at the stove.

Her mother did not turn when Hannah came in. She had a dishcloth over her shoulder and the wooden spoon in her right hand, watching the pot with the particular quality of attention she brought to anything she was doing, which was all of it, all at once, and was not the same as the absence of attention it sometimes resembled from the doorway. Hannah hung her school coat and came to the table.

Albrecht looked up. He said: *Das Südfeld braucht morgen früh Aufmerksamkeit.*

She said she would do it before school.

He nodded and looked back at the almanac. He had been reading it in sections all month and it did not appear to change anything about how he farmed.

Her mother brought the pot to the trivet and went to the counter for the bread and the butter and the pickled beets they had put up in September, Albrecht's beets, which always went farther than the canning jars could hold, and set everything on the table and sat down and they ate.

Hannah's private theory about her mother's silence had been with her long enough now that it had stopped being a theory and become a working assumption: Magda had decided somewhere around April that language was not a safe material for the duration and had set it down the way you set down a tool you had no use for this season. The doctor in Rockland had listened and examined and found nothing physically wrong. It moved through the kitchen with purpose. It knew where everything went.

They ate. The stove ticked. The draft at the kitchen window came and went, the window she had been meaning to stuff with rags since September.

Her mother ate and cleared and refilled the water glasses without setting anything down harder than it needed to be set, and then she cleared the rest and Albrecht went for the almanac again and Hannah washed the dishes while Magda dried them, which they did in the silence that was ordinary now, the kitchen sounds filling in what the voices didn't. The dishes went to their shelves in the same order they always went. Outside the window the yard was dark already, the maple at its edge a mass against the sky, barely any leaves left.

---

Albrecht went out while Hannah was wiping down the table.

She heard the back door close, and then through the wall from the direction of the icehouse came the low sound of his voice. She couldn't make out the words. She knew there would be an answer through the window from Karl — the icehouse window that had been cracked two or three inches since August — but Karl's voice didn't reach this far and she couldn't hear it. She could hear her father's voice going, a sentence, then a pause, then another sentence, going past where a simple answer would have stopped.

She turned on the kitchen radio.

The Philco on the counter was old and received unevenly: some nights clear, some nights mostly static, with the sense of something being said underneath it — a voice in another room. Through the wall, her father's voice continued.

She turned it off at eight. Her mother had already gone upstairs. The kitchen was quiet. She banked the stove for the morning and took the lamp to the stairs.

---

The hallway upstairs smelled of the cedar her mother kept in the linen chest. Hannah's room was the second door, the one with the view of the maple, and she set the lamp on the dresser and wound the alarm clock to four-fifteen and undressed in the lamp's reach and got into bed with the extra blanket.

The maple outside the window was almost bare. Two weeks ago the color had still been in it — a yellow that her father would call Goldgelb if he were naming it, which he wouldn't, because color was not what he named — and now the branches were branches, the sky behind them going from dark gray to black as the clouds moved east.

What Dr. Klein had said sat in her the way a stone sits in a boot: not sharp, but there. Not the grammar, which had an answer. The other thing.

He had heard her father in her German and he had named where he heard it — south, east of Munich — and she had said where and he had said yes. And that had been the whole of it.

She didn't know what he'd heard, exactly. She knew what she'd heard, which was that he'd recognized something she hadn't known was recognizable. Her father's German: the verb placed where her father placed it, the vowels her father used, which were not the vowels in the textbook and had never been. She had been speaking textbook German in that class since September, or she had thought she was, and somewhere in the line about the larch trees in October she had apparently stopped.

She didn't try to do anything with this. She turned onto her side.

From below — from the direction of the icehouse, the geometry of the farmhouse making it hard to fix precisely — she could hear her father's voice again, low and going, the German in the dark coming through the floor and through the wall at once, talking to Karl through the cracked window on the other side of the wall. She couldn't hear what he said. She hadn't been able to hear it since the first night she had noticed it, in August, and she had not gotten any closer to the words since then.

The maples had been yellow. Now they were branches. November was coming in the next few days, and after November came the months that took everything you had and didn't offer much back, and the south field needed its attention before school tomorrow, and the alarm was set for four-fifteen and would do what it did, and she was already closing before it.

Her father's voice went on below her in the dark.

She was asleep before it stopped.

**Fix applied:** Removed italics from `Goldgelb` (Hannah's narration, final bedroom section). Style guide is explicit: German vocabulary items in Hannah's narration are "not italicized, treated as part of the narrative's texture." *Goldgelb* is a single embedded word in Hannah's free indirect voice and should sit without typographic marking. (Full German dialogue sentences — *Ihr Akzent kommt aus dem Süden...* and *Das Südfeld braucht morgen früh Aufmerksamkeit.* — are a distinct case; those italics signal "spoken in German" and are consistent with standard convention for full-sentence foreign-language dialogue.)

---

**Flag 1 — Translation line after Klein's German (writer judgment required):**

> *Ihr Akzent kommt aus dem Süden. Östlich von München.*
>
> Your accent places you south, east of Munich.

The style guide says German in this manuscript is "untranslated." The bare line "Your accent places you south, east of Munich" reads structurally as an author-gloss for the English-speaking reader. However, it could equally be Hannah's immediate comprehension rendered in free indirect discourse — she grew up in her father's German and would parse this instantly. If the latter is the intent, consider a small FID anchor ("She heard it, understood it") or let the German stand alone and trust the reader; if the intent is to keep the German accessible to readers who don't know it, this is a deliberate departure from the style-guide rule that needs to be a conscious choice. Compression has already passed this chapter, so this line cannot be cut here — but the writer should confirm the intent.

---

**Flag 2 — Pronoun ambiguity: "It moved through the kitchen" (writer judgment required):**

> The doctor in Rockland had listened and examined and found nothing physically wrong. It moved through the kitchen with purpose. It knew where everything went.

"It" in the third sentence is intended to refer to Magda's silence (the subject of Hannah's theory two sentences back). But the sentence immediately preceding — about the doctor — creates a false referent: "it" reads momentarily as the doctor's conclusion (nothing physically wrong) rather than the silence. The ambiguity clears on re-reading but stalls on first pass. The fix is at the level of sentence order or a pronoun clarification ("The silence moved through the kitchen with purpose") — either of which is a compression-adjacent choice, so flagged for writer decision rather than applied here.

---

**Flag 3 — Possible Marcus-register bleed in Doris observation (low severity, writer awareness):**

> accurately, with a quality of not wanting to give the language more of herself than the task required

The phrasing "a quality of not wanting to give the language more of herself than the task required" carries a subordinate-clause formality that sits closer to Marcus's register than Hannah's. Hannah observes sharply, but her observations tend to stay in the concrete or the sensory; this clause is more analytical and abstract in its construction. The sentence is not wrong — a perceptive adolescent can think this — but if the chapter accumulates several such formal observations, they could collectively shade Hannah toward Marcus. At a single instance it's within tolerance; flagged in case it recurs.

# At the Harbormaster's

The freight notification had arrived Wednesday on the mail boat from Rockland — a printed form clipped to the corner of his classroom door when he came in that morning, the school's copy of the bill of lading for one crate, forty-three pounds, textbooks, consigned to Coldwater Reach School, language department. He had moved it to his desk and for two days been aware of it in the way he was aware of small formal obligations that required a kind of navigation he was still learning in this place: the combination of institutional procedure and local geography that made even straightforward tasks, in a town of nine hundred people, require some advance calculation about approach.

The form required a counter-signature from the harbormaster's office before the crate could leave the dock. Friday was a mail-boat day; the boat turned around at four-thirty. He left the school at three o'clock with the notification in his breast pocket and the afternoon already going gray.

---

He recognized the preparation now, turning the freight notification in his coat pocket as he walked down from the school.

He knew who Eira Bowman was. Nine hundred people in the town, and he had been here since March of the previous year; she was the harbormaster and had been for eight years, which he had gathered not from any single conversation but from the accumulated texture of a dozen conversations that had been about other things. He had seen her from the ridge road on his morning walks — a figure in a dark peacoat, moving with purpose along the dock's planking — and had not spoken to her beyond the incidental nod of people who have recognized each other without occasion to speak. He was curious about her relation to the body on the breakwater. What he had, concretely, was what the school hallway had given him in October: *no papers, no name, Coast Guard took the log*. The removal of the log was a fact that continued to interest him, in the way that the excision of pages from a manuscript continued to interest a reader who had not been present for the excision. He had turned these two facts over for three weeks without arriving anywhere with them.

The wind at the corner of the harbor road arrived before his coat was ready for it.

At the turn where the road dropped toward the dock, the breakwater was briefly visible through the stripped maples — the granite running out two hundred yards across the inner cove, the seaward-end light not yet lit in the pale afternoon. He looked at it for the seconds the road allowed. Then the seine sheds came between, and he went on.

---

The dock in early November: the planking worn pale at the center where foot traffic ran, darker at the edges, the smell of diesel and herring bait and cold salt arriving as a fact rather than an impression, sharpened by the temperature. The mail boat — the Heron, a white-sided vessel of perhaps sixty feet — was tied at the dock's eastern end, engine silent, flag moving in the wind off the inner cove. Two men in heavy rubber-bottomed boots were transferring freight from her hold to the dock in the methodical manner of people for whom this was not a new activity. One of them gave Marcus the particular look a working dock extends to a person who is evidently not a dock person. Marcus acknowledged this without addressing it and found the harbormaster's office at the head of the dock.

He knocked.

---

The interior was smaller than the exterior suggested. A desk against the wall facing the harbor window. A filing cabinet beside it. The BC-1206 radio set on the south wall, its panel angled slightly toward the desk. A tide clock mounted above the harbor window, its face calibrated in something other than the hour — a wheel rather than a hand, reading the tidal cycle against a scale marked for this harbor specifically. The log ledger lay open on the desk, a pen laid in the binding.

Eira Bowman was at the desk and looked up without appearing to have been waiting or surprised. She was in her early fifties, he thought — harbor-worker's hands visible at the desk's edge, her manner without the performance of welcome or its opposite. The peacoat on the nail behind the door was the coat she actually wore.

He said: Dr. Klein, from the school. He had a freight notification requiring the harbormaster's counter-signature before the school could take possession of a crate.

She said yes, and extended a hand for the form.

He gave her the notification and watched her read it — both hands flat at the form's edges, oriented without needing adjustment, read with the quality of attention that indicated genuine reading. She asked was the crate for the school's general inventory or a specific department. He said it was for the language classroom. She made a note in the margin, produced the freight manifest from the filing cabinet without searching for it, placed it alongside the notification, and read both documents again before handing him a pen with the cap already removed.

He signed on the line she indicated. She countersigned below his name, returned the pen, and told him the crate was on the dock, stenciled with the school's name; the dockhands knew which one.

Four minutes, perhaps. He thanked her.

He did not leave.

---

He turned toward the harbor window and looked out at the dock. The Heron's crew had gone aboard; the dock was quiet. The afternoon was darkening from the east, the overcast settling without urgency. The fixed red light at the breakwater's seaward end was just becoming visible, not quite lit yet but distinguishable against the gray.

He said, without turning from the window: had there been any further word on the man who was found on the breakwater in October.

A pause of approximately two seconds.

The matter had been received by the Coast Guard, Eira Bowman said. The First District office in Portland held the record. There had been no identifying information that she was aware of.

She said this in precisely the register in which she had read the freight form: complete, without inflection, with the care of someone who has established what she will say and verified that what she says is accurate. He had known people who gave testimony on difficult subjects in exactly the register they used to note the hour — scholars, primarily, and certain officials he had encountered in other years in other countries — and he had always found it more informative than the alternative.

He said yes, of course. He was quiet for a moment.

He asked whether there had been any indication from the vessels that put in during the three-day blow — any connection between those arrivals and the individual who was found.

She said: no. The investigation had found no connection between the individual and any vessel that had logged a Coldwater arrival in that period.

He said yes. Of course.

He asked — his hands at his sides, looking at the harbor, in the tone of a man conducting a professional inquiry on a neutral subject — whether it would have been unusual, in that kind of weather, for someone not connected with any particular vessel to come into the dock area after dark.

There was a pause of similar length to the first.

The three-day blow before the twelfth, she said, had pushed a number of boats to seek shelter in the harbor and in the coves east of the breakwater. It was not unusual in that kind of weather for a skipper who knew the channel to come in after dark. The harbor had seen heavier traffic than normal in that period.

He said yes. Of course.

The answer was precise, complete, and had left the space around his actual question entirely intact, in the way a text can be accurate in every particular and still withhold what the reader came to find.

---

He turned from the window and gave the room the attention he brought to documents.

The tide clock above the window: specific, locally calibrated, read correctly only by someone who knew this harbor's tidal pattern. The BC-1206's panel tilted toward the desk in the way of equipment calibrated to a particular user's position over a long period of use. The log ledger open on the desk — he could see the handwriting of the current pages without reading the entries, a compressed and regular hand, and the ledger as a physical object had the accumulated weight and edge-quality of something in continuous use for years: the pages toward the binding thicker, handled more, the spine worn at its lower third where a hand would grip it to open it. If he looked at it as he looked at a manuscript — which was how, after twenty years of professional training, he looked at any document that had accumulated across time — the impression was there of a different hand, earlier in the record. Looser, wider in its letter spacing, not careless but distinct, the letterforms of someone who had learned to write in different conditions from whoever was writing now.

The change of hand in a manuscript was primary evidence.

He said nothing about it.

He said he supposed the Heron would be leaving at four-thirty and he should let her continue.

She said yes.

---

He picked up the freight manifest from the edge of the desk.

She said: that's the school's copy. You can keep it.

He looked at the manifest. Above the freight description — one crate, forty-three pounds, textbooks, Coldwater Reach School — she had written in her compressed hand: *Collected 7 November 1943, 14:10.*

The annotation was not required by the form. The crate was still on the dock; it had not yet been collected. The time was given to the minute, which was a precision the freight procedure did not call for.

He stood with the manifest looking at the line. He could not account for its purpose in any documentation chain he knew. He folded the manifest along its crease and put it into his breast pocket.

He said good afternoon. She said the same. He went out.

---

The dockhand with the school's crate was the one who had not looked at him when he arrived. He thanked the man and took the rope handle and carried the crate up the dock.

Forty-three pounds, and the rope handle was not made for carrying any distance: it cut across the fingers and there was no angle of the wrist that improved matters. He stopped at the top of the dock incline and shifted the weight to the other hand and looked back at the harbor. The Heron's engine had started; the sound of it carried up on the wind, steady and low. The seine sheds stood to the east with their weathered boards and the dark water-stain at their footings. The breakwater ran out across the cove, granite, the tide continuing to fall from it, and the red light at its seaward end had come fully on — fixed, clear, visible from five miles offshore and from the top of a dock incline in a town of nine hundred people on a Friday afternoon in November.

He picked up the crate and walked.

What she had done was not something that clarified itself slowly. It was clear by the time he reached the road. There was only the answer she gave, and around it, in the exact contour of what she had said, the silence of everything she hadn't.

He knew the skill. He had used it — in Vienna, in Paris, in other rooms in other years, in circumstances where imprecision had a cost he had not been in a position to absorb. He had not expected to encounter it here, in a working harbormaster's office on a Maine dock, in a conversation about a freight crate that had lasted seven minutes.

He had the manifest in his pocket. He had the shape of what she had not said. He had, as a matter of habit and of long practice, a tolerance for beginning from incomplete information toward a conclusion that might not arrive for some time.

The road bent at the top of the hill. The harbor went behind the seine sheds and then behind the hill's shoulder, and then it was the road up through the stripped maples and the early dark coming in from the east and the rope handle working at his fingers one by one, and he carried his books the rest of the way.

# November Log

The barometer had been dropping since midday. By three-thirty it was past the threshold where she would have preferred to already be at the shack, and she went.

She came down from the harbor road with her kit bag over one shoulder and her flashlight in the other hand, though it wasn't yet dark. The harbor smell met her at the dock head: diesel from the draggers in the inner slips, cold salt, the brine of the tide running out past the seine sheds.

The two draggers in their slips first. She went over each in the failing light: mooring lines tensioned, dock cleats solid, the breast lines on the Callie B. doubled as she had planned. The bilge pump had been running clean since early October; she checked it anyway — the fitting, the discharge, the reservoir — and found nothing to object to. Then the spring lines on the *Agnes Mae* at the inner slip, then the dock cleats running east along the planking, then the open eastern end where the wood roughed out at the breakwater access steps. The full length of the dock. The breakwater light was on and fixed. She looked at it for a moment and went to the shack.

---

Inside, four o'clock. She lit the lamp and let the BC-1206 warm. When it came in she raised the *Agnes Mae* first: Gilmore, twelve miles south-southwest, still running. She gave him the barometer reading and the sea state and told him to come in. He said he had already turned. She said come in anyway.

The *Carrie Holt* was closer in, seven miles out, Brewer at the wheel. He had seen the sky and was already heading for the cove. She told him to stand off the breakwater until he had slack water, then come through on the flood tide; the channel would be workable. He said he understood.

She set the radio to receive. She moved the chair so she could see the harbor window and the door both from the desk. She opened the log to November 14, 1943, and wrote the time and the barometer: 29.4, dropping steadily. Wind southwest, twenty-two knots, gusting to twenty-eight at the anemometer mount. Sea state rough at the harbor mouth, three-to-four-foot chop with a building swell. Visibility two miles and closing. She listed the vessels: *Agnes Mae* inbound, twelve miles south-southwest. *Carrie Holt* inbound, seven miles. Positions and times. She set the pen in the binding.

The shack was cold. She had kept it unheated during the day so as not to waste the kerosene, and the November air had settled through the south wall completely. She went to the door hook and took down Owen's peacoat and put it on.

The wool smelled of salt and oil and the cedar block she kept in the breast pocket — a small dry piece she replaced each fall, since the cedar in the original lining had long since given out. The coat had been taken in at the shoulders in spring of 1936, Mrs. Thibodeau in town doing the alterations: shoulders taken in, hem raised one inch, lining re-sewn at the cuffs. Eight years of wearing had done the rest — the pockets worn soft at the lips, the cuffs showing use at the outer edge where her wrists rested on the dock railing. The shoulders were right. She buttoned it and sat down.

---

Outside the harbor window, the last light left the sky. The dock light at the slip head came on automatically at five. The inner cove surface was gray and agitated — not whitecapping yet but building from the southwest fetch — and the seine shed rooflines stood dark against the pale strip still left in the east. The breakwater ran out to her right, the seaward light on, doing its twenty-second sweep.

By seven the blow was proper. Brewer raised her from the outer cove at six-forty to say he was ready to come through. She told him the flood was making and the north side of the channel was manageable if he kept his speed down coming in. He came through and tied the west slip at seven-oh-two. Gilmore's *Agnes Mae* ground into the inner slip at seven-fifty with the motor coughing in the cold. She logged both in: *Agnes Mae* inbound 1950, *Carrie Holt* inbound 1902. Both vessels in and accounted for.

She lit the small stove in the corner. When the shack warmed she took the peacoat off and laid it over the chair back.

At eight she put it on again and went out to check the dock.

The blow drove the rain near-horizontal, the kind that found the collar gap no matter how you angled into it. She went with the flashlight and the rubber overshoes and was wet in the first minute. She kept the beam low on the dark planking and went cleat to cleat: the Callie B.'s breast lines, the *Agnes Mae*'s spring lines, the eastern cleats at the corner where the planking met the breakwater steps. All holding. The sound of the harbor was a low continuous roar — not the sharp crack of violent weather but the sound of a storm that had set and would hold.

The breakwater light showed through the rain and the spray coming up off the stone, fixed red, visible through the murk. She confirmed it and turned back.

She stripped off the overshoes at the shack door, hung the peacoat on the hook, wiped down the rubber. The stove had the shack fully warm. She put the peacoat back on and sat.

---

The storm did not break but settled — found its pitch and held it. The barometer at ten o'clock had barely moved from where it had been at six. She poured coffee from the flask and sat at the desk with the lamp burning and the radio quiet and the wind working steadily at the south wall.

She opened the log and wrote the dock check: 2008, all lines secure, no damage, both vessels in. Then the barometer: 29.2 at 2145, holding. Wind southwest, twenty to twenty-two knots sustained.

The log volume had been running since January. Her handwriting throughout: regular, compressed, the notation of someone who knew what a log entry needed and put nothing else in it. Eight years of this kind of writing. The entries did not vary much except in their details — the barometer and the wind, the vessel count, the incidents or the absence of them — and that constancy was what made them useful.

This binding held the older pages as well. She had re-covered the ledger the previous spring and assembled it from two sources: her current year's entries and, bound at the back, the pages from before. Owen's pages. She knew they were there each time she opened the log, the way she knew the peacoat's weight before she put it on — without needing to verify.

She put the pen in the binding to mark her place and turned to the back.

---

Owen wrote with a slight leftward lean and a fully closed *o*, an *r* with a small curl at the tip, the *s* compressed as if his pen moved faster than he did. He had a tendency to crowd the final letters of long words — *barometer* came out a little rushed at the end, *northwest* with the *t* tight against the *s*. She had read his handwriting enough times that she read it without slowing.

She found the page she was looking for.

*November 12, 1935. Weather deteriorating, wind NNW increasing, barometer 29.1 and falling. Putting out additional mooring lines on —*

The sentence ended there, mid-line. The pen had come up from the page and not come back. She had looked at this page perhaps two dozen times in eight years and the sentence still ended where it ended.

She held it for a moment. The sound of the wind. The stove settling.

Then she closed the ledger and turned it to November 1943.

---

She wrote the barometer — 29.2 at 2230, holding — and the wind and the time.

Then the pen stopped.

---

She had been at the dock around eleven o'clock. The bilge pump on the Callie B. — Farber had mentioned it needed attention and she had let the day get away from her, so she went down after the harbor lights came on. The pump was running clean when she got there. She was checking the discharge fitting when she heard the engine.

A small wooden motorboat. She heard it before she saw it — a single-cylinder engine, throttled back to idle — and then it rounded the dock's southern end without running lights and came in slow toward the eastern end. The open end. The end near the breakwater steps.

She stood up from the fitting and watched.

The man on the boat sorted his lines before the engine was fully off and made fast at the far cleat in two passes. He knew what he was doing. Not rushed, not fumbling: the efficiency of someone for whom dock lines were familiar. He had a lantern with him, shuttered down to almost nothing, and in its very low light she could see his hands working the knot — bare hands, working quickly, the knot made and tested with a tug.

She was at the head of the Callie B.'s slip. Forty feet away, or near enough. She did not move.

He stepped off the boat with the lantern and walked east along the dock planking toward the breakwater steps. He did not look in her direction.

She watched him go. The low orange glow of the lantern dropped below the level of the dock as he went down the breakwater steps, and then she could see it on the granite path that ran along the top of the breakwater — a small light moving steadily outward, not hurrying, not stopping. She watched until the dark took it.

She could not have described him. He was an adult man, not young. That was what the dark and the distance gave her, and she had had perhaps twenty seconds: from the moment he rounded the dock's southern end to the moment the lantern went out of sight down the steps. She had looked and she had not seen.

She did not call out. There was nothing irregular enough to call out about — coming in without lights was careless, tying at the open end was unusual, but neither was prohibited, and it was eleven o'clock at night and whatever the man was doing was his business. She finished with the pump and walked home.

In the morning he was at the end of the breakwater.

---

She did not write this in the log.

She wrote the barometer. The wind. The time. She wrote the page and set the pen in the binding and did not look at what she had not written.

---

The storm eased toward two, as she had expected. Barometer at 29.4 and climbing. The wind had come down from twenty knots sustained to fifteen, and the harbor's sound changed with it — lower, more regular, the surface settling from a slap to a chop. She knew the sounds of this harbor in every weather. She knew when the worst had cleared.

She went out at two-fifteen.

The dock was quiet. The rain had settled to mist — present but not driving, the kind that beaded on surfaces and didn't move. She went to the eastern end and found one of the spring lines on the corner cleat had slipped its keeper and needed reknotting. She worked the knot in her gloves, which was slower, but the rope told her hands what to do. She tied it and tested it and found it sound.

She looked up. The breakwater ran out ahead of her in the dark, two hundred yards of wet granite, the fixed red light at the seaward end clear and on. She could see the full length of it in the mist where she couldn't in the rain.

She went back to the shack.

---

At the desk she wrote the time: 0218. Barometer 29.4, rising. Wind southwest, fifteen knots and easing. Visibility improving. Two vessels in. No vessels out. No additional contacts. Eastern spring line at the corner cleat rerigged; otherwise all lines secure.

She set the pen in the binding.

Owen's coat was warm from the hours she had had it on, and she did not take it off. The lamp was turned down. Outside, the mist was the kind that thinned slowly — it would still be there in an hour, in two hours, lightening by degrees as the barometer climbed. The sound of the harbor was water on dock planking and the low creak of the *Agnes Mae*'s lines as the tide shifted her weight in the slip.

She sat in the shack with the lamp low and the log closed on the desk and the tide clock doing what it always did, and outside the window the mist and the dock light and the breakwater running out in the dark toward the fixed red light at its end.

She sat there until it was light enough to walk, and then she went home.
